News.title: Fury at torment of Brit dad facing jail in Cyprus over hotel plunge death of son, 2… how tragedy was ‘waiting to happen’
News.content:
Next

WITH its waterpark, spa and four swimming pools, the King Evelthon in Cyprus appears to be the perfect “luxury beachfront resort” for a family to wind down in.

But as Joshua Foster waited to take the lift down from the fourth floor to an evening meal in July with his wife and two children his life plunged into an unimaginable nightmare.





Unknown to the 38-year-old AI expert from Essex, the window next to him had been left open.

And in a moment of sheer terror, his two-year-old son fell through it to his death four storeys below.

Joshua rushed down to try to save him, but it was too late.

Next Friday the broken father faces a possible jail sentence on the Mediterranean island, having been convicted of causing death through a reckless, rash or dangerous act.

Friends and relatives believe he had already been punished enough by the torment of losing his son.

And now questions are emerging as to whether the hotel could have done more to prevent this tragedy.

The window is below a ledge just over a metre high, so it is not difficult for an adventurous child to reach.

Two holidaymakers who stayed at the King Evelthon have told The Sun it was an accident waiting to happen.





One came close to seeing his son fall from the same deadly ledge two years ago and the other feared a child could fall through it.

Both claim to have warned hotel staff about the danger.

The window, though, remained a risk.

Caroline Green, 66, from Poole, Dorset, stayed at the King Evelthon beach hotel in 2023.

She claims: “At one point we were standing next to elevator on the floor, when my friend turned around and went, her very words were, ‘Oh my god, that window is open’.

“You couldn’t tell the window was open. The only thing that gave it away was a breeze coming through that made her turn around to look.

“Then she said, ‘Can you imagine if someone put their child on the ledge?’ We all shuddered. We didn’t dare to think about what could happen.

“When we got to the ground floor we went to reception and said ‘Do you know the window is open? It’s really dangerous or could potentially be.’”

According to Joshua’s legal team, that cruel scenario took the life of his son.

Waiting for the lift in a ”good mood” he had not realised the window was open.



The doting dad placed his son on the ledge and the next thing he knew, he was gone.

The prosecution claimed Joshua had been swinging his boy playfully, but he denied this.

Whichever version is right, a parent should be able to safely lift their child in the air in a moment of fun.

In the UK a window that high up in a hotel would not be allowed to open more than 10cm, preventing such a tragedy.

Yet, in Cyprus the regulations permit the window to be open as long as the ledge is 1.1m high.

One dad, who doesn’t wish to be named, realised that is far too lax.

His own son came close to falling from the same window in 2015 as Joshua’s son at the King Evelthon.

The 52-year-old holiday park salesman, from Lancashire, revealed his youngster clambered onto the sill when they were waiting for a lift on the fourth floor of five star hotel.



He says: “I was on holiday there for a week with my wife and two kids and the exact same thing nearly happened to us.

“We were going out for dinner one night and we turned around and my son was on that ledge.

“I went over to get him. I didn’t think much of it because it’s quite a low window.

“But as I got there my heart sank when I saw how far down it was.

“My wife and I were both quite shaken by it.

“You know what young boys are like, they climb everything and he’d climbed up and got his bum on there and swizzled round to look back into the corridor.

“We didn’t see him do it and that’s why it was such a shock because we could have turned round and he might not have been there.

“I still talk about it to this day the way parents do with near calls with their kids. We were so lucky.”

Just like Caroline, he reported his concerns to staff.

He says: “I went straight to reception and I complained, I said that is absolutely deadly.”



Yet, when Joshua’s boy got onto that ledge the window was still open.

The dad does not think that Joshua should be going to prison.

He says: “I couldn’t believe it when I read about this awful tragedy when a child had actually fallen from that window.

“It was absolutely horrendous for that family. My heart goes out to this poor man who is now facing jail and his family.

“This was an accident waiting to happen.

“There is no way that he should be jailed. He’s been punished enough already.”

Caroline agrees: “My heart really goes out to that poor dad, it really does. This was something that could have been prevented.

“I think the dad is being treated appallingly in my personal opinion.

“The friend who spotted the window open, she is a grandmother and so she said how easy it would have been to put a child on the windowsill, not knowing it was open.

“A toddler wouldn’t be able to climb up onto a windowsill but maybe a 10 or 11 year old could – anyone who is taller than 4ft would have been able to get up there.”



Joshua’s lawyer asked for the case thrown out on humanitarian grounds – but in the end advised him to plead guilty.

He now awaits a potential four years behind bars, with his wife facing the prospect of comforting their five-year-old daughter alone.

They are not the only guests to leave the King Evelthon with their world in tatters.

In less than five years, two other Brits have died while staying at the Cypriot resort.

Ben Woods, 21, from Leigh in Greater Manchester drowned in the hotel pool in July 2022 while Ruaridh Nairne, six, from Inverness, drowned there in 2024.

An inquest was told that lifeguards were on their phones when Ben got into trouble while playing volleyball in the pool.

It was left to guests to perform CPR on him, according to witnesses.

Other hotels in the Cypriot chain Tsokkos Hotels & Resorts have also come under fire for their safety records.



In 2015, Thomas Cook reportedly moved 50 Brits from the Anastasia Beach Hotel to another hotel after guests claimed three people had tried to snatch children from the hotel.

A Bulgarian man was arrested and released without charge, according to the Cyprus Mail, while Tsokkos Group categorically denied the claims.

The previous year Brit tourists were horrified when staff killed a sickly stray dog by putting him in a waste crushing bin. Tsokkos apologised for the incident at the time.

Tsokkos have not responded to a request for a comment about allegations that staff were warned about the open window on the fourth floor of the King Evelthon hotel.

Antonis Sivitanidis, general manager of the King Evelthon hotel, previously told The Sun: “Allegations made by guests [on health and safety] I will not comment on as everyone has their own opinion.

“Our hotel is fully licensed and complies with all regulations. It is safe for visitors to come and stay.”

But those guests will need to be vigilant. Anything less than total focus could be fatal.

As Joshua’s lawyer Alexandros Alexandrou said in his appeal for mercy yesterday: “He admitted guilt, and he admits the momentary lapse that will haunt him for the rest of his life.

“We are allowed, even when we are happy, to lose our concentration.”

News.title: Margaret Hamilton, woman behind software that helped land Apollo 11 on Moon, dies aged 90
News.content:
Next

THE pioneering computer scientist whose groundbreaking software helped put the first humans on the Moon has died aged 90.

Margaret Hamilton played a crucial role in one of mankind’s greatest achievements, leading the team behind the computer systems that made NASA’s historic Apollo 11 mission possible.



Her death on September 30 was confirmed by the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), where she worked for more than 15 years.

Hamilton helped revolutionize space exploration after developing software that prevented the Apollo 11 mission from ending in disaster during its final moments.



In July 1969, astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin were preparing to touch down on the lunar surface when alarms suddenly began flashing inside their spacecraft

The onboard computer had become overloaded, threatening to derail the historic landing just moments before touchdown.

Read more on SPACE SPACED OUT Wild NASA photos from Mars capture strange 'jellyfish' figure sparking theories

But thanks to Hamilton and her team’s pioneering work, the computer was able to prioritize critical operations over less important tasks.

Their revolutionary “priority-driven software” allowed the spacecraft to continue its descent, helping Armstrong and Aldrin land safely on the Moon.

The achievement cemented Hamilton’s place in space exploration history, although her contribution would not receive widespread recognition until decades later.

Paying tribute to the scientist, MIT said: “To say Hamilton was a pioneer – to say she was ahead of her time – would be a dramatic understatement.”



Hamilton joined MIT in 1959 and went on to manage its Software Engineering Division, overseeing the development and testing of onboard flight software for NASA’s Apollo missions.

She also helped popularize the term “software engineering” at a time when computer programming was still an emerging field.

Speaking to The Guardian in 2019, Hamilton recalled being drawn to the extraordinary challenge of sending humans into space.



“I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired,” she said.

Her work was immortalized in a famous 1969 photograph showing her standing beside a towering stack of printed computer code developed for the Apollo missions.

The enormous pile of documents stood almost as tall as Hamilton herself, highlighting the sheer scale of the work required to send astronauts to the Moon.

Born in Indiana in 1936, Hamilton initially studied mathematics at the University of Michigan in 1955 before transferring to Earlham College.

She graduated with a mathematics degree in 1958 and moved to Boston the following year with her husband.



But what began as a way to support her family would eventually lead to a career that helped change the course of space exploration.

After leaving MIT in the mid-1970s, Hamilton went on to establish her own software companies, including Massachusetts-based Hamilton Technologies.

Her remarkable contributions were recognized in 2016 when President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom, one of America’s highest civilian honors.

At the ceremony, Obama said Hamilton “symbolises that generation of unsung women who helped send humankind into space”.

Her former college also paid an emotional tribute following news of her death.



Earlham College said: “We are saddened by her death, but grateful for the opportunity to have celebrated her extraordinary achievements throughout her long life”.

“Her pioneering spirit and remarkable legacy will continue to inspire generations of Earlhamites,” the statement added.

Hamilton is survived by her daughter, son-in-law, two grandsons and four great-grandchildren, according to MIT.

News.title: Man ‘running around naked trying to hug people & walking into traffic’ outside UK shopping centre is arrested
News.content:
NAKED ARREST Man ‘running around naked trying to hug people & walking into traffic’ outside UK shopping centre is arrested







Next

A MAN has been arrested after he allegedly took off his jeans and roamed the street naked while trying to hug strangers.

Cops were called to Clarence Street in Gloucestershire city centre at 5am on October 5 following reports of a man, believed to be in his 40s, acting “erratically”.

A member of the public called the police after a man was spotted running in the street stark naked.

Police say he put a pair of jeans on and then took them off again.





The man also attempted to approach strangers, trying to touch and hug them.

At one point, the man reportedly walked in front of traffic and stopped by a bus stop near King’s Walk shopping centre.

It is believed he was under the influence of drugs.

The man was subsequently arrested on suspicion of exposure.



He has been released on bail with conditions while an investigation is ongoing, with CCTV in the area being reviewed.

Police are now urging any witnesses who saw the incident or anyone who was approached by the man to come forward.

You can provide information to police online by going to their website and quoting occurrence 53260085851.

News.title: Kemi’s grip on the Conservative Party is now iron-clad – one key moment from her speech was red meat for Tory faithful
News.content:
POLITICS FIX Kemi’s grip on the Conservative Party is now iron-clad – one key moment from her speech was red meat for Tory faithful







Next

SCRAPPING inheritance tax on family homes puts traditional Tory convictions back at the heart of the party.

Kemi Badenoch burnished her conservative credentials by taking an axe to one of Britain’s most hated taxes while allowing couples to pass on an additional £1million tax-free.



It was red meat for the Tory faithful, and they lapped it up.

The Conservative leader walked on stage in a far stronger position than at the last party conference in Manchester.



One year ago Robert Jenrick was breathing down her neck, waiting in the wings and widely seen as a potential challenger.

Now her grip on the party looks iron-clad, with support from both the grassroots and the top of the party.

The key moment came an hour into her speech when she finally turned to inheritance tax, a policy Tory MPs and members have been demanding action on for years.

She said: “Just because I can’t give you everything that you want, doesn’t mean I can’t give you some of what you want.”

Badenoch says the changes will more than halve the number of families dragged into paying inheritance tax.

She summed up the Tory pitch in one line: “No stamp duty when you buy your home, no mansion tax when you live in your home and no inheritance tax on your home when you pass it to your children or grandchildren.”



Badenoch is drawing a dividing line with Reform and Labour on tax, property and aspiration.

The offer will inevitably appeal most strongly to better-off homeowners, particularly across London and the South East.

Her calculation is after years of Tory drift she wants to replace managerial politics with sharper dividing lines.

Whether it works remains to be seen.

But it will leave wavering voters across Britain in no doubt where the party stands for on the economy once again.

News.title: Several people trapped after seven-story building collapses in Turkey as rescuers scramble to find trapped residents
News.content:
Next

A SEVEN-STORY apartment block in Istanbul has suddenly collapsed leaving residents trapped under the rubble.

Only three people have been rescued so far with desperate emergency crews rushing to the site to try and clear the devastation.



The first three floors of the building collapsed in Istanbul’s Maltepe district at around 5.40am local time this morning.

At least seven people were reportedly inside the fallen section of the apartment block at the time.



Everyone on the upper floors managed to be evacuated safely as rescue crews moved in to start the search for people trapped under the rubble.

Thirty- three people lived in the buildin, g which also had several shops on the ground floors.

Istanbul Governor Davut Gul said teams have been in contact with the remaining four people but that they are still stranded.

Gul added: “The collapsed seven-story building was constructed in 1987. A total of 33 people live in the building.”



It remains unclear what caused the building to collapse.

An investigation has been launched to find out the cause.

Minister of Environment Murat Kurum said: “Our state is on the ground with all its institutions and resources.

“Work is continuing uninterrupted with great care and determination, leaving no possibility unconsidered, in order to reach our citizens under the rubble as soon as possible.

“We wish all our citizens a speedy recovery. May God grant a quick recovery to the injured.”



It comes after a huge suspected gas explosion blew up several buildings in Istanbul back in March.

The enormous blast took down two buildings in the Ayvansaray area of Istanbul.

Dramatic photos show the impact of the explosion as survivors are pulled from the wrecks of the buildings.

News.title: Girl sexually assaulted during Gunna show at Reading Festival – as cops release e-fit in hunt for man
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

FESTIVAL SEX ATTACK Girl sexually assaulted during Gunna show at Reading Festival – as cops release e-fit in hunt for man







Next

A GIRL was sexually assaulted during a Gunna show at Reading Festival as cops release an e-fit amid the hunt for a man.

The alleged incident happened at Reading Festival on Saturday, August 29, when a man inappropriately touched a girl.

Officers say the reported sexual assault unfolded at The Gallery Stage during Gunna’s set.

Detectives have since released an e-fit of a man as they work to investigate the alleged sexual assault.





The suspect is described as south Asian with dark skin and in his late 20s to early 30s.

Investigators say he has dark short hair and was wearing a beige jacket and similar coloured trousers.

Anyone who recognises the man or has any information that may assist cops is asked to contact Thames Valley Police.

Investigating officer Detective Constable Kate Hawkins said: “I am releasing this e-fit image and would ask anybody who believes that they recognise the man depicted, or who believes they witnessed this incident to please get in contact with us.



“You can make a report online, or by calling 101, quoting reference 43260451414.

“Alternatively, for 100% anonymity, you can also call the independent charity Crimestoppers on 0800 555 111.”

It comes after a woman in her 20s was allegedly sexually assaulted during a packed Gunna concert at the O2.

Cops have arrested a man, 26, after she was “approached from behind and sexually assaulted.”



It was reportedly filmed in the crowd during the concert by American rapper Gunna in March.

Police officers arrested him a suspect at the venue after he was stopped by staff.

News.title: First death row inmate killed by lethal injection since Christa Pike’s botched execution after 3 desperate appeals fail
News.content:
Next

A MURDERER has been killed by lethal injection in the first execution since Christa Pike cheated death.

Jamaal Howard, 46, was given the same deadly drugs despite his lawyers making three last-minute appeals to halt his execution after witnessing what had happened to Pike just days earlier.



Howard’s death was confirmed just after 8pm in Texas on Wednesday.

He received a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville.



Pike, 50, managed to survive two doses of the same drug on September, 30, in Tennessee as she was rushed to hospital after a botched execution.

The convicted killer is now said to be awake but “angry and confused” over the lethal injection failure as her lawyers have vowed to fight to stop her from being executed again.



Howard’s own lawyers had argued that he faced the same risks as Pike and could suffer if the drugs didn’t work.

They filed two requests to stop the execution at the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals.



His lawyers claimed the drugs were “degraded” and “far past the original beyond-use dates” – a concern also flagged by Pike’s legal team.

After being denied, his lawyers also argued unsuccessfully to the US Supreme Court over Howard’s mental disabilities.

Howard has the IQ of a 12-year-old boy.

He was convicted and sentenced to death in 2001 for the murder of a convenience store clerk during a robbery a year earlier.

Howard was just 20 when he shot Vickie Swartout, 42, in Texas and stole a carton of cigarettes and just $114 (£86) from the cash register.



Speaking to The Sun earlier this week, Howard’s spiritual adviser Rev Dr Jeff Hood said: “The day after everything happened with Christa, I told Jamal because I didn’t want him to find out and just be terrified and not know the whole story.

“We’re just talking about the drugs and he said ‘well, I don’t do drugs.’

“And he goes ‘well, don’t worry, if the drugs don’t work, they just pull out a gun and shoot me in the head.’



“And it’s like, ‘no, that’s not what happens.’”

Texas has now executed six people this year with two more lethal injections scheduled for the next three months.

Tennessee, where Pike was unsuccessfully put to death, has halted all executions for 2026.

Pike’s lawyers claim she has no memory of the lethal injection ordeal that nearly killed her.

They say among her first haunting questions after regaining consciousness were, “where am I?” and “who are you?”.



Despite remaining in hospital, Pike is still under heavy security.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Her attorney said she is shackled at both feet and by her right arm.

Pike has reportedly been overheard asking about the family of Colleen Slemmer, the 19-year-old she was convicted of murdering in 1995.

News.title: Jailed Albanian mayor uses AI video of himself to pledge free school meals from behind bars
News.content:
Next

AN ALBANIAN mayor has used a deepfake to make a bizarre AI-video, despite being behind bars.

In an Instagram video, Tirana mayor Erion Veliaj used an AI avatar to make a pledge to his voters, promising free school lunches for children.



The post has sparked confusion, not for its use of AI but because the disgraced Mayor is currently in prison awaiting trial.

The odd footage, which Instagram has labelled as “AI content”, shows a digital likeness of the politician standing in front of Albanian and municipal flags.



The AI-mayor claims he has been “held hostage for 20 months”, while he awaits trial.

He says: “I cannot send this greeting except through artificial intelligence.”



The avatar then goes on to list his achievements in office before repeating his pledge to provide free food in schools.

He adds: “However much they want to keep me away from the city, and from you, Tirana is the honour of my life.



“To repay that honour, I will keep working even from the cell where they have locked me up.”

Veliaj’s words drew instant backlash in Albania, with many likening the strange video to the AI-generated speeches made by other incarcerated politicians,

In July, an AI-generated avatar of Jair Bolsonaro, the former president of Brazil, was used during his son’s presidential campaign.

Pakistan’s former prime minister, Imran Khan, made several AI-generated videos, most notably to falsely claim victory in the country’s 2024 general election.

In February 2025, Veliaj was arrested for taking part in a scheme with his wife that took around €1 million in bribes and city funds.



The pair denied all charges against them, which included corruption, money laundering, and hiding assets.

Last month, Albania’s High Court ruled that Veliaj must remain in police custody during the case.

Shockingly, he remains the city’s mayor, despite Tirana’s council voting to remove him from office in 2025.

Albania is also no stranger to AI in politics.

Prime Minister Edi Rama introduced Diella in 2025, the world’s first AI-virtual minister.



The government appointed Diella to the cabinet, tasking her with finding corruption in government projects.

A few months after the announcement, Albanian actress Anila Bisha claimed that her face, voice, and likeness were used to create Diella without her full consent.

She stated that she only agreed to a one-off government chatbot, not a permanent political cabinet role.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Bisha also said she faced harassment and abuse from public backlash to Diella.

The Albanian government dismissed her claims as “nonsense”.

News.title: Burnham to hold security talks with German chancellor in Berlin
News.content:
Burnham is set to be greeted with military honours at the German capital's Chancellery ahead of his first face-to-face meeting with the chancellor.

On Thursday, the two leaders will formally ratify the 2025 Kensington Treaty, a partnership committing both countries to tackle hostile activity through deeper cooperation on science, technology, defence, security and growth.

Speaking ahead of the visit, Burnham said the UK and Germany were "joining forces to find, expose and disrupt" threats.

He continued: "Attacks on our infrastructure, our businesses and our democracies are not a distant threat.

"They reach into people's homes and workplaces, and they are designed to make us weaker and more divided."

European leaders have warned the threat of hybrid attacks against Europe by Russia has intensified in recent weeks.

Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary - for example cyber attacks, sabotage or misinformation.

Last month, a senior Russian diplomat was summoned by the British government over an "egregious and reckless attack" on Leipzig airport.

It is a major international freight hub used for providing support to Ukraine. Moscow has denied any involvement in the incident.

Meanwhile, questions have also been raised this week about Germany's reliability as an intelligence partner, following the bombshell arrest of a former spy chief on suspicion of espionage.

August Hanning has been accused of espionage, treason and obtaining classified information for a foreign power, the German Federal Prosecutor's Office says.

He ran the Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005 and has since been working as a private consultant.

The talks also come during a period in which Merz's own political future has come under intense scrutiny.

Burnham replaced Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer in July after the former leader was forced out by his own MPs just two years after winning a landslide election victory.

Similarly, Merz has faced persistent rumours he could be replaced by his party due to his poor approval ratings and following setbacks in regional elections.

Although the chancellor appears to have overcome an immediate crisis in his leadership, questions remain over his future.

Additional reporting by Ottilie Mitchell.

News.title: 'Come all the way' back to EU, French finance minister tells UK
News.content:
French finance minister Roland Lescure has invited Britain to "come all the way" back to the EU, after Prime Minister Andy Burnham signalled a second Brexit referendum was "possible" in a future Labour election manifesto.

Lescure said being in the bloc comes with some difficulties, but it enables members to better address the challenges facing the world.

Last week, Burnham said the UK needed to "consider the options", ranging from staying as is, rejoining the customs union or single market, or going "all the way".

Asked about the PM's comments, Lescure told the BBC: "British people decided, and that's obviously their 100% right, and if they're willing to come back, they will have to decide."

He added: "But what I can tell them is: come back, anytime."

Burnham recently warned that planned EU rules to help European manufacturers would damage the UK.

The prime minister expressed concerns about how British industry and supply chains could be affected by the planned Made In Europe scheme.

The proposals aim to protect EU industry from Chinese competitors by giving companies inside the bloc priority for public contracts and subsidies. The EU's car industry has called for the UK to be included to prevent disruption to its own supply chains.

Asked about the possibility of Britain being kept out of the scheme, Lescure said: "Come back, and you'll be at the table, and we discuss all these things together."

News.title: Most UK diplomats to leave East Jerusalem consulate as Miliband says 'mission' to remain
News.content:
Most diplomats will leave the British consulate in occupied East Jerusalem, Israel says, but the UK insists the building "will not be closing", and will operate as a "UK Mission"

"We did not want it to come to this," Israeli Foreign Minister Gideon Saar wrote on social media, as he said 20 diplomats and the Consul General would leave Israel while a task force of seven could remain in the building "with a very limited scope of activity".

UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband responded that some staff had been "temporarily withdrawn" for security reasons, but stressed the mission will " work with the Palestinian people".

Israel said in September it would shut the consulate, in retaliation for UK sanctions on Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank which are illegal under international law.

News.title: We spent thousands on a Tui river cruise but ended up on coach trips
News.content:
David Mallon and a group of five others were due to travel on 21 September. But they decided the new itinerary presented to them a few days before departure was so different from what they had booked that they didn't want to go.

"What they were planning to give us was not a cruise but a glorified coach trip," says David.

One reason for not wanting to accept the new plan was that a member of the group was meant to be avoiding long periods of sitting down - such as coach journeys - for health reasons.

With no offer of a refund, the group booked a last-minute holiday to Kos instead and decided to try and claim money back on their return.

"We don't blame Tui for the water levels, but it's the way they've handled the consequences of that," David says.

He has now submitted a complaint to Tui and says he will take his quest for a refund to the small claims court if necessary.

The BBC contacted Tui River Cruises about passengers' unhappiness with the extensive itinerary changes and the fact they were not offered any refund.

In a statement, a spokesperson said: "Extreme heat across Europe this summer caused low water levels on the Danube, affecting river cruise operators across the region. We review every sailing individually with our nautical partners.

"Customers on the Tui Isla departures on 14 and 21 September were sent revised itineraries before travelling. Where the ship couldn't sail sections of the river, we arranged coach transfers, hotel stays and adjusted travel arrangements to minimise transfer times so customers could still visit destinations, including Budapest, Vienna and Bratislava.

"We reviewed the revised arrangements carefully and customers continued their holiday on the amended itinerary under our standard booking conditions. While customers were still able to visit the key destinations on their itinerary, we're sorry some did not get the river cruise experience they had anticipated."

News.title: 'Every day there is killing': Gazans face Israeli strikes despite ceasefire as peace deal stalls
News.content:
In her tent in central Gaza early one morning last month, 31-year-old Fida al-Toutah, a mother of five, was combing her daughter's hair when the sound of gunfire erupted.

"My mother shouted at us to get down," her son Ezz recalled, weeping as he spoke.

He only realised Fida had been hit when he saw the bloodied hands of his younger brother, who had been clinging onto his mother as the bullets came in.

"Our mother was so kind and generous. What did she do wrong?" Ezz said.

Fida died on 21 September from a gunshot wound to the head.

She is among more than 1,400 people in Gaza who have been killed in Israeli attacks since the start of the ceasefire on 10 October last year, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN.

News.title: 'I was blamed for my baby's death now NHS needs to change'
News.content:
When Poppy Russell died shortly after birth, her parents were left bereft.

What followed made matters harder to bear - her mother was blamed for the death.

An inquest would later conclude that Poppy's death was preventable.

But instead of walking away from the trust that had failed them, Neil and Katie Russell are now working with it to bring compassionate care back into the NHS.

"We could have very easily been consumed by hate and anger and rage at what happened â and those feelings are still there," said Katie.

"But if no change comes from what happened to Poppy, then what's the point?"

Poppy Russell died in April 2021 at the Princess Royal Hospital in Telford.

She was just 12 hours old.

During her pregnancy her mother told midwives that she had tokophobia, a fear of natural birth and wanted a caesarean section.

Katie said she was repeatedly told however that she "couldn't just ask for a c-section."

When she went into labour, Katie was induced and then "we were left in a room for long periods of time where I had no care," she explained.

"Finally, when we got into the labour suite, I wasn't monitored appropriately and they missed signs that Poppy was in distress."

In a bitter irony, Poppy had to be delivered by emergency caesarean.

By then however, she had developed a hypoxic brain injury and died later the same day.

An inquest into her death found that had Poppy been born an hour earlier, she would have survived.

The Shrewsbury and Telford NHS Trust (SaTH), which ran the hospital, subsequently blamed Katie for her daughter's death.

They said she had refused foetal monitoring; the inquest concluded that was untrue.

"The trust left us in an appalling position," said Neil Russell.

"Not only were they found to have neglected our care, but in the months and years following, we uncovered that members of staff had tried to cover it up.

âLosing your daughter is one thing, but then to find that there was a cavalcade of lies was almost as bad."

Following the inquest in 2023 the trust said: "We recognise there were failings in the care we provided and we are truly sorry."

It said the death of any baby was a "tragedy" and promised improvements to maternity services.

In March 2024, the couple had a meeting with the trust to discuss all that had happened.

From the discussions, Neil and Katie decided they needed to honour Poppy.

"The first conversations about Poppy's Promise were about being human," said Neil, 45.

"It spun from our treatment, and not being treated like human beings."

News.title: UK bluefin tuna comeback shows nature can recover, says WWF
News.content:
Bluefin tuna have returned in huge numbers off the British coast after almost disappearing from UK waters.

The return of the giant predatory fish is one of several wildlife recoveries highlighted in a major new report from WWF, which it says shows conservation can work.

However, the Living Planet Report 2026 also found that monitored wildlife populations around the world have fallen by an average of 73% since 1970.

The wildlife conservation charity said nature remains in "freefall" but it called the report one of hope.

"It's not too late," Mike Barrett, chief scientific adviser at WWF-UK, told the BBC.

News.title: 'Stop throwing shade' - the woman trying to stop firms leaving the UK
News.content:
The UK needs to do more to back its own companies at a time when a growing number are choosing to list their shares in the US rather than at home, the boss of the London Stock Exchange (LSE) has told the BBC.

Dame Julia Hoggett said the government needed to make it "more attractive" to invest in the UK stock market, otherwise big firms would continue to look overseas for their next stage of growth.

Over the last few years, scores of big firms have left the London market, are considering a move or have been bought by private foreign investors.

The fear is this weakens the UK economy by reducing tax revenues and depressing business valuations.

News.title: Badenoch says Tories would scrap inheritance tax on family homes
News.content:
Rival parties hit back and said the proposals for IHT, which is levied on the value of someone's estate when they die, would prioritise support for wealthier people in the country.

Badenoch arrived in Birmingham's Symphony Hall with a message to Conservative Party members that they face a "battle for the soul of the this nation".

She argued her party is "renewed" and "coming back" as she continued efforts to convince voters that it has changed following an historic defeat at the 2024 general election.

In a nod to those who have defected to Nigel Farage's party, Badenoch said: "The Conservatives have had an export boom of drama queens going to Reform.

"This party is now the no drama party, we are the no-nonsense party."

With the party trailing Labour and Reform in the polls, Badenoch acknowledged that people are "looking through the shop window", they "like what they see" but "not enough of them are buying yet, we need to fix that".

Her inspiration for how to revive a long-standing brand was Marks and Spencer (M&S), saying they have "adapted their style for today's market and people are flooding back".

Badenoch added: "Just like M&S, we must learn from our mistakes, win back trust and make people feel good about our party again."

One of the biggest responses in the room from members came as Badenoch made clear she did not want to do an election deal with Reform.

She described many Reform voters as "our people", adding: "We let them down and we want them to come back home."

Following a section of the speech mocking some of Reform's senior figures, Badenoch said: "To those who say 'unite the right', we are not uniting with that.

"People deserve better than that and we are going to give them better than that. Character, conduct, and standards matter."

She also said she did not want to live in a country run by people who "debate whether my mixed-race children are English".

In one of many jibes aimed at Burnham, Badenoch labelled him a "Paddington Bear prime minister" who was "hoping that the problems will just go away".

News.title: Shocked NHS colleagues grieve 'exceptional doctor'
News.content:
The colleagues of a GP found dead at her home have spoken of their "profound shock" at the loss of an exceptional doctor.

Hannah Cain, 45, known to her patients as Dr Hannah Terry, was found at a property in Fern Hill, Dersingham, Norfolk, on Sunday. Her husband, Mark Cain, is due at King's Lynn Crown Court later, charged with her murder.

The GP was based at Grimston Medical Centre and had previously been at Heacham Group Practice for several years.

"We have lost an outstanding doctor, a cherished colleague and a friend, and her absence will be felt deeply across our health community," said a statement issued on behalf of primary care organisations across west Norfolk.

"The profound sense of shock and sadness across our practices and the wider NHS community speaks to the impact Hannah had on so many people."

It said its thoughts were with everyone who knew and loved Hannah, and it was grateful for the compassion and understanding shown by patients, communities and partner organisations.

News.title: Holborn and St Pancras by-election gets under way
News.content:
Voting is under way in the Holborn and St Pancras by-election as candidates from across the political spectrum vie to become its new MP.

About 30 polling stations - at churches and community centres - in the north London constituency opened at 07:00 BST and will close at 22:00, when a count will begin.

The seat became vacant after former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer announced he was standing down to focus on a role in international affairs.

Some 15 candidates are standing in the by-election, one of whom is an independent.

Voters will need to show a form of acceptable ID - such as a driving licence or passport - to be able to vote.

Who are the candidates up for election? Read the full list here.

Listen to the best of BBC Radio London on Sounds and follow BBC London on Facebook, external, X, external and Instagram, external. Send your story ideas to hello.bbclondon@bbc.co.uk, external

News.title: 'Kemi's family home pledge' and 'Badenoch invokes core Tory values'
News.content:
Most of the front pages lead with Kemi Badenoch's Conservative conference speech yesterday. "We're ready for the fight", external" is the Daily Telegraph's verdict on the Tory leader's message. The Financial Times, external says her promises to cut taxes represent a return to core Conservative values, but the Guardian describes them as "prioritising the wealthiest", external. The Daily Express believes Badenoch is a "no nonsense" leader, external - a phrase used by several papers - and that she heads a party that will stop what it describes as inheritance tax "raids". The Times says the Conservatives are now focused on wooing "Middle England"., external

"Reform not dodgy, says Reform", external is the Daily Mirror's review of the party's internal investigation finding it did not breach electoral law, when senior officials were recorded by an undercover journalist discussing foreign donations. The paper describes the probe as a "white wash".

The i reports that a major government review will call for schoolchildren to be given help for ADHD,, external autism and mental health issues even before they are diagnosed. The paper says the report will also question whether the conditions are being over-diagnosed and recommend community-based support.

The Guardian warns that the government's reforms to the special education system , externalin England could "unravel" because parents are rushing to secure support before any changes are implemented. It says experts are now urging ministers to review the timeline for their plans, which they claim are based on optimistic assumptions. The Department for Education says it's committed to implementing its plans by 2030.

A new daily pill could represent the biggest Parkinson's breakthrough, external since the 1960s, according to the Times. It says a clinical trial of Solengepras found it reduced patients' stiffness, slowness and tremors, as well as keeping them more alert.

The Telegraph says scientists could have found a key to helping us live longer in a 194-year-old giant tortoise , externalcalled Jonathan. He lives on the island of St Helena in the South Atlantic and is estimated to have hatched in 1832. Researchers say he has the "super genes" of a 5-year-old that reduce inflammation, regulate insulin and suppress cancer.

News.title: Hedgehog among four animals chosen to feature on new banknotes
News.content:
Banknotes are getting a nature makeover - and the Bank of England has revealed the four creatures that will feature on our money.

The Atlantic puffin, barn owl, buff-tailed bumblebee and European hedgehog will appear on the redesigned notes in years to come - although no decision has been made about which animal will be shown on which banknote.

The owl, bumblebee and hedgehog topped a public vote in their specific categories, and the puffin was included to celebrate marine life, the coastline and bring variety to the notes, the Bank said.

Wildlife is replacing notable figures from history, such as Sir Winston Churchill, on our cash in a decision that angered a number of leading politicians.

News.title: Eckert free to stay as Southampton boss as Spygate ban suspended
News.content:
Tonda Eckert is free to continue as Southampton manager after being given a suspended ban for his role in the Spygate scandal.

A Football Association (FA) independent regulatory commission handed the German a six-week ban from all football, but suspended it until the end of next season.

Eckert has also been given a Â£28,000 fine and reprimand but avoided a lengthy ban that could have cost him his job.

The FA had proposed a three-month ban, but the commission gave credit to Eckert for what they called "considerable mitigation in this matter, most particularly around the genuine contrition".

The FA is yet to confirm whether it will appeal.

In a statement, Southampton welcomed the decision.

"We hope this now brings a conclusion to a regrettable period of our history, and measures have been put in place to ensure that such errors in judgement never happen again at our club," the club said.

"We want to take this opportunity to thank the supporters for their unconditional backing throughout this process."

Saints owner Dragan Solak said the club had "already suffered enough".

"We appreciate the panel's recognition of that," he said.

"We are confident the manager has learned from this matter, and a suspended sentence allows him to continue in his role.

"I firmly believe that Tonda is one of Europe's most exciting young coaches, and with this distraction removed, I am confident he can lead the team to a successful season."

Solak said the FA process had been a "positive experience", but criticised the English Football League (EFL), saying "the way they have treated us is not something we will forget".

Saints were expelled from the Championship play-offs in May after admitting spying on training sessions involving Oxford United, Ipswich Town, and Middlesbrough before the play-off semi-final.

They were also handed a four-point deduction for this season.

An English Football League (EFL) independent disciplinary commission ruled at the time the espionage was authorised by Eckert and was a "contrived and determined plan from the top down".

The 33-year-old apologised in June - claiming he was unaware the practice was banned and that it had no impact on his team's performances - but the FA charged him with misconduct, and a hearing took place at the end of last month.

Eckert has been sanctioned for three breaches of FA Rule E3.1. The six-week ban from all football activity would be triggered if he was found to be involved in any other spying between now and the end of next season.

Eckert was appointed permanent Southampton manager in December 2025 after taking interim charge when they were 21st in the Championship. They finished the season in fourth place.

Saints, who face local rivals Portsmouth this weekend, are 13th in the Championship this season with four wins from their eight matches so far.

The FA did not charge Leeds United's former manager Marcelo Bielsa after the club were found guilty of spying on Derby in 2019, instead issuing a formal warning.

The EFL fined Leeds Â£200,000 - which Bielsa said he paid - and introduced a rule prohibiting any club from observing a rival's training session within 72 hours of a match between them.

The most recent precedent for this case came at the 2024 Olympics women's tournament, when Fifa banned Bev Priestman - Canada's head coach - from all football for a year after opponents New Zealand were spied on.

News.title: Man jailed for killing ex days after early release
News.content:
When he was arrested on suspicion of Nurse's murder, Sabat claimed he had killed before and was planning a "murder spree".

He told officers: "I'm a murderer, I don't want to come back out, I wanna go to jail... I've been let out a week.

"Let me back... I'm happy in there, I've done wrong. I killed before and got away with it.

"I've murdered three people so far. I'm gonna go on a murder spree."

Outlining the facts of the case, prosecutor Catherine Farrelly KC said Sabat and Nurse had been in a relationship and had known each other for many years as the defendant was brought up by her father.

Two days after Sabat was released from prison, Nurse's children visited her and on returning home, told their father her "friend or cousin" had been there.

On 22 October, Nurse told a neighbour Sabat was at her address and would not leave. Another neighbour saw her in the street shouting: "Get out of my house."

Two days later, a neighbour heard a single scream coming from the victim's home, the court heard.

Nurse was last seen on CCTV on 25 October. Her children tried to visit the following day but got no response when they knocked on her door.

Her family raised concerns on 27 October and paramedics entered the flat, where the defendant, armed with a knife, charged at a paramedic, the court heard.

The London Ambulance Service crew and family members withdrew from the property and police were called, Farrelly said.

Soon after, armed officers forced entry to the property and used Tasers as they detained Sabat.

Farrelly said officers found Nurse on a bed with a pillow over her face and with multiple stab wounds to the face. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

A post-mortem examination found she had sustained about eight stab wounds, including to the left side of her face, neck and hands.

News.title: Greens investigate party member behind Zionism motion
News.content:
Speitan, a British-Palestinian artist, proposed the Green Party conference motion defining Zionism as an ideology supporting "an ethnonationalist Jewish state".

The motion - which was approved by party members by 1,022 votes to 813 - also called for a "single democratic Palestinian state in all of historic Palestine".

Under Green Party rules, motions supported by members become official party policy, but will not necessarily be included in the party's manifesto at the next general election.

The motion attracted criticism from opposition parties and some Jewish groups, who labelled it an "attack on the Jewish community".

Four out of five Green Party MPs also opposed the motion.

Adrian Ramsay, a former party leader and Green MP for Waveney Valley, said the motion was an "unhelpful distraction" and "wrong in principle" as "the Green Party has always supported the right to self-determination and that has to apply to all peoples".

Asked if he would consider leaving the party, Ramsay told Matt Chorley on BBC Radio 5 Live he was "not ruling anything in or out at this stage".

"What I'm doing at this stage, and we're only a few days after the motion, is to talk carefully with colleagues to reflect both with Jewish Greens but also with Green MPs and other people in leading roles in the party to look at how best can we get things back on track," he said.

On Tuesday, the Jewish Chronicle reported, external the existence of a 2015 letter from Speitan in which she offered to testify as a defence witness in the trial of Minh Quang Pham.

US prosecutors said Pham had been directed by al-Qaeda leader Anwar al-Awlaki to detonate explosives in Heathrow's arrivals area after spending several months in Yemen being trained by him.

He was jailed for 40 years in the US after pleading guilty to supporting al-Qaeda. He denied planning a suicide attack.

In US court documents from 2015, Speitan was listed as a "close friend" who could provide "critical testimony regarding Pham's mental state".

In a later letter to the US District Judge, Speitan said Pham was one of the "few people I regard with such high respect and esteem".

She said if the judge "truly knew the Minh [Pham] that I and others grew to love and respect", they may have "probably had the whole case dismissed".

She acknowledged he "may have had and developed some behavioural issues" but added: "He turned out to be one of the kindest, honest, most sincere, trustworthy and respectful people I have ever known."

There is no suggestion in the documents Speitan knew of Pham's criminal activities at the time they knew each other.

Following the emergence of the letter on Tuesday afternoon, a Green Party spokesperson said: "Where members have expressed views that do not fit in with the party's values, we have internal processes to investigate."

On Wednesday, the party released an updated statement adding "an investigation is under way".

The spokesperson said: "Lubna Speitan holds no party positions other than being a member."

News.title: Trump makes late Nobel Prize pitch: ‘Not bragging ... but I settled eight wars’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Donald Trump on Wednesday reiterated his call for the Nobel Prize committee to award him with its Peace Prize as he leaned back into talk of his peacemaking efforts.

Those peacemaking efforts, which he claims to tally at eight thus far, are ongoing, he says, and will soon include “another one” — even though there’s no sign yet of meaningful progress in talks between the U.S. and Iran regarding another ceasefire. Setting aside that it would come amid a war he himself started.

The president spoke to reporters at an announcement on his “Trump accounts” for children, after returning to Washington briefly amid his near rally-a-day spree of campaign appearances across the country.

“I’ve done stuff that nobody else has ever done. I’m not bragging, I’m just telling you the facts,” the president told reporters on Wednesday. “No president has probably ever settled any wars. I settled eight wars."

He then went after his first-term predecessor, President Barack Obama, whom he accused of not knowing why he’d received the 2009 Nobel Peace Prize. They gave the peace prize to Obama, then less than a year into his presidency, for his diplomatic efforts to reestablish ties with the Muslim world after nearly a decade of warfare in Iraq and Afghanistan led to a perception held by some that America was at war with the entire Muslim world.

open image in gallery Donald Trump once again lashed out at former President Barack Obama over Obama's Nobel Prize on Wednesday ( Reuters )

The 47th president insisted on Wednesday that he was more deserving of the prize than Obama.

“Look, Obama got it, and he didn’t do anything-- he still doesn’t know what he got it for,” said Trump. “He got it when he was elected, right? Right at the beginning.”

“Whether I get it or not, I have done far more,” the president said.

The president frequently cites the “eight wars” statistic as a reference for his supposed peacemaking abilities, but the figure is not true. Several of the “wars” on Trump’s list were not wars at all, such as disagreements between Serbia and Kosovo which never escalated to real armed conflict during either of Trump’s two presidencies. Another one of the eight is the conflict between Iran and Israel, which very much remains ongoing as part of a three-way conflict also now involving the U.S. — that conflict has been ongoing for nearly eight months.

Still, the Iran war he unilaterally launched has largely shattered Trump’s image as a steward of global affairs, even in the minds of his own supporters, who embraced that depiction of the president during his 2024 campaign for a second term as he hammered Joe Biden and Kamala Harris over Israel’s relentless strikes against Gaza and the ongoing Russian invasion of Ukraine, both of which he pledged to end.

A year and a half after coming to power, Trump has made little to no progress in his efforts to negotiate an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine. A ceasefire exists in the Gaza Strip, where the majority of fighting has died down, but most Gazans remain in appalling conditions with much of the region’s infrastructure and housing destroyed. Israeli strikes continue to be carried out on camps of refugees, with continued civilian casualties.

open image in gallery Donald Trump spoke to reporters before departing the White House on Wednesday and claimed that the war in Iran was already 'won' ( AP )

The president’s touting of his diplomatic credentials also ignore one truth about his 2024 campaign: his promise to stop getting the U.S. into endless wars with murky objectives. His critics, both within and outside of the Republican Party, now accuse him of doing just that as the war in Iran has shifted from an effort to dislodge the Iranian government and take control of its remaining nuclear materials to ending disruptions over shipping in the Strait of Hormuz.

Obama has long been a fixation of Trump’s, however, and the president attacks him nearly as frequently as he attacks Biden, who defeated him in the 2020 election. On Wednesday, he warned that his allies wanted to see the Justice Department wielded against Obama, Biden and Hillary Clinton, but claimed that he was respecting the sanctity of his office by declining.

open image in gallery Donald Trump touted his peacemaking efforts Wednesday even as war continues between the U.S. and Iran in the Strait of Hormuz ( Reuters )

"I could've done very bad things to Hillary Clinton. I could've done very very bad things to Joe Biden. I could've done very bad things to Barack Hussein Obama,” said Trump.

As he departed the White House for a campaign rally in San Antonio, Texas, the president reiterated his confusing claim that the war in Iran was already “won”, but not yet “over”.

“It's a war that's been won from the standpoint of what we have to do. We have to get rid of-- no nuclear weapons for, as you know, for Iran,” said the president.

“We've taken away their nuclear power. If they would have had nuclear power, you would have had problems like you've never had before. So we did this for that reason. We've essentially accomplished that. Their military is now wiped out. Their whole country right now is wiped out. It'll be over very quickly. And when it does, and when it does, oil prices will come tumbling down.”

News.title: Nobel Prize in literature to be awarded in Stockholm
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

The Nobel Prize in literature will be awarded Thursday by the Swedish Academy in Stockholm.

Last year, Hungarian writer László Krasznahorkai, whose surreal and anarchic novels combine a bleak world view with mordant humor, won the Nobel Prize in literature for work the judges said upholds the power of art in the midst of “apocalyptic terror.”

Three science awards were announced earlier this week. The Nobel for medicine went to three scientists whose work led to a tool that uses light to help unravel how the brain works. The physics award recognized a scientist’s efforts to demystify a rare group of neutrinos. The chemistry prize recognized two scientists for untangling mysterious mirror images in molecules, a discovery that has been used to develop countless drugs.

This week ends with Friday's peace prize. The Nobel Memorial Prize in Economic Sciences will be announced Monday.

The prize money this year is 12 million Swedish kronor (about $1.2 million), whether for an individual, small group of laureates or organization.

___

Dazio reported from Berlin.

___

News.title: Trump says he ‘could have done very bad things’ to Hillary, Obama and Biden
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

President Donald Trump raised eyebrows Wednesday when he told reporters he “could’ve done very bad things” to Hillary Clinton and former Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama.

Trump made the off-the-wall claim during an Oval Office announcement touting his “Trump Accounts” for children after returning to Washington, D.C. from a series of campaign events across the country ahead of the midterms. The top Democratic figures are often targets of Trump’s tirades.

At the event, a reporter asked the president about his previous claim that Democrats would impeach him if they gained control of Congress in November.

“For what?” the reporter asked.

“They don’t know,” Trump said, before he pivoted to attacking his 2016 rival Clinton and his Democratic predecessors in the White House.

open image in gallery President Donald Trump said that he ‘could’ve done very bad things’ to Hillary Clinton and former Presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama during an Oval Office event ( AFP/Getty )

“I could've done very bad things to Hillary Clinton,” Trump began. “I could've done very, very bad things to Joe Biden. I could've done very bad things to Barack Hussein Obama. I …thought it was inappropriate to do so because you have to treat the office of the presidency with respect.

“Then I found out that they impeached me twice and I certainly, to this moment, I can do whatever I want, if I want,” the president continued. “They’ve done some very bad things.”

“I’ve had plenty of people say, Let’s go get them.’ And I said no, you can’t do that to the presidency,” Trump added.

Trump was impeached twice during his first presidency, but was not removed from office by the Senate. Neither Clinton, Obama nor Biden had any hand in those actions, and the Constitution only empowers Congress with such power to impeach.

open image in gallery A handful of Democrats have floated impeachment if they win in November, but others have dialed down talk of the idea ( AFP/Getty )

House Speaker Mike Johnson has warned that Democrats are “raring to go” and impeach Trump if they reclaim the House in November — which also serves as a rallying cry for him and his party as they face a tough road ahead in the midterms.

“It’s guaranteed, probably on the first day – first or second day,” Johnson told conservative commentator and CNN contributor Scott Jennings this week. “Remember, they’ve already filed articles of impeachment in this Congress.”

A handful of Democrats have floated impeachment should they win back the House in November, but others in the party have dialed down talk of the idea.

“This is something, oftentimes, I think the right-wing media wants us to talk about,” said California Rep. Pete Aguilar, chair of the House Democratic Caucus. “But it’s not anything that is top of the agenda for House Democrats.”

Last month, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries said that Democrats “haven’t ruled anything out” but also added, “we haven’t ruled anything in.”

Illinois Rep. Brad Schneider, the chairman of the New Democrat Coalition, said earlier this year that “we've already seen twice unless you're going to get a two-thirds majority in the Senate ... the president will not be removed from office.”

News.title: UK and Germany to launch security pact against Russian sabotage and cyber attacks
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Prime minister Andy Burnham will head to Berlin on Thursday for his inaugural face-to-face talks with German chancellor Friedrich Merz.

The leaders are set to establish a joint UK-Germany security framework aimed at countering cyber attacks, sabotage and other hybrid threats from hostile foreign actors, particularly Russia.

The strategic agreement will see both countries share intelligence and coordinate action to monitor, deter and disrupt potential dangers, while building greater resilience around critical national infrastructure.

Mr Burnham and Mr Merz are also scheduled to discuss aid for Ukraine, responses to Middle East instability, and the disruption of key global shipping lanes such as the Strait of Hormuz.

Furthermore, the pair will convene a UK-Germany Regional Growth Forum featuring British and German business leaders, aimed at driving investment, deepening industrial ties and ensuring economic benefits reach communities in both nations.

Thursday will also mark the formal ratification of the Kensington Treaty, which was signed in July last year, committing both nations to significantly deeper cooperation across science, technology, defence, security and growth.

open image in gallery Mr Burnham and Mr Merz will also discuss support for Ukraine, responding to instability in the Middle East and addressing the impact of disruption to global trade routes, such as the Strait of Hormuz ( Getty )

Ahead of the visit, Mr Burnham said: “Attacks on our infrastructure, our businesses and our democracies are not a distant threat.

“They reach into people’s homes and workplaces, and they are designed to make us weaker and more divided.

“Britain and Germany are joining forces to find, expose and disrupt this activity.

“Security and growth go hand in hand, and both must be felt in every town and city in our two countries.”

The Prime Minister’s trip comes amid an intelligence scandal that has rocked Germany; its former spy chief has been arrested on suspicion of espionage.

August Hanning, who headed Germany’s Federal Intelligence Service (BND) from 1998 to 2005, is “strongly suspected of treasonous espionage, spying out state secrets, attempted treason, and espionage”, the federal prosecutor’s office said in a statement.

Mr Hanning, 80, is accused of using classified intelligence to “draft an analysis” for an employee of one foreign intelligence service, and of “passing on information” to an employee of another foreign spying service.

open image in gallery Mr Burnham’s visit also comes at a time when concerns about sabotage and hybrid threats are on the rise in both the UK and Germany ( Reuters )

A former aide, identified as Manfred D, was also arrested and has been charged with aiding and abetting attempted treason and treasonous espionage.

The prosecutor’s office said Manfred D worked as Mr Hanning’s chief of staff and later served as chief of staff for several subsequent BND presidents from 2012 until 2026.

Mr Burnham’s visit also comes at a time when concerns about sabotage and hybrid threats are on the rise in both the UK and Germany.

Last month, the British Government summoned a senior Russian diplomat to protest over an “egregious and reckless attack” at Germany’s Leipzig airport, a major international freight hub used for providing support to Ukraine.

A drone carrying explosive was found near Ukrainian cargo planes in August, but failed to explode and was subsequently defused.

Investigators suspect a second drone collided with a cargo aircraft nearby and a third drone was reportedly found near the airport 10 days later.

Germany’s interior minister Alexander Dobrindt said the Leipzig airport attack followed the “well-established pattern of Russian hybrid operations in Europe” and the assumption was that Germany would be targeted again.

Moscow denied involvement and Russian president Vladimir Putin accused Germany of planting evidence to blame Moscow.

News.title: Eritrean soldiers entered northern Ethiopian towns, government-allied commander says
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Eritrean soldiers entered two towns in northern Ethiopia, a commander allied with Ethiopia’s government said, with military officers conducting surveillance in one of them, as residents reported that Tigrayan opposition forces had withdrawn from Shire.

Ermiyas Ababu, a Tigray Peace Force commander based in Mekelle, said Eritrean personnel entered Adigrat on Tuesday and Idaga Hamus on Wednesday. He said Eritrean military officers and commanders were conducting surveillance in Idaga Hamus, citing reports from his personnel in the area.

Separately, conflict monitoring group ACLED said Eritrean troops crossed the border at Zelambesa on Wednesday and Ethiopian military drones targeted them at Guada as they traveled toward Idaga Hamus.

The Associated Press could not independently verify either account. ACLED, which provided its account through East Africa analyst Jalale Getachew Birru, had not responded Thursday morning to an inquiry about the basis for its claims.

The allegations come amid renewed fighting between Ethiopian government forces and an opposition alliance that includes the Tigray People’s Liberation Front, or TPLF.

Eritrean Information Minister Yemane Gebremeskel accused Ethiopia on Wednesday of fabricating allegations to justify military action against his country. In a post on X, he accused Ethiopia’s ruling party of creating “a fallacious narrative of ‘self-defense.’” He did not specifically address the movements or strikes described by ACLED.

Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed reiterated Monday that his landlocked country must have access to the Red Sea. Ethiopia lost its coastline when Eritrea became independent in 1993. Ethiopia’s Foreign Ministry said Monday that it remained committed to dialogue and peaceful engagement with its neighbors.

Eritrea has denied Ethiopia’s allegations that it supports the TPLF. Last week, it announced it was severing diplomatic ties after Ethiopia expelled 10 Eritrean diplomats and closed its embassy in Asmara.

In Shire, residents Mesu’ud Ahmed and Abadi Halefom told the AP by telephone Wednesday evening that they had witnessed TPLF forces withdrawing earlier that day. Government troops and allied forces had not entered when they spoke, Mesu’ud said.

Shire has been a major refuge for people displaced by fighting in Tigray and a base for humanitarian aid operations.

“TPLF left but the government forces and their allies did not enter the town but we hear that they are coming,” Mesu’ud said. “Everyone has closed their shops in Shire, and moved their merchandise for fear of looting.”

Government-allied fighters entered Mekelle, Tigray’s regional capital, on Sunday after the TPLF announced its withdrawal. The Tigray Peace Force imposed a curfew there Wednesday from 8 p.m. to 6 a.m.

The force includes former members of the TPLF’s armed wing. Ermiyas said Tuesday that it was working with Ethiopian federal troops to expand its control.

The TPLF joined six other opposition groups last month in an alliance seeking to oust Abiy. Fighting escalated late last month, undermining the November 2022 peace agreement that ended a devastating two-year war.

_________

Filmon Equar Hailu in Mekelle and Amir Aman Kiyaro in Hamburg, Germany, contributed to this report.

News.title: Indian actor and filmmaker Nana Patekar dies at 75
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Nana Patekar, an acclaimed Indian actor and filmmaker, died Thursday at his home in the western state of Goa. He was 75.

Patekar died of a suspected cardiac arrest, the Press Trust of India news agency reported, citing a doctor at the hospital where he was pronounced dead.

Born in 1951 in India’s western state of Maharashtra, Patekar built a career spanning nearly five decades in Hindi- and Marathi-language cinema. He was known for intense performances and roles that often portrayed complex or unconventional characters.

Patekar made his film debut in the 1978 Hindi film “Gaman,” and later earned acclaim for “Parinda” and “Krantiveer.” He gained wider international recognition with filmmaker Mira Nair’s Oscar-nominated “Salaam Bombay!”

He won three National Film Awards, India’s highest film honors, and received the Padma Shri, one of the country’s highest civilian honors.

Prime Minister Narendra Modi mourned Patekar’s death, praising his “intensity, individuality and unmistakable presence” as an actor.

“He brought remarkable versatility and creativity to every role and gave us characters that will be remembered for generations,” Modi wrote on X.

Patekar is survived by his wife and son.

News.title: Tesco sales boosted by online shopping as consumers hunt for ‘value’
News.content:
Become an Independent member to bookmark this article Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today. Already a member? Log in

Tesco has unveiled a jump in sales for the first half of the year amid an online shopping boost and raised its annual profit outlook, despite cautioning that economic uncertainty was weighing on consumer confidence.

The UK’s biggest supermarket chain said sales, excluding fuel and VAT, totalled £33.8 billion for the 26 weeks to August 29.

Sales were 1% higher when compared like-for-like with the same period last year, and 1.5% higher in the UK alone.

Online sales surged by 8.4% in the UK with average grocery orders growing, and sales for its rapid delivery arm Whoosh soaring by 37%.

The company revealed its adjusted operating profit jumped by 6.3% to £1.8 billon.

Tesco said a strong financial performance for the first half meant it was now expecting profits of between £3.15 billion and £3.3 billion for the full year – an improvement on the £3 billion to £3.3 billion range it had previously guided.

Consumer confidence has been “relatively resilient” but “ongoing political tensions continue to create uncertainty”, the company said, which was translating to demand for a better value weekly shop.

Nevertheless, the supermarket’s “Finest” range of more premium products saw sales jump by 9% in the UK.

Meanwhile, fuel sales surged by nearly a fifth year-on-year which it attributed to higher oil prices pushing up the cost for consumers.

Ken Murphy, Tesco’s chief executive, said: “Against an uncertain external backdrop, we have continued to invest in giving customers the very best value for money.

“Our focus remains on helping customers get the best possible value from their weekly shop.

“Looking ahead, we’re excited to bring our new Christmas ranges to customers and help them enjoy a great festive season.”

News.title: Kenyan authorities scramble to find passengers on Ebola flight
News.content:
Authorities are racing to track down passengers who boarded a flight from Uganda to Kenya on Saturday alongside a man infected with Ebola.

The man travelled by bus from the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the epicentre of an Ebola outbreak that has killed 4,000 people, to Kampala, Uganda. He then boarded a flight to Nairobi on Saturday, October 3, which was operated by the African airline Jambojet.

The patient went to a hospital in Nairobi and died just 48 hours later, meaning the journey took place in the final days of infection, the stage at which patients who die of the disease are most contagious. By October 6 authorities had tracked down 28 contacts, including family members of the deceased, but said they urgently needed to track down 23 passengers and crew who had travelled on the same flight.

The man is Kenya’s first ever case of the disease. Ebola does not typically spread through the air like Covid-19 or measles, requiring close contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person to spread. However, an aeroplane cabin significantly intensifies these risks because passengers share cramped spaces for prolonged periods and touch the same surfaces, such as a cabin toilet.

“We are working closely with the Ministry of Health, Port Health Services and other relevant authorities to support the ongoing public health response, including the identification and management of the other guests and crew who may have been in contact with the individual,” a spokesperson for Jambojet said on Tuesday.

After landing in Kenya, airport staff screened the patient, standard protocol for people travelling from at-risk countries during the current Ebola outbreak, but allowed him to continue his journey into Nairobi.

Kenya’s health ministry director-general, Patrick Amoth, said the patient may have passed through airport screening because medication had masked his symptoms.

News.title: Africa embraces ‘Go to Work on an Egg’ to boost maternal health and nutrition
News.content:
The sun is barely up when villagers start queuing for eggs at the metal gate of Shamim Haried’s home.

By noon, all that day’s supply is usually sold out, but people keep coming and asking if there are any left.

Demand is so high that arguments can break out in the queue, says the mother-of-two who lives outside Malawi’s capital, Lilongwe.

Her eggs are cheaper and fresher than those sold in the market.

“The people almost fight for eggs: it’s hard to watch,” she explains.

“Eggs are the cheapest healthy protein that they can get and it’s better for them to buy here than anywhere else.”

Her flock of 1,400 chickens lay around 1,000 eggs each day, but she reckons she could sell three times that.

News.title: What is pneumonic plague? Symptoms and how it spreads
News.content:
The death of a researcher at a plague laboratory in Siberia has prompted the World Health Organization to press Moscow for answers.

Russian officials have yet to share details of what caused the worker’s illness, and this information vacuum has fuelled speculation.

But what is the disease, and how much of a threat does it pose?

What is pneumonic plague?

Plague is a rare and serious infection caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, usually found in small mammals such as rodents and their fleas. Pneumonic plague is the most virulent of plague’s three forms, and is a severe infection of the lungs.

The other types are bubonic plague – the Black Death that laid waste to much of Europe during the Middle Ages – which attacks the lymph nodes, and septicaemic plague, which attacks the blood. Either can develop into the pneumonic form if the infection spreads.

Pneumonic plague is rarer than the bubonic form, but more dangerous.

Each year, the world records an estimated 1,000 to 3,000 plague cases of all types, though the number fluctuates.

Most cases are bubonic, and spread by the bite of an infected flea, and most occur in Madagascar and the Democratic Republic of Congo. But infections are also found in countries including Russia, India, China and the United States.
