News.title: Weight loss jabs are safe for obese teenagers, WHO announces
News.content:
Obese teenagers can safely be given weight-loss drugs and undergo bariatric surgery, the World Health Organization (WHO) has said.

The recommendations form part of the first set of global guidelines released by the WHO for the treatment of obese children and adolescents.

Previously, the WHO only recommended weight-loss drugs like Mounjaro and Wegovy and bariatric surgery, which alters the stomach and reduces appetite, for the treatment of obese adults – defined as someone with a body mass index of 30 or above.

However, the new guidelines say children over the age of 10 can safely be given the drugs, as well as undergo weight-loss surgery, if all other options, like managed exercise and diet programmes, have been exhausted. Children under that age should not be given drugs or surgery.

Obese children in the UK are currently not eligible for weight-loss drugs or surgery on the NHS, although specialised clinics may offer them to children over 12 under very strict conditions.

The WHO recommends first and foremost that obese children and teenagers undertake a structured diet programme and physical activity, which for children over five should include an average of at least 60 minutes per day of moderate to vigorous activity across the week.

According to Unicef an estimated 188 million children and adolescents are obese, and last year, the number of overweight children exceeded the number of underweight children for the first time in history.

While obesity rates are beginning to plateau in many rich countries, childhood obesity is rising rapidly in the developing world, including in sub-Saharan Africa, which is home to nearly a quarter of the world’s overweight children.

The drivers of obesity are complex, but experts believe a switch from traditional, fibre-rich diets to cheap, high-fat, high-sugar food has played a significant role in growing global obesity rates.

Obesity at any age carries significant health risks – but the consequences are thought to be more acute if obesity begins in childhood, accelerating the development of severe and life-threatening conditions, including type-2 diabetes, cardiovascular dysfunction, and liver disease.

The WHO guidelines also emphasise the importance of addressing mental health issues that are often associated with obesity and contribute to unhealthy eating patterns – including anxiety and depression, low self-esteem, and bullying.

“Our priority must be to ensure that every child and adolescent can access quality care and supportive environments from an early age, helping them achieve and maintain a healthy weight and laying the foundation for lifelong health and well-being,” Dr Luz María De Regil, Director of the Department of Nutrition and Food Safety, WHO.

News.title: Russia’s plague shouldn’t scare us – its secretive bioweapons should
News.content:
The facts about the laboratory accident in Russia are scant.

A lab technician at the Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East in Siberia is dead, 200 people have been quarantined, and the state security services are saying “nothing to see here, folks”.

Denials from the country that has run a covert biological weapons programme since the Cold War have done nothing to quieten speculation about what is really going on in the vast Siberian tundra.

Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, demanded on Tuesday that Russia be “transparent” about the situation, which he said Washington was monitoring “very closely”.

“I think it’s incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world,” Mr Rubio said during a trip to Iceland.

A death from plague is a tragedy, but should not be something we need to worry about. We have moved on from the Middle Ages, when the Black Death laid waste to much of Europe.

It’s treatable with antibiotics and does not spread as fast as diseases like Covid. Its replication or R number does not get above 1.5 – measles, for example, has an R number of 12 to 18.

News.title: Kane’s record-equalling cap was no different to his first
News.content:
One expects that when the end comes it will not be as rancorous as the final exit of Cristiano Ronaldo from Portugal, a drama playing out elsewhere. At some point, Kane will take his leave and it is likely to be as unassuming as the rest of it. He will be back at Wembley, injury permitting, for cap No 126 next month against Croatia. He talks like a different person to the one he was even five years ago – with a confidence and certainty about his place in the world. As opposed to the younger Kane, who seemed to regard everything outside his goalscoring tunnel vision with a general sense of bemusement.

“Availability,” he said, “is one of the biggest strengths you can have at this level for any coach.” He was keen to emphasise his “all-round leadership” too, “a lot of assets off the pitch”. He still measures himself in goals, of course, and perhaps there will be a Ballon d’Or too later this month – a prize that has eluded generations of England players before him who have won much more for their clubs than Kane has done. The good news for Kane is that his last England years will be spent in a very good England team – one which was on another level to its opposition on this occasion too.

No team in the top tier of the Nations League has scored more goals than England – 14 in the last four match days. Tuchel’s name was sung at Wembley and even if the World Cup semi-final collapse in Atlanta in July has not been entirely forgotten, the roughest edges have been taken off somewhat. Another great performance from Jude Bellingham and also from Morgan Rogers, in place of Bukayo Saka. Another dominant Elliot Anderson performance in midfield. They left Wembley to applause and a sense of optimism renewed.

England kept the ball with such authority, and none more so than Bellingham. Trent Alexander-Arnold came back at right-back. Myles Lewis-Skelly returned for another bite at a Wembley midfield job. As in Prague last week, there was a self-inflicted Czech calamity in the first half. The captain Vladimir Coufal appeared to lose his cool at the threat of the England attack all over the Czechs’ half. No other reason for this Premier League experienced full-back to fling himself at Kane’s cross and drill the ball past Newcastle goalkeeper Lukas Hornicek on 27 minutes.

ANTHONY GORDON has risked riling his former Newcastle team-mates – after claiming Pedri is a huge playmaking upgrade.

The winger, 25, completed a blockbuster £70million move to Barcelona during the summer.



And Gordon was among England’s top performers during the international break after netting against Spain, Czechia and in the 7-0 demolition of Croatia.

The former Everton man had already made a stunning start to the season with Barcelona – notching five assists in six LaLiga outings.



But Gordon may have landed himself in hot water with his ex-Newcastle pals.

He appears to have made an unwitting dig at some big-names at St James’ Park after heaping praise on Barcelona midfielder Pedri, 23.



Gordon told Sport: “I’ve made many runs throughout my career that no one saw, but now I have Pedri, who sees absolutely everything.

“Adapting has been relatively easy because at Newcastle we already played a similar style – pressing hard and attacking with the team pushed high up the pitch.

“With the ball as well, now I play surrounded by some of the best footballers in the world.

“The best Barca side I’ve ever seen is Pep Guardiola’s – the one that won the Champions League with players like Xavi and Andres Iniesta. I want this team to be remembered forever.”

Sports.title: Man Utd fans left ‘speechless’ as Youri Tielemans reveals idol he wants to train with
Sports.content:

MANCHESTER UNITED fans have been left shocked after Youri Tielemans revealed a strange choice for who the idol he wants to train with is.

The midfielder was appearing in a video published by the club on social media which asked players: ‘If you could train with anyone in the world who would it be?’



Tielemans was one of several players who was in the hot seat for the question, alongside Kobbie Mainoo, Amad Diallo, Andrey Santos, Carlos Baleba, Ayden Heaven and Matheus Cunha.

But while many of his team-mates opted for well-known sports stars, Tielemans went for a quite unique pick.



When asked, the 29-year-old replied: “Jason Statham.”

The Belgian explained: “Yeah, I really like him as an actor but also like his presence.

“It’s really good, so I’d say him.”

Fans were left stunned by the selection, with one writing online: “One million guesses who Youri Tielemans goat is. Speechless.”

A second said: “I had to watch it twice to make sure I heard it right.”

A third added: “Fried head when I heard that.”



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Another said: “Asked for a goat and he’s picked the bloke from Transporter.”

A fifth said: “Expected some mad answer, never ever expected it to be that.”

Statham is best known for his roles in Hollywood action movies such as Fast and Furious, The Meg, The Expendables, Transporter, Lock, Stock and Two Smoking Barrels and Snatch.

What many people don’t remember, however, is that the 59-year-old was once on the path hoping to land medals for Great Britain.



Statham, then 22, competed for Team GB at the 1990 Commonwealth Games in Auckland, New Zealand.

He competed in the 1m springboard, 3m springboard and 10m platform events.

But he could only manage eighth in the 1m springboard alongside a pair of 11th-place finishes in the other two events.

There were also two failed events to qualify for the Olympic Games in 1988 and 1992 before he quit diving to pursue a career in acting.

Sports.title: Sir Alex Ferguson reveals emotional moment he broke down in tears after telling Man Utd stars he was retiring
Sports.content:
Next

SIR ALEX Ferguson cried after he told his Manchester United players he would be stepping down as manager in May 2013.

News of Ferguson’s impending exit leaked on the Tuesday night before he gathered the United squad and his backroom staff at their Carrington training complex on the Wednesday morning.



Ferguson writes in Games of My Life.: “It wasn’t until I got back to the office and shut the door that everything caught up with me; I just sat at my desk and cried.

“After I wiped my eyes, I thought I had better clear out quickly before the news was made public. The last thing I wanted was to have to deal with the press.”



Before his final match in charge at West Brom – a 5-5 draw – United players presented Ferguson with a scrapbook charting his career and a Rolex watch with “Thanks for everything” inscribed on it.

Having penned two autobiographies, two seasonal diaries in the Nineties, a book on his first six years in charge of United and a study in leadership, Ferguson has released a seventh book at the age of 84.

His latest memoir sees him pick the 21 matches that have meant the most to him, dating back to his schoolboy days in Glasgow.

Ferguson also wonders what might have materialised had his New York dinner with future Manchester City manager Pep Guardiola in September 2012 taken place two months earlier.

Guardiola had started a year-long sabbatical after his departure as Barcelona coach and Ferguson claims the Catalan had already agreed to take over at Bayern Munich in the summer of 2013.

Fergie wrote: “If I could rewind time, we would have dined some months earlier, I would have poured plenty of Tignanello and I would have tried my hardest to convince him that his future lay in Manchester.



“Unfortunately for us, it did. Enough said.”

In his previous book, Leading, Ferguson suggested that Guardiola had not “signed on the dotted line” with Bayern, writing: “I asked Pep to phone me before he accepted an offer from another club, but he didn’t and wound up joining Bayern Munich in July 2013.”

The death of Ferguson’s sister-in-law, Bridget, in October 2012 convinced him to retire at the end of that season and he informed his late wife, Lady Cathy, around Christmas time.



The book is dedicated to Lady Cathy, who passed away in October 2023.

Ferguson mentions United’s owners, the Glazers, only once in the 336 pages but there is no mention of co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who stripped Ferguson of his £2million-a-year ambassadorial role.

However, Fergie does muse on the current United structure of a chief executive and director of football above the head coach.

He writes: “I suppose the owners like the idea of a ‘coach’ because he, in their minds, is just one part of a bigger machine.

“If he goes, the machine is intact – or, at least, that’s the theory.



“Even though at the big clubs, the authority has moved away from the touchline to the sporting director or football CEO, in the eyes of the press and the fans, it remains the head coach who shoulders the responsibility if things go wrong.”

Ferguson pointedly stresses: “Formidable, sustainable financial strength is closely correlated with success on the pitch.”

United’s debt now stands at £1.15BILLION.



The Scot also offers an olive branch to Roy Keane, his captain at United for more than eight years.

Ferguson and Keane have never repaired their relationship since the former midfielder was unceremoniously sacked by United in November 2005, and they have barely spoken since Keane’s stint as Sunderland manager ended in 2008.

United’s 3-2 comeback triumph at Juventus in the 1999 Champions League semi-final, one of Ferguson’s defining games, is best remembered for Keane’s Herculean performance, which the Scot dwells on again.

Ferguson says: “I know Roy isn’t an attention-seeker and shrugs off the praise that others heap on him.

“He poured every ounce of his being into that game. It was his greatest night in red.



“For as long as tales are told about the exploits of United, Roy’s performance amid the smoke flares and drumming of the Stadio Delle Alpi is one that will stay with me for ever and deserves to be passed down through the generations.”

“Fergie time” is referred to nine times by Ferguson: “The words ‘The fourth official has indicated there will be a minimum of . . .’ are among my favourite in the English language.”

He fondly recalls Michael Owen’s 96th-minute winner against Manchester City in September 2009 and quips that the “the wonderful fourth official probably should, at the very least, have been awarded an MBE”.

The fourth official was Alan Wiley.

Less than a month later, Ferguson complained that Wiley “wasn’t fit enough” during United’s 2-2 home draw with Sunderland.



Ferguson received a two-match touchline ban.

Fergie also randomly reflects on his chalk-and-cheese dynamic with Nottingham Forest legend Brian Clough.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Clough arrived for a game at Old Trafford and asked the United apprentice Deiniol Graham to shine his shoes.



Ferguson says he was “furious and handed [Clough] his shoes, which I had instructed Deiniol and our kit-man not to touch, and told him never to pull that stunt again.”

Sports.title: Arsenal ace Max Dowman presented with three Guinness World Records certificates after record-breaking rise
Sports.content:
Next

MAX DOWMAN has been presented with three Guinness World Record certificates.

The 16-year-old Arsenal star has officially been honoured as the youngest player to both score a goal in and win the Premier League, and as the youngest player in Champions League history.



Dowman made his Premier League debut from the bench against Leeds, aged just 15 years and 235 days in August 2025, becoming an instant fan-favourite at the Emirates.

He went on to overtake Borussia Dortmund’s Youssoufa Moukoko to become the youngest-ever Champions League player at 15 years and 208 days.



By scoring his first league goal against Everton aged 16 years and 73 days he also picked up the record for youngest scorer in the Premier League.

This was followed by being crowned as the youngest-ever Premier League winner at 16 years and 144 days after the club ended a 22-year wait for the title.

Dowman has been snapped with his certificates outside the Gunners’ training base to kick off Guinness World Records‘ Class of ’27.

Senior Editor of Guinness World Records Football Edition 2027, Tom Beckerlegge, has praised Dowman’s remarkable rise through professional football.

Beckerlegge said: “The youngest player on our list, Max sums up what the Class of ’27 is all about. To have already achieved three Guinness World Records titles before turning 17 is extraordinary, and his story captures exactly why this generation of players is so exciting.

“Football never stands still. Records are broken, new stars emerge and every season brings fresh moments of genius that light up the game. The Guinness World Records Football Edition 2027 celebrates all of that – from the biggest stars in world football to the young players whose stories are only just beginning.”

Sports.title: Sir Alex Ferguson reveals hopes to attend new Manchester United stadium opening in ‘person or spirit’
Sports.content:
Next

SIR ALEX Ferguson hopes to live long enough to attend the opening of Manchester United’s new stadium.

United co-owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe outlined his preference to build a new 100,000-seater stadium in February 2024, dubbing the proposal a “no-brainer”.



Architects Foster+Partners unveiled designs in March 2025 and United bought land near their 116-year-old stadium for £63.5million in the summer.

The club initially eyed a move-in date of 2030 but that has been scrapped, with no specific date now targeted.



United do hope to host games during the 2035 Women’s World Cup, though.

Ferguson, 84, has been a regular at Old Trafford since he retired from management in 2013 and has a seat reserved in the directors’ box.

In his latest book, Games of My Life, Ferguson admits that the prospect of United moving into a new-build left him in a reflective mood.

He writes: “I found myself wondering whether I would be around to celebrate its opening.

“I hope they get to break ground quickly, because if it takes five years to complete, I’ll be pushing ninety.

“However, I know I’ll be at the ceremony one way or another – in person or in spirit.”



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

The 13-time Premier League winner first visited Old Trafford in 1984 to watch Celtic face Rapid Vienna in a European Cup Winners’ Cup replay, relocated to Manchester after crowd trouble at Celtic Park.

Ferguson was appointed United manager in 1986 and took charge of 724 games at Old Trafford, although he missed the December 1998 defeat to Middlesbrough to attend a funeral in Scotland.

The United great suffered a brain haemorrhage in May 2018 and left Old Trafford in an ambulance shortly after arriving for the fixture against Liverpool in May this year due to a heart issue.

Ferguson also arrived for United’s first home game of the season against Ipswich Town in August with his left foot encased in a protective boot, having injured his Achilles.

Old Trafford’s North Stand was renamed the Sir Alex Ferguson Stand in November 2011 to commemorate Ferguson’s 25th anniversary at the club.



United then installed a statue of Ferguson outside the stand bearing his name in November 2012.

A nearby road was also renamed Sir Alex Ferguson Way in 2013.

Games of My Life by Alex Ferguson is published on Thursday October 8 by Macmillan.

Sports.title: Sir Alex Ferguson brands Arsenal fans who abused Arsene Wenger ‘a stain on the club’ despite epic Man Utd rivalry
Sports.content:
Next

SIR ALEX Ferguson has dubbed Arsenal fans’ treatment of Arsene Wenger during his latter years as manager as a “stain on the club’s reputation”.

Wenger left the Gunners in May 2018 after almost 22 years in charge, having won three Premier League titles and seven FA Cups.



Arsenal did the double in two of their title triumphs and went the whole season unbeaten with their third in 2003-04.

However, they failed to add to their title tally during Wenger’s final 14 years in the dugout and there were repeated calls for him to walk.



During an FA Cup tie at Brighton in 2013, Gooners unfurled a banner that read, “Arsene thanks for the memories but it’s time to say goodbye”.

Arsenal endured a nine-year trophy drought between 2005 and 2014 until they won the FA Cup.

They retained the trophy in 2015, yet those domestic successes failed to quieten a vocal contingent of the support.

The rise of fan TV in the mid-2010s saw Wenger repeatedly targeted by Arsenal’s performative fans on YouTube and social media.

In his latest book, Games of My Life, Ferguson declares him and Wenger as the “last two monuments in Premier League management”.

The Manchester United legend sympathises with his rival’s struggles, which he pins on Arsenal’s move from Highbury to the 60,000-capacity Emirates Stadium in 2006.



CASINO SPECIAL – BEST CASINO BONUSES FROM £10 DEPOSITS

Wenger had the opportunity to manage Real Madrid before Arsenal upped sticks for Ashburton Grove but remained in north London. Ferguson feels Wenger’s “loyalty” contributed to Arsenal’s “faltered form”.

Arsenal lost several key players shortly after the relocation. Manchester City signed Kolo Toure, Emmanuel Adebayor, Gael Clichy and Samir Nasri within a third-year period after their 2008 takeover by the Abu Dhabi United Group.

Cesc Fabregas left for Barcelona the same summer that Nasri headed to Manchester in 2011 and Thierry Henry and Alexander Hleb moved to Catalonia in successive summers.

Ferguson even prised Robin van Persie from Arsenal in 2012 after the Dutchman entered the final year of his contract, a move that inspired United’s last title victory in 2013.

And Fergie has now written of Wenger’s struggles: “I’m glad I never felt such pressure at Old Trafford.



“The banks even made a contract extension for Arsene a condition of their financing. He was trapped.

“The way he was treated by some Arsenal fans at the end of his managerial career was a stain on the club’s reputation.”

Despite a bitter rivalry during Wenger’s first 12 years at Arsenal, Ferguson and Wenger had a warmer rapport from around 2008.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Ferguson presented Wenger with a gift to mark his retirement ahead of his final match as Arsenal manager at Old Trafford in April 2018.

Games of My Life by Alex Ferguson is publishing on Thursday 8th October by Macmillan.

Sports.title: Mikel Arteta’s new £80m Arsenal deal is more bad news for Man City after he left club in sliding doors moment
Sports.content:
Next

JUST when Manchester City fans thought things could not get any worse, Mikel Arteta has signed a new contract at Arsenal.

The Spanish boss extending his seven-year stay at the Emirates until 2030 was the least surprising event of an extraordinary international break which saw City found GUILTY of breaching Premier League finance rules.



Arteta’s new deal underlines that while things are uncertain at the Etihad, the Gunners are rock solid and seem certain to dominate English football for years to come.

In September 2019, Pep Guardiola claimed he was “pretty sure” Arteta, his City assistant at the time, would succeed him.



But two months later, the Basque returned to former club Arsenal to become manager.

There were theories that Arteta could still return to City to take over from Guardiola.



But after securing the Prem title in North London five months ago — the first time Arsenal had been crowned champions since 2004 — that was never going to happen.

Arteta has faced some tough questions as his spell in Manchester overlapped with the period of City’s alleged rule-breaking.

And he has always offered a firm “no” when asked if he had witnessed any wrongdoing at the Etihad.

He will be quizzed on the crisis at his old club again tomorrow when he addresses the media ahead of Saturday’s lunchtime clash with Leeds.



SUN VEGAS WELCOME OFFER: GET UP TO £100 BONUS

Yet there appears to be no stopping Arteta and Arsenal.

Aside from City, it looks as though their biggest rivals — Liverpool, Chelsea and Manchester United — are playing catch-up and are unlikely to get close this season.

They appear to have the strongest squad, and much of that is down to the financial investment of owners Stan and Josh Kroenke, who ploughed over £1billion into transfers.



Arteta, who was already on £10million a year, will see his salary rocket to £20m including bonuses.

It feels a world away from the Covid era when he was still finding his feet as manager.

When the pandemic struck, Arteta and his players accepted a pay cut.

His job title changed from head coach to first-team manager back in September 2020 and, since then, he has been all-powerful.

Arteta was under huge pressure as Arsenal kept coming close but failed to win anything before it all fell into place in May.



The Gunners also went agonisingly close to winning the Champions League — only losing to Paris Saint-Germain on penalties.

Being crowned European champions for the first time is the ultimate aim this season.

Even Arsene Wenger was unable to achieve that — losing the 2006 final 2-1 to Barcelona — so Arteta is determined to rewrite history.

Arteta can be a control freak and a bit paranoid, particularly regarding referee and VAR decisions.

But he is a perfectionist and, by winning the Prem, he finally got the reward his efforts deserved.



His deal had been due to run out at the end of this season.

What are Man City charged with? THE Premier League claim Man City hid £900m in 'sham' deals across a nine-year period. They were found guilty on 114 of the initial 115 charges – with the number now up to 130 charges – which fit into six categories… Failing to give accurate financial information over sponsorship revenue, related parties and operating costs between 2009-10 and 2017/18. Total charges: 50

Failing to provide full details of managerial remuneration between 2009/10 and 2012/13. Total charges 8

Failing to provide full details of player remuneration between 2010/11 and 2015/16. Total charges 12

Failing to comply with Uefa Licencing and Financial Fair Play regulations between 2013/14 and 2017/18. Total charges 5

Breaching Premier League Profitability and Sustainability rules between 2015/16 and 2017/18. Total charges 25

Failing to co-operate with the Premier League investigation between 2018/19 and 2022/23. Total charges 30

Total charges: 130

Arsenal chief executive Richard Garlick said: “It ends any speculation about him going into the final year of his contract, which happens with managers.

“We’re delighted. It’s a real partnership we have with Mikel.

“He’s got the title of manager and I’ve got the title of CEO and Andrea Berta is sporting director.

“But it’s a partnership and it gives us a competitive advantage.



“I look at the teams in the Premier League and Mikel is the only manager to have won the Premier League who is currently managing.

“You look at all the other teams in the traditional top six and they have all gone through managerial changes in the last 12 months.

“We’ve now got a manager who has been with us for a significant period of time and has been allowed to build and develop a team over a period of time.

“The excitement is we see that platform and we’ve built from there.



“That’s not the end of it. This is a really exciting new beginning for us.”

Arsenal may have spent heavily in the summer, but they still attracted criticism for not signing another left winger or central striker.

It seems the players they coveted most in those positions were unavailable.

It may be in January or it may be next summer — but the Gunners intend to spend big again.



Garlick added: “We need to keep finding that edge that gives us that advantage.

“And we have to be brave, because it would be very easy just to simply say just roll over what we did last year and that’ll be enough.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

“Everybody is out to get you. When you’re champions, everybody wants to beat you.

“We need to find a way of taking those opportunities and taking those advantages and pushing forward all the time. That is always forward when we are so much ahead.”

Sports.title: Cristiano Ronaldo puts aside long-running rivalry with Lionel Messi to send classy message after Argentina retirement
Sports.content:
Next

CRISTIANO RONALDO has sent a classy message offering his “respect” to rival Lionel Messi after his Argentina farewell.

Messi, 39, closed the chapter on his 21-year spell with the national team this week after playing his final game against Benin.



The former Barcelona superstar bid an emotional goodbye as he started the 3-0 victory and finished on 208 caps.

It was the perfect ending for Messi as he chipped in with two assists and scored from the penalty spot.



Messi – who helped Argentina win the 2022 World Cup – struggled to hold back tears after the game while giving his send-off speech.

He also released a lengthy statement on Instagram later on.

And his biggest footballing nemesis Ronaldo put aside their long-running rivalry to pay tribute to the veteran star in the comments.

He said: “Leo, so many years defending your country and a story that will live on forever.

“You have all my respect for everything you’ve achieved with Argentina. A hug.”

Messi and Ronaldo duelled each other for the Ballon d’Or on a number of occasions, with the Argentine winning eight and the Portugal captain claiming five.



BEST ONLINE CASINOS – TOP SITES IN THE UK

Ronaldo himself is an icon for Portugal after appearing 234 times for his country – but this week he ruled out his own retirement despite his fallout with boss Jorge Jesus.

Messi released a full statement after his Argentina farewell hailing his “incredible journey”.

He wrote: “Yesterday was my last match, and I already miss wearing the sky blue and white. I know I’m making the right decision.

“It was an incredible journey, full of joy and some sadness, but I know for sure that every step I took was worth it.



“This journey would have been impossible without my family, who were always by my side and supported me, especially during the difficult times when I needed it most.

“My friends, all the teammates and coaches I had, along with their staff, were also essential.

“Thank you to the clubs I played for, for always respecting my feelings and allowing me to dedicate myself to my country when it was time to wear the national team jersey.

“And of course, thank God: without His guidance and His will, we wouldn’t even be dreaming of having gotten this far.



“I am so grateful. I love you all so much, I’m going to miss you, and I will always thank you for being by our side, by my side.”

Messi walked out for the game with his three sons – Thiago, 13, Mateo, 10, and Ciro, eight.

He was given in incredible send-off by an 85,000 sell-out crowd in Buenos Aires as he gave a speech lasting around ten minutes.

His team-mates were left in tears as he claimed he wished he could play for Argentina forever.

RECOMMENDED STORIES

Messi added: I’m going to miss playing here so much. I love you all, and I’m proud to be Argentine.



“I leave grateful, proud and at peace. Thank you for everything.”

Sports.title: 'Sandpapergate' Q&A: The 2018 ball-tampering scandal explained
Sports.content:
​​​It was the ball-tampering scandal that rocked world - and particularly Australian - cricket.

For the first time since 'Sandpapergate', which resulted in Steve Smith, David Warner and Cameron Bancroft receiving bans for the roles they played in the plot to alter the condition of the ball, Australia are preparing for a Test series in South Africa.

Ahead of the first Test in Durban from Friday, live on Sky Sports from 7.30am (8.30am first ball), here is an explainer of what transpired in Cape Town and its subsequent fallout…

What was 'Sandpapergate'?

Image: The ball-tampering scandal rocked Australian cricket

That was the name given to the March 2018 ball-tampering scandal during Australia's Test tour of South Africa after Bancroft was caught on camera trying to rough up one side of the ball with sandpaper in order the make it swing through the air.

The incident occurred on day three of the third Test in Cape Town while South Africa were batting in their second innings, with Bancroft aiming to hide the sandpaper, which he initially said was a piece of tape, in his trousers after realising he had been spotted.

At the end of the day's play, Bancroft and Australia captain Smith admitted to ball-tampering in a press conference - albeit not to the use of sandpaper at that stage - with Smith saying the plan had been cooked up by the 'leadership group' at lunch.

What happened next?

Image: Steve Smith departed as Australia captain following the ball-tampering scandal

Smith and vice-captain Warner stood down from their leadership roles for the remainder of the Cape Town Test but still took to the field as the Baggy Greens, now captained by Tim Paine, slumped to a 322-run defeat after being rolled for just 107 in their second innings - Warner top-scoring with 32, Bancroft making 26 and Smith seven.

Smith, Warner and Bancroft were sent home ahead of the fourth Test, in which Australia were hammered by 492 runs to fall to a 3-1 series defeat, and later received hefty bans from international and domestic cricket, ranging from nine months to a year.

They were each found by Cricket Australia to have engaged in conduct against the spirit of the game and harmful to its interests.

What were the exact punishments?

Image: Warner was found to be the architect of 'Sandpapergate'

Warner was found to have led the plot to alter the condition of the ball, including guiding Bancroft on how to use the sandpaper.

He was slapped with a one-year ban and told he would never be considered for a leadership position within the team again.

Smith - who would go on to be succeeded permanently by Paine as captain - was also suspended for 12 months after failing to prevent a plan he was aware of and making misleading comments.

He was also informed he would not be able to take a leadership role until at least 12 months after the conclusion of his ban.

Bancroft was suspended for nine months.

What else did the players lose?

Image: Smith was also removed from the 2018 IPL

Smith and Warner were removed from the 2018 IPL, where they were due to play for - and initially captain - Rajasthan Royals and SunRisers Hyderabad respectively, while Bancroft saw Somerset cancel the deal he had signed to play county cricket.

Australia coach Darren Lehmann was among the collateral damage.

Lehmann - now coaching Northamptonshire in county cricket, leading the Steelbacks to the 2026 T20 Blast title - was cleared of any involvement in the ball-tampering scandal but opted to resign after the fourth and final Test against South Africa.

Without Smith, Warner and Bancroft, Australia would go on to lose Test series away to Pakistan and at home to India, before a 2-0 win in Sri Lanka preceded their comeback series - the 2-2 Ashes draw in England in the summer of 2019.

Were the ball-tampering bans too harsh?

Some argued that the sanctions meted out were too severe, including former India internationals Gautam Gambhir and Harbhajan Singh and broadcaster and ex-Hampshire captain Mark Nicholas - a view shared by the late, great Shane Warne.

Leg-spin legend Warne, who died in 2022, said while it was "embarrassing" for Australia to be caught up in the scandal, he felt worldwide "hysteria" led to a punishment "not fitting the crime".

Image: The late, great Shane Warne felt the ball-tampering punishments did not fit the crime

Smith and Bancroft gave emotional press conferences on their returns to Australia after being sent home, while Bancroft later admitted he had considered quitting and becoming a yoga teacher during his enforced break from the game.

While all three players went on to represent Australia again - Smith is still doing so - Bancroft's international career arguably never truly recovered with the opener's two Tests at the start of the 2019 Ashes his, at this point, last international matches.

Warner, who retired from internationals in 2024, applied to have his lifetime captaincy ban lifted but then revoked that in 2022.

The suspension was ultimately lifted and he went on to lead Sydney Thunder in the Big Bash League.

How does Smith reflect on 'Sandpapergate'?

Image: Smith felt he was 'thrown to the wolves" in the immediate aftermath

Speaking to News Corp recently, Smith said: "That was a traumatic experience in my life and when I hear the flash of a camera it makes me revisit that, in a way.

"The 24-48 hours after being told I was getting banned for a year, going through the airport in Johannesburg getting absolutely mobbed, and then flying back and doing a press conference... I still have little flashbacks here and there of it.

"I felt like I was kind of thrown to the wolves through [Johannesburg] airport. I didn't have any support there at all.

"It was certainly a difficult period, particularly the initial few days after. The mental state I was in was not great.

"That's somewhere I'd like not to get to again, but I certainly learned from that and have been able to move forward with my life.

"I've tried to kind of erase a lot of 2018 and what happened. I can't remember a lot about the series. I've tried to block most of it out of my memory bank."

What reactions can Australia expect in South Africa?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Former South Africa captain Shaun Pollock describe his experience working as a pundit during the infamous 'Sandpapergate' Test in 2018

Australia have returned to South Africa since 'Sandpapergate' but only for white-ball cricket with a proposed Test tour in 2021 cancelled due to Covid-19.

England fans regularly teased their Ashes rivals after the ball-tampering scandal, with some dressing up as sandpaper to make their point, so what sort of response can Smith and the current players expects from South Africa supporters?

Former Proteas all-rounder Shaun Pollock told the Sky Sports Cricket Podcast: "I don't think it'll be overly hostile.

"Over here, there's been quite a few replays of the [2018] series over the last few weeks, just to create a bit of animosity, I suppose, but when you play against Australia, people in South Africa won't need a reason to have a go at them about some particular reason.

"I'm sure there'll be a few people coming dressed up in accordance with 'Sandpapergate', I'm sure there'll be some continual reminding of it, but I don't think it'll be over the top or too intense."

Finally, is there any more to come out over 'Sandpapergate'?

Image: Cameron Bancroft considered becoming a yoga teacher during his suspension from cricket

Who knows?

While Cricket Australia found only Warner, Smith and Bancroft were party to the plot, Bancroft said in an interview in 2021 that it was "self-explanatory" bowlers in the team had to be aware the ball was being meddled with.

Cricket Australia said they were open to investigating any new information brought to light.

The whole episode is one Australia will want to forget but will likely never be allowed to.

Watch the first Test between South Africa and Australia live on Sky Sports Cricket from Friday (7.30am on air, 8.30am first ball). Get the latest Sky Sports deals or stream with no contract.

Sports.title: Why Sprint in Singapore adds new twist to F1's toughest race
Sports.content:
Formula 1 stages its sixth and final Sprint event of the year this weekend to conclude the first flyaway triple header of the sport's busy 2026 season run in.

And, for the first time, the Sprint format is being used at the Singapore Grand Prix and its Marina Bay street track, home of the sport's original night race.

But on a track not known for its overtaking, what kind of weekend can we expect with two qualifying sessions and two races?

How the Singapore GP weekend will be different to normal

When the Sprint format was first introduced at three races for the 2021 season, the tracks selected - Silverstone, Monza and Interlagos - were ones deemed to be particularly good for racing so to justify the addition of a 100km race on the Saturday as an appetiser to the main Sunday Grand Prix.

That has generally continued to be the case in the selection of Sprint venues up to this year, with perhaps the inclusion of Imola in 2022 the surprise exception.

Street tracks, which by their nature traditionally aren't as overtaking-friendly as conventional permanent tracks, have generally not featured on that yearly list.

Azerbaijan did host a Sprint in 2023, but Baku's wall-lined street track features the longest straight on the calendar and so allows passing.

Singapore certainly falls more into the category of conventional street track - there are no long straights of note and overtaking opportunities are severely limited around the confined, twisty layout.

Image: The Singapore GP takes place this weekend, live on Sky Sports F1 (HOCH ZWEI/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images)

The floodlit race is instead most known for its physicality owing to the hot and humid conditions of the Asian country and the fact the 62-lap race pushes towards the two-hour limit around a 19-corner lap that features plenty of 90-degree turns.

So, holding a second race this weekend appears counterintuitive in one sense to the original purpose of the Sprint format. However, there are flip sides to the decision.

The first relates to qualifying. Given the lack of passing opportunities in the race, qualifying is always considered absolutely essential at Marina Bay and, like all street tracks where the walls are so close, the Saturday spectacle is often spectacular.

The circuit was the scene of one of the most famous qualifying laps in the sport's recent history when Lewis Hamilton surged to pole position for Mercedes in 2018, while numerous drivers have come a cropper against the barriers over the years when pushing for a decisive, grid-defining lap.

This year there will be two such sessions - Sprint Qualifying on Friday followed by Grand Prix Qualifying on Saturday - which means double the qualifying challenge and, therefore, double the jeopardy for drivers.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights from qualifying at the 2025 Singapore Grand Prix.

The Sprint format also means drivers and teams will have two-thirds less time to hone their cars' set-ups and settings for the competitive sessions given there is only a single one-hour session of practice running instead of the usual three.

Building up rhythm and confidence is crucial on a street track so drivers know they will have to shortcut that process this time in Singapore. However, that is clearly easier said than done, increasing the likelihood of mistakes in sessions that count and teams going down set-up cul-de-sacs.

A further potential twist comes in the scheduling of the sessions.

That sole practice takes place in the hours before sunset at 4.30pm local time (9.30am BST) whereas Sprint Qualifying is at 8.30pm (1.30pm BST) when the floodlights will be in full effect and temperatures will be a little cooler, creating a set-up conundrum for teams as cars, engines and tyres won't necessarily behave the same in different conditions.

Parc-ferme conditions mean teams can't then touch the cars again for Saturday's Sprint, which takes place during the late afternoon like practice.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the 2025 Singapore Grand Prix from the Marina Bay Street Circuit.

A precursor to Monaco 2027

Next season the Sprint format is being expanded to 10 events and, when the full 2027 calendar was published last month, the surprise news came from the fact that Monaco had been selected to host one of them.

The Principality's street circuit is even narrower and harder to pass on than Singapore's, which has increasingly made qualifying the standout aspect of that particular race weekend as cars have become wider and more reliable.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player F1 drivers share their opinions following the announcement that the Monaco Grand Prix will get a Sprint race next year.

Staging two races there next year therefore appears to be as counter-intuitive as it does in Singapore, yet the opposite thinking in terms of doubling up on qualifying and building in the potential for more unpredictability now appears to be a balancing factor.

It will be interesting to hear what drivers, who have mostly been supportive about bringing the Sprint to Monaco next year, make of the Singapore Sprint experience as it unfolds.

A four-team fight for Singapore victory?

Irrespective of how much unpredictability there is this weekend on Singapore's Sprint debut, the weekend promises to be competitive in the battle for victory at the front.

Max Verstappen's impressive win for Red Bull last week in Malaysia means F1's 'Big Four' teams have now all won at least one race in the first year of the sport's new regulations, with Mercedes' early-season dominance a thing of the past despite the Silver Arrows' continued command of both world championship races.

Marina Bay was actually one of only two races that Mercedes won last year although George Russell, who dominated that weekend, already knows his hopes of going back-to-back are effectively over thanks to a grid penalty for excessive engine usage that will send him to the back of Sunday's grid.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Craig Slater explains why George Russell's Singapore GP grid penalty could end his chances of a world title this season.

Russell will still hope to be a factor at the front in Saturday's Sprint, though, where the grid penalty does not apply.

But it is clearly championship leader Kimi Antonelli, who dominated Monaco but crashed in Baku qualifying, who will be carrying Mercedes' front-running hopes into Sunday on a weekend the team bid to get a handle on why their big aerodynamic upgrade brought to Malaysia did not deliver the expected step forward.

Who has won on 2026's Sprint weekends so far? Race weekend Sprint winner Grand Prix winner China George Russell Kimi Antonelli Miami Lando Norris Kimi Antonelli Canada George Russell Kimi Antonelli Britain Kimi Antonelli Charles Leclerc Netherlands George Russell Lando Norris

The in-form Verstappen will also likely be a factor at the front for resurgent Red Bull as he finally looks to win the Singapore Grand Prix - at the 10th attempt.

Marina Bay is the one long-standing track on the current calendar (Madrid, where Verstappen finished second last month, only joined the schedule this year) that the Dutchman has yet to win at.

Verstappen has qualified and finished second in each of the last two years, so has certainly been knocking on the door to do so. Red Bull will hope their recent performance gains elsewhere transfer to the unique demands of Singapore.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player On the F1 Show podcast, David Croft looks at Red Bull's strengths following Max Verstappen's dominant win at the Bahrain GP in Malaysia.

Then there is McLaren, who claimed dominant victories with Lando Norris on F1's last visits to high-downforce tracks in Hungary and Zandvoort but have hitherto not enjoyed great success across the first two legs of the Azerbaijan-Malaysia-Singapore triple header.

Sports.title: What's next for Littler? Can he still qualify for Players Championship Finals?
Sports.content:
Two-time world champion Luke Littler can still qualify for the Players Championship Finals in Minehead – but what else can he win?

His unprecedented 12-month clean sweep may be over following a crushing 10-4 defeat by Jonny Clayton in the quarter-finals of the World Series of Darts Finals in Amsterdam and a shock first-round exit at the World Grand Prix, but he can still qualify for next month's Players Championship Finals.

The world No 1 had won the first six premier events of the season following his World Championship triumph at Alexandra Palace in January with the World Masters, UK Open, Premier League, World Cup of Darts and World Matchplay.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Dan Dawson discusses Luke Littler's early World Grand Prix exit

Darts in 2026 Event Winner Dates World Championship Luke Littler Dec 11-Jan 3 World Masters Luke Littler Jan 29-Feb 1 UK Open Luke Littler March 6-8 Premier League* Luke Littler Feb to May World Cup* Luke Littler and Luke Humphries June 11-14 World Matchplay Luke Littler July 18-16 World Series of Darts Finals* Ross Smith September 17-20 World Grand Prix Luke Humphries Sept 28-Oct 4 European Championship October 22-25 Grand Slam of Darts November 14-22 Players Championship Finals November 27-29 *Non-ranking event

He had been hoping to add the World Series of Darts Finals, World Grand Prix, European Championship, Grand Slam of Darts and Players Championship Finals trophies to complete a historic clean sweep of the year. But his bid was derailed by Clayton, who reeled off seven of the final eight legs to defeat the teenager before overcoming Luke Woodhouse in Leicester, where he suffered a 2-1 defeat in the double-in, double-out tournament.

At the weekend, 19-year-old Littler was beaten by Cam Crabtree in the semi-finals of the World Youth Championship.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking on Love The Darts, Paul Nicholson has backed Littler's reduced schedule for the rest of the season

Had he gone on to win the title, Littler would have become the first player to hold both the World Championship and World Youth titles.

The final will take place on Sunday, November 29, in Minehead as part of the Players Championship Finals, a tournament Littler won last year but has yet to qualify for this time around.

What could the rest of Littler's year look like? Players Championship 33 (Leicester) November 4 Players Championship 34 (Leicester) November 5 Grand Slam of Darts* (Wolverhampton) November 14-22 Players Championship Finals* (Minehead) November 27-29 World Championship* (Alexandra Palace) December 11-January 3 *denotes major

With just two floor events remaining before the Players Championship Finals, Littler can still earn enough prize money to qualify for the tournament - but will he make the trip to Leicester on November 4 and 5?

The top 64 players on the ProTour Order of Merit qualify for the Minehead showpiece, with the projected cut-off expected to exceed £30,000 after all 34 events. Littler currently sits in 126th place with £10,500, while Mike De Decker occupies the final qualifying spot in 64th with £29,250.

That leaves 'The Nuke' with a slim route into Minehead, but he would likely need to reach the final of at least one - and potentially both - of the final two ProTour events to force his way into the field.

Littler won the 2025 title, defeating Nathan Aspinall 11-8 in the final.

"I also think there's a big misunderstanding about what that tournament was because there were people suggesting that maybe he shouldn't have been there. This isn't the Development Tour Finals. This was a world championship, and I don't ever want to exist in a world of sport where someone is excluded from a world championship for being too good.

Sports.title: Rahm to quit LIV Golf over 'unacceptable' terms
Sports.content:
Jon Rahm is set to quit LIV Golf after deeming the terms proposed to him for the relaunch of the series “unacceptable”; Rahm is reportedly owed up to $150m (£113m) from the contract he signed three years ago, with both sides now working towards a separation agreement

Jon Rahm withdrew from this week's Open de Espana as he expects the birth of his fourth child

Jon Rahm is to quit LIV Golf after deeming the terms offered for the proposed relaunch of the breakaway series “unacceptable”.

LIV Golf is currently going through Chapter 11 bankruptcy proceedings in the US after Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund withdrew its support at the end of the season, having invested $5bn (£3.7bn) over four years.

While players including Sergio Garcia successfully petitioned the court to lift the automatic stay on their contracts, effectively freeing them to explore other opportunities for next year, Rahm was not granted the same route out.

The Spaniard is one of LIV Golf's two biggest names, alongside Bryson DeChambeau, and is reportedly owed up to $150m (£113m) for the remainder of the contract he signed almost three years ago.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jon Rahm says he's willing to honour his contract with LIV Golf but his future beyond that remains a doubt.

"Mr Rahm has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0 and has determined that those terms are unacceptable to him, and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0," attorney John Beck told a bankruptcy hearing.

The Athletic has also reported that Rahm and LIV are working towards a separation agreement, with a deal expected to be finalised by October 15.

Rahm withdrew from this week's Open de Espana in Madrid to remain at home with wife Kelley, who is expecting their fourth child.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Geraint Hughes explains what is next for LIV Golf and what will happen to their players after they filed for bankruptcy.

The 31-year-old has already taken steps towards a potential return to the traditional tours. In May, he ended his dispute with the DP World Tour and paid around £2.21m in fines for playing in conflicting events, securing conditional releases for 2026 and making him eligible for the Ryder Cup.

Rahm previously declined the PGA Tour's offer of reinstatement through a specially created Returning Member Program, which was made available to him, Cameron Smith, Bryson DeChambeau and Brooks Koepka. Koepka was the only player to accept.

As a result, Rahm would face a mandatory one-year suspension before being eligible to return to the PGA Tour, meaning he could not play on the circuit until late August next year.
