Sports.title: Eckert’s Spygate ban may be lenient, but no sane manager will try the same trick again
Sports.content:
“Hi Tonda, are you a cheat?” That simple, succinct, question cut to the heart of a matter that has vexed the Football Association all summer. It was posed by the Northern Echo’s Dominic Shaw after Southampton overcame Middlesbrough in the second leg of May’s Championship playoff semi‑final and proved the cue for Tonda Eckert to walk out of his press conference at St Mary’s.

Although Southampton’s manager subsequently admitted to authorising spying on opponents, England’s football authorities struggled to decide what punishment best fitted an act some regard as heinous but which others fail to take seriously. Now, in autumn, we finally have an FA verdict, with Eckert given a six-week ban suspended until the end of the 2027-28 season, a £28,000 fine and a reprimand.

Despite the apparent leniency of the sanction, one thing is clear: Eckert’s summer in purgatory surely dictates no sane England-based coach would contemplate engaging in espionage now.

Eckert may wish he could turn back time to early May and rewrite history. On the eve of the playoff semi-final first leg on Teesside, William Salt, then an intern Southampton first-team analyst, was caught lurking awkwardly beside a tree while filming a Middlesbrough training session on his iPhone. Spygate was born and an independent disciplinary commission convened by the Football League (EFL) expelled Southampton from the playoff final against Hull after their win against Boro across two legs. The governing body also decreed the Saints would begin the current Championship season on minus four points.

View image in fullscreen Tonda Eckert on the touchline at Middlesbrough’s Riverside Stadium during the first leg of Southampton’s playoff semi-final. Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/Reuters

By then Southampton had also admitted to spying on Oxford and Ipswich training. There is a certain irony that Eckert’s team won none of the three games – albeit Middlesbrough were ultimately beaten on aggregate – involving covert surveillance. Yet the EFL independent disciplinary commission panel made plain its discomfort regarding the “particularly deplorable” pressure placed on a young worker hired on a temporary contract. Salt has since been given a staff job as an analyst in Southampton’s academy and is reportedly progressing well.

With the EFL empowered to sanction clubs but not individuals in such cases, it was down to the FA to punish Eckert. The 33-year-old German issued a public apology in June but was not charged with misconduct by the FA until late July. A further hiatus ensued before a hearing at Wembley on 24 September.

This extraordinary delay afforded Eckert ample time to regret dispatching Salt to Middlesbrough’s training ground adjacent to the luxury Rockliffe Hall Hotel and golf course just south of Darlington. Salt’s primary mission was to discover whether Hayden Hackney, Middlesbrough’s star midfielder and the Championship player of the season, was fit after injury. Unfortunately, clandestine manoeuvres were evidently not his strong suit. Salt soon found himself being chased into hotel toilets, and realised that using his bank card to buy a coffee at Rockliffe had not been the smartest move. That payment facilitated a search for his name on Southampton’s website. It was swiftly identified, enabling Steve Gibson, Middlesbrough’s owner, to make a formal complaint to the EFL regarding a breach of its anti-spying regulations.

It is understood that, until this point, Southampton’s manager remained unaware of the Bev Priestman precedent. The former head coach of Canada Women was banned from all football activity for a year by Fifa after being found guilty of initiating spying. During the 2024 Paris Olympics her staff secretly filmed a New Zealand training session using a drone and the former England women’s assistant manager paid a high price.

It is unclear whether Eckert has since been in touch with the 40-year-old, now in charge of Wellington Phoenix. Priestman met such extreme hostility in previously welcoming Canada that she relocated her family to New Zealand. During ‘Spygate’, Eckert’s wife was heavily pregnant and based in Berlin, preparing for the birth of their first child. Back in Hampshire, her husband received death threats via LinkedIn. Southampton supplied the manager with protection while police advised him that driving his own car was unsafe and that he should restrict his movements.

Plenty of people were extremely angry, with St Mary’s regulars polarised between those who believed the manager had shamed their club and should be sacked, and others who reflected that what is euphemistically called “training observation” of opponents is commonplace and largely unpunished across tracts of Europe. The second camp remembered that, seven years ago, Leeds were fined £200,000 after the club’s then manager, Marcelo Bielsa, sent an analyst to monitor a Derby training session. Frank Lampard, then in charge of Derby, complained after spotting him perched up a tree.

After that incident the EFL tightened its regulations regarding espionage appreciably. Nonetheless, Eckert’s advocates claim that, given he started last season as Southampton’s under-21s coach and became the manager after Will Still’s sacking in November, he had missed the EFL’s annual managerial summer rules refresher course.

View image in fullscreen ‘I would lie if I said this summer’s been easy,’ Eckert said last month. Photograph: Cody Froggatt/PA

Eckert, who began his career as a Germany national team analyst before moving into coaching at Cologne, RB Salzburg, RB Leipzig, Bayern Munich, Barnsley and Genoa, was only half-joking when he recently told reporters that the EFL handbook was his staple bedside summer reading. He also made contact with Gareth Southgate and visited the former England and Middlesbrough, manager, with the pair discussing English football culture and its zero tolerance for spycraft at length.

“I would lie if I said this summer’s been easy,” said Eckert last month. “I’ve asked the FA for forgiveness.” He has had unwavering support from Southampton’s board who made it clear they had no desire to sack him in the face of considerable dressing room hostility on the part offrom players who felt betrayed by ‘Spygate’.

With first-team hearts and minds since seemingly recaptured by the coach who led them so close to promotion last season, Southampton have won four and drawn two of their opening eight Championship games. Next up on Sunday is the visit of Portsmouth. South-coast derbies are invariably tense but Eckert’s reprieve may ensure he cuts an unusually relaxed figure in the technical area.

Sports.title: All aboard the Tuchel train? England camp has clear winners and losers
Sports.content:
Thomas Tuchel’s original idea had been for continuity. The England manager wanted to build on the positives from the World Cup and he was minded to stand by the vast majority of the players who had been a part of the journey to the semi-finals in North America over the summer. His squad for the four-match Nations League window and the beginning of a new international cycle would not be defined by radical change. What was it about the best-laid plans?

As Tuchel prepared to name his group in mid-September, he knew that he would be without a clutch of World Cup players because of injury. He then lost another handful after the announcement. Fast forward to the Czechia game at Wembley on Tuesday night – the final one of the quartet – and, after further withdrawals, Tuchel could count only 12 players who were available to him during the World Cup. He knows the train moves quickly in football, stopping for nobody. That flexibility is a prerequisite in his line of work. This felt like something else.

Tuchel and his staff were resolved to road-test an updated game model as they sought to move on from the devastation of the World Cup semi-final loss to Argentina. Again, nothing too radical because the principles were in place. They wanted to give the players greater freedom in terms of where they could roam on the pitch; encourage them to trust their instincts and take risks, all within a framework where covering for a teammate was fundamental. Tuchel would need some new players to execute it and, as he reflects on a positive window, in which defeat by Spain was followed by three wins, two against Czechia either side of the 7-0 dismantling of Croatia in Rijeka, he will feel he has found them.

There are always winners and losers from an international camp and maybe they are more pronounced on this occasion because of the timing; the sense of a fresh start, the desire to turn the page after Argentina. It was always going to be a tone-setter for the ultimate goal of Euro 2028 glory.

The biggest winners were Alex Scott and Lewis Hall, with Myles Lewis-Skelly getting an honourable mention. James Trafford pushed his claim to supplant Jordan Pickford as the first-choice goalkeeper, and then there was Trent Alexander-Arnold, ever tantalising, ever nuanced.

As for the losers, well, take your pick from those who were not present, with Tuchel making it clear that it would be harder for them. “It is always like this,” he said. “Everyone should be desperate to come because the train is rolling. Full credit to the players who bought in to that. We can only put our full energy into the camp and the players who are in camp. They make the camp special.”

View image in fullscreen Alex Scott (centre) caught Thomas Tuchel’s eye before being forced to withdraw with injury. Photograph: Sebastian Frej/Getty Images

Tuchel described Scott and Hall as “really excellent”. In the case of the former, Tuchel cannot contain his excitement. He does not want to. Scott did well when he came on as a 70th-minute substitute for his debut against Czechia in Prague and was very good from the start against Croatia, catching the eye with his smoothness on the half turn, his dynamic surges.

It was noticeable that when Tuchel’s assistant, Anthony Barry, spoke on Monday about fluid, hard-running midfielders to fit the team’s style, he name-checked three: Declan Rice and Elliot Anderson, who are well-established, and Scott. It is such a frustration that he aggravated a thigh problem against Croatia and is out for two months, which will rule him out of the matches in November against Croatia and Spain. Tuchel worked with Scott in November 2025 and at the pre-World Cup camp in Florida. “Alex came in here now and was on a completely new level,” Tuchel said. “He was super-strong.”

It was a positive window for Lewis-Skelly, who Tuchel counted on as a midfielder rather than a left-back for the first time. The 20-year-old started three of the games and came on as a 79th-minute substitute against Croatia. The worry was how he picked up bookings in both matches against Czechia; he is now suspended for the home game against Croatia. “I wasn’t aware of the yellow card,” Tuchel said of Tuesday’s one at Wembley, rather surprisingly. He knows about the need to stay out of red card territory.

Kobbie Mainoo is a potential loser from the emergence of Scott and Lewis-Skelly. Tuchel was at pains to sympathise with the Manchester United midfielder over the injury that forced his withdrawal, particularly after he did not play him for a single minute at the World Cup. But with Rice certain to return after an agreed rest this time this out, and James Garner in the frame, Mainoo has work to do. Ditto Jordan Henderson, who was not up to speed fitness‑wise after his broken arm at the World Cup.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Trent Alexander-Arnold made his mark after being brought back into the fold. Photograph: Catherine Ivill/AMA/Getty Images

Hall has taken his chance at left-back, stepping up after Nico O’Reilly played against Spain and was then forced to withdraw. Hall started in each of the subsequent games – “three top matches from him”, Tuchel said – and if he is plainly in possession of the shirt, he deserves to keep it in November. Which is bad news for O’Reilly and Djed Spence, who has not yet played this season.

Did Alexander-Arnold do enough at right-back after his surprise recall? He could not have done much more with his starting opportunities in both Czechia games. There was the lovely cross for Anthony Gordon’s breakthough goal in Prague and a driving, attack-minded performance at Wembley. Everybody knows what Alexander-Arnold can do; he showed it again and the argument remains that he must be included for his points of difference.

On the other hand, what does Tuchel do when Reece James, Tino Livramento and Spence are available? The manager has previously made it plain he considers all three to be ahead of Alexander-Arnold. He said he might have called up Ben White if he were fit and also has Jarell Quansah, even if the Bayer Leverkusen player would rather be considered in central defence. That was where Tuchel started him against Czechia at Wembley – ahead of Trevoh Chalobah and Jarrad Branthwaite.

Cole Palmer has found himself under an unforgiving spotlight after his withdrawal, particularly after Tuchel questioned whether he wanted to play for England. It looks a long way back for the Chelsea No 10 and the same is true of Phil Foden. Both were overlooked when Tuchel gave a late call-up to Morgan Gibbs-White, and neither looks an easy fit for this team’s aggressive style. “I don’t know [if they are],” Tuchel said. “That is the honest answer. They were not here. This team took another step and it’s always about the guys who are here.”

Tuchel has plenty to ponder before the November matches. He will hope to see John Stones recover his fitness and form at Inter. There is a belief that the centre-back’s move to Serie A, where the tempo is slower, can help him find his rhythm. Marcus Rashford will be expected to return; he has credit in the bank with Tuchel, even if Gordon has nailed down the starting spot on the left wing.

Can Noni Madueke stage a comeback on the right after being dropped? And what of the strikers in the Saudi Pro League, Ollie Watkins and Ivan Toney, who were also dropped? Tuchel now sees Jude Bellingham as the back-up No 9 to Harry Kane. He gave Dominic Calvert-Lewin only brief substitute appearances against Spain and Czechia at Wembley. The train hurtles on.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi’s Argentina career turned football into a sacred mystery
Sports.content:
“What Argentina is doing in this World Cup is of a sacred order,” Brazilian writer Milly Lacombe posted at the height of the tide of anti-Argentinian sentiment during this year’s tournament. She was exploring the contradiction she felt around her support of Lionel Messi: “a player who is a God and a man who shakes Trump’s hand”.

Lacombe highlighted the importance of acknowledging the complexities around Messi and the Argentinian team. How is it possible that Messi was not speaking out against the racist incidents we all saw around the Argentina team, she asked. “That’s why it hurts so much to see someone with Messi’s power choosing to make himself small,” she wrote.

Much was made of Messi’s silence at the time. Then again, much has been made of his visible discomfort with words throughout his epic career. Journalist John Carlin once said that having interviewed Messi twice, he would decline a third opportunity, such was the challenge of getting the little giant to say anything of consequence. In 2010, Juan Sebastián Verón said he had never seen Messi as nervous as when he had to address his teammates for the first time as Argentina captain. In terms of public speaking, perhaps Messi’s most famous outburst was at the 2022 World Cup when he told a Dutch player to “go away”.

View image in fullscreen A giant number 10 shirt was displayed on the pitch before Messi’s farewell apperance. Photograph: Rodrigo Abd/AP

Despite this reticence, Messi has always meant something, even when he doesn’t speak. Messi and Argentina were treated as darlings when they won the World Cup in 2022. By the time the 2026 final ended in defeat to Spain, they had become villains.

“That’s why it’s important to understand that when Messi, in the middle of a game that was lost, looks at the sky, and then after that he turns the game around and smashed it, there is something very mysterious there. Right? That we can’t explain. That we just feel,” Lacombe said after Argentina’s semi-final victory over England this summer. “I started supporting England but by the end of the match I was weeping, surrendered to the commitment, the passion, the love that I saw the Argentina team pour on to the pitch. It’s only in that moment of intense passion that we reach the sacred.”

Not everyone surrendered to the sacred in the same way. The final against Spain lacked sublime power and opened the floodgates of vitriol from all corners of the globe. Argentinian fans were offended, hurt, defensive and aware they may have just seen Messi’s last appearance in an Argentina shirt. When he confirmed he would end his international career – his final appearance for Argentina came against Benin on Tuesday – a wave of grief and gratitude swept the nation.

View image in fullscreen An 18 yr old Lionel Messi grapples with Hungary’s Vilmos Vanczák and is sent off after 44 seconds on his Argentina debut. Photograph: Michael Mayhew/Getty Images/Allstar

Messi grew up in Barcelona’s youth system, and he was eligible to play for both Spain and Argentina. His debut for Argentina – in a youth match against Paraguay – set up a rush to ensure he pledged his allegiance to the country of his birth, before Spain could tempt him. He was already one of the Barcelona’s academy most promising stars, but he was little known in Argentina. His father, Jorge, wanted nothing more than for his son to represent Argentina, and sent videos to then-manager Marcelo Bielsa hoping to expedite the process. For years, Jorge endured an uphill struggle to consolidate the ties between Lionel and Argentina. Messi’s prowess, seemingly unstoppable in a well-oiled Barcelona system, did not come through at national level. For a long time, Jorge would ask his compatriots the same question. How can we get Argentina to love my son?

Now, as we start to write Messi’s football obituary, some of the most grievous incidents against him are resurfacing. There was the time when a panel of pundits stood in a minute’s silence in protest against Messi’s performances for his country. He was criticised for not singing the national anthem. We learned that before Argentina matches he suffered bouts of vomiting and diarrhoea. Diego Maradona mocked him, saying he was no leader (although he would later make Messi Argentina’s captain). And when the campaign to win over the nation stepped up and he gave interviews, his discourse was shockingly basic and he gave little away.

But Messi never gave up. He missed penalties, wept, and stood to take them again. “What characterized Messi in the national team is that he lost. He lost a lot. He’s constituted in defeat” Argentinian journalist Alejandro Wall says.

View image in fullscreen Adoring fans cheer for Messi before the match against Benin. Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/Reuters

But the vitriol more often came from the press than the people. When he quit the national team in 2016, a spontaneous show of love and desire swept the nation, and he reversed his decision. From then on, the Argentinian Football Association’s main priority mirrored that of Jorge Messi: finding a coach who could adapt the entire system to Lionel. It wasn’t easy.

Perhaps it was only after Maradona’s death in 2020 that the new Messi started to emerge. He walked taller, more confident and comfortable in his role as leader. In 2021, Argentina won the Copa América, and snippets of Messi’s pep talks to his teammates filtered out. He made simple statements in his unmistakable Rosario accent, aspiring the ‘s’ and not pronouncing most final consonants. His – and Argentina’s – achievements since then speak for themselves.

Tuesday’s farewell at the Monumental Stadium – much like that first youth game against Paraguay – had a rushed, improvised air. The Argentinian FA struggled to secure opponents, not wanting to share box office with another footballing power. Benin were mocked by some as unworthy, and even Lionel Scaloni made reference to a desire to face bigger opponents than Bolivia and Burkina Faso, the other teams Argentina played this window. Burkina Faso ended up sending an Under-23 side who arrived a few hours before the match, and the stadium was not filled to capacity. Ticket prices were extortionate, and diehard fans refused to fall for what they called “a scam”.

View image in fullscreen An electric atmosphere at Estadio Monumental. Photograph: Rodrigo Valle/Reuters

But against Benin they turned up in numbers. Earlier, Messi had picked up an honorary doctorate from the University of Buenos Aires, in a small and shabby ceremony in a back office of the Argentinian FA. Delicately produced homages to No 10 were aired. Social media posts full of hyperbolic emotion appeared. “Like Scheherazade, he mocked destiny match by match, to gift the Argentina people another day of his magic. The thousand and one nights of Lionel Messi with the light blue and white come to their end,” read one post. “Whoah, hold it! It’s 9am. I can’t start weeping yet” came a swift reply.

To paraphrase Wayne Rooney, the entertainment around the match was crap. There was a drawn out homage by Soledad Pastorutti, who sang the same number she had once performed with Maradona. A veteran of the Falklands/Malvinas War sang the national anthem, and then clad himself in the same flag that fell on the pitch in Atlanta. The terraces chanted against AFA president Chiqui Tapia in a beautiful chorus, which went some way to atoning for the drone show at the end, with adverts for an insurance company glittering in the sky.

But football is about redemption, and the night was redeemed. Benin actually put up a fight, bookended by the team’s captain gifting Messi a statue of a Dahomey Agojie, the group of women who fought against French occupation. Messi set up three of his team’s three goals and took a penalty. He didn’t miss.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi salutes his adoring fans after his final match for Argentina. Photograph: Roberto Tuero/ZUMA/Shutterstock

The cameras zoomed in on weeping faces but the sounds from the concrete terraces were decisively celebratory, relentless, trembling. It was football through and through. And Messi loved it. You could tell. He picked up the microphone and launched into a speech so articulate and confident that it merits a dissertation studying its every word. He addressed conspiracy theories surrounding the World Cup final: “Nothing odd happened. The match against England wore us out at an emotional level”. He warned of hard times to come but said team unity is the way through.

“We had the dream of fulfilling our dream,” he said, adding: “I don’t know, I’m talking more than ever. I don’t want to leave here. I love you”. And Argentina loves him back.

As Lacombe said, when Messi looks at the sky, then turns a situation around and smashes it, there is mystery. There is something sacred.

Sports.title: Robertson rant and the wrong system? Pocognoli’s Scotland start raises questions
Sports.content:
What is the general situation after four games?

Scotland are staring at a third-place finish in Group B1 of the Nations League, which will have repercussions for their seeding in Euro 2028 qualifying. More striking, though, was the general standard of performance over Sébastien Pocognoli’s first four games as manager.

Scotland were dismal for a half in Slovenia before a decent but scoreless recovery. They capitulated after an early sending-off against Switzerland, failing to register a shot on target in a meek 3-0 loss. North Macedonia were as poor an international team as Scotland have faced in recent times, rendering the 2-0 win in Skopje worthy of little more than a shoulder shrug. Pocognoli’s men rounded off this extended window by being played off the Hampden Park pitch by Slovenia. Andy Robertson, the captain, strikingly questioned the attitude of his teammates. There has been no new manager bounce.

Pocognoli was given only a two-year contract, which was odd given the pedestal he was placed on by the Scottish Football Association when hired in August. The likelihood remains host-nation status will secure the Scots a place in the next Euros, but the country cannot arrive at the event under the cover of darkness. The alarming nature of the performance against Slovenia – it really had no redeeming qualities – places a huge emphasis on November’s fixtures.

Are Scotland suited to the way Pocognoli wants to play?

It does not look that way. The manager deploys a three-man backline as routine, with an emphasis on pressing high and wingbacks being crucial to attacking phases. Scotland do not have an obvious two-man central defensive pairing, meaning they most definitely struggle when the number is increased by one. Time and again, they leave far too much space in behind and look woefully exposed. Counterattacks bypass Scotland’s midfield all too easily. Pocognoli’s Scotland are a dream to play against.

Success for the Scots under Steve Clarke came from being well-drilled, compact and difficult to beat. Unsexy perhaps, but effective. Playing with gay abandon is all well and good when having a level of security Scotland simply do not possess currently. Scotland allowed Slovenia to be just as menacing as Morocco and Brazil, top-quality opposition they faced at the World Cup. Pocognoli’s desired methods may be impossible to implement without day-to-day involvement with players. Ideology is fine when club football permits an overhaul of personnel.

When Scotland switched to a defensive four in the closing stages of the Slovenia clash, players appeared generally confused. This was a bad look for Pocognoli, who has insisted he is “flexible” in a tactical sense and disputed the idea he had a touchline row with Robertson. Scott McTominay’s return for the next set of fixtures would provide an iota of hope, were it obvious where the Napoli man fits in. The setup as is will not maximise the abilities of McTominay, John McGinn, Ryan Christie and Billy Gilmour.

View image in fullscreen Sébastien Pocognoli consoles Billy Gilmour after Scotland’s feeble defeat at home against Slovenia on Tuesday. Photograph: Robbie Jay Barratt/AMA/Getty Images

Didn’t fans want a revolution?

A reality is Scotland have qualified for three of the last four major tournaments. Noise directed towards Clarke underappreciated the scale of his work. That said, after seven years, Clarke’s tenure had run its course.

The obvious move at that point was to turn towards a coach who had succeeded in tournament football with a similarly sized nation. With the level of available talent dropping or ageing, there was also a requirement for pragmatism and realism. Instead, Scottish FA officials spoke of a data-led search for Clarke’s successor, which led them to a coach who had never managed in international football before. Trying to be too smart by half? This team was not fundamentally broken, it just needed to progress.

Nobody of sane mind should insist upon Scotland morphing into the Ajax team of the 1970s. The baseline, created by Clarke, is now tournament participation. This summer’s World Cup was the latest example of how finals involvement positively alters attitudes within and outside Scottish football to an unparalleled level. That is the important thing. The rest is fluff.

There were 34,000 at Hampden for Slovenia’s visit; hardly disastrous in broader Nations League context but almost 20,000 short of capacity. The public are yet to buy into Pocognoli and the blue-sky vision sold by his employers.

How does Pocognoli handle Ben Gannon-Doak?

Some in Scotland would have us believe Gannon-Doak is the tartan equivalent of a young Ryan Giggs. The truth is that at 20 Gannon-Doak is a player who is lightly raced at club level and, at this point, looks unlikely to make a first-team impact at Bournemouth. He has searing pace and a directness that scares defenders, which is offset by woeful decision making. Whether these shortcomings can he improved upon very much remains to be seen.

What is clear is that Gannon-Doak cannot operate as a right wingback for Scotland against credible opposition. Deploying him there also denies a start to Aaron Hickey, who is undeniably one of Scotland’s best players. Gannon-Doak is a winger (as are Josh McPake and Findlay Curtis). Pocognoli’s first-choice method does not involve wingers. Something has to give.

View image in fullscreen Ben Gannon-Doak, pictured holding off Slovenia’s Erik Janza, is not a wingback. Photograph: Andrew Milligan/PA

What is the wider scenario that Pocognoli is part of?

The Scottish FA suddenly has a chief football officer in Craig Mulholland, and a head of strategy, operations and performance in Graeme Mathie. The latter was plucked from the Scottish second tier and the former was present in the dressing room during Scotland’s Nations League fixtures. The move to insert this level of middle management carrying wishy-washy job descriptions is strange, not least when neither of the individuals in question can provide working examples of markedly improving the big picture with an equivalent nation. Meanwhile, the new Scotland Under-21s manager, Tony Docherty, who is fielding teams in the same formation as Pocognoli, last took charge of a plummeting Ross County.

Scottish football in general has a reluctance to let others mark its homework. Those in high office, typically very pleased with themselves, fail to convince on umpteen levels. Scotland have to work far, far harder at finding resource for the men’s A team. Six starters against Slovenia were 30 or older. Clarke could be obstinate but there was no raft of exciting footballers he chose to ignore.

There is no question of the Scottish FA becoming anxious towards Pocognoli. Indeed, as was the case with Clarke, they seem beholden to him. If this goes wrong, however, there will be significant questions to be answered about a chosen direction of travel.

Sports.title: ‘I wanted to depart in the best way possible’: Kieran McKenna on Ipswich exit and future plans
Sports.content:
It was on the Portman Road pitch, bathed in bright early May light while immersed in the relief and joy of a third promotion in five years, that Kieran McKenna realised the moment was right. The thought had flickered earlier in the season that this might be his final campaign at Ipswich, only to be pushed into the subconscious by the Championship’s remorseless grind. “But standing out there, I felt this was probably time,” he says of those moments after QPR had been swept aside and a return to the Premier League assured. “Another big victory, a full stadium, in front of my family and the fans. It was an amazing way to go out on a high.”

Five months later McKenna has no regrets about electing to cut things short while the going was so good. The golf bag lying outside his garage speaks of a man enjoying the break and, more pertinently, of something bigger. His son has recently become interested in the sport and sharing those moments with loved ones, whether out on the greens or spending part of the summer travelling along the East Anglian coastline in a camper van, were among the biggest reasons to pause a soaring career. At 40, McKenna had spent two decades immersed in coaching; it was time to appreciate life’s essentials while continuing professional development at his own speed.

He had, as usual, been linked with moves away but the idea of a voluntary career break was hard for many to fathom when the decision was finalised in June. “For people on the outside it’s maybe a bit more difficult,” he says. “But those who know my path and my values, the ones closest to me who know me really well, I think they understood why I wanted to step out and what the benefits were of having a period like this.”

Not everyone in football saw it that way: the phone has rung with proposals for his next move but McKenna says those overtures arrived “too soon, especially given the way I left Ipswich”. Leaving through the front door, a luxury rarely afforded, made him proud and there is no desperation to leap back into the fray. “I’m certainly in no rush,” he says. “I’m enjoying the time I’m having and hopefully an opportunity will come along that’s right. I have an idea what that would feel like but football doesn’t always follow your plan.”

Since early September he has dipped his toe back in. That has involved tuning back into the process of watching and assessing games, while travelling to spend time with Bayern Munich, the Wigan Warriors rugby team and Colorado Rapids, who are managed by his friend Matt Wells. He has been working on foreign languages, topping up an already competent level of Spanish. This week he is visiting clubs in Spain and, next Wednesday, he will begin work as a technical observer for Uefa when Shakhtar Donetsk play AEK Athens at Stamford Bridge. “I wanted to give myself the best possibility to learn before taking on the next challenge,” he says.

View image in fullscreen McKenna basks in Ipswich’s promotion in May. ‘All we get is people coming up telling the story of how much the last few years have meant for them,’ he says. Photograph: John Sibley/Action Images/Reuters

More than once McKenna repeats an assertion he made after promotion in May: that 2025-26 was the hardest of his four-and-a-half seasons at Ipswich, during which he masterminded a dizzying rise from League One to the top flight that marked him among football’s hottest managerial properties. The pressure was heightened last season: Ipswich had gone down and were expected to bounce back, even though the remarkably close-knit core who had propelled them through the divisions were drifting away. In effect, he took two different teams to the top.

“You can see how it could really have gone in two distinct directions,” he says, making a comparison with the fall Luton experienced after a brief reacquaintance with the elite. “We had the feeling internally that if we didn’t work really hard to pull everyone together then it could have gone in a negative way.”

McKenna pulled them over the line and reached the end of his own journey. Along the way he had come close to departing more than once but jumping ship earlier would have jarred. “I had a lot of different opportunities to leave, could have left in many different circumstances really,” he says. “But I was always aware I wanted to depart in the best way possible, with the club on a high, back in the Premier League and with a great chance to build for what will hopefully be a really successful period.”

The hardest aspect of his final day, he explains, was looking down a camera and addressing the supporters with a five-minute speech in which he did not attempt to suppress his emotion. He reels off a list of coaching staff and other colleagues with whom the goodbyes were touching, meaningful, joyful. Many of the friendships, particularly with members of the “really, really special team” that he led to those successive promotions, will be lifelong. The night before this interview, he spent most of a journey back from London speaking to one of them.

View image in fullscreen Kieran McKenna acclimatising to the Premier League in 2024. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

He laughs off the idea he would have relished getting his hands on the £200m summer transfer spend – not to mention a new training ground whose design he influenced – that appears to have given his successor, Gary O’Neil, a better shot at survival. If anything, he suggests, it shows the club have begun their own new chapter. McKenna also emphasises the thought of potential reputational damage from a second relegation did not factor into his decision to quit. “It wasn’t about the thought of a worst-case scenario or what could go wrong,” he says.

It was about prioritising life where we meet, in the family’s home a brisk half-hour walk from Portman Road. He and his wife chose to stay in Ipswich, where their two children attend school, having become more than mere itinerants passing through. It so happens Sir Alf Ramsey and Sir Bobby Robson kept homes nearby after moving upwards. McKenna has hero status here too, in these unassuming yet football-crazed surroundings. Although he keeps a low profile and locations for socialising are chosen judiciously, the overwhelming affection of a town and county often rear up.

“Everyone is respectful; all we get is people coming up telling the story of how much the last few years have meant for them, their family and their friends, and wishing me the best,” he says. “Moving down here together, going all in, making ourselves part of this community, it’s been another of the really positive things. It’s a little bit different living in the area where you were managing but it’s the right thing for us at this time.”

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Has muscle memory ever taken him on an early-morning drive to the training ground? “You’d think it might, but it’s just a different life. You’re not setting the alarm for 5.30am and driving there in the dark. You’re getting up with the kids and having breakfast with them, and you’re around when they go to bed. Although the geography is the same, the life is different.”

He does not think such a heady half-decade, in which a talent honed at Tottenham and Manchester United blossomed gloriously, has changed a grounded personality honed in rural County Fermanagh. “I probably feel about 20 years older,” he says. “But my friends at home were telling me in the summer that I haven’t changed since I was 10. I couldn’t have arrived at Ipswich with a better background as a coach but, on the other hand, if you’d given me a list of the things I’d have to deal with in the next five years I really wouldn’t have believed it. After going through so many things you’re wiser for the experience.”

Nonetheless the fact remains: taking a breather when the world is your oyster feels vanishingly rare in football management. Maybe everyone should do it. “But what’s right for me, after two decades coaching, might be different for a manager who only stopped playing three years ago,” he says. “It’s been a massive body of work. You leave United, pick your bags up, get in the car and five-and-a-half hours later you’re in Ipswich. At 35 you’re leaving your family behind, checking into a hotel 10 days before Christmas; you absolutely throw yourself into the job for the next four and a half years and the family do the same. I want to enjoy the time we have now, take this period to reflect and be in the best position I can for the next role.”

View image in fullscreen McKenna says his two decades in coaching have taken a toll. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA

So what would that next iteration of McKenna’s career look like, in a perfect world? He has been linked with any potential vacancies at Celtic and his old employers Spurs; his name will be circling once the season’s sackings start, although Ipswich will be owed a sizeable fee for any role he takes this year.

“I’m always going to want to be somewhere where I can improve players, play attacking football and win games,” he says. “But beyond that I’m a manager who wants to enjoy having that connection with a club, a community, trying to build something memorable. It was a really special opportunity at Ipswich and you want to do that again in your career. But you have to be ready to come in somewhere and get some short-term success as well.”

The chance will surely arise soon; it does not take a giant leap to imagine McKenna in a Champions League dugout in the next few years if the stars align. Until then the self-growth will continue and there will always be dispatches from Portman Road, where his brother and children are regulars. McKenna would rather look forward and will not beat that path for now. “I think that’ll be some way down the line,” he says. “They’re cracking on with the season. There’s nothing that can lessen my pride and love for everything we’ve been through. Hopefully I’ll be back in the stadium as an old hand, and some of the people will remember the times we had.”

They are unlikely to forget; McKenna’s aim is that, by then, at least one other set of supporters will have felt the magic too.

Sports.title: ‘This is only the beginning,’ vows Mikel Arteta after signing £80m-plus Arsenal deal
Sports.content:
Mikel Arteta has promised “this is only the beginning” of what he can achieve as Arsenal manager after signing a new long-term contract that would take his reign at the club beyond a decade if he sees it out.

The Spaniard is understood to have signed a four-year deal worth more than £20m a season, making him the best-paid Premier League manager. That is a hefty pay rise in recognition of his success last season as Arsenal ended their 22-year wait to be crowned champions after three successive runners-up finishes.

Arteta, who took over from Unai Emery in December 2019, is the Premier League’s longest-serving manager after the departure of Pep Guardiola from Manchester City. After losing the Champions League final last season to Paris Saint-Germain in a penalty shootout, the 44-year-old is targeting more success as he seeks to build a winning dynasty at Arsenal, where he previously served as captain under Arsène Wenger.

“It’s a privilege to commit my future to the club and to continue to work with exceptional people who want the best for Arsenal,” Arteta said. “This club is unique, its character and the way it makes you feel, and I have a great sense of privilege that our journey together will continue. We have already built a special bond and created memories that will last a lifetime, and what is so exciting is that this is only the beginning of what we can achieve together.

“This is such a proud moment for me and my family. I feel the love and respect from our fantastic supporters, and they have mine – and ours – in return.”

Arteta’s previous contract, which was due to expire at the end of this season, was believed to be worth about £10m a season plus a £5m bonus for reaching the Champions League. The new deal, to June 2030, cements his status as one of the best-paid managers in the world. His coaching staff have also signed extended deals.

“It has been an incredible journey so far and we are excited for what lies ahead in this special relationship,” said Arsenal’s co-chairs, Stan and Josh Kroenke. “Last season was an incredible moment in Arsenal’s history, a moment in which we created memories that will last a lifetime. We’re determined to create many more in the years ahead.

“We share a special bond with Mikel. We are so proud of everything we have achieved since he returned to the club in 2019. He has a deep understanding of Arsenal’s values and carries them in his heart. He knows what this club means to everyone connected to it and is committed to building on everything we have achieved together.”
