A few hundred people then marched from Puerta del Sol to the Spanish Congress, chanting "We will not tolerate a single eviction more" and "the fight will continue, Mari Carmen is still alive". There were other chants against fascism and against the police.

Many protesters seemed to feel the police have been complicit in the evictions, as under court orders they have to remove tenants who have been served eviction notices.

After a couple of hours, the chants near Congress gave way to another minute of silence. Then, a big collective shout of "murderers".

One protester told the BBC that people would remain in the square "as long as necessary".

World.title: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo 11 on the Moon, dies at 90
World.content:
The computer scientist behind groundbreaking research that helped land Nasa's astronauts on the Moon, has died aged 90.

Margaret Hamilton was a trailblazer in her field, leading the team who developed the software for Nasa's Apollo missions, which coined the term "software engineering".

Hamilton's former employer, the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), confirmed her death, adding she died on 30 September.

"To say Hamilton was a pioneer - to say she was ahead of her time - would be a dramatic understatement," MIT said in its statement, before acknowledging that she was a software engineer before it was mainstream.

Hamilton worked at MIT from 1959 until the mid-1970s and managed the Software Engineering Division.

It was in this division that she led a team of engineers writing and testing all onboard in-flight software for Nasa's Apollo 11 project that guided US astronauts Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin to land safely on the Moon.

"I was attracted both by the sheer idea and the fact that it had never been done before. I was the first programmer to join and the first woman they hired," she told the Guardian in 2019.

In 1969, moments before the historic Apollo 11 Moon landing, an onboard computer raised an alarm, signalling an error was occurring.

The error detected the computer was overloaded, and for a moment it looked like the complex landing might not be achieved.

But Hamilton and her team had planned for such an error by engineering "priority-driven software" to shut down any background tasks and favour the most important - the Moon landing - according to MIT.

The team's famous software engineering was immortalised in a 1969 photograph of Hamilton standing beside the stack of printed code that towered beside her.

World.title: France's school protests: What lies behind the anger
World.content:
Since late September students across France have been holding protests against underfunding in education, and have been blocking access to many high schools.

The movement has turned violent in places â hundreds of students, teachers and police officers have been injured. Thousands of people â including an unknown number of outside troublemakers â have been arrested.

The protesters are complaining about staff shortages and dilapidated facilities in the country's lycÃ©es, schools which are attended by 15-18-year-olds.

"Sometimes our teachers are absent for several weeks without being replaced," Madalena, a Paris student, told the BBC on Tuesday as demonstrations brought out hundreds of thousands across France. Her school buildings, she added, were "boiling hot" during the recent heat waves.

There is a variety of other complaints. Some resent the banning of mobile phones or school days that last until 18:00. "You get home at 7 pm, and have no time to sleep or do your homework," one lycÃ©en told France 2.

France's online platform that allocates places in higher education, Parcoursup, is another sore point.

The frustration has deep roots. About 80% of each cohort now passes the baccalaurÃ©at, which entitles students to a university place - though not necessarily their preferred choice. This leads to a scramble for desirable courses, and an anxiety focused on Parcoursup, which many regard as opaque.

World.title: New York court hears arguments in ongoing 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia
World.content:
Bayoumi, who is now retired from government work, has denied knowing the two men were hijackers or that he had any involvement in 9/11, while Saudi Arabia has said that any allegation that it or its officials are complicit in 9/11 is categorically false.

The Kingdom has argued that, as a foreign sovereign state, it has immunity from prosecution in US courts.

The families, who first filed the lawsuit in 2002, spent several years lobbying US Congress to pass an amendment to the foreign sovereign immunity law to allow the case to go ahead.

In 2016, Congress passed the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act (JASTA), which allows civil claims against a foreign state or official for injuries, death, or damages from an act of international terrorism.

In August 2025, the Manhattan District Court ruled that the 9/11 families had presented enough evidence to meet the terms of the act and the case was allowed to proceed towards a trial.

Saudi Arabia on Wednesday asked the Court of Appeals to reverse that decision.

Counsel Gregory Rapawy argued core issues of fact â including the central question of the nature of Bayoumi's employment by the Saudi state â had not been decided and needed to be done so before the country could be stripped of immunity.

9/11 families' lawyer Gavin Simpson argued that the District Court had already found that Bayoumi's actions "were not just acts of a good Samaritan or an innocent participant".

"He was, in fact, following Saudi Arabia's instructions when assisting the hijackers," said Simpson, and that these were points that Saudi Arabia had "failed to rebut."

One option the judges seemed to wrestle with was whether to send the case back to the district court to make more concrete findings, which could involve taking testimony from live witnesses.

Asked by Judge Guido Calabresi which witnesses Saudi Arabia could call in that eventuality, Rapawy suggested that if the issue ultimately came down to Bayoumi's credibility, "we would have to see" if he could be called to testify.

As he drew the hearing to a close, Judge William Nardini said "it's a difficult case, and we will take it under advisement", meaning that the panel would issue a ruling at a future date.

Speaking outside the courthouse, Terry Strada, whose husband Tom was killed in the World Trade Center, told the BBC she felt positive about the hearing.

"25 years is an extraordinary time to go without accountability and justice for the murder of your loved one. What we hope is that the judges will uphold [District Court] Judge Daniels' decision and move to a trial."

World.title: Trump wants a new Camp David-like retreat at his Florida golf club
World.content:
US President Donald Trump is looking to create a presidential retreat similar to Camp David at his Florida golf club.

The club would foot constructions costs as a "gift" to Americans and provide free memberships to future presidents - and accommodations to visiting foreign dignitaries.

"It's only about two minutes away from the airport â¦ and they could spend the weekend there, like a retreat, like a sort of Camp David retreat," Trump said on Wednesday.

If it comes to fruition, Trump's transformed golf estate would stand in stark contrast to the rustic Camp David, once a Great Depression-era camp in the woods for federal employees. It would also mark another tradition transformed by Trump.

World.title: Former Venezuelan President Nicolás Maduro expected to face more charges this week
World.content:
Federal prosecutors are expected to bring additional charges against former Venezuelan President NicolÃ¡s Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores, the BBC's US media partner CBS has reported.

The new charges accuse them of playing a role in the torture of Americans who were held in Venezuelan prisons, according to CBS.

US forces seized Maduro and Flores from their compound in the Venezuelan capital, Caracas, in a dramatic, night-time raid on 3 January, and brought them to New York to face charges for alleged weapon and drug offences, which they deny.

The BBC has contacted Maduro's lawyer for comment as well as the US Attorney's office in Manhattan âwhich brought the charges.

Additional people may be charged for their role in torturing more than a dozen Americans who were wrongfully detained by the Venezuelan government under Maduro, CBS reports.

Maduro's attorney, Barry Pollack, told CBS that he was not provided notice about any additional charges.

Flores, who is facing drug trafficking and weapons charges, is scheduled to appear in federal court for a bond hearing on Thursday in New York.

The trial for both Maduro and Flores is set to begin in June 2027.

The US has accused Maduro of narco-terrorism conspiracy, cocaine-importation conspiracy, and possession of and conspiracy to possess machine guns and destructive devices.

He and 14 others were first indicted in 2020, during President Trump's first term.

Prosecutors have alleged that Maduro, his wife and son, and their accomplices engaged in a cocaine-trafficking conspiracy and partnered with cartels designated as terrorist groups.

They said the accused "abused their positions of public trust and corrupted once-legitimate institutions to import tons of cocaine into the United States".

Maduro has previously called such charges a tool to further "imperial" plans for getting access to Venezuela's rich oil reserves.

He and his wife's lawyers have asked the court to dismiss the charges because he is the leader of a sovereign country and therefore immune from prosecution. They contend the US taking him by force is illegal. The judge has not ruled on their requests.

World.title: Kwara APC: How a succession battle became a political earthquake, By Ehi Braimah
World.content:
Politics is rarely only about elections; it is also about succession, control, alliances, interests and the management of political expectations. In Kwara State, these forces have combined to produce one of the more intriguing intra-party crises ahead of Nigeria’s 2027 general elections.

What began as a contest over who would succeed Governor AbdulRahman AbdulRazaq has gradually turned into a full-blown political rupture within the All Progressives Congress (APC), with Senator Saliu Mustapha and other influential party stakeholders moving to the People’s Democratic Party (PDP), followed by defections among elected officials and grassroots members.

The immediate issue is the 2027 governorship election, but underneath it is a much bigger question: who controls the political future of Kwara after AbdulRazaq leaves office? AbdulRazaq will complete his second term in May 2027 and cannot seek a third term. Inevitably, therefore, the question of succession has become the defining issue within the Kwara APC.

The governor has an obvious political interest in what happens after his tenure. His opponents, equally, have ambitions of their own. Senator Saliu Mustapha, representing Kwara Central, was one of the prominent figures interested in becoming the next governor of Kwara State. The disagreement between him and AbdulRazaq did not begin with the APC primary, but the primary appears to have converted a simmering political rivalry into an open confrontation.

The dispute between both politicians is a struggle over political influence, succession and control of the APC structure. The governorship primary on 22 May, was the defining moment. Yakubu Danladi-Salihu, speaker of the Kwara State House of Assembly, emerged as the APC’s governorship candidate, polling more than 94,000 votes. His emergence followed intense negotiations and controversy within the party.

The choice was politically significant for another reason. Danladi-Salihu is from Kwara North, a zone that has long argued that it should have an opportunity to produce the governor. Thus, the primary was about the individual aspirants and the politics of zoning and power rotation, but the controversy surrounding the primary has been difficult to contain. Aggrieved APC stakeholders have alleged that the process was manipulated to favour a preferred successor. Some have gone as far as describing the emergence of Danladi-Salihu as the product of an imposed process.

A group of former aspirants subsequently rallied around what Senator Mustapha calls the “Rainbow Coalition”, bringing together the G15 of aggrieved governorship aspirants, Otoge Progressives and elements of the party’s elders’ caucus. Those are allegations and political interpretations, not established facts, to the best of my knowledge. The APC has defended the legitimacy of its processes and continues to support AbdulRazaq and its governorship candidate.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Indeed, 51 APC ward chairmen in Kwara Central recently declared their support for the governor and Danladi-Salihu and dismissed the significance of Mustapha’s defection. But in politics, perception matters. Once a substantial group of party members believes that a process has been predetermined, the damage to trust can be considerable – even where the party insists that its procedures were followed.

The legislative primaries added another layer of tension to the furore. In May, the APC initially screened out 105 of 158 aspirants seeking its State House of Assembly tickets, with several serving lawmakers among those initially declared “uncleared.” The development generated anxiety across the party.

There is, however, an important correction to the earlier narrative about this episode: the APC subsequently reversed that initial screening outcome and cleared all 159 Assembly aspirants in a revised exercise.

That reversal itself illustrates the intensity of the political atmosphere. The initial decision created the impression of a dramatic purge, but the subsequent reversal showed that the party was capable of adjusting its position when the consequences became politically sensitive. It is therefore too simplistic to say that the governor personally “handpicked” every National and State Assembly candidate. That remains an allegation by some aggrieved party members.

The more defensible conclusion is that candidate selection became a battleground over control of the party and the political configuration that will emerge after AbdulRazaq. That distinction matters. Mustapha’s eventual defection transformed the internal APC dispute into a broader political realignment. His move to the PDP was because he lost an internal contest but it also represents part of a wider coalition of dissatisfied APC stakeholders. That is where the PDP has acquired an unexpected opportunity.

The irony is difficult to miss. The APC’s political ascendancy in Kwara was built around the historic “Otoge” movement of 2019, which ended the dominance of the political structure associated with former Senate President Bukola Saraki.

Seven years later, the political landscape has changed dramatically. Some of the forces that helped establish the APC’s dominance are now divided, while the PDP is attempting to rebuild around some of the same political networks that were weakened in 2019 and harvest what appears to be a political fortune.

The APC’s internal crisis has consequently become an opportunity for the PDP to reconstruct its grassroots organisation. The defections are particularly significant because they are no longer confined to prominent politicians. Last month, more than 2,000 APC members in Adewole Ward, Ilorin West Local Government Area, reportedly defected to the PDP. Adewole is the ancestral ward of Governor AbdulRazaq, making the development symbolically important. The defectors said they were supporters of Mustapha and were following him into the PDP.

There have also been defections in Offa, including from Shawo Central Ward, the political base of Senator Lola Ashiru. Reports say hundreds of APC members moved to the PDP, citing their confidence in Saraki’s political leadership.

Two APC members of the Kwara State House of Assembly – Saba Yisa Gideon and Olusola Odetundun – have also defected to the PDP. The Assembly subsequently declared their seats vacant after the APC argued that they had no constitutional basis to defect in the absence of a division within the party.

This is the point at which an internal party disagreement becomes a political earthquake. The real significance of these defections will not simply depend on the number of people leaving the APC but on whether the defectors can convert their movement into an effective political organisation.

That is the challenge before both sides. Will there be more defections? Only time will tell because in politics, 24 hours is a long time.

For the APC, the central question is whether it can reconcile its competing factions before the 2027 election. For the PDP and the Rainbow Coalition, the challenge is different. Defections make headlines, but elections are won through organisation, candidates, voter mobilisation and sustained grassroots engagement. Moving prominent politicians and thousands of supporters from one party to another is only the beginning.

There is also an interesting federal dimension. Mustapha’s realignment does not necessarily translate into opposition to President Bola Tinubu. His camp has sought to distinguish its disagreement with the Kwara APC structure from its position on the President. This reflects the fluidity of Nigerian politics, where alliances can be different at federal and state levels.

The 2027 contest in Kwara could therefore produce unusual alignments: support for one political platform at the presidential level and another at the state level. At the heart of everything, however, is succession. A governor nearing the end of his tenure naturally wants to influence what comes next. Aspirants want a fair opportunity to succeed him; legislators want to retain their seats; party leaders want to remain relevant, and political blocs want assurances that they will not be excluded from the next dispensation. It is the same playbook used by politicians to advance their interests.

When these interests collide, a party primary can become much more than a primary – it becomes a struggle over the future. That is what appears to have happened in Kwara, but it would be premature to declare that the APC has lost Kwara. Nigerian political parties have repeatedly demonstrated their ability to survive internal crises, reconcile factions and rebound before elections because of the absence of what we may describe as ideological orientation.

What is clear, however, is that the APC’s succession problem has become a serious organisational challenge. As I noted earlier, the irony is that the 2019 Otoge movement was built on the rejection of political dominance by one entrenched structure. Today, the forces that emerged from that political revolution are engaged in another struggle over who gets to shape the next political order.

That is the deeper meaning of the Kwara crisis which has escalated beyond just merely seeing it as AbdulRazaq versus Mustapha, or APC versus PDP. The 2027 election will eventually determine which political coalition commands the mandate of the people. For now, however, one thing is unmistakable: a succession battle inside the APC has escaped the confines of the party and became a wider contest for the political future of Kwara.

The political earthquake has happened, but the real question is how the aftershocks will end.

Ehi Braimah is a public relations specialist, marketing strategist and publisher/editor-in-chief of Naija Times and Lagos Post. He is a strong advocate for African prosperity and can be reached through: [email protected].

World.title: Sierra Leonean President Bio, Elumelu rally West African private sector to turn regional potential into investment, jobs
World.content:
The President of Sierra Leone and immediate past Chair of the ECOWAS Authority of Heads of State and Government, Julius Maada Bio, and leading African investor and Chairman of Heirs Holdings, Tony Elumelu, have called on West Africa’s private sector to move decisively from the promise of regional integration to its delivery.

They both called for support to mobilise capital, build competitive industries, create jobs, and transform the region’s vast economic potential into shared prosperity.

Hosting President Bio in Lagos ahead of the inaugural West Africa Integration and Investment Summit (WAIIS), Mr Elumelu brought together leading private sector and financial institution leaders for the inaugural physical meeting of the WAIIS Private Sector Advisory Board.

The meeting focused on four strategic areas with the potential to reshape West Africa’s economic future: energy trade and industrialisation, strategic minerals, agribusiness, and digital transformation.

President Bio set out an ambitious vision for WAIIS to consolidate a regional market of more than 400 million people and mobilise businesses from within West Africa and across the world to deepen trade, investment and economic cooperation.

“We are partners in execution — let us transform ideas into partnerships, partnerships into investments, and investments into lasting prosperity for our continent,” Mr Bio told members of the Advisory Board.

He added: “But potential is not prosperity. Our task is to convert these advantages into productive enterprises, competitive industries, regional value chains, jobs and wealth.”

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

Mr Elumelu welcomed President Bio’s initiative to place private capital and enterprise at the heart of the regional agenda, reaffirming his commitment to mobilising African and international investment alongside leading African financial institutions, including the Africa Finance Corporation, Afreximbank, United Bank for Africa (UBA), Ecobank, etc., to support the execution of priority projects.

The approach reflects Mr Elumelu’s philosophy of Africapitalism—the belief that the African private sector has a defining role to play in catalysing the continent’s economic transformation through long-term investment in critical sectors.

Mr Elumelu stressed that Africa’s businesses must increasingly look beyond national borders and combine capital, expertise and capabilities to build enterprises and industries capable of competing at scale, while creating jobs and expanding opportunity across the sub-region.

“This is consistent with our aspirations to create jobs for our young people,” Mr Elumelu said. “We have all it takes to be prosperous.”

But private sector ambition, he noted, must be matched by decisive government action.

“Governments must provide the policy certainty, regulatory efficiency and security required to give investors the confidence to commit capital for the long term.”

Lagos State Governor, Babajide Sanwo-Olu, underscored the importance of industrialisation and the free movement of goods and services in building a truly integrated West African market. He stressed that political leaders must provide the enabling environment, certainty and assurances required for businesses to invest, produce and trade across borders.

At the centre of the discussion was a shared conviction that West Africa has the scale, resources, talent and entrepreneurial capacity to become one of the world’s most dynamic economic regions.

With the Summit now less than two months away, Mr Bio called on members of the Advisory Board to move from advocacy to active mobilisation: engaging prospective investors directly, matching them with viable projects, and identifying the financing gaps, policy decisions and other interventions required to move transactions forward.

WAIIS will take place on 17–18 November 2026 at the Julius Maada Bio International Conference Centre in Lungi, Sierra Leone, bringing heads of state, investors and business leaders together to advance investment across energy, strategic minerals, agribusiness and digital transformation.

Notable names on the WAIIS Private Sector Advisory Board are Tony Elumelu — Chairman, Heirs Holdings; Aliko Dangote— Group President/Chief Executive, Dangote Group; Folorunso Alakija — Executive Vice Chairman, FA Limited; Samuel Dossou-Aworet — Founding Chairman, Petrolin Group; George Elombi — President & Chairman of the Board of Directors, Afreximbank; and Abdul Samad Rabiu, Chairman/CEO, BUA Group.

Others are Wale Tinubu — Group Chief Executive, Oando PLC; Samaila Zubairu — President & Chief Executive Officer, Africa Finance Corporation; Alain Ebobissé — Chief Executive Officer, Africa50; Jean-Claude Kassi Brou — Governor, Central Bank of West African States; Paulo Gomes — Founder and Chairman, Orango Investment Corporation; Benedict Okey Oramah — Chairman, Africa Trading Minerals (ATMIN); and Habib Yérim Sow — Group Chairman & CEO, Teyliom Group.

World.title: How Nigeria’s Population Commission mismanaged N245 billion on undelivered products, other controversial contracts – Auditor-General
World.content:
The National Population Commission (NPC) awarded and paid for census-related contracts worth billions of naira without adequate evidence of delivery, according to the Auditor-General for the Federation, who said it also inflated the prices of some contracts and breached procurement rules.

The findings are contained in the Auditor-General’s 2024 Annual Report on Non-Compliance, submitted to the National Assembly in July.

The report examined the commission’s activities for the 2023 financial year and identified several breaches involving contracts for Personal Digital Assistants (PDAs), mobile device management, local content, information technology infrastructure and other census-related procurements.

The findings on the NPC involve more than N245 billion in contracts and payments. The office attributed the irregularities largely to weaknesses in the NPC’s internal control system and recommended that the commission’s Director-General account to the National Assembly’s Public Accounts Committees and recover billions of naira for remittance to the Treasury.

In several of the cases, the NPC did not respond to the audit queries. The auditor general consequently said the findings remained valid until the commission implemented the recommendations.

During the 2023 audit period, Ojogun Osifo served as the Director-General of the National Population Commission (NPC). He was appointed to the position by the late former President Muhammadu Buhari in August 2022. His tenure expired in July 2026, after which President Bola Tinubu appointed Abuh Muhammed as his successor.

Issue 1: N131.5 billion paid for PDAs without evidence of delivery

The largest finding concerns N131.56 billion paid for the procurement of 800,000 PDAs and accessories for the planned 2023 population and housing census.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

According to the report, the NPC awarded contracts worth N131 billion to six contractors between 1 December 2022 and 2 May 2023.

The commission told auditors that it had received 760,000 of the 800,000 devices.

But the auditors said the NPC failed to provide credible evidence that the devices had been delivered.

The report said there were no store receipt vouchers, delivery notes, waybills or inspection reports to substantiate receipt of the devices. Instead, the commission relied on handwritten entries on unofficial papers.

The audit team was also denied access to physically inspect the locations where the devices were supposedly stored or deployed.

The auditor general said the failure was attributable to weaknesses in the NPC’s internal control system.

The finding breached paragraph 708 of the Financial Regulations, which provides that payment should not be made for goods not supplied or services not performed. It also cited paragraph 603(i), which requires payment vouchers to contain full particulars and be supported by relevant documents.

The NPC did not respond to the query.

The auditor-general recommended that the NPC Director-General account to the Public Accounts Committees for the entire N131.56 billion, recover and remit the money to the Treasury and submit evidence of the remittance to the committees.

The report further recommended sanctions under paragraphs 3106 and 3115 of the Financial Regulations for irregular payments and failure to account for public funds.

Issue 2: Inflation of three PDA contracts by N1.45 billion

The auditors also found that the NPC inflated three PDA contracts by a combined N1.45 billion.

The report said the Bureau of Public Procurement (BPP) had approved the supply of 80,000 Gisen Tab A7 Lite 8 devices for N7.36 billion. The NPC, however, awarded a contract for Seedstar PDAs at N7.85 billion, resulting in an alleged N485.57 million increase.

The auditors said the BPP-approved Gisen devices had been tested and certified by the original equipment manufacturer for compatibility with biometric applications, encryption systems and census data capture software.

The Seedstar devices, by contrast, lacked BPP validation and OEM recognition and had weaker processors, lower resolution and shorter battery life, according to the report.

The auditors said this created a risk of device failure and inefficiency during enumeration.

In another case, the BPP approved a contract for 70,000 Digi Tab A7 devices for N6.399 billion. The NPC subsequently instructed the contractor to supply unspecified Tab A7 Lite devices for N6.865 billion, resulting in an alleged N465.34 million inflation.

A third contract for 50,000 Itec Tab A7 devices and accessories was also approved by the BPP at benchmark prices. The NPC later instructed the contractor to supply Tab A7 Lite devices at inflated unit rates, according to the report.

The resulting inflation was put at N496.72 million.

The three contracts therefore produced a combined alleged inflation of N1.447 billion.

The auditor-general said the actions violated Section 31(3) of the Public Procurement Act 2007, which prohibits price changes or substantive changes to bids after the procurement process.

The report identified diversion and loss of government funds as risks and said the NPC did not respond to the audit query.

The director-general was asked to account for the N1.447 billion, recover and remit it to the Treasury and provide evidence of payment to the National Assembly.

Issue 3: N4.43 billion census technology subscription questioned

The report also questioned the NPC’s handling of a N4.429 billion Mobile Device Management contract.

The contract was awarded on 19 April 2023 for the execution of the 2023 population and housing census.

But the auditors found an inconsistency between the award and the executed agreement. While the award was for the Mobile Device Management contract, the executed agreement described it as the “Development and Implementation of a Mobile Device Management Solution.”

The NPC subsequently paid the full N4.429 billion on 15 May 2023, through voucher NPC/CC/1966/2023.

That payment was made almost three weeks after the census had been officially postponed on 29 April 2023.

The auditors said the subscription was time-bound and expired without being used for census purposes, meaning the project received no operational benefit from it.

The commission’s director-general reportedly told the auditors that the subscription was used “in the course of carrying out normal official activities.”

But the auditor-general said no verifiable evidence was provided to support the claim.

The report said the explanation did not resolve the concern because the subscription was procured specifically to manage 800,000 census devices and not for routine administrative activities.

According to the auditors, using such a high-value licence for routine operations did not demonstrate value for money and instead pointed to wastage.

The finding was linked to paragraph 415 of the Financial Regulations, which requires officers responsible for expenditure to exercise due economy.

The audit team said the NPC’s failure to respond meant the finding remained valid.

The director-general was asked to account to the National Assembly, explain why the subscription was used for routine operations rather than census activities, recover and remit N4.429 billion to the Treasury and provide evidence of the remittance.

The report also recommended sanctions for irregular payments.

Issue 4: N96.8 billion local content contract breached BPP directive

The auditor-general also accused the NPC of disregarding a BPP directive on local content in the procurement of PDAs worth N96.8 billion.

The report said a BPP Due Process Report dated 15 November 2022 directed the NPC to ensure that Zinox Technologies Limited and TD Africa did not participate as local content suppliers because they were already engaged as representatives of the original equipment manufacturer for the same procurement.

Despite the directive, the NPC awarded a contract worth N85.27 billion for 480,000 PDAs and accessories to a company to cover the 60 per cent foreign content approved by the Federal Executive Council.

The auditors said the commission subsequently awarded an additional N11.57 billion contract to the same company for 80,000 PDAs and accessories, despite the BPP recommendation that the company should not participate in the 40 per cent local content component.

The auditor general said the arrangement allowed one supplier to dominate both the foreign and local content allocations and effectively excluded indigenous firms from participating in the project.

The report said the decision weakened procurement governance and undermined the objective of the local content policy, including fair competition and the development of domestic capacity.

It put the value of the affected contracts at N96.8 billion and identified diversion and loss of government funds as risks.

Again, the NPC did not respond to the query.

Consequently, the auditor-general recommended that the NPC director-general account for the N96.8 billion, recover and remit the money to the Treasury and provide evidence to the National Assembly.

Failure to do so, the report said, should attract sanctions for irregular payments under paragraph 3106 of the Financial Regulations.

Issue 5: N6.23 billion ICT project awarded without bill of quantities

The audit also uncovered a N6.23 billion ICT contract executed without an approved Bill of Quantities (BOQ).

The NPC awarded the contract for the supply, installation and implementation of ICT components for the 2023 census. It also included the construction of an ICT Disaster Recovery Centre in Kaduna.

According to the auditor-general, the contractor constructed the ICT building without an approved BOQ.

The auditors described the BOQ as a critical technical and financial document for determining material requirements, labour inputs and unit costs.

Its absence, they said, left the NPC and the contractor without a standard basis for assessing costs and project requirements.

The report said the situation left pricing decisions, variations and material specifications vulnerable to ad hoc treatment, creating risks of inflated claims, hidden costs and weak oversight.

It also made it difficult for the commission to monitor performance, assess value for money and ensure that the infrastructure met the required technical standards.

The auditors said the absence of a BOQ increased the likelihood of cost escalation, material shortages and disputes after construction.

The finding was linked to Section 16(1) of the Public Procurement Act 2007, which requires public procurement to be conducted transparently, equitably and in a manner that ensures accountability and conformity with the law.

The risks identified were diversion and loss of government funds.

The NPC did not respond to the query.

The auditor-general recommended that the director-general account to the National Assembly for the N6.2 billion, recover and remit the money to the Treasury and submit evidence of the remittance.

Issue 6: N4.73 billion ICT contract awarded to allegedly unqualified firm

The report also faulted the award of a N4.735 billion ICT contract to a contractor the auditors said lacked the required technical and professional capacity.

The contract covered the supply, installation and implementation of ICT components for the 2023 National Population and Housing Census.

The auditor-general said the contractor submitted a conditional Advance Payment Guarantee instead of the mandatory unconditional guarantee.

The company was also not registered with relevant professional bodies prescribed in the invitation to tender, including the Computer Society of Nigeria and Cisco, according to the report.

The auditors further said the contractor lacked recognition as an original equipment manufacturer in Nigeria.

The report said the award of a high-value and sensitive ICT contract to a company without demonstrated technical competence, professional certifications and industry recognition compromised the assurance of technical competence and reliability required for the project.

The auditor general linked the finding to Section 23(1) of the Public Procurement Act and paragraph 2909 of the Financial Regulations, which require bidders to meet specified qualification and eligibility requirements, including the necessary technical capacity, equipment, manpower and legal capacity to execute a contract.

The NPC again provided no response to the audit query.

The auditor-general recommended that the director-general account to the National Assembly for the N4.735 billion, recover and remit the money to the Treasury and provide evidence of payment.

The report said the finding would remain valid until the recommendations were implemented.

What next? Auditor-General seeks recovery of billions

Across the findings on NPC, the auditor-general repeatedly identified the risk of diversion and loss of public funds and linked the irregularities to weaknesses in the NPC’s internal control system.

The report’s recommendations place the burden on the director-general to account to the National Assembly, recover disputed payments and remit the funds to the Treasury.

The auditor-general also repeatedly noted that the NPC failed to respond to the audit queries. Consequently, the office said the findings remained valid pending implementation of its recommendations.

The findings raise questions about the commission’s procurement controls in the preparations for the postponed 2023 census, particularly the handling of the procurement of hundreds of thousands of digital devices and the supporting ICT infrastructure.

The report also shows that the concerns went beyond documentation. They included alleged payments without evidence of delivery, changes to BPP-approved specifications and prices, failure to comply with local content directives, payments for time-bound services after the census had been postponed, and the award of sensitive ICT work to a contractor the auditors considered unqualified.

The auditor-general recommended that the relevant sums be recovered and remitted to the Treasury, with sanctions applied where the commission fails to account for the funds or address the identified breaches.

World.title: Economic expert seeks redesign of FG’s cash transfer programme
World.content:
Uche Uwaleke, an economy and capital market expert, has urged the Federal Government to redesign its conditional cash transfer programme.

Mr Uwaleke, a professor and the President, Capital Market Academics of Nigeria (CMAN), made the call in an interview with the News Agency of Nigeria (NAN) in Abuja.

He said the cash transfer programme, one of President Bola Tinubu’s administration’s principal poverty reduction interventions, required fundamental redesign to improve transparency and public confidence.

The expert said the programme could provide temporary relief and protect vulnerable households from severe economic shocks.

He, however, said its effectiveness would depend on credible beneficiary identification, payment integrity, adequate transfer amounts and the ability to monitor outcomes.

Mr Uwaleke said a programme whose beneficiaries could not be independently verified risked excluding deserving households, creating opportunities for abuse and weakening public trust.

“I recommend that the government should replace the existing approach with a more transparent, independently verifiable and better targeted social protection framework.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“A strengthened social register should be regularly updated and linked, with appropriate privacy safeguards, to credible data from relevant government institutions.

Access services

“Community-based verification should complement digital identification to ensure that people in remote and underserved communities are not excluded,” he said.

He also recommended a payment architecture that allowed traceability, alongside accessible grievance redress mechanisms and periodic impact assessments.

Speaking on food production, Mr Uwaleke called for the revival of the Directorate of Food, Roads and Rural Infrastructure (DFRRI) programme.

He said the revival would help address challenges affecting food production, rural access and basic infrastructure across the country.

Mr Uwaleke said national development could not be achieved by concentrating investment in major urban centres.

He noted that rural communities where much of the country’s agricultural production took place, needed stronger links to markets and essential services.

According to him, the underlying logic of the programme is to bring development closer to rural communities by addressing food production, rural access and basic infrastructure.

Mr Uwaleke said a renewed DFRRI-type programme should not reproduce past institutional arrangements but be redesigned as a community-centred rural productivity and infrastructure initiative.

He said the initiative should be jointly implemented by the federal, state and local governments, with clear accountability mechanisms and measurable outcomes.

According to him, these commitments must be translated into a coordinated national agricultural productivity programme with measurable targets, clear institutional responsibilities and adequate funding.

“Its priorities should include feeder roads, small-scale irrigation, rural electrification, water supply, produce aggregation centres, storage facilities, primary healthcare access and market infrastructure.

“Such a programme can accelerate grassroots development by connecting farming communities to markets, reducing transportation costs, improving access to agricultural inputs and creating employment through rural infrastructure projects.

“The emphasis should be on raising output per hectare, increasing multiple cropping, improving yields, reducing post-harvest losses and strengthening linkages between farmers, agro-processors and domestic markets,” he said.

Mr Uwaleke said the programme would provide a practical means of ensuring that economic recovery reached communities that had remained disconnected from the benefits of national growth.

“The emphasis must be on functional infrastructure and productive assets rather than politically distributed projects that have little lasting economic value,” he said.

Mr Uwaleke noted that beyond agriculture, the cost of energy remained a major constraint on domestic production.

He said manufacturers, small businesses and service providers continued to face high operating costs because of unreliable electricity supply and dependence on alternative energy sources.

The CMAN president said expansion of gas infrastructure, renewable energy, embedded generation and reliable grid supply must become integral components of the government’s prosperity agenda.

He said reducing energy costs would improve industrial competitiveness, encourage domestic production, reduce dependence on imported goods and create employment opportunities.

“The same logic applies to transportation and logistics.

“The completion of strategic roads, railways, ports and inland logistics infrastructure should be prioritised according to their economic returns and capacity to reduce the cost of moving people and goods.

“A well-connected agricultural or industrial production centre can generate substantially greater economic value than an isolated project with limited linkages to productive activity.

“Infrastructure investment must consequently be evaluated not only by the amount spent or kilometres constructed but also by its contribution to productivity, trade and employment,” he explained.

Mr Uwaleke said Nigeria needed a deliberate strategy to deepen domestic manufacturing, strengthen agro-processing, develop industrial clusters and encourage production of goods where the country had competitive advantage.

He noted that achieving this would require more than incentives and policy declarations.

The expert said it demanded reliable energy, efficient ports, affordable long-term finance, predictable taxation, effective trade facilitation and a stable regulatory environment.

Mr Uwaleke also called for stronger coordination between the fiscal and monetary authorities.

(NAN)

World.title: Poor record-keeping caused confusion over NAF crash manifest – Ex-SSS director
World.content:
A former Director of the State Security Service (SSS), Mike Ejiofor, has attributed the conflicting figures surrounding the number and identities of people aboard the Nigerian Air Force (NAF) aircraft that crashed in Ondo State to poor record-keeping.

Mr Ejiofor said proper documentation of passengers and crew members aboard the aircraft would have made it easier to establish the exact number of people on board and identify the casualties.

The NAF released the names of 25 people aboard the aircraft, rather than the 32 earlier reported by government officials.

Mr Ejiofor spoke on Arise Television’s Daybreak programme on Wednesday.

Commenting on the conflicting figures, he said the authorities should have been able to rely on the aircraft’s manifest to establish the identities of everyone on board.

“It goes again to the issue of data keeping; it would have been easier to get the manifest,” he said.

He said there was a possibility that some people aboard the aircraft might not have been included in the available manifest.

“I think they should rely more on the manifest of the aircraft if it was actually compiled from the people in the aircraft and their names were contained in a manifest,” he said.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“It’s a sad situation that this simple record-keeping can just be having conflicts.”

NAF recent aircraft crash

The NAF aircraft crashed on 5 October in a riverine swamp in the Igbokoda area of Ondo State.

According to the information provided by the authorities, the ATR-42 military aircraft, with tail number NAF 931, was on a routine maritime patrol and transport mission from Benin City to Lagos when air traffic controllers lost contact with it.

The NAF said all 25 people on board – 20 passengers, mostly military personnel, and five crew members, died in the crash.

The wreckage was located in a dense, muddy swamp opposite a local naval base. Recovery efforts have reportedly been hampered by the terrain and the fact that much of the wreckage became submerged in water and mud.

President Bola Tinubu declared three days of national mourning and ordered an investigation into the cause of the crash.

The incident has also renewed concerns over the safety and maintenance of military aircraft in the country.

‘Investigate NAF aircraft operations’

Mr Ejiofor said the crash should prompt a broader examination of the Nigerian Air Force’s aircraft fleet, including the maintenance history and operational condition of its aircraft.

He described the frequency of military aircraft crashes as a concern that should be investigated thoroughly.

“What is the state of maintenance of all these aircraft? How long have they been serviced? From records we have, there have been over 10 crashes in the last 10 years,” he said.

“We should look into the general operations of the Air Force.”

He also cited the 21 May 2021 crash in which Ibrahim Attahiru, then chief of army staff, and other military personnel were killed.

Mr Ejiofor said the recurring incidents warranted a comprehensive review of military aviation operations rather than investigations being limited to individual crashes.

Crash site poses rescue challenge

On the search and rescue operation following the latest crash, Mr Ejiofor said the difficult terrain had posed a significant challenge to rescuers.

He said the proximity of the crash site to military and police facilities would ordinarily have raised expectations of a swift response, but the swampy terrain complicated the operation.

“The terrain posed a very serious challenge, and as we speak, the forces of the aircraft have not been recovered yet. So, there’s no hope that there will be any life,” he said.

He, however, cautioned against blaming those involved in the rescue operation, given the conditions at the crash site.

Mr Ejiofor also cautioned against drawing conclusions about what caused the loud sound reportedly heard before the aircraft crashed.

He said it was too early to determine whether the aircraft exploded before hitting the ground or whether the impact itself produced the sound.

“For me, these are speculations,” he said.

“It’s possible the impact on crashing was the deafening noise, it might not.”

He added that an explosion could also have occurred before impact, potentially contributing to the scattering of debris and body parts.

“It’s also possible that there was an explosion before the impact, which led to the dissemination and finding of body parts,” he said.

He stressed that the cause of the crash could only be established after a proper investigation.

“So, until the investigation is complete, we can’t be specific about whether it was an explosion in the air or the impact on the ground,” he said.

World.title: Plane Crash: Aiyedatiwa visits site, says aircraft’s main body yet to surface, human parts recovered
World.content:
Search operations continued on Wednesday at the site of the crash of the Nigerian Air Force plane at Igbokoda, headquarters of Ilaje Local Government Area of Ondo State. Still, divers could not locate the main body of the aircraft.

The divers, comprising the Police, Navy and locals, including members of the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), only managed to bring out some human body parts as well as pieces of the aircraft.

Ondo State Governor Lucky Aiyedatiwa disclosed this to journalists during an assessment visit to the crash site.

Mr Aiyedatiwa visited the site alongside personnel of the Nigerian Navy and Nigerian Air Force, divers, the South-west Director of the National Emergency Management Agency (NEMA), the Director of the State Emergency Management Agency and residents who had participated in rescue efforts since Monday.

The ill-fated ATR-42 aircraft, which was carrying Nigerian Air Force personnel on a special mission from Benin to Lagos, crashed at Igbokoda on Monday morning.

NAF authorities said 26 people were on board the aircraft at the time it crashed.

According to the governor, no survivors had been found, noting that only parts of bodies, clothes and jackets belonging to Air Force personnel and broken aircraft parts were recovered and preserved for further investigation.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

He said the main body of the aircraft had not been sighted as it was believed to be submerged in the swamp.

Mr Aiyedatiwa, from the local government area where the crash occurred, explained that the difficulty of accessing the site prompted him to direct the Ministry of Works to deploy two amphibious machines, popularly known as swamp buggies, to open wider access through the waterways.

He said the machines had enabled rescue teams to move bigger boats closer to the crash site and were being used to excavate the soil in search of other parts of the wreckage or the main body of the aircraft.

The governor further said the aircraft had still not been sighted as of the time of his visit. At the same time, Navy personnel and local divers continued searching the deeper sections of the area for possible bodies and the cockpit.

Mr Aiyedatiwa said only the pilot could have explained the cause of the crash, adding that the occupants were believed to have died.

He said the swamp’s nature and depth could have caused the aircraft to become deeply submerged in the mud.

“From construction experience and analysis of this area, for you to get to refusal level, it’ll get to about 30 metres deep,” he said, adding that the aircraft could have gone completely into the mud.

He said jet fuel was flowing into the water, polluting the area with aviation fuel.

He said he was grateful the aircraft did not crash in the middle of the community, adding that it would have been a major catastrophe.

According to him, residents who witnessed the incident said the aircraft appeared to be coming down with a sound suggesting a bad engine and was almost landing within the community.

He said the pilot managed to manoeuvre the aircraft away from the community before it landed about 200 metres away and went straight into the swamp.

The governor said only the pilot could have explained the effort made to manoeuvre the aircraft away from the community.

Mr Aiyedatiwa also sympathised with the families of the deceased and the Nigerian Air Force, describing the victims as able and young Nigerians who had signed up to defend and protect the territorial integrity of the country.

He, however, said that based on what had been seen at the crash site, he doubted whether any of the victims could return to life.

“May their souls rest in peace,” he prayed.

Mr Aiyedatiwa, however, urged the search and rescue teams to intensify efforts to get out the remaining parts of the aircraft and the bodies of the victims.

Earlier, the Commander of the Nigerian Navy Forward Operating Base, Igbokoda, Andy Alemongwa, briefed the governor on the progress of the search-and-rescue operation.

Also on Wednesday, the Flag Officer Commanding, Western Naval Command, Abubakar Mustapha, and the Air Officer Commanding, Logistics Command, Nigerian Air Force, Abubakar Suleh, inspected the crash site of the Nigerian Air Force ATR-42.

Mr Mustapha, a rear admiral, conveyed the appreciation of the Chief of Defence Staff, Olufemi Oluyede, a general, and the service chiefs to the Ondo State Government, communities, emergency agencies and other stakeholders for their support since the incident occurred.

He urged stakeholders to remain calm and continue to cooperate with the various agencies involved in the recovery operation.

At the site, the team assessed the situation and provided technical guidance to facilitate the timely recovery of the submerged aircraft and its contents.

As part of the recovery efforts, the team began an underwater survey using side-scan sonar equipment to map the crash site and determine the submerged aircraft’s position.

The sonar survey is expected to help divers and other technical personnel locate the aircraft and plan subsequent recovery operations, including deploying a swamp buggy to facilitate excavation in the difficult terrain.

World.title: 2027 Polls: ‘84% intend to vote, but only 41% committed’ – Yiaga survey
World.content:
A new voter intention survey by Yiaga Africa has revealed a wide gap between Nigerians’ stated intention to vote in the 2027 general elections and their actual commitment to participating in the polls.

The survey found that while 84 per cent of respondents said they were likely or very likely to vote in the 2027 elections, only 41 per cent of that group said they were certain and committed to voting.

The findings were presented in the third edition of Yiaga Africa’s National Voter Intention Survey (NVIS 3.0) at a policy roundtable on voting intentions ahead of the 2027 general elections in Abuja on Wednesday.

The survey was designed to assess voter interest and participation and identify factors that could encourage or discourage Nigerians from taking part in the elections.

According to Yiaga Africa, 2,470 Nigerians aged 18 and above across the 36 states and the Federal Capital Territory participated in the September 2026 survey.

Of the respondents, 2,066 were interviewed by telephone, while 404 were interviewed face-to-face, particularly in rural communities.

The Senior Manager and Head of Knowledge Management and Learning at Yiaga Africa, Safiya Bichi, said the mixed approach ensured that people without access to telephones, especially those in rural communities, were not excluded.

Stay Ahead with Premium Times 

“Over 2,400 people were surveyed. We used a mixed method where we used telephone lines and traditional surveys to reach out to people and administer the survey questions,” Ms Bichi said.

She said the survey was intended to provide a broader picture of Nigerians’ attitudes towards the 2027 elections.

Ms Bichi said the 84 per cent intention to vote recorded in the latest survey did not necessarily translate into a firm commitment to participate in the election.

“84 per cent of citizens said they intended to vote, but only 41 per cent are committed to vote in this election,” she said.

She explained that a significant proportion of those who said they intended to vote had not yet decided which candidate they would support.

According to her, 44 per cent of the 84 per cent who said they intended to vote had not yet settled on their preferred candidates.

This, she said, presents political parties and candidates with a large pool of voters who could still change their preferences before the election.

She also said between six per cent and 10 per cent of respondents were either disinterested or undecided about participating in the election.

The latest figure represents an increase in overall voter intention compared with the first two rounds of the survey.

Yiaga Africa said 77 per cent of respondents indicated that they were likely to vote in the first NVIS, conducted in December, while the figure dropped to 73 per cent in the second survey before rising to 84 per cent in the third round.

However, the survey showed that the proportion of respondents who were “very likely” to vote has continued to decline.

According to the organisation, 52 per cent of respondents in the first survey said they were very likely to vote. That figure fell to 48 per cent in the second survey and 47 per cent in the third.

Ms Bichi said the difference suggested that although more Nigerians expressed an intention to vote, their certainty about actually participating in the election remained a concern.

Insecurity threatens participation

Insecurity emerged as one of the most significant threats to voter participation.

The survey found that 61 per cent of respondents feared that violence could prevent them from voting.

The concern was particularly pronounced in the North-East, where 78 per cent of respondents identified violence as a potential barrier to voting.

The survey also found that 82 per cent of respondents were very concerned that insecurity could affect the conduct of the elections.

The findings point to a dual concern among voters: fear of violence during the electoral process and doubts about the ability of security agencies to protect voters.

Only 48 per cent of respondents said they trusted security agencies to protect their votes during the elections.

Ms Bichi said improved security remained the strongest factor likely to motivate Nigerians to participate in the 2027 elections.

According to the survey, 83 per cent of respondents said improved security would motivate them to vote.

Another factor, 38 per cent of respondents identified as better logistics, while 20 per cent cited stronger candidates.

Ms Bichi said security and the quality of candidates had remained among the major factors influencing voter participation across the three rounds of the survey.

Confidence in INEC falls

The survey also revealed declining confidence in the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC).

Only 34 per cent of respondents said they were confident in INEC ahead of the 2027 elections.

This is down from 45 per cent in each of the first two rounds of the NVIS.

Confidence in INEC was particularly low in some regions. Yiaga Africa said 62 per cent of respondents in the South-east expressed a lack of confidence in the electoral commission. In comparison, the North-East recorded 62 per cent in another measure cited during the presentation.

The survey also found that Nigerians had greater confidence in some technological components of the electoral process than in the institution administering the election.

Forty-nine per cent of respondents said they trusted election technology, including accreditation and the IReV results-transmission system, compared with the 34 per cent who expressed confidence in INEC.

Ms Bichi said the finding suggested that Nigerians were increasingly placing their trust in electoral technology rather than solely in the institutions responsible for conducting elections.

Trust in electoral process becomes partisan

Yiaga Africa also found a relationship between citizens’ assessment of the current government’s performance and their confidence in the electoral commission.

The survey found that 54 per cent of respondents approved of the current government’s performance, while 71 per cent rated the state of the economy as poor or very poor.

Ms Bichi said confidence in INEC appeared to have taken on a partisan dimension.

She said respondents who rated the current government’s performance highly were also more likely to express confidence in INEC. In contrast, those dissatisfied with the government’s performance tended to have lower confidence in the electoral commission.

This, she said, suggested that public trust in the electoral process was not merely institutional but was increasingly influenced by political perceptions.

Low confidence in judiciary

The judiciary also recorded low levels of public confidence in its ability to resolve electoral disputes.

The survey found that 63 per cent of respondents were not confident that the judiciary would resolve electoral disputes fairly and effectively after the elections.

The South-South recorded the highest level of distrust, with 81 per cent of respondents in the region expressing a lack of confidence in the judiciary’s handling of electoral disputes.

The finding adds another layer to concerns over public confidence in Nigeria’s electoral process, from voting and security to the electoral commission and the post-election dispute resolution system.

Desire for change drives voter intention

The survey also examined why Nigerians intended to vote.

The desire for change in leadership emerged as the leading motivation, with 49 per cent of respondents identifying it as their main reason for voting.

Only 20 per cent identified civic duty as their motivation, while 16 per cent pointed to specific candidates.

Ms Bichi said the findings suggested that candidates themselves were not currently the primary motivation for participation.

Rather, the desire for a change in leadership appeared to be the dominant factor influencing voter intention.

Vote buying remains a concern

The survey also highlighted the continuing influence of vote buying on Nigeria’s electoral process.

Nineteen per cent of respondents, about one in five people surveyed, said they received money as an incentive to vote for a particular candidate in an election.

The prevalence was higher in some regions, with 32 per cent of respondents in the North-West saying they had received money to vote for a specific candidate.

Young people also featured prominently in the findings, with 24 per cent of young respondents saying they had received money to vote for a candidate.

The findings suggest that despite ongoing electoral reforms and efforts to curb inducement, financial incentives remain a significant feature of voters’ experiences.

The survey recorded a significant increase in public awareness of electoral reforms.

Only 24 per cent of respondents were aware of the electoral reform process during the first NVIS conducted in December.

The figure increased to 37 per cent in the second survey conducted in March and rose sharply to 62 per cent in the third survey.

Yiaga Africa attributed the increase to growing public awareness following the passage of the 2026 Electoral Act.

Among the reforms respondents were aware of were changes relating to accreditation and the electronic transmission of election results.

Young people less likely to vote

Despite the prominence of young Nigerians in the country’s electorate, the survey found that younger respondents showed weaker intentions to vote than older Nigerians.

Only 40 per cent of respondents in the younger age group indicated that they were likely to vote.

In contrast, 64 per cent of respondents aged 61 and above indicated that they were likely to participate.

The finding suggests a significant participation gap between younger and older voters and raises concerns about political parties’ and electoral stakeholders’ ability to mobilise young Nigerians ahead of 2027.

The survey also found a gender gap in voter intention, with 65 per cent of men indicating a likelihood to vote compared with 57 per cent of women.

INEC responds

Responding during the panel session, Victoria Eta-Messi, director of the Voter Education and Publicity Department at INEC, acknowledged the concerns around public trust and voter participation but defended the commission’s efforts to improve the electoral process.

Ms Eta-Messi said continued focus on the 2023 elections without recognising improvements made since then was concerning.

“The fact that people just keep holding on to 2023 rather than seeing the small steps that we’re making is a bit worrisome,” she said.

She, however, acknowledged that INEC still had significant work to do to increase participation and restore public confidence.

She cited the recently concluded Osun election as an example of improvements the commission was seeking to build on.

According to her, INEC had been concerned about the Osun election because of the attention it would attract as a test of the commission’s preparations ahead of 2027.

She said the commission was encouraged by the conduct of the election, particularly improvements in the deployment of personnel and materials.

Ms Eta-Messi said INEC was also working to improve its infrastructure and logistics, while engaging transport unions, including the National Union of Road Transport Workers and the National Association of Road Transport Owners, to address challenges experienced during previous elections.

She said training of INEC staff and ad hoc personnel was also being strengthened to ensure that officials understand the electoral process and perform their duties effectively at polling units.

Technology and logistics

The INEC official said the commission was also working to ensure that technology was deployed appropriately during elections while maintaining human safeguards.

She said technology would not be allowed to operate without checks and controls, stressing that human oversight would remain part of the electoral process.

She also identified logistics as one of the areas requiring continued attention.

According to her, the commission’s experience during the Osun election showed that better planning could improve the movement of personnel and electoral materials and ensure that polling units opened on time.

Need for grassroots mobilisation

Ms Eta-Messi said improving electoral participation would require greater engagement with Nigerians at the grassroots.

She said a significant proportion of the electorate lived outside major urban centres and that electoral stakeholders must therefore use available platforms to reach citizens in local communities.

She said INEC was engaging organisations and institutions that could assist in voter education and mobilisation, including the National Orientation Agency (NOA).

World.title: Afrilition and the prophesy of an African renaissance, By Adéwálé Àjàdì
World.content:
Afrilition is a call to service to be the generation that is willing to sacrifice comfort so that posterity will stand in excellence. Like the story of Joseph, prophecy is not determinism but a call to duty and commitment in faith so that our vision becomes our fate.

Afrilition expresses ancestral promise and affirmation, and it inevitably strays into a prophetic voice, not just as a spiritual invocation but also as critical engagement with trends and patterns. For me, as a writer, this is not new territory. In the early 2000s, I wrote a piece for Vanguard newspaper based on my experience of a Venezuelan film titled Sequestro Express. It dealt with kidnapping that had become endemic in this oil-rich but deeply divided society. It awakened something in me, and I wrote to warn that kidnapping on a mass scale was coming to our beloved Nigeria if we did not address the social cracks urgently. The comment section was devastating to my ego, as responses mocked and attacked me; they especially seemed to suggest that living abroad dislocated me from understanding Nigeria. Well, we have watched kidnapping replace armed robbery as Nigeria’s violent pathology. Join the Premium Times WhatsApp Community For Quick Access To News and Happenings Around You. Open in WhatsApp The thing about prophecy is that only God sees all and is always right; even with the highest gift, we prophesy only in part. Afrilition as part prophecy is showing early signs of alignment. This last week, the IMF published the top 20 countries with the largest GDP based on Purchasing Power Parity (PPP). The report has two African countries ranked 18th and 19th, respectively: Egypt and Nigeria. PPP ranking provides a better reflection of each country’s true market size, production volume, and domestic purchasing power, without exchange rate distortion. In line with Afrilition‘s prediction, the trend towards economic transformation is emerging. IMF further predicts that Nigeria will be the sixth largest contributor to Global Economic Growth in 2026 by driving 1.5 per cent of all new economic activity in the world.

Some African institutions are acting in very visionary ways, especially in processing African mineral wealth and developing industrial capacity to change patterns from being producers of raw and primary commodities to adding value through industrial processes and producing secondary and finished goods. Kenya has banned all unprocessed minerals, starting September 2026, whilst constructing three local gold refineries. Zimbabwe added to its restrictions on raw lithium concentrate, the extraction of antimony and tungsten in September. Both Guinea and Ghana have prohibited the export of unrefined gold, with stricter raw gold export regulations in Guinea. Malawi and Botswana have also implemented bans on critical transition minerals like cobalt, lithium, manganese, and rare earth elements. There is the boom in agro-processing and its effect on import substitution, like the ongoing effort of Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire to translate their 60 per cent of world cocoa production into processing chocolate, with a 2030 plan to process 80 per cent of their own cocoa beans locally. Ethiopian coffee is going through something similar, and so is the West African cashew.

The Dangote case study is worthy of a standalone, as the level of intention to transform here is a force of true Pan-African imagination. In 2003, at the end of the Obasanjo administration in Nigeria, the outgoing government offered that Nigeria’s moribund refineries in Port Harcourt and Kaduna be sold to a consortium that included Dangote. There was a major public outcry that this was the worst kind of cronyism. Editorial after editorial depicted this proposal as state capture. In my own family, this fuelled a major disagreement between my youngest brother and me. He saw it as part of my glorification of Obasanjo because it seemed, in those days, that he could do no wrong in my sight (things have since changed completely). My brother’s position had a lot of merit, and so did the editorials because, in a privatised public business, the questions of true value will never end. Had Dangote taken over the Nigerian government refineries, he would have had to go through business by attrition. Today, he has built the largest refinery on the continent and is expanding it towards the largest in the world. He has also broken ground on another refinery for East Africa, while the wind of war has benefited his refinery, so that the closure of the Strait of Hormuz put wind beneath his business wings. The emergence of these patterns and policies is in line with Afrilition. These are just the beginnings, and the battle to keep Africa as an extractive provider of primary commodities will enter a new and more sophisticated phase beyond the blatant violent destabilisation we see in many corners of the continent. The most egregious of which is in Sudan and the DRC Congo.

There is the boom in agro-processing and its effect on import substitution, like the ongoing effort of Ghana and Côte d’Ivoire to translate their 60 per cent of world cocoa production into processing chocolate, with a 2030 plan to process 80 per cent of their own cocoa beans locally. Ethiopian coffee is going through something similar, and so is the West African cashew. The emergence of these patterns and policies is in line with Afrilition. These are just the beginnings, and the battle to keep Africa as an extractive provider of primary commodities will enter a new and more sophisticated phase beyond the blatant violent destabilisation we see in many corners of the continent. The most egregious of which is in Sudan and the DRC Congo. The dreams that Joseph told his brothers did not say they were not stars themselves, but their own insecurity led the brothers to nearly kill him and eventually sell him into slavery. Over the next few decades, there will be many tests of African will to transform and realise its civilisation. Despite African excellence not being to dominate others, this will not stop them from doing all in their power to maintain their chokehold. They will try to keep Africa as an extractive and consumer- or importation-dependent space. Afrilition is a call to service to be the generation that is willing to sacrifice comfort so that posterity will stand in excellence. Like the story of Joseph, prophecy is not determinism but a call to duty and commitment in faith so that our vision becomes our fate. Stay Ahead with Premium Times

World.title: Justice Adefope-Okojie leads debate on judicial intervention in Nigeria’s elections
World.content:
By Innocent Anaba

Justice Oludotun Adefope-Okojie, retired Justice of the Court of Appeal, will deliver the 2026 Gavel International Annual Lecture slated for November 17, focusing on the increasingly debated role of the judiciary in Nigeria’s electoral process.

The lecture, entitled “Electoral Process in Nigeria: Managing the Boundaries of Judicial Intervention,” will examine the relationship between judicial intervention in electoral disputes and the constitutional right of Nigerians to determine their representatives through the ballot box.

The event will hold at the Main Hall of the Lagos Chamber of Commerce and Industry, Nurudeen Olowopopo Road, Central Business District, Alausa-Ikeja, Lagos.

Former Attorney-General and Commissioner for Justice of Bayelsa State, Chief Anthony George-Ikoli, SAN, will chair the event. George-Ikoli is also the first Senior Advocate of Nigeria produced by Bayelsa State.

Lawyer and activist, Mr. Femi Falana, SAN, will moderate the panel discussion following the lecture.

The organisers said the theme was chosen against the backdrop of continuing public debate over the role of the courts in determining electoral disputes and the implications of judicial decisions for the votes cast by Nigerians.

The lecture will examine the constitutional and practical boundaries of judicial intervention and the need to balance the adjudicatory role of the courts with the electorate’s authority to choose its political representatives.

Justice Adefope-Okojie brings extensive judicial experience to the discussion, having served both on the High Court of Lagos State and the Court of Appeal, where she participated in the adjudication of electoral and other constitutional disputes.

Gavel International said her extensive judicial experience, particularly in electoral adjudication, placed her in a strong position to lead the discussion on the relationship between the judiciary and the electoral process.



The organisation said her experience on the Bench and commitment to justice, constitutionalism and the rule of law would provide useful perspectives for policymakers, legal practitioners, academics and other stakeholders engaged in Nigeria’s democratic process.

Gavel’s record of public engagement

Founded by journalist Mustapha Ogunsakin in 2008, Gavel International is a legal and judicial news platform covering the administration of justice, constitutional governance and the rule of law.

The organisation has also used its platform to convene public discussions on important legal and governance issues.

The 2026 edition will additionally feature the presentation of awards to Nigerians who have distinguished themselves through contributions to law, justice, business, human rights, education and public service.

The organisers said the event is expected to draw senior judicial officers, lawyers, academics, policymakers, public officials, members of the diplomatic community, business leaders, journalists and other stakeholders.

The panel discussion, to be moderated by Falana, is expected to extend the debate beyond the lecture and provide perspectives from the legal profession, academia and the media on the appropriate limits of judicial intervention in Nigeria’s electoral process.

World.title: DR Congo Ineligible Player: NFF sent petition to wrong email – FIFA
World.content:
Mpasi

One of the technical grounds on which FIFA dismissed Nigeria’s protest against DR Congo for fielding an ineligible player in the world cup qualifiers was that the mail which they used in sending the petition wasn’t the right one.

DR Congo pipped Nigeria to book a place in the intercontinental playoff with a 4-3 win on penalties after both teams stayed locked at 1-1 after extra time.

According to the New York Times, FIFA discovered that Nigeria’s petition against Lionel Mpasi who was in goal in the playoff final didn’t fulfill the requirements of his nationality

switch from France to Congo, before taking part in the game.

However they dismissed the appeal by Nigeria on what they term as technical grounds following the late filing of the case by Nigeria. A bogus claim which has now put them under intense

scrutiny from the world at large.

According to a highly placed source at the National Sports Commission (NSC), FIFA cited the fact that the petition was sent to the General Secretary (GS) rather than the legal portal as part of the technical ground on which it was dismissed.

A laughable claim because all petitions and correspondence are first and foremost routed to the GS, who most times reply nations and give directions on where complaints should be forwarded to.
