Another ground was that it was filed late. A lame excuse because doing the right thing after an infraction of such magnitude shouldn’t be time barred.

World.title: Family of 6 killed in Oyo over damaged phone as police parade suspects
World.content:
The suspects

By Adeola Badru, IBADAN

The Oyo State Police Command has paraded several suspects arrested in connection with three separate criminal cases, including the alleged murder of a family of six at Oloba Village in Lagelu Local Government Area of the state.

The command said the suspects allegedly attacked the family over a damaged mobile phone belonging to one of them.

The other cases involved an alleged armed robbery at Wofun Olodo, Ibadan, during which a 44-year-old woman, Mrs Wahab Rukayat, was reportedly killed, as well as the arrest of a suspected unqualified medical practitioner accused of posing as a doctor.

The suspects were paraded at the Police Command Headquarters, Eleyele, Ibadan, where the command provided details of the separate investigations and displayed some of the items allegedly recovered.

In the Lagelu case, police identified the three suspects arrested over the alleged murder as Hammed Akinbami, Ojo Akinbami and Padonu Edward.

According to the command, the suspects allegedly invaded the residence of Ifeanyi Chukwu, his wife and their four children at Oloba Village, armed with a locally made Dane gun, two cutlasses and a wooden club.

Police said the suspects allegedly attacked the family in retaliation for damage to a mobile phone belonging to one of them.

The command alleged that the suspects robbed the family of N200,000, a motorcycle, a Doma machine with chainsaw and a spraying machine before using a wooden club to kill four members of the family.

It further alleged that the two children who survived the initial attack were taken to the Osun River, where their hands and legs were tied before they were thrown into the river.

The police said the remains of the woman had been recovered from the river, while efforts were ongoing to recover the remains of the other members of the family.

The command said the suspects were being investigated to establish their individual roles in the alleged attack and the circumstances surrounding the deaths.

Three arrested over robbery

In a separate case, police paraded three suspected members of an armed robbery gang identified as Oluwatobi Akinrinola, Mathew Okunola and Ibrahim Rabiu.

The suspects were arrested over an alleged robbery operation at Wofun Olodo, Ibadan, during which 44-year-old Rukayat was reportedly killed.

The command said the suspects allegedly attacked their victims and stole mobile phones, wristwatches, $400 and other valuables estimated at N3.493 million.

Police said an iPhone 7 Plus belonging to one of the victims was recovered from the suspects, while surviving victims reportedly identified them during an identification parade.

Some of the victims who were invited to the command headquarters to identify the suspects alleged that they were subjected to severe torture during the attacks and that property worth millions of naira was stolen.

The police said investigation was ongoing to determine the extent of the suspects’ alleged involvement in the robbery and killing, as well as establish whether other members of the gang were still at large.

Suspected fake doctor arrested

In the third case, the command paraded Benjamin Adeniyi, described as an auxiliary nurse, for allegedly practising medicine as a doctor without the requisite qualifications and professional training.

During an interview, Adeniyi reportedly admitted to the police that he had been practising as a medical doctor since 2022 despite lacking the required qualifications.

The police also accused him of operating two hospitals under the name LIFE IS GOOD, with branches in the Olodo and Academy areas of Ibadan, where he allegedly provided medical services, including fertility treatment.

The command said investigation was aimed at determining the extent of his activities and identifying patients who may have been exposed to risks as a result of the alleged illegal practice.

Reacting to the cases, the Police Public Relations Officer of the command, DSP Olayinka Ayanlade, said investigations into the three incidents were ongoing.

Ayanlade said the command was intensifying efforts to establish the full circumstances surrounding the incidents and apprehend other persons who might have been connected with the alleged crimes.

He added that the police would continue with the investigations and ensure that anyone found culpable was brought to justice.

World.title: Overhaul security, cut food, transport costs – NSCIA to FG
World.content:
By Luminous Jannamike, Abuja

The Nigerian Supreme Council for Islamic Affairs, NSCIA, has called on the Federal Government to overhaul Nigeria’s security architecture and urgently reduce the cost of food and transportation.

The Council said the twin pressures of insecurity and rising living costs required faster and more effective government action, while acknowledging efforts to revamp the economy.

The position was contained in a communiqué issued at the end of the NSCIA General Assembly in Abuja and signed by the Sultan of Sokoto and President-General, Alhaji Muhammad Sa’ad Abubakar, and Secretary-General, Prof. Is-haq Oloyede.

“The Council called for an urgent and comprehensive reform of Nigeria’s security architecture, while supporting decentralised policing,” the communiqué said.

It, however, said decentralised policing must be anchored on professionalism, constitutional safeguards, impartiality, accountability, sustainable funding, respect for fundamental rights and effective coordination between federal and state security institutions.

The Council also pressed the Federal Government to move faster on reducing the burden on ordinary Nigerians.

“The Federal Government should expedite action on drastically reducing the cost of transportation and food to alleviate the hardship being faced by ordinary Nigerians,” it said.

On religious rights, the NSCIA called on government agencies to respect the right of Muslim female students, Muslim NYSC members, female security personnel and Muslim women in other workplaces to use hijab.

It also faulted the University of Ibadan, Obafemi Awolowo University and University of Lagos over what it described as hostile dispositions to Supreme Court judgments favouring hijab in their international schools.

The Council urged the universities to retrace their steps and comply with the law.

It similarly called on the Rivers State Government and management of Rivers State University to implement the Supreme Court judgment on the mosque sought by Muslim students on the university campus.

The Assembly urged Muslims to contribute more effectively to nation-building, obtain their National Identification Numbers and Permanent Voter Cards, and participate fully in choosing leaders at all levels.

It also called for greater emphasis on quality education combining Islamic knowledge with Science, Technology, Engineering, Arts and Mathematics, while urging Muslim organisations to strengthen economic independence through lawful investments, Zakat and Waqf.

The Assembly adopted the 2026 report of the National Hajj Commission of Nigeria, NAHCON, and endorsed its recommendations for repositioning the Hajj industry.

It also approved an expanded National Executive Committee, including Prof. Mahfouz A. Adedimeji as Deputy Secretary-General, National Affairs; Prof. Salisu Shehu as Deputy Secretary-General, International Affairs; Abeni Obomeileh Mohammed, SAN, as Deputy Secretary-General, Corporate Affairs; and Dr Umar Jibrilu Gwandu as Public Relations Officer.

World.title: Insecurity: Nigeria in state of war, TUC laments
World.content:
President of TUC, Festus Osifo

— Says kidnapping still a booming business

— Urges FG to double efforts against insecurity

By Johnbosco Agbakwuru

ABUJA — The Trade Union Congress of Nigeria (TUC) on Wednesday lamented that the country has been in a state of war for over a decade due to insecurity, declaring that kidnapping remains a booming business for criminal elements.

The union said insecurity has undermined government efforts to attract foreign investment and advised the Federal Government to double its efforts in the fight against insecurity.

Briefing journalists after its National Executive Council (NEC) meeting in Abuja, TUC President Comrade Festus Osifo urged the government to strengthen the naira to between ₦700 and ₦800 to one US dollar, saying the high exchange rate remained central to the rising cost of goods, including the petrol pump price.

Osifo said the Federal Government should take decisive steps to end the insecurity ravaging the country.

He noted that while macroeconomic indicators were improving, with inflation gaining some stability and the exchange rate strengthening, the government could do better.

The TUC president recalled that in 2024, the congress presented a 15-point demand to the Federal Government, with the exchange rate at its centre.

“We cannot be tired of talking about the exchange rate because it is central to literally everything. Today, the official rate is just a little above ₦1,300 to the USD, but we see that the government can still do better,” he said.

“We commend CBN Governor Cardoso for the great work he is doing at the Central Bank, but we can still do much more because we still believe that ₦1,300 to $1 is still undervalued.”

Comrade Osifo stressed that the naira should trade between ₦700 and ₦800 to $1, insisting that at ₦1,300 it remains undervalued.

“From all international commentators, from economic think tanks, both local and international, and from scholars, currently our naira is undervalued and is not trading at the strength it should.

“Yes, we knew that before, when it was around ₦400, it was overvalued, but today at ₦1,300 it is still undervalued. So the government should do everything possible to move the naira to the right value,” Osifo said.

He also commiserated with the families of security personnel who died in recent incidents, noting that one of the pilots involved had gotten married just weeks earlier.

On insecurity, Osifo said the TUC wanted the Federal Government to deal decisively with the problem ravaging almost every part of the country.

He said the union was urging the government to provide security agencies with the needed funds and equipment to prosecute the fight against terrorists and bandits, adding that without a stable country there would be no economic progress.

He condemned the incident in Niger State that led to the death of about 37 persons in the custody of the Nigeria Security and Civil Defence Corps (NSCDC), describing it as an aberration.

“We are quite happy that the government immediately swung into action by setting up a committee, but we don’t want the committee’s report to just be another report gathering dust. Whoever is culpable, no matter how highly placed, must be decisively dealt with according to the letter and spirit of the law,” he said.

Addressing the country’s many security challenges, the TUC president said: “First, as you know, gentlemen of the press, today we have been facing the issue of insecurity in our country, maybe in the last 15 years at best.

“And in our last press briefing, we extended a thank you to the DG of the DSS for the great work he has been doing, seeing the number of convictions in recent times, with a number of apprehensions without paying ransom. We still commend him on that.

“And we still wish that they continue on that trajectory. Same with the National Security Adviser; we know that they don’t sleep on a daily basis in order to make the rest of us sleep.

“Having said that, we know, as a country, that we are still faced with a huge level of insecurity. For example, recently, as we all know, the level of kidnapping and killings in the Bakin Ladi area in Plateau State has even increased much more.

“We know very well, for a fact, that in some areas in our country—states like Zamfara, Borno, Katsina, even in the southern part of the country, and Nigeria in general—we have kidnappings still going on as a business.

“We have killings still going on. We have proposed at a time, as the Trade Union Congress of Nigeria, that the government should even carry out what we call virement in the budget to move funds to that area to procure the necessary equipment, to procure all the necessary gadgets to wipe out these people once and for all, because Nigeria has been in a state of war for over a decade, and we must stamp this out once and for all.

“It is very difficult to attract foreign investment. It’s very difficult to even get local investors to put their money into the economy where there is this level of uncertainty and this level of insecurity.

“So for us, the government should double its effort. The funds going to fight the state of insecurity should be increased. Yes, we love road construction. Yes, we love investment in power. We love investment in education and so on and so forth. But beyond that, we must first of all live well. We must first of all be alive to enjoy the dividends of the infrastructures—to be able to drive on those roads, to be able to feed and to send our children to school.

“So the protection of life and property should be paramount to any government. Yes, we could see that a lot is being done, but we are encouraging them to do much more.”

On the health sector dispute involving members of the Joint Health Sector Unions (JOHESU), Osifo said the union had resolved to send a letter to the Coordinating Minister of Health and Social Welfare to hasten action on the workers’ demands.

World.title: FG releases 8-month consolidated allowance to non-academic staff
World.content:
Dr Tunji Alausa, Minister of Education

…moves to avert fresh crisis in tertiary institutions

By Joseph Erunke, Abuja

The Federal Government has released eight months’ arrears of the Consolidated Non-Academic Staff Tertiary Institutions Allowance, CONTA, to non-academic workers in federal universities, polytechnics and colleges of education, in a move aimed at strengthening industrial harmony and preventing disruptions in the nation’s tertiary education system.

The allowance, covering January to August 2026, was announced by the Minister of Education, Dr Tunji Alausa, on Wednesday, barely two days after the government commenced payment of the Consolidated Academic Tertiary Institutions Allowance, CATA, to academic staff.

The twin payments signal the Federal Government’s efforts to address staff welfare concerns across the tertiary education sector and ease tensions that could threaten the stability of the academic calendar.

Alausa said the release of CONTA demonstrated the administration’s commitment to workers’ welfare and recognition of the critical role played by non-academic personnel in keeping tertiary institutions functional.

According to him, the welfare and motivation of both academic and non-academic staff remained central to ensuring stable institutions and producing the skilled manpower required for national development.

He said the payment was also part of the Federal Government’s broader efforts to address legitimate welfare concerns, promote industrial harmony and minimise disruptions to academic activities nationwide.

The minister said the administration would continue to strengthen institutions responsible for developing Nigeria’s human capital, stressing that a stable tertiary education system was essential to the country’s socio-economic development.

Alausa further assured stakeholders that the Federal Ministry of Education would sustain consultations with relevant unions, heads of institutions and other stakeholders to resolve outstanding issues and build a more stable and productive tertiary education system.

He appealed for continued cooperation from academic and non-academic staff, institutional authorities and unions as the government implements its reforms in the sector.

The minister reiterated that the ministry under his leadership would continue to prioritise staff welfare, institutional stability, human capital development and improved learning outcomes.

He added that the Federal Government remained committed to fulfilling its obligations to personnel in the tertiary education sector and addressing outstanding welfare issues in line with the human capital development objectives of the Renewed Hope Agenda.

World.title: 66 years on, Nigeria must escape the fragility trap, by Olu Fasan
World.content:
Olu Fasan

How fragile is Nigeria? That is one question Nigerian leaders don’t want to confront. Indeed, it irks them when anyone says that Nigeria is a fragile state. What’s more, some Nigerians, out of sheer romantic or sentimental patriotism hate it when the word “fragility” is used to describe Nigeria. It is unpatriotic, they reckon, for anyone to suggest that Nigeria is a fragile state. But this is not a subjective matter, rather it is an objective reality, based on rigorous assessment of key political, economic and social indicators. Nigeria may choose to be the judge and the jury in its own matter and declare itself strong and stable, the world simply does not see it that way, and the evidence points to a deeply fragile state. In their seminal report on state fragility, published in 2018, Professor Sir Paul Collier, from Oxford University, and Professor Sir Tim Besley, from the London School of Economics, provided a useful analytical framework for understanding state fragility. They came up with what they called the Six Symptoms of State Fragility. They are 1) the prevalence of organised non-state violence; 2) a government lacks legitimacy in the eyes of many citizens; 3) a state has a weak capacity for essential functions; 4) the environment for private investment is unattractive; 5) the economy is exposed to shocks with little resilience; and 6) deep divisions in the society. Anyone who examines these symptoms carefully would admit that they perfectly describe Nigeria.

Think about it. Is there anyone who would say there is no prevalence of organised non-state violence in Nigeria when, according to media reports, there were at least 4,326 civilian deaths between January to March in this alone? Or can anyone say that the Nigerian government has the capacity to provide essential amenities for its citizens? Or is the environment attractive private investment when several long-term foreign investors are deserting Nigeria and the country is only attracting volatile portfolio investment? What about cohesion? Is Nigeria united? The truth, except for the self-deluded, is that Nigeria is a deeply fragile state. Indeed, international indexes show it. For instance, in the 2024 Fragile States Index, published by The Fund for Peace, Nigeria was ranked the 15th most fragile state out of 179 countries. Nigeria has also been ranked the 15th most fragile state in the 2026 Fragile States Index, published by the World Population Review. In both indexes, Nigeria is more fragile than other African countries except six: Democratic Republic of Congo, Central African Republic, Chad, Ethiopia, Mali and Libya. This is a deeply depressing picture for Nigeria, Africa’s third largest economy and its most populous and most endowed nation.

Now, how could a country that is so blessed with abundant human and natural resources be the world 15th most fragile state? How could a country whose citizens provide global leadership, running major international organisations, be unable to govern itself well? How could a so-called “Giant of Africa” be more fragile than most African countries? But what happened? Well, while some see Nigeria’s problems as economic in nature, I see them as political and institutional, because Nigeria’s economic and social challenges have their roots in the failure of politics and political institutions. One of the greatest insights came from the famous book Why Nations Fail, written by Daron Acemoglu and James Robinson, both economics Nobel laureates. In the book, the authors said: “While economic institutions are crucial for determining whether a country is poor or prosperous, it is politics and political institutions that determine what economic institutions a country has.”

For instance, it is politics and the political process that produce leaders that Nigeria has had and thus their economic and social policies. If President Goodluck Jonathan had been re-elected in 2015, he would not have implemented the misguided economic policies and the divisive political and social policies that his successor, President Muhammadu Buhari, implemented. Similar, if President Bola Tinubu loses his re-election bid next year, his successor will almost likely reverse some of his economic policies. Furthermore, it is Nigeria’s political institution, or, if you like, its Constitution that allows someone to become president with only 36 per cent of the popular vote, gained by deploying the wedge issues of ethnicity and religion, and yet control 100 per cent political power under a “winner-takes-all” political process. What about the 64 per cent that did not vote for him? Such a perverse political system causes a government to lack legitimacy in the eyes of many citizens.

Let’s face it, Nigeria’s deeply flawed political and governance structure is the root cause of its fragility, characterised by political instability, economic inequality, ethnic tensions, religious intolerance and social divisions. No country that faces those multiple challenges can be described as anything but fragile because such a country cannot achieve the unity and stability needed to transition from poverty to prosperity, from chaos to order, and from extractive political and economic systems to inclusive ones. Yet, Nigeria is too structurally fragile that it cannot achieve any meaningful progress unless it breaks free from its deeply flawed Constitution, governance structure and democratic practice. For instance, the Nigerian Constitution tells three lies. First, the Constitution starts with the declaration that “We the people … Do hereby make, enact and give to ourselves the following Constitution.” But the people of Nigeria did not enact the Constitution, the military did, and they did not, as with most constitutions, submit it to the people for popular ratification. Unfortunately, thanks to path-dependent institutional development, the civilian leaders have refused to give Nigerians a genuine people’s Constitution. Until Nigeria gets a people’s Constitution, the words “We the people” in the 1999 Constitution are oxymoron.

Then, the Constitution describes Nigeria as a “Federal Republic”. But Nigeria is neither a true federal state nor a true republic. According to the Encyclopaedia Britanica, a true federal system must have three essential features: non-centralisation, local autonomy and elements that promote common nationality. But Nigeria has one of the most centralised political systems in the world, with a constitution that has an “Exclusive Legislative List” that reserves 67 items and “any matter incidental or supplementary to them” to the centre. Most constitutional lawyers say that no other federal constitution has such many items concentrated at the centre. Second, there is no genuine local autonomy in Nigeria, the kind that exists in genuine federal systems where the subnational units can pursue policies that are completely different from those of the centre. But even in the Concurrent Legislative List, which contains matters on which both federal and state governments can legislate, federal laws trump state laws in the event of a clash. That’s not true federalism; it’s a unitary system!

What about the third characteristic: elements that promote common nationality. Tell me, how can the mismanagement of Nigeria’s diversity promote common nationality. President Buhari was accused of a Fulanisation agenda because he put his fellow Fulanis in virtually all critical security positions, completely excluding Igbos. Bola Tinubu ran for president on a Muslim-Muslim ticket, and, in power, he has been accused of a Yorubanisation agenda by putting his fellow Yorubas is virtually all economic, security and justice positions. It’s as if people from other ethnic groups are not smart enough to hold such pivotal roles.

Now, let’s come to republicanism. Is Nigeria a true republic. Of course not. In his book The State We’re In, Will Hutton argues that, in a true republic, “political power and authority are firmly rooted in the people, with the state ruling for the people rather than over them”. But in Nigeria, power flows from the top down, not bottom up. Elections are frequently rigged, and governments never act as the agent of the people. Nigeria is not a true representative democracy because it does not have a social contract. What’s more, Nigeria’s president is one of the most powerful and yet most unaccountable in the world. He rules like an absolute monarch. Truth is, with such deeply flawed political and governance structure, Nigeria risks being trapped in fragility. Only root-and-branch restructuring can help it escape the fragility trap and unlock its potential.

World.title: 2027 election cases: Your conduct will be monitored, CJN warns tribunal judges
World.content:
Chief Justice of Nigeria, CJN, Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun

By Ikechukwu Nnochiri

ABUJA—Ahead of the 2027 general elections, the Chief Justice of Nigeria, CJN, Justice Kudirat Kekere-Ekun, yesterday warned that judges appointed to election tribunals would be closely monitored.

Speaking during the flag-off ceremony of the 2026/2027 legal year of the National Industrial Court of Nigeria, NICN, the CJN, who noted that some judges of the court could be called upon to serve as members of election petition tribunals, said the nature of such an assignment demanded a great degree of impartiality and restraint.

She equally implored lawyers to avoid duplicating court actions, which could lead to conflicting judgments capable of not only damaging public confidence but also exposing the judiciary to disrepute.

The CJN maintained that the court must remain intellectually prepared to meet modern-day challenges, while ensuring that its decisions remained firmly anchored in the Constitution, applicable legislation, binding precedent and established principles of judicial reasoning.

She said: “As we approach another electoral season, these responsibilities assume even greater importance.

“Some of Your Lordships may, in accordance with the applicable constitutional and legal framework, be called upon to serve as members of Election Petition Tribunals.

“In that capacity, Your Lordships will be called upon to decide politically sensitive disputes which attract considerable public attention.

“The nature of such assignments therefore demands an even greater degree of impartiality, restraint and detachment.

“Whether sitting in this Court or performing a Tribunal assignment, you must remain conscious that your conduct will be closely scrutinized.

“You must ensure that nothing in your associations, public engagements or other conduct creates a reasonable perception of political alignment or predisposition.

“The Bar must never become an instrument through which the judicial process is manipulated for partisan or strategic purposes.

“The proper forum is determined by law, not by the perceived likelihood of success before a particular Judge or court.

“There is also a need for restraint in public commentary. The right to criticise a judgment or judicial process does not extend to personal attacks on Judges, deliberate misrepresentation of proceedings or attempts to bring pressure to bear on the Court through public opinion.

“Where there are genuine concerns about judicial conduct, the appropriate institutional channels remain available and should be used,” the CJN added.

She also cautioned lawyers on the use of Artificial Intelligence (AI), noting that although it could be a handy research tool, it should not, however, displace their professional responsibility.

“An AI system may produce an answer that appears authoritative, complete with names of parties, citations, quotations and even a seemingly convincing account of the decision.

“That does not make the authority genuine. A non-existent case, an incorrectly stated decision or a quotation attributed to a judgment in which it does not appear has no place in a court process

“For counsel, the consequences can be serious,” the CJN warned.

In his address, the President of the NICN, Justice Benedict Kanyip, disclosed that the court was inundated with cases in the past legal year.

According to him, over the past twelve months, a total of 2,236 cases were disposed of across the Judicial Divisions of the court, significantly cutting down its historical backlog.

“Despite the pressure occasioned by this, my colleagues, in their characteristic manner, demonstrated unwavering commitment to duty and concluded significant numbers of these cases.

“I am pleased to report that through the dedication of our judges, we achieved a significant increase in case disposal rates compared to previous years.”

However, he decried the poor utilisation of the court’s Alternative Dispute Resolution (ADR) Centre by litigants and their counsel.

He noted that only 31 cases were referred to the ADR Centre across the various Judicial Divisions of the court in the last year.

“We must note that ADR is a valid and special component of, especially, labour justice delivery. Judicial efficiency cannot rely on litigation alone.

“Despite our efforts to promote ADR in the Court, we have not received any reciprocity in that regard from litigants and their counsel,” the NICN President stated.

While the Attorney-General of the Federation and Minister of Justice, Prince Lateef Fagbemi, SAN, pledged the continued support of the Federal Government to the court, the President of the Nigerian Bar Association (NBA), Mrs. Oyinkansola Badejo-Okusanya, SAN, stressed that Nigerian labour jurisprudence must remain dynamic but firmly rooted in the rule of law.

Dignitaries at the legal year ceremony, which was preceded by the official commissioning of the court’s headquarters building, included former CJNs, Justices Mahmud Mohammed and Walter Onnoghen; the President of the Court of Appeal, Justice Monica Dongbam-Mensen; and several Senior Advocates of Nigeria and lawyers.

World.title: Military, DSS, Police, Others Rescue 20 Abducted Youth Corps Members
World.content:
•Uzodimma hails security agencies

Amby Uneze in Owerri and Linus Aleke in Abuja





The Nigerian military, in collaboration with Department of State Services (DSS), Nigeria Police, and other security agencies, has rescued 20 prospective members of the National Youth Service Corps (NYSC) and a civilian, who were abducted in Imo State.

The prospective corps members, who spent seven days in captivity, were abducted on October 1 around Umunoha, in Imo State, while travelling to their orientation camp.

Director of Defence Media Operations, Major-General Michael Onoja, who confirmed the rescue in a telephone conversation with THISDAY, did not provide further details.

But the Nigeria Police, in a statement last night, said the victims were rescued about 4:28 pm on October 7, at Amakohia Ubi Village in Imo State, following sustained and coordinated search-and-rescue operations by the security agencies.

The police statement said, “Following their safe recovery, the victims have been taken for medical examination and necessary medical attention as part of the post-rescue process.

“The successful rescue followed sustained operational coordination and collaboration among the security agencies involved in the search-and-rescue effort.”

The force added that efforts were ongoing to apprehend the suspects responsible for the abduction, as the police and other security agencies continued to intensify operations to bring those responsible to justice.

“The Nigeria Police Force appreciates members of the public for their cooperation and support and reiterates its commitment to the protection of lives and property and the prompt response to threats to public safety,” the force said.

The police further assured the public that updates would be communicated as necessary.

Earlier, Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, had deployed Deputy Inspector-General of Police in charge of Operations, DIG Shehu Nadada, to Imo State to coordinate the search-and-rescue operation for the 20 prospective NYSC members and other passengers abducted along the Owerri-Onitsha Road.

The deployment followed appeals by the victims’ parents to the Olubadan of Ibadanland, Oba Rashidi Ladoja, and the police authorities for urgent intervention.

Uzodimma Hails Inter-agency Alliance

Imo State Governor, Senator Hope Uzodimma, applauded security agencies for their quick intervention and for securing the release of the 20 corps members kidnapped along the Onitsha-Owerri Road.

Uzodimma said he was particularly pleased with the security agencies for their collaboration and patriotism in ensuring that the corps members were rescued unharmed.

In a statement he personally signed, Uzodimma expressed satisfaction with the collaborative efforts of both the Oyo and Imo State governments towards the quick release of all 20 captives.

He said since the issue involved the security of lives, the government was cautious about releasing too much information to the public, hence the discreet manner it was handled.

The governor said he was particularly grateful to the security agencies for the discreet and collaborative manner in which they tackled the challenge.

He also praised the parents for their patience during the trying period and urged Nigerians to always have faith in the federal government to overcome the current security challenges in the country.

Sources informed THISDAY in Owerri that the kidnapped victims were rescued following joint security operations involving five days of planning and execution.

Director-General of NYSC, Brigadier-General Olakunle Nafiu, met with the rescued victims at the DSS medical facility.

Nafiu was accompanied by senior security officials, including Imo State Commissioner of Police, State Director of DSS, and Commander of 34 Artillery Brigade.
