World.title: MultiChoice Group, a Canal+ Company, Teases the New Era of DStv
World.content:
MONROVIA — A major transformation is brewing for television screens across Liberia, and the continent’s biggest entertainment player is dropping its biggest hint yet.

MultiChoice Group, operating under Canal+, has begun teasing a sweeping overhaul of its satellite television service—rallying under a bold new tagline: “DStv Expect More.”

Rather than a simple refresh, the company promises a complete reinvention of the DStv platform built entirely from the ground up. The vision? A hyper-customized viewing experience designed around how people actually watch TV today.



While full details remain under wraps, MultiChoice hints that a brand-new suite of tailored packages is on the horizon. Whether you live for live sports on the pitch, binge-watch movies and series, or try to keep a crowded household happy, a custom-built DStv experience is heading your way.

“This is the next evolution for Africa’s most loved storyteller,” the company teased in a recent statement, promising subscribers more choice, greater value, and control over their screens.

What these newly designed packages look like, which channels are making the cut, and how localized pricing will shape out for the Liberian market remain closely guarded secrets for now. Viewers across the country will just have to sit tight and stay tuned as MultiChoice prepares to reveal the full picture in the coming weeks.

World.title: Liberia: Ex-Mines Minister Paye Says Liberia Must Adopt “Resource Sovereignty” to Break Mining Cartels, Stop Reliance on Foreign Loans
World.content:
MONROVIA – Former Minister of Mines and Energy, Wilmot Paye, has called on the Liberian government to adopt a policy of resource sovereignty, arguing that the country cannot substantially benefit from its natural wealth unless it breaks the hold of cartels and outside influence over the minerals sector.

By Obediah Johnson

Mr. Paye spoke on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, as a guest on Voice of Liberia 104.1 FM in Monrovia.



Cartels and “extended influence”

Mr. Paye said Liberia is more richly endowed with natural resources than other countries in the region, but that its minerals sector continues to be threatened by cartels and extended influence. He recalled that during the previous administration, the mining cartel was very strong and powerful in the country.

He said many African countries are already promoting resource sovereignty and are taking charge of their own destinies instead of depending on others for survival. Liberia, he said, should do the same.

According to Mr. Paye, a sound policy approach, effective implementation and the removal of hurdles and outside influence would make the energy and minerals sectors more vibrant for the benefit of citizens.

“While I was in government I believe in it, while I’m out I believe in it and I will continue to believe in it,” he said of resource sovereignty, adding that Liberia needs to change its approach and mindset.

“Not relief agencies”

The former minister cautioned that mining companies operating in Liberia are not relief agencies. If steps are not taken to promote resource sovereignty, he warned, such companies could deplete the country’s resources without bringing significant benefits to citizens.

Against reliance on loans

Mr. Paye argued that Liberia should stop treating loans and borrowing as the answer to its difficulties, given the abundance of its natural resources. He said that by promoting resource sovereignty, the country would not need loans from the World Bank or other international financial bodies to fund its development programs.

He identified minerals as a very significant part of the country’s natural wealth, but said greed among some past and current public officials, whom he did not name, is a contributing factor depriving the nation of the benefits.

Allegations of “double standards”

Mr. Paye noted that Liberia’s new mineral law prohibits public officials, employees and agents of the Ministry of Mines and Energy from holding mining licenses. However, he said some of these officials continue to play double standards to influence the sector.

He observed that some public officials interfere in the sector by being awarded contracts by companies operating in it. He did not provide specific names or examples.

China-Liberia mineral survey

Mr. Paye also disclosed that China and Liberia reached an agreement and carried out a mineral resource survey across the country as part of efforts to strengthen bilateral relations after years of strained ties.

He said the survey was conducted jointly by the Ministry of Mines and Energy, during his tenure, and the China Geological Survey, with support from the Wuhan Center in China. It provided additional insights into Liberia’s mineral potential and identified more than two dozen minerals found in the country, he said.

“Liberia is a resource-rich country; there is no country in our region that is as blessed as Liberia,” Mr. Paye said, adding that the country’s potential spans forest, mineral, renewable and non-renewable resources.

Court cases during his tenure

Mr. Paye recalled that his administration at the ministry rejected unfavorable requests from influential people inside and outside government that were not in the interest of the country and its citizens. He said his firm stance on carrying out the ministry’s statutory responsibilities led to the ministry being taken to court on numerous occasions.

The claims in this article are those of Mr. Paye. The officials and companies he referred to were not named, and no response from the government was available at the time of publication.

World.title: Liberia: Founder of Change Agent Network Eric Wowoh Charged by Police Over Alleged Land Fraud Involving US-Based Couple
World.content:
According to the charge sheet, investigators reviewed bank transfers, Zelle, Cash App and other electronic payments showing the couple paid US$18,741 toward the price. Mr. Wowoh, however, admitted to investigators that he received only US$9,200 from Mrs. Acquah as part payment, the charge sheet says

MONROVIA – The Liberia National Police has charged Eric W. Wowoh, founder and executive director of the civil society organization Change Agent Network, with theft of property, receiving money under false pretences and criminal conveyance of land, in connection with a land transaction involving a couple based in the United States.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]



According to a police charge sheet dated October 6, 2026, Mr. Wowoh was arrested on September 16, 2026, by Detective Joseph S. Nagbe at the LNP headquarters in Monrovia. The document lists no accomplices and says the case is to be forwarded to court.

Complaint filed through lawyer

The case stems from a complaint filed on September 11, 2026, by Mrs. Rebekah Acquah and her husband, Mr. John Acquah, who reside in Rhode Island. They reported the matter to the police’s Crime Services Department through their lawyer, Atty. Stephen B. Lavelah of the Kailando and Associates Law Firm.

The couple alleges that Mr. Wowoh, who is associated with the organization, received US$18,741 toward the purchase of a property valued at US$30,500. The property consists of two lots of land with a structure under construction in the Rock Church Community, Duazon, Margibi County.

How the deal allegedly unfolded

Police say the Acquahs approached Mr. Wowoh in 2024 to help them find land in Liberia. In December 2024, he allegedly agreed to sell them part of his own property: US$5,500 for the two lots and US$25,000 for the house, totaling US$30,500.

According to the charge sheet, investigators reviewed bank transfers, Zelle, Cash App and other electronic payments showing the couple paid US$18,741 toward the price. Mr. Wowoh, however, admitted to investigators that he received only US$9,200 from Mrs. Acquah as part payment, the document says.

Police say that in February 2025 Mr. Wowoh handed the couple the legal documents for the property, including the administrator’s deed, warranty deed and transferred deeds. The charge sheet describes the deed as valid and legitimate.

But investigators allege that he later secretly retrieved the same documents and sold the property to another buyer, acting with criminal intent to resell it. The charge sheet also notes that Mrs. Acquah paid US$482.34 in taxes to the Liberia Land Authority (LLA) for the property.

Charges and legal basis

After its investigation, the police resolved to charge Mr. Wowoh with theft of property/receiving money under false pretense and criminal conveyance of land. The charges are brought under Chapter 15, Subchapter A, Sections 15.5 and 15.23 of the Revised Penal Code of the Republic of Liberia.

Concerns for civil society

The charge against the head of a civil society organization is likely to draw attention to the conduct of leaders in Liberia’s non-governmental sector. The charge sheet does not say the alleged transaction involved the organization’s funds or activities, and it does not accuse the organization itself of wrongdoing.

The document was signed by Commander-in-Charge R. Smith. It records Mr. Wowoh as a Liberian of Lorma descent, born in Fissibu Town, Lofa County. Mr. Wowoh could not be reached for comment.

World.title: Liberia: GTMS Liberia Launches Legal Action Against Two Men Over Alleged Fake Executive Appointments
World.content:
MONROVIA – Global Tracking & Maritime Solutions Liberia Inc. (GTMS Liberia) has instructed lawyers to begin civil and criminal proceedings against two men it accuses of falsely presenting themselves as senior officers of the company, while warning the public, customers and business partners to have no dealings with them.

By Selma Lomax, [email protected]

The company named the men as Presley S. Tenwah and Elvis D. Johnson. In a statement, management said it was alarmed by their purported appointments as General Manager-Liberia and as Public Relations Executive and Operations Manager, respectively.



According to GTMS Liberia, the appointments were allegedly made by Sahr H. W. Ngegba, who claims to be a Director of the company. Management said he has no such authority.

“Not associated with the company”

The company said Mr. Ngegba is not associated with GTMS Liberia in any capacity. It stated that he does not appear in its corporate structure, staff register or list of authorised officers, and that he holds no position as director.

“These appointments were issued by a person with no authority to act on behalf of this Company,” the statement said in substance, describing Mr. Tenwah and Mr. Johnson as impostors.

Distance from UK entity

GTMS Liberia also moved to separate itself from GTMS-UK. It said it is neither a subsidiary of nor in partnership with the British company, which it says has been wound up and is currently undergoing liquidation in the United Kingdom.

Management described the two entities as entirely separate and distinct. It further alleged that the appointments were a deliberate attempt to mislead the public and to exploit GTMS Liberia’s name and reputation in order to shield the UK entity, which it says is under investigation by British authorities over alleged administrative failures and serious financial irregularities.

Public warning

The company issued what it called a strict warning to the general public, its customers and its business partners. They were told not to transact any business with Mr. Tenwah or Mr. Johnson in the name of GTMS Liberia. Management said any dealings with the two men would not be recognised as binding on the company.

Legal proceedings

GTMS Liberia said it has instructed the Global Lead Counsel of AFDASA Global to immediately commence civil and criminal proceedings against Mr. Tenwah and Mr. Johnson. They are accused of falsely representing themselves as officers of the company, misleading the public, and causing significant operational disruption and reputational harm.

“We will pursue all available legal remedies to protect our name, our stakeholders, and the public,” the company said.

The statement did not provide details of the alleged disruption to operations or say when the legal filings would be made. Mr. Ngegba, Mr. Tenwah and Mr. Johnson could not be reached for comment.

World.title: Liberia: ‘The Money Gave Us Hope, But Three Months Is Too Short’ — Grand Cape Mount Women Tell LWEP
World.content:
TOSOR, Grand Cape Mount County — When the money reached some women in Grand Cape Mount County, it did more than put cash in their hands. It opened doors to small businesses, helped pay school fees, provided food for families and gave women greater control over their economic lives.

By Patience M. Jones, [email protected]

But for women benefiting from the Liberia Women Empowerment Project (LWEP), the opportunity has also come with challenges.



Some women in Tosor Community say they need more time to repay the funds, particularly as seasonal conditions make it difficult to generate enough income within three months. Others are still waiting for grants they say they were promised, while one group is seeking urgent intervention after an error in its payment processing left members with only a portion of the amount they expected.

The concerns emerged Tuesday when the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection (MGCSP), the World Bank and LWEP implementation partners visited Grand Cape Mount County for a technical review aimed at hearing directly from beneficiaries about the impact of the project.

The visit brought together county authorities, community leaders, women beneficiaries, Village Savings and Loan Associations (VSLAs), health workers and other stakeholders.

The delegation was welcomed through traditional drumming, music and the presentation of white rice, kala and two white chickens by the town chief and community members.

But beneath the celebration was a more personal story: women who say LWEP has allowed them to improve their livelihoods, while also calling for changes they believe could make the support more sustainable.

‘The Money Is Helping Us Send Our Children to School’

For Sao G. Sando, a beneficiary and member of a village savings group, the project’s value goes beyond the money itself.

She said the training has taught women how to save, keep proper records, manage their businesses, and use borrowed funds responsibly.

Sando now sells water and soft drinks while encouraging other women in her savings group to expand their businesses.

For her, one of the clearest signs of the project’s impact is its contribution to children’s education.

“We tell you people thank you because you’re making us able to send our children to school, for them to be educated,” she said.

Sando said women are increasingly taking responsibility for the welfare of their children and households rather than depending entirely on others.

Her experience mirrors that of other beneficiaries who say access to small amounts of capital has allowed them to start or expand businesses and generate income for their families.

But not every woman has received the support.

When the Money Does Not Arrive

Korpu, Chairlady of the Women of Success group, said her members completed the required training and were prepared to invest their grant in their businesses.

Instead, a discrepancy in the payment process has left the group waiting.

According to Korpu, the group was expecting an US$8,000 grant, with an initial payment of US$4,000. However, US$4,000 was entered into the system as the approved amount and was subsequently split, resulting in a payment of US$2,000.

Korpu said the group rejected the amount because it did not correspond with the US$8,000 they had requested.

“We were told that $8,000 would be given to us,” she explained.

She said the delay has been particularly frustrating for members who had already planned businesses around the expected funding, including single mothers and older women.

Colonel Sharman, Chairlady of Women of Substance in Robertsport, said her group is facing a similar situation.

The group has not yet received its grant, despite completing the necessary training.

“We are dying hard for this grant,” Sharman said.

She said the existing village savings system has helped sustain the women while they wait, but the grant would provide additional capital to expand their businesses.

Project Explains Payment Error

An LWEP project representative acknowledged during the meeting that an error occurred in the processing of the Women of Success grant.

The representative explained that the group requested US$8,000, but a fee officer mistakenly entered US$4,000 into the system. That amount was then divided into two payments, resulting in the group receiving US$2,000.

Because of the project’s approval procedures, the technical team could not simply alter the amount without going through the formal process.

The project representative said the group was right to refuse to sign for an amount that did not correspond with its request.

He said formal communication would be sent to the Project Management Unit (PMU) to correct the error and facilitate payment of the appropriate amount.

He expressed hope that the matter could be resolved within the coming month.

For beneficiaries, however, the issue is not only about how much money they receive, but how much time they are given to make the money work.

‘Three Months Is Too Short’

Tarlor N. Kannedy of Togarana Savings Club in Gwonzudwa said the three-month repayment period is placing pressure on women whose businesses are affected by seasonal challenges.

She said the women appreciate the assistance but need enough time for their investments to generate returns, particularly during the rainy season when some businesses slow down.

“Even though we have the money, the three months is looking short to us,” Kannedy said.

She called for an extension of the repayment period or a system that would allow beneficiaries to operate through established village savings arrangements.

Under traditional village savings systems, members contribute regularly, borrow money, pay interest and, in some cases, extend repayment by paying additional interest.

Kannedy said such flexibility would allow women to grow their businesses without the constant pressure of a fixed three-month deadline.

“Even though it brings happiness to us, it brings tension to us in other ways,” she said.

Small Businesses, Big Responsibilities

For other women, the money has already produced visible changes.

Massa J. Fahbulla said she invested in the dry-fish business and uses the income to support her children, including paying school expenses and providing food.

Other beneficiaries reported investing in petty shops, cold-water businesses, dry goods and fishing.

A beneficiary from Toso United Savings Club said he received 25,000 Liberian dollars from his group and used it to purchase fishing nets.

He said the investment has helped him expand his fishing activities and repay the money within the first three months.

Massa J. Fahbulla said her group has also used project funds to provide loans to members and generate interest, allowing the money to circulate among women who need capital.

For these women, the project money is not simply cash received and spent. It is capital that must be managed, repaid, and reinvested.

Village Savings: A Lifeline Beyond the Grant

Across Grand Cape Mount County, women repeatedly pointed to village savings groups as one of the strongest foundations supporting their economic activities.

Some groups have existed for years, allowing members to save regularly, borrow money, pay interest, and reinvest their earnings.

Estella Nkenene, Chairlady of a village savings group in Robertsport, said her group has operated for about five years.

She explained that members contribute regularly and loans are given to trusted members based on their ability to repay.

When LWEP funds arrived, the group created a separate system to protect and manage the project money.

Nkenene said the group has generated interest by lending the money to members and is using the proceeds to increase the amount available for women.

“We don’t look at the project money as free money,” she said. “We will be checking on you.”

For Nkenene, accountability is essential because the money must continue benefiting women beyond the first cycle of beneficiaries.

Training Beyond the Money

Beneficiaries said the impact of LWEP extends beyond financial assistance.

Hawa Balla of Togetherness Savings Club said training taught members how to manage money, avoid using funds for prohibited activities and invest in productive businesses.

She said members returned from training and shared the lessons with others in their communities.

Another village savings leader said the project also provided training on climate-smart agricultural practices, including soil fertility, crop rotation and the use of organic materials to improve farming.

The women said the training has helped them think differently about managing businesses, savings and household income.

A Project Built Around Women’s Economic Empowerment

Abdullai Sheriff, Lead Service Provider Manager for LWEP, said the project is a five-year Government of Liberia initiative implemented through the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection with financing from the World Bank.

He said the project is expected to run until June 2027 and is being implemented across six counties and 498 communities.

According to Sheriff, the project has an overall financing envelope of approximately US$44.6 million, including US$18 million allocated for grants.

He said LWEP is expected to reach approximately 267,200 people through interventions covering livelihoods, grants, gender-based violence prevention and response, education, community participation and accountability.

Sheriff encouraged beneficiaries to use the project’s grievance redress mechanisms to report complaints and seek solutions.

“We are here for you,” he told the beneficiaries, encouraging them to share their experiences, concerns and recommendations.

Who Is Behind LWEP ?

The Liberia Women Empowerment Project is a Government of Liberia initiative funded by the World Bank and implemented through the Ministry of Gender, Children and Social Protection (MGCSP).

The project is designed to strengthen the social and economic empowerment of women and girls by improving access to livelihoods and basic services, addressing harmful social norms, preventing and responding to gender-based violence, strengthening community participation and building institutional capacity.

Plan International Liberia serves as the Lead Service Provider, working with a consortium of partners that includes Catholic Relief Services (CRS), ActionAid Liberia, Medica Liberia, Defence for Children International (DCI), Foundation for Community Initiatives (FCI), Kids Educational Engagement Project (KEEP), Raising Voices, Women NGO Secretariat of Liberia (WONGOSOL) and VIAMO.

The project is being implemented in Montserrado, Bomi, Gbarpolu, Grand Cape Mount, River Cess and Grand Gedeh counties.

Its interventions include support for women-led businesses, Village Savings and Loan Associations, farmer-based organizations, grants, community mobilization, gender-based violence prevention and response, education and institutional strengthening.

From the Community to the Health Center

The technical review did not end with community meetings.

The delegation also visited a health facility in Robertsport, where members interacted with doctors, nurses and other health authorities.

Health workers discussed challenges affecting services for survivors of gender-based violence and other vulnerable community members.

The engagement provided the World Bank, MGCSP and project partners with an opportunity to hear directly from frontline health workers about gaps in service delivery and the needs of survivors.

Superintendent Welcomes Delegation

Grand Cape Mount County Superintendent Hon. Foley J. Kiatamba welcomed the World Bank, MGCSP and LWEP delegation to the county.

Kiatamba acknowledged the presence of government officials, development partners, community leaders and beneficiaries, saying the county appreciated the visit and the opportunities created through the project.

He assured the delegation of the county’s welcome and support.

Beyond the Numbers

For the women gathered in Tosor, the field visit was more than a routine project review.

It became a rare opportunity for beneficiaries to speak openly about what is working, what is not, and what they believe needs to change.

For some women, the project has already become school fees, food on the table, fishing nets, petty shops and growing businesses.

For others, the promised support remains just that — promised.

And for those who have received the funds, the message is equally clear: the opportunity matters, but three months may not be enough time to turn a small investment into sustainable income.

The women are not simply asking for money.

They are asking for time, flexibility, and a system that allows the opportunity they have been given to grow.

World.title: Lungu eyes first silverware with Pirates
World.content:
Chipolopolo forward Gamphani Lungu will be seeking his first silverware with South African giants Orlando Pirates when they face Mamelodi Sundowns in the MTN8 final this Saturday.

The highly anticipated final will be played at the sold-out Moses Mabhida Stadium at 18:00 hours.

Lungu is expected to feature when Pirates confront Sundowns in what promises to be a thrilling encounter.

The 27-year-old enjoyed good form after joining Pirates from Siwelele FC in June this year before an injury sidelined him for some weeks.

He has scored three goals in six appearances for the Buccaneers.

Lungu is fresh from featuring for Zambia in the back-to-back 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, AFCON, qualifiers against Algeria and Togo last month.

He trekked to South Africa in 2018 when he switched from Power Dynamos to SuperSport United.

Lungu has 17 caps for Zambia since making his debut in 2018.

World.title: Zambia’s Power Capacity Hits 4,722MW, Nearly Double Peak Demand, As Hichilema Warns The Grid Is Lagging
World.content:
Zambia’s installed electricity generation capacity has climbed to 4,722.3 megawatts, up from 3,777MW in 2024 and now nearly twice the country’s peak demand. President Hakainde Hichilema warned, however, that the transmission and distribution network needed to deliver that power is falling behind.

Peak national demand stands at around 2,400MW, Ministry of Energy data show. The gap between what the country can generate and what its grid can carry has become the central test of the energy push under the Grow Zambia Agenda.

The President set out the figures in a speech read on his behalf by Vice-President Mutale Nalumango at the third edition of the Energy Forum for Africa in Lusaka. The forum ran under the theme “Driving a Borderless Energy Future for Africa”.

“I must emphasise that although we have recorded positive gains and investment in the generation space, transmission and distribution space is lagging behind,” he said.

The President said the rise in generation has been driven by efforts to diversify the energy mix, particularly through increased investment in solar, thermal generation and battery energy storage.

Solar has led the charge. Installed solar capacity has risen almost six-fold, from 178MW in 2024 to 1,027.5MW, overtaking the 2026 target of 1,000MW. Solar photovoltaic generation now accounts for about 21.76 per cent of installed capacity, up from roughly five per cent in 2024.

He said the growth shows what can be achieved when policy direction, private investment, project development, financing and implementation are brought together.

The increase comes as Government pursues a target of 10,000MW under the Grow Zambia Agenda. The President said that target should not be viewed as an isolated energy ambition, but as a platform for the country’s wider economic transformation.

Reliable, adequate and affordable electricity, he said, is needed across agriculture, mining, manufacturing, tourism, irrigation, agro-processing, transport and digital services. He tied the power drive directly to the country’s farming goals.

“If we are to produce 10 million tonnes of maize, we need electricity for irrigation, mechanisation, storage, milling and processing,” he said.

Mining faces the same dependence. Expanding copper production and mineral value addition, the President said, will require dependable electricity for mines, concentrators, smelters and manufacturing.

For that reason, he said, the energy strategy should be measured not only by the number of megawatts added to the grid, but by the economic activity the additional power makes possible.

To close the gap, the President urged cooperating partners, the private sector and other stakeholders to prioritise investment in transmission and distribution infrastructure. Strengthening the grid, he said, is necessary so that new power can be evacuated and delivered to households, businesses and productive sectors.

He also looked beyond Zambia’s borders. Stronger cooperation among African countries, he said, is critical to cross-border electricity trade, and a borderless energy future would allow countries to share power during shortages while supporting industrialisation and growth.

Private capital is already moving in that direction. Global commodities trader Trafigura Group and partners agreed to build a US$300 million high-voltage transmission line linking Zambia’s grid to the Copperbelt of the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC).

The 200-kilometre Kalumbila–Kolwezi Interconnector Project will enable imports of up to 700MW to the DRC’s mining and industrial centres in Katanga and strengthen its connection to the Southern African Power Pool. The design allows capacity to be raised to more than a gigawatt. The project, approved on the Zambian side last year, will also link to a substation at First Quantum Minerals‘ Sentinel mine in Kalumbila.

The DRC’s Strategic Investment Fund, electricity trader EnPower and Gridworks Development Partners, part of British International Investment, plan to take equity, with Trafigura arranging a large share of the debt financing.

Gridworks chief executive officer Chris Flavin said both countries stand to benefit. “Zambia and the DRC both stand to benefit from closer interconnection, and this project will give the Copperbelt access to reliable, competitively priced power and lay the foundation for further cross-border transmission investment,” he said.

He added that the line would not serve the mines alone. “While the project is anchored by mining offtake, there is capacity on the line to serve the wider population.”

At the forum, Stanbic Bank Zambia chief executive officer Mwindwa Siakalima said financial institutions have a critical role in bridging the gap between energy ambition and actual project implementation.

“An integrated regional market can move power from areas of surplus to areas of deficit, strengthen energy security and unlock the investment needed to drive growth,” he said.

Energy Permanent Secretary for Electricity Arnold Simwaba called on investors holding signed implementation and power purchase agreements to move to the ground and begin their projects. Several projects are advancing towards implementation and financial close, he said, but commitments must translate into actual projects.

Regional projects could add more. Zambezi River Authority dam management services engineer Patrick Sipatela said regional cooperation could unlock more than 5,000MW of renewable energy. That includes the 2,400MW Batoka Gorge hydro-electric scheme, which has advanced to procurement preparedness, and the 1,000MW Kariba floating solar project, whose pre-feasibility studies have been completed.

Zimbabwe’s Minister of Energy and Power Development, July Moyo, told the forum that African countries must invest in inter-connectors so that power can move across borders.

With generation now well ahead of demand, Government’s next measure of progress is the grid. The President’s call to prioritise transmission and distribution now sits with cooperating partners, financiers and private investors.

World.title: Chitala Declares August Election Not Credible, Calls For Unity Government And Audit Of 13,529 Polling Stations
World.content:
Zambia Research Foundation director Dr Mbita Chitala declared the August 13 general election not credible, warning that the vote has left the country fractured. He called for a government of national unity to heal what he described as the deep governance wounds the election inflicted on the nation.

In a statement setting out his case, Dr Chitala, a co-founder of the MMD in 1990, listed a series of failures he said had compromised the polls. He cited a six-hour blackout at the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ), reports of stolen ballots in Mandevu Constituency, tear gas lobbed into a vote tallying centre in Kabwe and a variance of more than 800,000 votes.

Those failures, he said, warranted an independent audit of all 13,529 polling stations.

The central charge in his statement concerns the closure of the courts during the window for challenging the presidential result. Dr Chitala placed the shutdown above every other grievance arising from the election.

“The closure of all courts on 24th August 2026 during the seven-day petition window under Article 103 is the most urgent constitutional crisis,” he said.

He added that the challenge had to take an unusual route. “A petition was filed electronically through Chief Justice Mumba Malila after physical filing became impossible.”

Governance activist Brebner Changala turned the same issue on the legal profession. He accused the Law Association of Zambia (LAZ) of abetting a breach of the Constitution by remaining silent on the closure of superior courts during the seven days allowed for filing the presidential petition.

Mr Changala demanded full disclosure on who ordered the shutdown at a time when the opposition was expected to file its challenge to the disputed election.

“I am asking for full clarity and disclosure on why the courts were closed at a critical moment of a seven-day requirement by the Republican Constitution for filing a presidential petition,” he said.

The activist described the closure as an assault on the Judiciary by the Executive that weakens the separation of powers. He said the lawyers’ body had failed in its duty.

“LAZ, as defender of the rule of law, should have condemned the abrupt closure of the Judiciary which botched the electoral process,” Mr Changala said.

He also questioned the decision by Chief Justice Dr Mumba Malila to swear in President Hakainde Hichilema while acknowledging that a petition was before the Constitutional Court. Administering the presidential oath with a petition pending, he said, was a serious constitutional violation, and the only proper course would be for Dr Malila to resign on moral grounds.

Mr Changala pointed to former Chief Justice Matthew Ngulube, who resigned on principle, and commended Judge Catherine Makungu for stepping aside to preserve institutional credibility. In his view, the Judiciary under its current leadership is compromised, its integrity now on trial, while the international community closely monitors developments.

Beyond the polls themselves, Dr Chitala raised concerns about what he called the selective prosecution of opponents. He cited the 2024 conviction of Patriotic Front (PF) secretary general Raphael Nakacinda for defaming the President after the offence had been repealed.

He also linked the rising tension to two further developments. The first is what he described as the assassination of former Minister of Transport and Communication Mutotwe Kafwaya. The second is the post-election treason charges against National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP) leader Brian Mundubile and his running mate Makebi Zulu.

To support his case, Dr Chitala drew on reports by Human Rights Watch, Freedom House and a UN Rapporteur on the restriction of opposition rallies under the Public Order Act and the harassment of journalists. He also questioned judicial independence following the suspension of three Constitutional Court judges in September 2024.

Having set out the problem, the former MMD founder turned to the remedy. He said his statement was intended to provide a factual framework for dialogue, truth and reform, and was inspired by Chipata Bishop George Lungu‘s call for reconciliation.

His proposal is an eight-pillar national reconciliation and constitutional restoration process. It would cover political dialogue, a review of political prisoners, independent electoral fact-finding, constitutional justice, security-sector neutrality, electoral reform, a national compact and a government of national unity modelled on those formed in Zimbabwe and South Africa.

Dr Chitala was clear that such a process could not become a cover for wrongdoing. Reconciliation, he said, should not mean impunity, but must follow truth, justice, reconciliation and reform.

His intervention comes amid high political tension after the August 13 vote. That tension has been fed by the treason charges against Mr Mundubile and Mr Zulu, the killing of Mr Kafwaya and unresolved grievances over the stoppage of vote counting and results announcements, as well as the closure of courts as the opposition prepared to challenge the presidential result.

The demands for an audit, a reconciliation process and answers on the courts closure now stand before the Government. President Hichilema addresses Parliament on Friday

World.title: M’membe Says Renegotiated US$1.5 Billion Health Deal Leaves Zambia Chained To Foreign Aid
World.content:
Socialist Party president Dr Fred M’membe rejected the UPND administration’s US$1.5 billion health compact with the United States, saying the removal of contested clauses on biological specimen sharing and data exploitation does not free Zambia from foreign dependency. He also demanded that the Ministry of Health publish the full agreement.

In a statement, Dr M’membe said the Government’s celebration of the deal confirmed a leadership “completely devoid of Pan African and revolutionary vision”. Zambians, he said, were being asked to applaud a renegotiation instead of a clean break from aid dependency.

The opposition leader was responding to claims by Health Minister Prof Roma Chilengi that the Government had “negotiated away” the most objectionable conditions in the compact. Those provisions, covering the sharing of biological specimens and the use of health data, had drawn months of public anger before the revised terms were announced.

For Dr M’membe, the changes do not alter the nature of the arrangement. “Let us be completely clear: renegotiating the terms of our dependency does not make us free,” he said.

He accused the Government of failing to understand what he called Western transaction aid, or of choosing to ignore its nature. In his view, sovereignty cannot be secured by bargaining over conditions one clause at a time.

“True sovereignty cannot be bargained for in bits and pieces,” he said.

The Socialist Party leader pointed to Ghana and Zimbabwe as countries that took a different path. Both, he said, refused to compromise their national dignity over conditional Western compacts, because their leaders understood that the health data and sovereignty of their citizens were not commodities for the global market.

Zambia, by contrast, was behaving “like a desperate sub-contractor” under the current administration, Dr M’membe said. He described the Government as celebrating that the chains had been padded rather than broken.

Having set out the party’s objection in principle, the statement turned to three specific demands on the Government.

The first is full disclosure. The party called on the Ministry of Health to immediately publish the complete, unedited Memorandum of Understanding. Dr M’membe said the public had a right to know exactly what structural alignments and long-term policies Zambia had committed to in exchange for the money.

The second concerns the country’s natural resources. The party said it would remain vigilant against any attempt by foreign powers to use health aid as a Trojan horse to secure backdoor access to Zambia’s copper, cobalt and wider mineral wealth.

The third demand goes to the structure of the funding itself. Dr M’membe described the US$1.5 billion, spread over five years, as an “ad-hoc band-aid” that would keep Zambia’s clinics and hospitals permanently reliant on the shifting political whims of Washington.

Beyond criticising the compact, the statement laid out how the Socialist Party would approach health financing. Dr M’membe said the party would not go cap-in-hand begging global powers to fund the health of Zambian children and the wider population.

“True health security is built on national self-reliance,” he said.

Under the party’s plan, public healthcare would be funded by stopping tax evasion by multinational mining corporations. The recovered revenue and the country’s own mineral wealth would then be reinvested directly into Zambian doctors, Zambian laboratories and local manufacturing.

That position ties the health compact to the party’s wider case on mining revenue. Where the Government presents the US$1.5 billion as support for the health sector, the Socialist Party presents domestic mineral wealth as the alternative source that would remove the need for conditional foreign funding.

Dr M’membe closed the statement with a call for a different measure of national progress. “We must stop measuring our national success by the size of the foreign grants we receive and start measuring it by our ability to stand on our own two feet,” he said.

The Socialist Party’s demand for the complete, unedited Memorandum of Understanding now stands before the Ministry of Health, alongside its call for public disclosure of every long-term policy commitment attached to the US$1.5 billion compact

World.title: K1 Bet Pays Out K634,053 for Zambian Farmer
World.content:
LUSAKA, Zambia: A K1 bet has paid out K634,053.60 for a farmer in Kalomo District, after all 14 of his selections came in on betPawa.

Clever’s betslip had 14 selections at combined odds of 409,066.84. On its own it returned K409,065.84. The betPawa Win Bonus then added K224,986.76, a 55% increase on his winnings.

The Win Bonus grows as more qualifying selections are added to a betslip, up to 1250%, and every selection has to win for the bet to pay out.

Clever built the bet on a Friday night using Japanese league matches, a choice his wife found funny at the time. He was working in his field the next morning when betPawa called to tell him he had won.

“I could not believe it. I had to breathe and check,” he said.

He has put part of the money into fertiliser and supplies for the winter maize season.

“People think this is fake, but it is real,” he said. “Bet small, and you never know what could happen.”

World.title: Milk boosts Romase school attendance in Lundazi
World.content:
School attendance at Lundazi’s Romase Primary School has significantly increased following the government’s initiative of introducing milk to the school feeding programme for the early child learners.

School headteacher, Henry Banda, told the media in an interview that the move has also prompted parents to approach the school administration with the request to have their children enrolled outside the enrollment school calendar.

“Eight parents came to the school to request the school to admit their children in Pre-school so that they can also benefit from the fresh milk sachets that the school is providing to the learners,” Mr Banda said.

He has since commended the Government for the initiative, adding that not every home has all the food requirements.

Mr Banda said the school anticipates high enrolment levels this November for next year’s Early Childhood learners.

“As a school, we would be very happy if enrolment levels will be increased next year as it would be a step in the right direction, reducing illiteracy levels in the District,” he said.

He further urged the government not to relent in providing food to the learners.

And an Early Childhood Education (ECE) teacher, Mwanida Banda, said class attendance has improved after milk sachets were introduced to the ECE learners late last term.

Ms Banda added that pupils no longer report late for school and that absenteeism due to sickness has also reduced.

“Since the introduction of milk to the ECE learners, I have noticed that concentration in class has improved as well as general body health for the children,” Ms Banda noted.

World.title: ZCCM-IH approves new KCM tailings leach plant in Chingola
World.content:
ZCCM-Investments Holdings Plc (ZCCM-IH) has approved a 498 million United States Dollar Tailings Leach Plant at Konkola Copper Mines (KCM)’s Nchanga operation in Chingola.

The approval means that ZCCM-IH which holds a 20.6 percent stake in KCM has given the firm a go ahead to proceed with implementation of the project.

ZCCM-IH Corporate Affairs Manager, Loisa Mbatha has told the media in a statement that the project will reprocess tailings from the TD5 dam at Nchanga to deliver approximately 70,000 tonnes of copper cathode a year at full capacity.

Ms Mbatha said the plant will be funded by KCM and is outside Vedanta Resources’ initial 1 billion United States dollar investment programme for KCM.

“Importantly, the project will not require any capital contribution from ZCCM-IH, as KCM’s equity contribution will be financed from internally generated resources,” she said.

Meanwhile, ZCCM-IH Chief Executive Officer, Kakenenwa Muyangwa described Nchanga’s tailings as one of the largest secondary copper resources in Africa.

Mr Muyangwa said the project will support the Grow Zambia Agenda by contributing to the 3 million metric tonnes target of copper production per annum by 2031.

He pointed out that the project will allow KCM to acquire copper from existing resources without mining a single tonne of the mineral.

“Using the latest technology, this plant turns them into around 70,000 tonnes of LME Grade A cathode a year without mining a single new tonne of ore. It is exactly the growth we want across our portfolio. It means more copper from assets that already exist, in support of Zambia’s path to 3 million tonnes and the Grow Zambia agenda,” Mr Muyangwa said.

The project is expected to be constructed in two years following KCM’s decision to sign a 498 million United States dollar engineering, procurement and construction agreement with China NERIN Engineering last month.

World.title: Mwanakampwe calls for investment in rain, underground water harvesting
World.content:
Central Province Permanent Secretary, Milner Mwanakampwe, has called for investment in rain and underground water harvesting to mitigate the impact of climate change on the livestock sector.

Dr Mwanakampwe says water harvesting should be prioritised to safeguard the future of the livestock sector and contribute to the Grow Zambia Agenda of beef exports.

Provincial Permanent Secretary was speaking when a delegation from the German International Cooperation paid a courtesy call on him in Kabwe.

“We need to harvest rain water to ensure our livestock is safe in the time of drought. We can also use the same water for gardening,” he said.

Dr Mwanakampwe noted that rain water has continued going to waste because of lack of investment in appropriate water harvesting infrastructure.

He therefore stressed the need for cooperating partners to support the government’s efforts in mitigating the effects of climate change.

Dr Mwanakampwe said water harvesting is one of the measures that could be undertaken to mitigate the effects of climate change.

“As provincial administration, we look forward to continuous collaboration with cooperating partners in water harvesting in Central Province. Districts like Mumbwa are prone to drought,” he said.

He also noted that the livestock sector can only be safeguarded from climatic shocks through the harvest of rain and underground water.

World.title: South Africa: Anti-Immigration Groups Disrupt Home Affairs - South African News Briefs - October 8, 2026
World.content:
press review

Anti-Immigration Groups Vow to Disrupt Durban Home Affairs Centre

Anti-illegal immigration groups have vowed to continue disrupting operations at the Home Affairs Refugee Reception Centre in Durban, reports EWN. About 1,000 foreign nationals seeking asylum and other immigration services were chased away by demonstrators carrying sticks and sjamboks. The protests follow a Home Affairs directive allowing all foreign nationals to apply for asylum, regardless of their legal status. This comes after a Constitutional Court ruling found restrictions on such applications unconstitutional.

10 Killed in Minibus Taxi Crash in Durban

Ten people have died in a minibus taxi accident on the MR385 Road in Cato Ridge, Durban, reports SABC News. Preliminary reports indicate the taxi lost control and collided with a tree. The KwaZulu-Natal Department of Transport said that a Road Traffic Inspectorate and road safety team have been deployed to the area. Increased traffic law enforcement is planned across the province during Transport Month.

State Links AKA Murder Weapon to Accused

The State has begun presenting its case in the murder trial of rapper Kiernan "AKA" Forbes and Tebello "Tibz" Motsoane by seeking to link the alleged murder weapon to the accused, reports EWN. Seven men are on trial at the Durban High Court over the February 2023 killings. The first witness, a retired police officer, testified about a firearm recovered after a May 2022 shooting in Mayville, which the State says was later linked to the AKA and Tibz murders.
