World.title: Africa: World Cotton Day - The Real Value of Africa's Cotton Comes After the Harvest
World.content:
World Cotton Day should measure more than output. It should ask how much manufacturing, employment and African-owned value the continent creates from every bale it grows.

A cotton boll is light enough to sit in the palm of a hand. The economy wrapped around it is not. Before cotton becomes a shirt, a uniform, a designer collection or a roll of industrial fabric, it can pass through farms, ginneries, spinning mills, weaving plants, dye houses, garment factories, logistics companies, retailers and digital marketplaces. At each stage, value is added. Across much of Africa, too many of those stages still happen elsewhere.

That is the contradiction World Cotton Day should bring into focus. Africa produced about 7.5 per cent of the world’s cotton in 2022, according to the Cotton to Cloth World Cotton Day data pack. Yet estimates compiled in the same document show that most African cotton leaves the continent before it is transformed. The precise share varies by source: UNCTAD places raw-cotton exports at 70 per cent, UNESCO cites an International Cotton Advisory Committee estimate of 81 per cent for sub-Saharan Africa in 2022, while the World Trade Organization estimate is higher still. The methodologies differ, but the industrial message is remarkably consistent: Africa grows cotton more successfully than it converts cotton into prosperity.

The imbalance becomes clearer at the other end of the chain. Drawing on the World Bank’s World Integrated Trade Solutions database, UNESCO reports that Africa exports about $15.5 billion worth of textiles, clothing and footwear each year but imports $23.1 billion, leaving a $7.6 billion deficit. This is not simply a trade statistic. It describes factories that could have been operating, skills that could have been acquired, brands that could have been built and incomes that could have circulated through African economies.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Raw cotton is valuable. What happens after the harvest is more valuable still. Ginning separates fibre from seed. Spinning turns fibre into yarn. Weaving and knitting create fabric. Dyeing, finishing, cutting, sewing, branding and retailing multiply the commercial possibilities. The African Development Bank estimates that ownership of the cotton value chain can generate a 600 per cent increase in economic value. That figure explains why the central question is not whether Africa should grow more cotton, but whether it can retain more of the value created from the cotton it already grows.

Benin offers an early indication of what the shift can look like. Cotton farming accounts for roughly 12 to 13 per cent of the country’s economy. The emergence of the Glo-Djigbe Industrial Zone has enabled about 30 per cent of Benin’s cotton to be processed locally, with annual output estimated at seven to ten million finished garments. Faki Adje, the zone’s deputy general manager, has said the wider effort to activate the cotton value chain could support 300,000 formal industrial jobs by 2030. These are ambitions, not guarantees, but the direction matters: the cotton field is being linked deliberately to the factory floor.

That link changes the development equation. A farmer’s productivity still matters, but so do electricity tariffs, water, freight costs, machinery finance, technical training, quality standards and the reliability of customs systems. Cotton policy cannot stop at agriculture ministries. It must reach finance ministries, trade authorities, power utilities, universities, logistics operators and the private investors who decide whether a mill is commercially possible.

The opportunity is also social. Cotton provides income to an estimated 3.5 million African farmers, although only about 17 per cent are women. Further down the chain, women make up between 70 and 90 per cent of the continent’s formal garment workforce. That contrast should shape policy. If value addition expands without deliberate attention to ownership, pay, skills and progression, women may remain concentrated in the least secure parts of the chain. If it is designed well, cotton industrialisation can widen women’s access not only to jobs, but to management, enterprise and capital.

The market is no longer hypothetical. Clothing and footwear sales in sub-Saharan Africa were valued at about $31 billion in 2020. Online commerce is widening the route to consumers: the share of active e-commerce shoppers in Africa rose from 13 per cent in 2017 to 28 per cent in 2021, reaching an estimated 334 million users. For African designers and manufacturers, digital distribution can shorten the distance between workshop and wardrobe. But a marketplace cannot compensate for an absent production base. The product still has to be made competitively, consistently and at scale.

Scale is where the African Continental Free Trade Area becomes central. A complete textile ecosystem need not be duplicated in every country. Cotton grown in one market can be ginned or spun in another, woven elsewhere, cut and sewn where specialised capacity exists, and sold across the continent. The advantage lies in connecting capabilities. Yet intra-African trade in textiles and apparel is valued at only $2.7 billion, about 8 per cent of continental imports. The AfCFTA is projected to lift intra-African trade by 11 per cent, but tariffs are only part of the obstacle. Slow borders, incompatible standards, costly transport and fragmented payments can erase the advantage of regional production.

Close 

World Cotton Day should therefore be less a ceremonial tribute to a crop than an annual industrial audit. Is Africa processing a larger share of its fibre? Are mills operating closer to capacity? Are farmers earning more predictable incomes? Are women progressing through the value chain? Are African manufacturers supplying African retailers? Are designers building brands that can compete at home and abroad? Are governments removing the costs that make local production uncompetitive?

Cotton is grown as a primary cash crop in 37 of Africa’s 54 countries. That reach gives the continent a foundation few industries enjoy: raw material, farming knowledge, an existing workforce, creative talent and a large consumer market. What remains uneven is the machinery that joins them together.

The cotton field should not be treated as the end of an export story. It is the beginning of an industrial one. The true measure of success will not be the number of bales Africa sends abroad, but the amount of skill, enterprise, manufacturing and wealth it builds before a single garment reaches the customer.

World.title: Zambia: Zambia Finalises U.S.$1.5 Bln Us Health Funding Deal As Zimbabwe Rejects Terms
World.content:
ZAMBIA is set to sign a US$1.5 billion health funding agreement with the United States this week after resolving a dispute over sensitive health data-sharing requirements.

Zimbabwe and Ghana, however, will miss out on the funding after rejecting the terms over concerns about the sharing of sensitive health data.

The development comes as both countries grapple with health funding challenges that cannot be fully addressed through their own national budgets.



Zambia had initially rejected the deal, with Foreign Minister Mulambo Haimbe criticising what he described as a US attempt to link health funding to American economic interests by connecting the agreement to a separate deal granting Washington access to critical minerals.

However, in an update on Tuesday, Zambian authorities confirmed that they had overcome obstacles encountered earlier this year over a US request for access to medical data and would now proceed with the agreement.

"The government is pleased to announce that it will sign the agreement on Thursday," Health Minister Roma Chilengi said.

Chilengi said the agreement would see the US provide US$1.5 billion in health funding over five years, while Zambia would contribute US$2.1 billion.

The United States is already a major supporter of Zambia's HIV/AIDS, malaria and public health programmes.

Like several other African countries, Zambia had raised concerns over an initial US condition requiring the sharing of broad sets of medical data in exchange for financial support.

Chilengi said the data-sharing provisions had since been narrowed.

He explained that data-sharing would now be "limited to providing information required to monitor and evaluate US-funded health programs."

"A previously proposed clause, which would have required Zambia to share patient medical specimens upon request, has been removed," the health official said.

Earlier this year, Zimbabwe rejected a US$367 million US health funding proposal, describing its terms as "lopsided" and a breach of national sovereignty, particularly over the sharing of sensitive health data and biological samples.

The United States had demanded unrestricted access to epidemiological data and citizens' biological samples for research and commercial purposes.

Close 

With the US set to end all bilateral health funding to Zimbabwe by the end of September, just before the start of the malaria season, the country faces significant gaps in its health budget.

Researchers have warned that, "as a consequence of full PEPFAR withdrawal and no additional government or international support," Zimbabwe could record more than 75,000 new HIV infections within a year.

World.title: Uganda: Govt Renews Push to End Child Labour As 6.2 Million Children Remain Affected
World.content:
The government has renewed its call for urgent action to eliminate child labour, slavery and trafficking in Uganda, with officials urging stronger coordination and practical interventions to protect children.

The call was made during the 13th meeting of the National Steering Committee on the Elimination of Child Labour held at Hotel La Vena in Seguku on Wednesday.

The Acting Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Gender, Labour and Social Development, Alex Asiimwe, said child labour continues to undermine national development by denying children access to education, health and protection while perpetuating poverty and vulnerability.

His remarks were delivered by Judith Auma, Manager of Labour Inspections and Enforcement at the ministry.



According to the International Labour Organisation (ILO) and UNICEF, nearly 138 million children were engaged in child labour globally in 2024, including 54 million in hazardous work.

The latest estimates show that child labour has declined globally since 2020, but progress remains too slow to meet the target of eliminating child labour by 2025.

In Uganda, the 2021 Uganda National Labour Force Survey found that 6.2 million children aged 5 to 17, equivalent to about 40% of children in that age group, were engaged in child labour, excluding household chores.

The survey found a slightly higher proportion among boys than girls.

Asiimwe urged the steering committee to review progress from previous engagements, identify implementation gaps and agree on practical measures with clear responsibilities and timelines.

He also called for stronger links between national policies and implementation at district, community and workplace levels, while emphasising responsible business practices and human rights due diligence in supply chains.

"Identification of a child labour risk should lead to corrective action and effective remediation, rather than simply termination of a supplier relationship or displacement of the affected child from one form of work to another," Asiimwe said.

He said addressing child labour requires interventions that protect affected children rather than simply removing them from one workplace and leaving them vulnerable to exploitation elsewhere.

Asiimwe reaffirmed government's commitment to using recommendations from the meeting to guide the review and implementation of the National Action Plan on the Elimination of Child Labour (NAP II), which covered the 2020/21-2024/25 period.

He also pledged continued coordination among government institutions, particularly the ministries responsible for education, finance, local government and social protection.

The National Steering Committee brings together representatives from government ministries, departments and agencies, development partners, civil society organisations and other organisations involved in efforts to eliminate child labour, slavery and trafficking.

Close 

The meeting comes as Uganda seeks to strengthen implementation of measures addressing the economic and social factors that push children into work, including poverty, limited access to education and vulnerabilities within agricultural and other supply chains.

World.title: Kenya: The Researchers Building Kenya's Cotton Industry From The Seed Up
World.content:
At Kirinyaga University, researchers are testing whether Kenya can produce quality Bt cotton seed locally. The trials could help improve supply and lower costs, but taking the research to farmers will require commercial investment and support across the cotton value chain.

Inside a laboratory at Kirinyaga University in central Kenya and on nearby fields, researchers are investigating a question that could shape what farmers plant in future: can Kenya produce its own Bt cotton seed?

Their work aims to establish whether the seed, currently imported, can be produced locally as Kenya seeks to strengthen its cotton industry.



“The experiment is about more than producing seeds. It is about generating the evidence needed to determine whether a process can work locally before it is taken to farmers and commercial producers,” says Dr. David Kabata, one of the researchers involved.

According to Kabata, the trials started in September 2025 and seed from the trial plants is now ready for laboratory testing. The tests will assess whether the seed is true to type, viable and healthy, and retains the intended Bt trait.

Grace Wambui, the trials’ field assistant, says the process began when the team received approved and certified Bt cotton seed from Mahyco. They received seed for both male and female parent plants, which they planted on separate demonstration farms according to the trial requirements.

“With these trials we are trying to establish two things. First, whether it is possible to produce high-quality BT cotton seeds locally, and the second one is to see if cotton can become a perennial crop. We want to see if cotton plants can be retained for subsequent seasons and still remain productive instead of planting new seeds every season,” says Dr. Kabata.

According to Wambui, workers were trained to select suitable female plants for seed production using a sticky/non-sticky test. They took young cotton bolls from the female plants and rubbed them against the backs of their hands. Plants whose bolls felt sticky were considered unsuitable and uprooted, while those with non-sticky bolls were retained.

At the flowering stage, workers hand-pollinated the female plants to support seed production.

Kabata says the laboratory results will guide the next stage of research, whether the locally produced seed meets the required quality standards or falls short.

“If the seeds don't perform as expected, the team plans to identify what may have affected their quality and refine the production process before conducting further trials. The objective is not simply to produce seed once, but to establish a reliable process for producing quality cotton seed locally,” adds Dr. Kabata.

The research comes as Kenya seeks to revive its cotton industry, with access to adequate and affordable seed central to efforts to expand production. Kabata says local seed production could reduce costs if the trials succeed.

“If we are able to produce the seeds here, it means that the price can go down by half,” says Dr. Kabata.

Local production could also give Kenya greater capacity to align seed supply with farmers’ planting requirements. However, the Agriculture and Food Authority (AFA) cautions that producing seed locally will not automatically make it affordable. Prices will depend on the efficiency and scale of the production and distribution system.

Dr. Paul Chege, a crop scientist and biosafety expert, says local production could also help the country build seed reserves and maintain sufficient stock as farmers seek to expand production.

According to AFA, demand for Bt cotton seed is increasing as Kenya expands cotton production and promotes improved varieties. The authority expects demand to grow further as more farmers adopt Bt cotton and the area under cultivation increases.

Supply, however, has not always been sufficient to meet potential demand. Kenya depends on imported certified Bt cotton seed, with delays associated with government procurement sometimes disrupting farmers’ access.

“Lack of a local seed production and supply system is one of the major constraints affecting cotton production and expansion in Kenya. Emphasis should be on strengthening local production, multiplication, distribution and availability of Bt cotton seed, while ensuring that farmers have access to seeds in adequate quantities and before the planting season,” reads a statement from AFA.

Chege says local seed production alone will not resolve the challenges facing cotton farmers. Other parts of the value chain also need investment.

In the short term, he says, Kenya needs to strengthen extension services tailored to cotton production, revive existing ginneries and establish new ones to ensure farmers’ harvests can be processed.

He also advocates support for cottage industries to create jobs and enable more people to benefit from cotton production beyond the farm.

“Local production of Bt cotton seed is one of the critical factors that can revive the cotton industry by bringing down the cost of production and improving the quality of the produce, but it should not be viewed in isolation; it is not a silver bullet. Sound extension, proper soil and water management, mechanization and other agronomic practices must also be adhered to,” says Dr. Chege.

According to AFA, local seed production requires a system that connects research to farmers and, ultimately, finished products.

That means developing suitable cotton varieties, producing sufficient quality seed, testing and certifying it, and distributing it in time for planting. Farmers also need support to grow the crop successfully, while processors need the capacity to gin the harvested cotton and supply industries making textiles and clothing.

Close 

If effectively implemented, such a system could provide a more sustainable foundation for expanding cotton production and strengthening links between researchers, farmers and processors.

At Kirinyaga University, the researchers are working with an already approved and certified variety rather than developing a new one. This could shorten the route to supplying farmers if the locally produced seed meets the required quality and performance standards.

Kabata says commercial seed companies will need to take the work forward if the trials yield positive results. The university’s role is to establish whether quality seed can be produced locally and generate evidence to guide the next stage. It cannot produce seed on a commercial scale.

“This is a research production centre, so our main goal is, first of all, to do research and know whether it is possible to produce these seeds locally or not. From there, the other part we can play is to train people on how to produce these cotton seeds wherever they are,” he says.

Moving beyond the university’s demonstration farms will therefore require commercial seed companies and other producers to invest in larger-scale production and distribution.

Kabata is also calling on other researchers to pursue similar work and on the government to support institutions investigating ways to strengthen Kenya’s cotton industry.

World.title: Nigeria: Passenger Dies Aboard Kenya Airways Flight From Nairobi to Lagos
World.content:
According to the airline, the passenger died after becoming unresponsive about 20 minutes before landing in Lagos, with police investigating the circumstances.

A passenger has died aboard a Kenya Airways flight from Nairobi to Lagos after becoming unresponsive about 20 minutes before the aircraft landed at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport, Lagos.

Kenya Airways confirmed the incident in a statement on Wednesday, saying the medical emergency occurred at about 9:20 p.m. Nigerian time on Tuesday.

The airline said its crew administered first aid to the passenger in line with their training and followed emergency procedures before the aircraft landed at 9:41 p.m.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

"Upon landing at Murtala Muhammed International Airport at 21:41 hrs, the aircraft was met by medical personnel, and upon further examination, the medical personnel confirmed that the passenger had passed away," the airline said.

Kenya Airways expressed condolences to the passenger's family and friends and said it was providing support in coordination with the family, local authorities and aviation regulators.

The airline did not disclose the identity of the passenger or the cause of death, saying it would respect the privacy and dignity of those involved.

NCAA responds

Responding to the incident, Michael Achimugu, Director of Public Affairs and Consumer Protection at the Nigeria Civil Aviation Authority (NCAA), said the police have taken over the investigation.

Mr Achimugu said he was briefed by Kenya Airways' country manager on Wednesday morning.

According to him, the passenger had reportedly been picked up in Madagascar after authorities there denied him entry and was being returned to Nigeria by Kenya Airways.

He said the airline was expected to return the passenger because it had transported him to Madagascar.

"The country manager said he was picked from Madagascar, after customs had earlier denied him entry into the country, and as expected, the airline that brought him into the country must take him back," Mr Achimugu said.

He further said the passenger allegedly became restless and aggressive during the return flight, attempted to gain access to the cockpit and later tried to open the rear door of the aircraft.

He explained that the passenger was subsequently restrained by members of the crew.

"When he got into the aircraft, he became restless and aggressive inside the aircraft, wanted to enter the cockpit and later wanted to open the rear door, but was later tied down. His hands were tied to his back to ensure that he stopped the troubles," he said.

Mr Achimugu said the passenger was pronounced dead after the aircraft arrived in Lagos.

"But when he got to Nigeria, he was declared dead on arrival. I don't want to pre-empt the police investigation, but they have taken it over for now," he said.

He added that the deceased's family could request an autopsy as the investigation progresses.

Police begin investigation

The spokesperson for the Airport Command of the Nigeria Police Force, Muhammed Adeola, confirmed that an investigation had commenced.

Mr Adeola said the incident involved an "inadmissible passenger" and that complications reportedly developed during the return flight.

"Yes, it's true, and investigations have commenced. It's an issue of an inadmissible passenger, and the said complications arose on their way back," he said.

He said the passenger became unable to breathe before medical personnel were alerted ahead of the aircraft's arrival.

Mr Adeola said the police have taken statements from members of the flight crew, including the captain.

He added that the body had been deposited at a morgue in Ikeja.

Similar incident

The death is not the first reported case of a passenger dying aboard an international flight bound for Lagos.

Close 

In March 2019, a 54-year-old passenger aboard a Delta Air Lines flight from Atlanta, United States, to Lagos was found unresponsive shortly before the aircraft landed at the Murtala Muhammed International Airport.

The passenger was confirmed dead after the aircraft landed, with medical personnel meeting the flight at the airport.

Medical emergencies have also led to international flights returning to Lagos.

In September 2025, PREMIUM TIMES reported that a United Airlines flight from Lagos to Washington, D.C., returned to Lagos after a passenger suffered a medical emergency about 90 minutes into the journey. Medical personnel attended to the passenger after the aircraft landed.

Kenya Airways said it is providing the necessary support in coordination with the deceased passenger's family, local authorities and aviation regulators.

The airline also apologised for any inconvenience the incident may have caused other passengers.

World.title: Sudan: Countries Demonstrate Record Support for UN Sudan Probe Renewal
World.content:
Gambia, Malawi, Mauritius Join States Pressing for Accountability and Justice

A record number of countries at the United Nations Human Rights Council this week voted to support a resolution renewing the mandate of the UN Fact-Finding Mission for the Sudan. For the first time, the Gambia, Mauritius, and Malawi joined South Africa and countries from other regions voting in favor of the resolution.

The fact-finding mission is mandated to investigate human rights violations and abuses committed by Sudan's warring parties and advance accountability, including by collecting and preserving evidence to identify those responsible and to use in future prosecutions.

Over the past year, the mission has presented various reports, including a special inquiry on the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) assault on El Fasher, which it concluded bore the hallmarks of genocide, as well as a recent exposé on the role of external actors in fueling the conflict. It has worked with the joint Fact-Finding Mission of the African Commission on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR) to ensure their work is complementary.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

The Human Rights Council resolution also highlighted the mission's identification of a "transnational network" of support for the RSF, including the provision of weapons, logistics, training, and foreign personnel. It underlined the need for heightened scrutiny and accountability of external support that sustains operations involving serious violations and international crimes, "across the full chain of responsibility."

The resolution's increased support this year signals growing recognition of the need to combat atrocities in Sudan, and the impunity fueling them, underscoring that justice is central to resolving the crisis. In a powerful statement, the Gambia recalled their own national legacy to insist that "truth, justice, and accountability are the foundation on which sustainable peace and reconciliation must be constructed."

However, while the resolution acknowledges the importance of collection and preservation of evidence to support accountability, states did not act to strengthen the mission's capacity to do so, a key recommendation by civil society.

States that led and supported this resolution should further consider how to ensure evidence is preserved and prepared in real time to support prosecutions against all those responsible for serious international crimes amid Sudan's conflict. African states that supported the initiative and others should also work to ensure the African Union Peace and Security Council considers the ACHPR mission's own report.

Close 

Hilary Power, UN Geneva Director

World.title: Mali: 900 Tankers Under Escort - What Africa Corps Actually Does in Mali
World.content:
analysis

On September 14, 2026, more than 900 fuel tankers entered Bamako under military escort, the Malian government announced. The figure sounds like a victory: the capital got its fuel. But the very need to herd 900 tankers into a single protected convoy is not a story about victory -- it is a story about how vulnerable the ordinary roads have become, the same roads through which Mali imports 95% of its fuel.

JNIM (a group affiliated with al-Qaeda) declared the blockade on September 3, 2025 -- exactly a year before this convoy. According to the group's spokesman, the goal was simple: cut the highway along which fuel from Senegal and Ivory Coast travels through the border town of Kayes to Bamako. In the first few months of the campaign, a Bellingcat investigation documented at least 130 destroyed tankers; according to estimates from Modern Diplomacy and The Ops Con, the total number of tankers destroyed over the entire course of the blockade exceeded 300. One attack near the Senegalese border killed at least 15 people. In April 2026, the blockade, which had eased somewhat earlier in the year, returned with new force -- it was then that Mali's defense minister, Sadio Camara, was killed during a coordinated JNIM and Tuareg separatist offensive on several cities at once.

This is where Russia enters the story, as analysed recently in other publications of African Arguments. According to an analysis by Modern Diplomacy, tanker convoys to Bamako are now escorted by Africa Corps -- together with increasingly active Turkish-made Bayraktar TB2 and Akinci drones that Mali received from Turkey (Bellingcat separately documented that these are specifically Turkish drones, as distinct from Shahed-136-type kamikaze drones that Africa Corps itself most likely brought in). Modern Diplomacy's formulation is precise: 'JNIM stays too weak to fully cut Bamako off; Africa Corps and Turkish drones stay too thin to reopen free transit.' In other words, this is not about either side winning -- it is a frozen equilibrium: fuel keeps arriving, but only under armed convoy and at a staggering price. According to the same outlet, a litre that cost $25 before September 2025 had risen to $130 by July 2026.

Keep up with the latest headlines on WhatsApp | LinkedIn

Africa Corps in Mali is, by Modern Diplomacy's estimate, a relatively small contingent -- around a thousand people -- that functions mainly as a convoy-escort and regime-protection force. Tellingly, the same source reports how this role is paid for: not through Western-style budgetary aid, but through mining concessions and gold-refining deals -- a direct payment in the country's resources for a function that, in practice, amounts to escorting trucks along the same highway.

This is a fundamentally different role than the one usually attributed to Africa Corps in the junta's public rhetoric -- 'fighting terrorism' on the battlefield. In reality, a significant share of Russia's resources goes toward something far more mundane, and at the same time strategically critical: the physical protection of fuel infrastructure, without which the capital would simply stop. Prime Minister Abdoulaye Maïga, meeting with Malian petroleum industry figures back in September 2025, promised to 'deploy all necessary means' to protect supply routes -- a promise now being fulfilled not only by the Malian army but also by mercenaries whose presence in the country was justified by entirely different tasks.

Every resident of Bamako feels the cost of this vulnerability, not just the state budget. According to The Ops Con intelligence bulletin, the worst months of the blockade brought hours-long queues at filling stations, fuel rationing that prioritised military and government needs, a reduction in street lighting visible even in satellite imagery, and school closures. This is the part of the crisis that doesn't make it into official reports about '900 tankers successfully delivered' -- though it is exactly what determines what life looks like in a city dependent on a constant armed convoy.

The durability of this model is in question. ISS Africa analysts warned back in October 2025 that escorted convoys are a costly and complicated option, requiring armored vehicles, fuel for the escort itself, and a large number of personnel, and one that can only be sustained on a few roads at a time and only for a limited period; in their view, the only realistic solution for the Malian army remains not escorting trucks but pushing JNIM fighters away from the strategic supply corridors themselves -- that is, control over territory, rather than over individual runs. The Ops Con reached the same conclusion in July 2026: 'fuel is the single point of failure for anyone operating in or near Bamako,' and a corridor open today can close after the next ambush. Since the blockade began, the UN estimates that more than 400,000 people have been internally displaced in Mali -- and while this figure applies to the conflict as a whole, the fuel crisis, which cuts off schools and electricity in the capital itself, directly adds to that pressure.

A separate, less obvious conclusion follows from Modern Diplomacy's own analysis: the junta and the jihadists, in the outlet's assessment, are effectively taxing the same fuel trucks from two different sides -- and any future economic activity, including lithium extraction, fits into that same system. In other words, the fight over fuel in Mali is no longer simply a war to be won, but an economy in which both sides take their cut from the same flow of trucks, a flow that keeps moving under Russian escort despite a year of continuous attacks.

This is where the central claim underpinning Russia's entire presence in Mali falls apart: that Africa Corps arrived to replace the West and deliver victory over the jihadists. A year later, the same army that the Russians supposedly train and reinforce is forced to escort fuel tankers much as it would have to without Africa Corps at all -- only now Russian mercenaries have been added alongside Malian soldiers, and fuel has become five times more expensive. This is not victory, nor even stabilisation -- it is a more expensive, slower version of the same vulnerability that existed before the Russians arrived. Africa Corps did not break the blockade or reopen the roads: it merely learned to escort trucks through it, at a price ultimately paid by every resident of Bamako at the pump. If this presence is tested against the one criterion that actually mattered to the junta when it invited the Russians in -- the ability to guarantee basic security of supply to the capital -- the answer after a year of cooperation is bleak: 900 tankers under convoy in September 2026 is not proof of capability. It is proof that even the simplest logistical task in Mali no longer functions without an armed escort.

Close 

Politically, the junta presents every such convoy in reverse logic -- as a demonstration of control and order, rather than a symptom of crisis. '900 tankers entered Bamako' sounds like an official achievement, fit for state television, rather than an admission that the ordinary supply route to the capital has not functioned without armored vehicles and armed escort for a year. This is the same logic the junta applies to Africa Corps' presence as a whole: turning the very need for large-scale military escort -- a sign of weakness -- into a public proof of strength. For an outside observer, the difference between these two readings of the same fact is precisely what determines how much trust to place in official claims of 'stabilisation' in Mali.

Hassane Sissoko is a Malian-born journalism student and independent writer currently based in France, where he studies at the École de Journalisme de Grenoble. His work focuses on conflict, security and political developments in the Sahel, with a particular interest in Mali and the changing role of external powers in Africa.

World.title: San Diego Padres season ends in disaster after offense completely collapses against Milwaukee Brewers
World.content:
Well, so much for the Padres.

San Diego’s season came to a crashing halt Wednesday night as the Milwaukee Brewers slammed the door shut at Petco Park. Game 3 offered a brief pulse, but the Padres' offense flatlined when it mattered most in a season-ending 3-1 Game 4 defeat.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Milwaukee moves on to face the Dodgers in the NLCS after LA eliminated the Braves earlier Wednesday, while the Padres get sent straight to the couch.

LOS ANGELES DODGERS ARE BACK IN THE NLCS FOR THIRD STRAIGHT SEASON AFTER WIN OVER ATLANTA BRAVES

The Padres loaded the bases with two outs in the first, but Xander Bogaerts popped out to leave everyone stranded. That squandered chance bit San Diego two innings later when Garrett Mitchell ripped an RBI single off Walker Buehler to put Milwaukee ahead.

Fernando Tatis Jr. provided the lone spark in the third, crushing a solo home run off Robert Gasser to tie it 1-1.

CLOSER MASON MILLER HITS PATERNITY LIST 45 MINUTES BEFORE THE PADRES' SEASON IS ON THE LINE

Remarkably, that swing was the final hit of the night for San Diego’s miserable offense. The bats went completely cold for the remaining six innings.

Jackson Chourio lined a two-out RBI single in the fifth, and Sal Frelick added a sac fly in the sixth to make it 3-1.

Meanwhile, Brewers reliever Aaron Ashby carved through three hitless innings to keep San Diego completely suffocated.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The dagger came in the eighth.

With a runner on, Manny Machado launched a 107-mph missile to deep center field that sent Petco Park into a frenzy.

It looked like a game-tying two-run bomb.

But Garrett Mitchell tracked it down, leaped at the wall, and robbed Machado on the warning track.

Trevor Megill slammed the door in the ninth, striking out the side to seal the 3-1 victory and send Milwaukee to the NLCS.

Tee times await, boys.

World.title: Anti-Israel protesters label Mamdani a 'traitor,' accuse him of 'genocide' outside Oct 7 vigil
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A group of anti-Israel protesters on Wednesday targeted New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, calling him a "traitor," accusing him of "genocide" and claiming he "cannot weaponize being brown anymore."

The crowd of more than 100 demonstrators marched from City Hall to Union Square, where a vigil was held to mark the anniversary of the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas terror attacks in Israel. The vigil was organized as an evening of mourning for those killed in the Oct. 7 attacks and the bloodshed that followed, including Israelis and Palestinians.

The anti-Israel crowd was just outside the barricades of the Israelis for Peace Vigil, beating on drums and attempting to drown out the speakers, according to City & State New York.

Mamdani was at the vigil and held a candle as protesters threw various insults at him, including accusations of genocide and "selling all your people out."

ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA'

"Zohran, what do you say? How many kids did you kill today?" the protesters shouted, according to the outlet.

"700,000 dead. Mamdani, your hands are red!" they also chanted.

"Traitor, traitor, come on out! You sold all your people out!" the group was also heard chanting.

The crowd also shouted: "Zohran, you can’t hide. We charge you with genocide!"

"We don’t care about where you’re from. You cannot talk about being Muslim anymore. You cannot weaponize being brown anymore. Identity politics can only get you so far," they said.

One protester also claimed to be a former intern for Mamdani, saying the mayor "was never working for the people."

Protesters also demanded that Mamdani take action against New York real-estate events that have marketed properties in Israeli settlements in the West Bank, which the demonstrators characterize as "stolen" Palestinian land, according to City & State New York.

"Mayor Mamdani, take a stand. Stop the sale of stolen land," the group chanted.

The protesters also called for abolishing the City University of New York's Board of Trustees, whose members are largely appointed by the mayor and governor. Protesters have previously accused the board of ignoring demands to divest investments linked to Israel and criticized its handling of anti-Israel demonstrations on campus.

Despite the protesters' accusations of genocide on Wednesday, Mamdani is a longtime critic of the Israeli government's actions in Gaza and has denounced its treatment of Palestinians in the aftermath of the 2023 attack.

MAMDANI SAYS IT WAS 'STRANGE' GETTING CALLED OUT BY NETANYAHU AFTER CALLING FOR HIS ARREST

In a statement on Wednesday, Mamdani condemned Hamas’ attack as a "horrific war crime" while also characterizing Israel’s subsequent military operation as a genocide.

"The suffering did not begin nor end that day," he wrote. "It instead continued through the Israeli government’s devastating, ongoing genocide in Gaza in which it has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians — including more than 21,000 children."

Israel has rejected accusations that it is committing genocide in Gaza, saying its military targets Hamas and other terrorist groups while seeking to minimize civilian casualties.

The mayor's statement sparked bipartisan backlash, with Rep. Dan Goldman, D-N.Y., calling it "egregious and insulting."

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"There are 364 days of the year to focus on that. This is a day that should just be focused on what was by all agreement a horrific terror attack," Goldman, who is Jewish, told Politico. "What the mayor’s statement did today was to blame Israelis for the attack that they suffered three years ago. Regardless of what you actually think of the conflict and what’s happened either since or before, there’s no excuse for victim blaming."

World.title: Texas executes Jamaal Howard despite concerns over lethal injection drug used in failed Tennessee execution
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

A Texas man convicted of killing a convenience store clerk during a robbery was executed Wednesday evening after the Supreme Court declined to halt the execution, despite his attorneys raising concerns about the lethal injection drug used in a failed execution attempt in Tennessee last week.

Jamaal Howard, 46, was pronounced dead at 8:03 p.m. He was sentenced to death for the 2000 killing of 42-year-old Vickie Swartout in Silsbee, Texas.

Prior to Howard's execution, his attorneys pointed to the failed execution of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike, who survived two doses of pentobarbital on Sept. 30, arguing that the same drug Texas planned to use could pose similar risks.

"Texas should not be eager to follow in Tennessee’s footsteps; a stay would keep that from happening," Howard's attorneys argued in their filing.

CHRISTA PIKE'S ATTORNEYS SAY SHE'S IN CRITICAL CONDITION AFTER BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTIONS

The Supreme Court rejected Howard's emergency appeal without explanation. Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson was the only justice to publicly dissent, Fox News reported.

The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals had previously rejected two requests to stop the execution based on concerns about the drug's use.

According to The Associated Press, as the pentobarbital began taking effect Wednesday evening, Howard took a couple of breaths and gasped.

Howard then began making snoring sounds, coughed and resumed the snoring sounds, which grew progressively quieter. His movements reportedly stopped entirely after around 30 seconds, and he was pronounced dead 19 minutes later.

CHRISTA PIKE’S BOTCHED LETHAL INJECTION TAKES FOCUS OFF VICTIM, JEOPARDIZES EXECUTION: FORMER POLICE CHIEF

Howard's attorneys also said in court filings that they had requested information about the dose of pentobarbital the Texas Department of Criminal Justice planned to use to carry out the execution.

The concerns stemmed in part from Pike's execution attempt, during which she reportedly survived two doses of pentobarbital.

Howard's execution took place the same day a Tennessee judge granted a request from Pike's attorneys to order the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence connected to the failed execution attempt.

According to the Death Penalty Information Center, Pike is the first person to survive a lethal injection in the modern era.

CHRISTA PIKE EXECUTION FAILURE SPARES MURDERER WHO BAILED VICTIM OUT JUST TO KILL HIM

Howard's attorneys also argued before the Supreme Court that his execution should be halted because he was intellectually disabled. However, the state said his attorneys had not presented evidence establishing that he met the legal criteria for intellectual disability.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Howard was convicted of capital murder in the killing of Swartout, who was shot once in the chest during a convenience store robbery.

Howard, who was 20 years old at the time, also took $114 from the cash register during the robbery.

Fox News Digital's Michael Ruiz and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

World.title: Rays sweep Yankees in ALDS after controversial spectator interference denies Anthony Volpe's homer
World.content:
The New York Yankees had a ton of momentum after crushing their AL East-rival Boston Red Sox in the Wild Card Series, and it seemed they were ready to take on another division foe in the ALDS.

Instead, the Yankees’ season has come to a close because of the stellar play of the American League’s best team this season: the Tampa Bay Rays.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The Rays defeated the Yankees, 4-3, to take Game 3 and sweep New York in yet another game of pure fundamentals, timely hitting and one turning point that went their way in this series-deciding matchup.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

With the season on the line, the Yankees sent Max Fried to the mound, their veteran left-hander who said he would pitch no matter what, even though his girlfriend is due to deliver their child any day.

But Fried didn’t have an ace-like outing in this one, giving up four runs on seven hits, including two home runs – solo shots to Ryan Vilade and Victor Mesa Jr.

It was Mesa Jr.’s that was the decider in this game, as he smashed a hanging breaking ball into the famous Yankee Stadium right field bleachers to make it a 4-2 game.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

While that moment was massive for Mesa and the Rays, the rookie outfielder would be involved in a game-changing moment in the bottom of the sixth inning.

As Mesa was enjoying what he did to help his team potentially reach the ALCS, Anthony Volpe was trying to change things for the Yankees when he turned on a Griffin Jax fastball and sent it soaring to left field.

Mesa was tracking the moonshot the whole way to the wall, but it looked like it was running out of room. As Mesa jumped up to attempt to make the out, the ball ended up in the first row. With a runner on base, Volpe sent the Yankees crowd into rapture as he tied the game at four apiece.

But … not so fast.

Spectator interference was called on the play, as video replay was clear after long deliberation that a fan in the first row reached over the wall and touched it before it went over the fence. So, instead of a two-run homer, it was decided that Volpe would go to second base with an RBI double.

It was a 4-3 game, and that ultimately became a deciding factor in this one.

The Rays’ bullpen was stellar from that point on, with manager Kevin Cash eventually giving the ball to his closer, Bryan Baker. Despite allowing his first baserunner of the series on a walk, Baker was able to secure the three outs needed, as he struck out Trent Grisham to start the celebration for reaching the next stage of the postseason.

And once again, the Yankees find themselves on the losing end of a ALDS series against an AL East opponent. Last season, it was the Toronto Blue Jays, who almost won the World Series if it weren’t for the Los Angeles Dodgers’ heroics, defeating the Yankees in the Bronx to send the pinstripes home packing.

Meanwhile, the Rays, hoping to get back to the World Series for the first time since the 2020 shortened season, will await the winner of the Cleveland Guardians and Chicago White Sox ALDS bout. Chicago is up on Cleveland, 2-1, after the Guardians’ 9-3 victory to stay alive earlier on Wednesday.

World.title: Ken Paxton calls out James Talarico's 11-day absence at Trump rally, prompting response from campaign
World.content:

Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton questioned Democratic Senate candidate James Talarico's absence from the campaign trail during President Donald Trump's rally in San Antonio Wednesday, prompting a response from his opponent's campaign less than a month before the November midterm elections.

Paxton led the crowd in chanting "Where is Talarico?" while asserting that the Democrat had not been seen campaigning in Texas for 11 days.

Talarico's campaign told Fox News Digital the Democrat has been sick with the flu and is expected to return to the campaign trail this weekend.

PAXTON VENTS OVER LACK OF CAMPAIGN CONTROL AS DC ESTABLISHMENT HE ONCE BATTLED COMES TO HIS AID

"After holding more than 100 public events and shaking tens of thousands of hands, James came down with the flu but will be back on the trail this weekend," JT Ennis, a campaign spokesperson for Talarico, told Fox News Digital.

"Ken Paxton has been ignoring Texans this entire campaign, and his priorities are clear: He doesn’t answer to the people of this state. He answers to his billionaire megadonors and special interests."

The statement from Talarico campaign spokesperson JT Ennis also criticized Paxton's campaign priorities, pushing back against the Republican's remarks as the two candidates compete for a U.S. Senate seat.

Trump also questioned Talarico's whereabouts during his remarks, repeatedly referencing the Democrat's absence while campaigning on Paxton's behalf.



TRUMP-LINKED MAGA INC POURS $10M INTO KEN PAXTON'S TEXAS SENATE RACE AGAINST JAMES TALARICO

The president suggested without evidence that Talarico had become sick after eating meat for political reasons, mocking the Democrat's dietary preferences.

Trump also criticized Talarico's positions on immigration, public safety and education, while praising Paxton's record as Texas attorney general and urging voters to support his Senate bid.

The president emphasized the importance of the Texas race to Republicans' efforts to maintain control of Congress, warning supporters about the consequences of Democrats gaining seats in the Senate.

MEET THE VOTERS WHO COULD BREAK THE GOP’S DECADESLONG GRIP ON A REPUBLICAN STRONGHOLD

Trump's appearance in San Antonio was part of a broader effort to mobilize Republican voters ahead of the midterm elections. He urged attendees to participate in early voting, which begins Oct. 19 in Texas, or cast their ballots on Election Day.

The exchange over Talarico's whereabouts comes as the candidates enter the final weeks of the campaign.

World.title: Los Angeles Dodgers are back in the NLCS for third straight season after win over Atlanta Braves
World.content:
It's a baseball cliché that pitching wins in the playoffs, but sometimes clichés exist for a reason.

The first three games of the NLDS matchup between the Los Angeles Dodgers and Atlanta Braves was a showcase of the quality of both teams' pitching staffs. In game one, Tarik Skubal was dominant for Los Angeles, though was nearly matched by the Atlanta bullpen. The Dodgers took control later in the game, but went hitless with runners in scoring position Wednesday despite the 5-3 win.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Game 2 was even better. Atlanta scratched across three runs against a shaky Blake Snell and a parade of Dodgers relievers, while Ray Kerr and Didier Fuentes, among others, held the powerful LA lineup to just two. That seemed to shift the series advantage toward the Braves, with Chris Sale scheduled to start Game 3 at home.

DODGERS HIT TWO HOMERS OFF CHRIS SALE TO STEAL GAME THREE OF NLDS BEHIND YOSHINOBU YAMAMOTO

Kike Hernandez and Freddie Freeman touched up Sale for two homers in the fourth inning, but again, LA couldn't score against the Braves relievers. Dodgers manager Dave Roberts got a shaky ninth inning from closer Edwin Diaz to finish it out after a leadoff double. Another low-scoring, 3-1 game between the two teams. Three games, just 17 combined runs.

Game 4? More of the same.

Tyler Glasnow started for Los Angeles, coming off a solid, but injury-plagued season. Atlanta countered with Tyler Mahle, who, out of nowhere, had the lowest ERA of any starter traded at this year's deadline. Yes, even better than Tarik Skubal. Significantly so, in fact. And once again, despite the talent in both lineups, runs were hard to come by.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Atlanta jumped out to a 1-0 lead in the first thanks mostly to the speed and baseball IQ of Michael Harris II. Harris singled to lead off the game, got a running jump to steal second, advanced to third on a grounder, then scored when Glasnow bounced a breaking ball and LA catcher Will Smith couldn't find the ball in time to make a play.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The Dodgers tied it through, well, shockingly similar circumstances. In the top of the second, Shohei Ohtani walked to lead off the inning, then stole second as Teoscar Hernandez swung through strike three. Catcher Sean Murphy's throw got into center, letting Ohtani advance to third. Max Muncy seemingly popped up to short left center, but Mauricio Dubon, one night after robbing Freddie Freeman of a home run, just...dropped it.

Ohtani came in to score, tying the game at one apiece.

It would stay that way for a long, long time.



Glasnow was effectively wild, walking five hitters through 4 2/3 innings, but never allowing Atlanta to break through with a big hit. While Ozzie Albies led off the sixth with a double for the Braves, Alex Vesia and Edgardo Henriquez got Drake Baldwin, Lane Thomas, and Mauricio Dubon to end the threat.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Finally, in the seventh, LA got to the Braves bullpen. Fuentes, virtually unhittable in game two in LA, couldn't find the strike zone after a Teoscar Hernandez single chased Mahle from the game. Rookie pinch hitter Josue De Paula walked with two outs, with Kyle Tucker following with one of his own. Braves manager Walt Weiss went to veteran Robert Suarez to face Andy Pages. But Pages, after starting the count 3-0, laced a line drive single up the middle on 3-2 to score two.

Henriquez pitched a scoreless bottom of the seventh, getting Ronald Acuna Jr. to ground out after Michael Harris II doubled with two outs. Tanner Scott got the heart of the Atlanta lineup in the eighth, sandwiching a grounder from Ozzie Albies around strikeouts of Olson and Drake Baldwin.

In the ninth, Max Muncy provided some further insurance with a long homer to right to stretch the lead to 4-1.

Roberts once again turned to Edwin Diaz to close, despite the veteran closer's awful, injury-filled regular season. But Diaz had a drama-free ninth, striking out Rowdy Tellez looking, getting Dubon and Austin Riley to fly out to right to clinch it.

For all the talk about LA's star-filled lineup, with Shohei Ohtani, Mookie Betts, Freddie Freeman and Kyle Tucker, it was Kike Hernandez, Andy Pages, and Max Muncy who helped carry the limited offense and the Dodgers' pitching that helped secure the series. The Dodgers had just one hit with runners in scoring position all series, but did just enough to support their starters and relievers.

The Dodgers have reached their third straight NLCS, after winning championships in 2024 and 2025. They'll face the winner of the Milwaukee Brewers-San Diego Padres series, and with the Brewers up 2-1 in that series, it could set up a matchup of the only two teams to win 100 games in the regular season. And if Milwaukee can avoid using Jacob Misiorowski in the remainder of the series, they'll be able to line him up for two starts in the NLCS, plus a likely relief appearance.

For Atlanta, it's another disappointing postseason exit after their title in 2021. The Braves lineup, even with Harris, Acuna, Olson, Baldwin, Albies, and Riley, had just 18 hits in 124 at-bats. That's a .145 batting average, and that's not nearly enough to win a postseason series. They scored eight runs in four games and never could find the big hit they needed to build a big inning against Yamamoto or Glasnow.

Once again, sometimes those clichés about pitching turn out to be true.

World.title: FIRST ON FOX: US Coast Guard recruits largest class in nearly 40 years, beats goals for third straight year
World.content:
NEW You can now listen to Fox News articles!

FIRST ON FOX: The U.S. Coast Guard recruited its largest enlisted class in nearly four decades during fiscal year 2026, surpassing its recruiting goals for the third consecutive year as the service works to expand its ranks.

According to the Coast Guard, 5,445 active-duty members enlisted in fiscal year 2026, up from 5,204 in 2025 and 4,422 in 2024.

The service also commissioned 346 active-duty officers, the second-highest total in its history.

"These record-breaking recruitment numbers prove that the call to serve still resonates deeply across our country," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.

US ARMY HITS 2026 RECRUITING GOALS FOUR MONTHS EARLY, PETE HEGSETH ANNOUNCES AT WEST POINT COMMENCEMENT

"I am incredibly proud to stand beside these new Coast Guard men and women who have stepped up to defend our homeland," he continued. "They represent the very best of who we are, and we are going to make sure they have the tools, the training and the support to get the job done."

During fiscal year 2026, the Coast Guard expanded its recruiting efforts, opening four recruiting offices in Miami, Florida; Long Island, New York; Austin, Texas; and the Netherlands.

Coast Guard Vice Commandant Adm. Tom Allan said the numbers reflect growing interest in serving.

COAST GUARD ENDING RACE-BASED ADMISSIONS FOR OFFICER COMMISSIONING PROGRAM UNDER TRUMP DEI CRACKDOWN

"We surpassed our recruiting goals because Americans are ready and willing to serve in the U.S. Coast Guard, conducting exciting missions that deliver results our Nation needs," Allan said.

"This momentum is about more than numbers; it is about being the world’s best Coast Guard and building the workforce America needs," he added. "We are proud to welcome our newest members and grateful to our recruiters for continuing to deliver exceptional results."

The service is also investing in new infrastructure to help train its expanding workforce.

The Coast Guard awarded a $400 million contract to modernize Training Center Cape May in New Jersey, marking the largest shore construction award in the service's history.

TRUMP TURNS TO EMERGING TECH GIANT IN MULTI-BILLION BID TO RAMP UP US SUBMARINE PRODUCTION

The facility serves as the Coast Guard's sole basic training center for enlisted recruits, and the improvements are intended to accommodate its growing workforce.

The recruitment gains come as the Coast Guard pursues a modernization initiative known as Force Design.

Among the initiative's goals is to expand the Coast Guard's military workforce by at least 15,000 members by the end of fiscal year 2028 to support an expanding fleet and growing mission demands.

World.title: Trump dominates the Iowa Senate debate from afar
World.content:
President Donald Trump was the main character in a televised Iowa Senate debate Wednesday night between Democrat Josh Turek, a state representative, and Republican Rep. Ashley Hinson.

Turek hammered Hinson for supporting Trump policies that he says are the culprit in rising costs for Iowa families — from “chaotic tariffs” to the war in Iran — whether they live in cities or on farms.

“The real issue is that Iowans are hurting, and they’re hurting uniquely,” Turek said. “I’m hearing ‘I’m struggling to keep food on the table, I’m struggling to pay my electric bill, I’m struggling to keep a roof above my head,’ and now with this war in Iran, ‘I’m struggling just to keep gas in my tank.’” He noted that Hinson voted seven times against curtailing the war and five times against reining in Trump’s tariffs.

Hinson fired back, accusing Turek of skipping out on votes in the Legislature, being “too liberal” for the state and lying when he accused her of using her position to enrich her family.

“It’s one thing to vote like an East Coast liberal; it’s another to lie like them,” she said. At another point, she jabbed Turek for flip-flopping on his willingness to legislate with Trump. “You trashed the president during the primary, and now you’re doing ads saying you’re going to work with him,” she said. “It’s a tale of two Tureks.”

But by modern standards, the debate over a Senate seat that is one of a handful that will determine party control of the chamber was unusually civil. Hinson expressed her sympathy over Turek’s sister’s being diagnosed with cancer, and Turek nodded to the pain negative ads caused both candidates. And both of them pledged to work with Trump or a future Democratic president.

“You work with the person who’s going to sign the bills, no matter who that person is, on things that are important to your state, and that’s exactly what I’ve done,” Hinson said. In particular, she pointed to laws President Joe Biden signed on preventing stillbirths and providing mental health services to rural veterans for which she was the lead Republican sponsor in the House.

Recent polls have found the race is more or less a dead heat, with several surveys showing each candidate with a lead within the margin of error. Iowa has been a reliably Republican state in recent years, with Trump having won it in all three of his bids for the presidency and the GOP controlling both Senate seats and all four U.S. House seats.

But Trump’s low approval ratings have been an anchor on Republican candidates in Iowa, as they have been across the country. Trump was about 1,000 miles south Wednesday night, campaigning in Texas as Hinson and Turek debated in Iowa, but he looms over virtually every contest approaching in the midterm election.

The last time Democrats won statewide federal races in Iowa was more than a decade ago, when Barack Obama carried the state in two presidential elections and when then-Sen. Tom Harkin was re-elected to a fifth term in 2008. The Senate seat is open because Sen. Joni Ernst, R-Iowa, is honoring a self-imposed promise to serve only two terms.

The one-on-one between Hinson and Turek, part of the Iowa Press debates series, was held at the local PBS studio in Johnston, about 10 miles north of Des Moines, and featured three journalists — from Iowa PBS, the Des Moines Register and The Gazette, a newspaper based in Cedar Rapids — asking questions.

Hinson and Turek sparred over taxes, Social Security and immigration, among other issues.

Hinson cited border crossings during Biden’s term as a reason Iowans should not trust Turek and Democrats on the issue, arguing that her rival supports “all the illegals.” Trump and Republicans, she said, deserve credit for clamping down on illegal immigration.

“We have now sealed off the border, that just took about six months to get that done, and now we have zero crossings happening at our southern border,” she said. “So, who do you trust to fix the problem — the arsonists, the people who started the fire or the people who are cleaning up the mess?”

Turek affirmed that he would not vote to fund the Department of Homeland Security without significant changes to immigration enforcement policies, including requiring the use of body cameras and revising use-of-force standards.

“Yeah, that is my position,” he said. He added that he believes that no one wants to see “Americans shot in the street,” a reference to federal officers’ killing Renee Good and Alex Pretti during an immigration crackdown in Minnesota this year.

“What I am talking about is we can have safe and secure borders, and we need to have a pathway to earn citizenship for those that have come here legally,” Turek said.

At several points, Turek accused Hinson of slashing Medicaid, Obamacare premium subsidies and food assistance funds to cut taxes for the wealthiest Americans. Hinson responded that she was proud to eliminate taxes on tips, overtime pay and Social Security checks, which were among the features of Trump’s signature “big, beautiful bill” last year.

Turek said he supports those provisions, but he also proposed eliminating the cap on Social Security taxes to keep the program solvent beyond the six-year time frame when benefits are expected to be reduced if Congress does not act. That cap currently shields income above $184,500 per year from Social Security taxes.

“I think that it is fundamentally wrong that you have every single teacher and police officer and firefighter that is paying payroll tax and Social Security tax year-round,” Turek said. “Meanwhile, you’ve got folks like Elon Musk and Bill Gates and Jeff Bezos that are paying just for the first few minutes of the year. The best way we can keep this solvent is by taking off the cap.”

Hinson countered that lifting the cap would not fully fund Social Security payouts and argued that a federal commission should be established to revamp the system and keep it solvent. Congress, which holds the actual authority to rewrite the Social Security law, would then vote on the commission’s plan.

“This is a serious issue for our seniors, and it is a promise we need to keep to them,” she said, accusing Turek of “fearmongering” on the issue.

The candidates ducked and weaved a little on the last questions posed to them. Hinson was asked whether Congress is abdicating its authority by allowing Trump to build a White House ballroom and promise to send $5,000 payments to Americans if Republicans win the House and the Senate.

“Well, speaking as someone who serves on the Appropriations Committee right now, I care very deeply about Article I of the Constitution, which is making sure that we have the power of the purse,” she said, without addressing whether Trump’s seizure of that authority is proper.

Turek declined to rule out voting to remove Trump from office if he is impeached by the House.

“I have no interest in looking at impeachment,” he said in response to a question. “I think that we need to look forward, not back.”

In a twist at a time when many Democratic Senate candidates are distancing themselves rhetorically from Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., Hinson said she could team up with him if Democrats win the majority and she wins the Iowa Senate seat.

“So, hopefully it’s not Chuck Schumer, but if it’s Chuck Schumer, I’ll work with him,” she said. “I got things across the line with [Rep.] Nancy Pelosi [D-Calif.] as speaker, so I think that shows that I can work with anyone.”

Earlier in the debate, she sought to undermine Turek’s boast that he is not taking money from corporate PACs by highlighting the Schumer-backed super PACs that have taken money from companies and spent heavily to help elect Turek.

“He is basically taking laundered corporate PAC money,” she said, challenging Turek to call for ads on his behalf to be taken down “if you don’t want to take that corporate PAC money, because that’s how it flows. It flows through people like Chuck Schumer, right to support you.”

Turek declined to denounce the political action committees backing him.

World.title: DNC sues administration over taxpayer-funded pro-Trump TV ads
World.content:
The Democratic National Committee sued the Trump administration Wednesday over its taxpayer-funded s that portray President Donald Trump in a favorable light, alleging the ads violate federal laws on government spending and propaganda.

The DNC cited a measure Trump signed into law this year that says funds appropriated by Congress can’t be used “for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States not heretofore authorized by Congress.”

The lawsuit also cites the Anti-Deficiency Act, which bars spending government money that hasn’t been appropriated by Congress, and the Purpose Statute, which says taxpayer funds can be used only for the specific purposes approved by Congress.

The DNC said the administration’s use of taxpayer dollars for “campaign-style s” deprived Democrats “of a fair electoral process by adding public funds to the resources available to support Republican candidates.” The use of public funds places Democratic candidates at an electoral disadvantage, it argued.

The watchdog group Common Cause filed its own suit making similar legal arguments, alleging the administration had violated appropriations statutes.

The ads, launched last month, sparked criticism from lawmakers on both sides of the aisle, many of whom questioned their legality.

Trump reversed course Monday, announcing on Truth Social he would no longer use government funds for the ads and saying he and his PAC, MAGA Inc., would foot the bill moving forward, instead. He didn’t say whether the government would be reimbursed for the ads that already ran.

Reached for comment on the lawsuits, the White House pointed NBC News to Trump’s Truth Social post. The Department of Homeland Security and the Office of Management and Budget, which are named as defendants in addition to Trump and the White House, didn’t immediately respond to requests for comment on the lawsuit.

Since Trump’s announcement, several of the ads have continued to run with the disclaimer that they were paid for by the U.S. government.

Asked by NBC News whether those were paid for before or after Trump pledged to cover the costs, the White House wouldn’t say either way.

A person familiar with the ads said that the ad buy for the spots, placed before Trump’s Monday announcement, will end this week. Afterwards, the person said, outside groups will begin paying for the ads.

NBC News has reported that a $20 million contract was awarded to a Maryland firm for the ad campaign. AdImpact, a political ad-tracking firm, estimated that at least $10 million had been spent to air the ads through Monday.

Attorneys for the DNC asked a federal judge in Washington to find that the administration acted unlawfully “by developing and airing the propaganda ads using Congressionally appropriated funds” and to prevent it from using those funds to develop and air the ads in the future.

DNC Chair Ken Martin condemned the administration for using taxpayer dollars as Americans struggle with a rising cost of living.

“Americans deserve better than to have their hard-earned tax dollars used for Trump’s illegal schemes,” he said in a statement Wednesday.

Omar Noureldin, Common Cause’s senior vice president of policy and litigation, said in an interview with NBC News Wednesday that the group is bringing forth the suit “because we want to make sure that no president, regardless of party, can hijack public funds to fund political self-promotion without congressional approval.”

“It appears that the $20 million that had been contracted for this has not all been spent yet, and so they will continue to run ads paid for by taxpayer dollars, and so we think we need to stop that now, and not another dollar of taxpayer dollars should be spent on these ads,” Noureldin said.

The federal money for the ads came from funds intended for Customs and Border Protection, an arm of DHS. NBC News reported that CBP leadership was cut out of the decision to run the ads.

Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr, a Trump appointee, said last week that the ads didn’t merit FCC review, arguing that they weren’t “anything at all out of the ordinary.”

The White House has defended the ads by calling them “clearly not political” and claiming they were about “reminding Americans to love their country.” It has also pointed to other administrations’ use of public safety announcements.

World.title: Florida poll: Republicans lead in the races for governor and Senate
World.content:
Republican Byron Donalds holds a 7-percentage-point advantage over Democrat David Jolly in the Florida governor’s race, according to a new NBC South Florida/Telemundo Station Group poll, while Republican Sen. Ashley Moody is up by 10 points in her matchup against Democratic challenger Angie Nixon.

Donalds, a congressman from the southwest corner of the state, is at 48% in the poll, compared with Jolly’s 41%, in a race in which Donalds has had a commanding financial advantage. (That advantage is just inside the poll’s margin of error, but Donalds has the edge in most of the range of possibilities.)

Moody is at 50% in the Senate race, compared with 40% for Nixon, a Democratic Socialists of America-aligned candidate who got into the general election after a surprise primary victory over Democrat Alexander Vindman in August.

The results come amid broad Democratic optimism about the 2026 elections, with public polling showing the party making races in some typically red states into competitive contests this year. This poll suggests limits to that apparent momentum in other places.

The poll also took a snapshot of the state’s hugely influential bloc of Hispanic voters, largely congregated in South Florida. In 2024, Donald Trump won Hispanic-heavy Miami-Dade County by roughly 11 points, a significant reversal in a part of the state that had long been Democratic-leaning. Joe Biden won the county by 7 points in 2020.

But now, Florida Hispanic voters — including large Cuban, Nicaraguan, Honduran and Colombian populations — appear to be swinging back away from Trump, even as other high-profile Republican candidates hold comfortable leads among Hispanic voters.

Donalds holds a 48%-43% lead over Jolly among Hispanic voters, according to the survey, while Moody is up 47%-40% over Nixon. Trump’s job performance rating, however, is underwater, with 49% disapproving of his job performance, compared with 45% who approve.

Overall, 48% of all Florida likely voters approve of Trump’s job performance and 48% disapprove.

Before Trump’s gains among Florida’s Hispanic population in 2024, Democrats had generally won the demographic in the state by comfortable margins. Democrats argue that recent special election victories in Florida show the party has already started winning back the Hispanic vote, in part because of Trump’s aggressive immigration enforcement policy. Unhappiness with prices and the cost of living has also affected Trump’s ratings among Hispanic voters.

“In legislative races in Florida, we have seen huge swings,” Suzan DelBene, D-Wash., chair of the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, told NBC News last week, speaking of the committee’s efforts in Florida House races. She said that on immigration, Trump and his party broke a promise “to go after the worst of the worst.”

By far the most important issue identified was inflation and the cost of living, with 30% saying it is likeliest to influence their votes. In both the overall sample and the sample of Hispanic voters, “direction of the state or country” (17%) was the second most important issue. The broader polling data put “immigration enforcement” as the third most important issue (16%), while the Hispanic sample put property taxes (13%) as the third most important issue. Immigration enforcement was the fourth most important issue among Hispanic voters (12%).

Questions about the Trump administration’s push to allow local and state policy to cooperate with federal immigration officials fell along party lines.

Among all voters, 85% of Republicans support the policy, compared with 18% of Democrats and 44% of those identified as independent voters who supported the harsher immigration enforcement tactics.

Property taxes have also been front and center in Florida during the midterms.

The state Republican Party and term-limited Gov. Ron DeSantis support a ballot measure, known as Amendment 3, that would increase property tax exemptions to the first $250,000 of a home’s value by 2028. The exemption cap is currently $50,000.

In the poll of all Florida voters, 55% back the amendment, 26% oppose it, and 19% are undecided. Nearly three-quarters (74%) of Republicans supported the idea, compared with 36% for Democrats and 43% for independents.

The overall survey questioned 625 registered voters, all of whom said they were likely to vote in the November elections. They were interviewed over the telephone by Mason-Dixon Polling & Research Inc. from Sept. 28 to Thursday, with a margin of error of plus or minus 4 percentage points. The same time frame and methods were used to survey 400 Hispanic registered voters, with a margin of error of plus or minus 5 percentage points.
