World.title: Cornell defendant is fighting AG Letitia James’ appointment as special prosecutor
World.content:
One of the seven men named in the lawsuit filed by a former Cornell University student who alleges that she was sexually assaulted at an on-campus fraternity house has filed a petition to block New York Attorney General Letitia James’ appointment as special prosecutor in the case.

The attorney for Gillio Lopes, who has denied that he sexually assaulted the woman, filed a petition in Albany County Supreme Court on Wednesday. His filing says James should not be the prosecutor in the case because she has “unequivocally demonstrated a bias and presumption of guilt against the defendants named in the Civil Case.”

The Article 78 petition, filed against James and Gov. Kathy Hochul, is a proceeding used to challenge an action by a state or local government officer or agencies in New York.

Hochul appointed James last week to independently investigate Jane Doe’s allegations in the lawsuit, in which she says she was plied with alcohol, sexually assaulted and gang-raped at the Chi Phi fraternity house in October 2024. In her role, James will determine whether criminal charges are warranted.

James’ office declined to comment on the Article 78 filing.

In a statement Monday, James said: “My office enforces our state’s laws to protect all New Yorkers. I am committed to leading a comprehensive investigation they can trust, guided only by the facts, the evidence, and the law.”

Hochul’s office reiterated support for James on Wednesday.

Reached for comment on Lopes’ filing, the governor’s office referred to her comments last week.

“I have every confidence in our Attorney General to do what she has always done: look at the facts, examine the record and draw the proper conclusions. That’s exactly what’s going to happen in this case,” Hochul said at the time.

Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed James as special prosecutor last week to independently investigate Jane Doe’s claims of being plied with alcohol and gang-raped at the Cornell University Chi Phi fraternity house in 2024. Heather Ainsworth for NBC News

Hochul appointed James after she expressed dismay over Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten’s investigation of Doe’s allegations. He has said his office found a lack of criminality at the time and declined to press charges, but he reopened the case after the lawsuit sparked national uproar.

Jane Doe’s civil suit was filed last month against Cornell, Chi Phi and seven fraternity brothers. None of the men named have been criminally charged.

The fraternity was suspended from campus, and it remains barred.

Cornell said in a statement Sept. 28 that it conducted a thorough, monthslong Title IX investigation in 2024 that handed down “a range of sanctions, which included expulsions and suspensions” from the university. Two of the fraternity members were expelled, and two others were suspended. A third, who had already graduated, was barred from campus, and the final two were issued no-contact orders and required to write “reflection papers,” according to a source who has seen the written decision of the Title IX investigation.

Lopes’ filing argues that James’ appointment is “improper” and cites a post her office shared on X on Sept. 28, three days before her appointment was announced. In the post, she said: “What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable. I’m holding her in my heart and in my prayers. To her, and to all survivors: you’re not alone. We stand with you.”

The post, the petition contends, “made clear that she has formed an opinion about the case” and that “she has already reached the conclusion that Petitioner and the other named Defendants are guilty.”

The petition also seeks to have the court review James’ appointment and asks that her appointment be annulled or modified so she is not personally directing the probe or any resulting prosecution.

Stuart Bernstein, an attorney for Lopes, said Wednesday: “As Governor Hochul has said, the public needs confidence in the individual leading this investigation. AG James, based upon her very public statements validating Jane Doe, certainly doesn’t instill confidence in a fair investigation.”

In her lawsuit, Doe accuses Lopes of kissing her and sexually assaulting her without her consent.

Attorneys for two of the seven men, including Lopes, have denied to NBC News that they sexually assaulted Doe. An attorney for a third man denied the allegations to ABC News. NBC News has not received responses to requests for comment from the other men.

On Tuesday, Andrew Miltenberg, an attorney for Lopes, said he welcomes Cornell’s decision to have an independent review of its handling of Doe’s allegations, which will be led by former acting U.S. Attorney General Sally Yates.

“In our experience, Cornell’s investigations have generally been thorough. That said, we have also seen due process problems that have affected respondents, and on at least two occasions we have gone to federal court to try to address those issues. In this case, we do not agree with the outcome as to Mr. Lopes,” Miltenberg said.

World.title: Isaias becomes first hurricane of 2026 Atlantic season, threatens Gulf Coast
World.content:
Hurricane Isaias strengthened from a tropical storm late Wednesday night and is expected to make landfall along the U.S. Gulf Coast this weekend, threatening parts of Mississippi, Alabama and the western part of the Florida Panhandle. It is the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season.

A hurricane warning was issued Wednesday for the northern Gulf Coast, from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, across Alabama to Florida's Bay/Gulf County line.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared a state of emergency for more than two dozen counties in his state, and Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties.

Maps show hurricane's path

Isaias had maximum sustained winds of 75 mph and was located about 460 miles southwest of the mouth of the Mississippi River, according to the National Hurricane Center.

Forecasters said they expected Hurricane Isaias, pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," to make landfall late Friday or early Saturday,

Map shows the potential path of Isaias, which strengthened from a tropical storm into a hurricane late Wednesday night. CBS News

"Isaias is expected to strengthen and be a strong hurricane when it approaches the northern Gulf Coast on Friday," the National Hurricane Center said. "A life-threatening storm surge is expected."

Along with the hurricane warning, a tropical storm warning was issued from Louisiana's Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish line to Ocean Springs, and from the Bay/Gulf County line to Florida's Aucilla River. A storm surge warning was issued from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown, Florida.

Isaias is expected to impact the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News

The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 7 inches of rain and as much as 10 inches in some places along the coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. Much of the Southeast, and as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas, could see heavy rainfall.

The latest for a first hurricane since 1905

Isaias' progression into a hurricane on Wednesday marked the latest date in 121 years for the Atlantic season's first hurricane to develop, just missing a record set on Oct. 8, 1905, according to National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration data.

The season, which has been unusually quiet in the Atlantic this year, runs from June 1 through Nov. 30.

An Atlantic hurricane season typically produces, on average, 14 named storms, seven hurricanes and three major hurricanes, according to the hurricane center, which used climate data collected between 1991 and 2020 to calculate those figures. A season's first named storm normally forms in mid- to late-June, while the first hurricane tends to form in early- to mid-August, and the first major hurricane often comes in late August or early September.

Forecasters predicted there would be less Atlantic storm activity than usual this year, but so far it has been even quieter than anticipated. Meteorologists say that's largely due to to the onset of a strong El Niño over the summer, which typically correlates with cooler water temperatures and greater fluctuations in wind patterns over the Atlantic, conditions that dampen the growth of tropical systems. The Pacific, meanwhile, has seen an unusually active series of hurricanes.

World.title: Democrats invest more heavily in Gina Hinojosa as Pritzker offers support
World.content:
National Democrats are stepping up their financial support for Texas Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa after recent polls showed a dead heat and more Democrats began to see an opportunity to potentially defeat three-term incumbent Republican Gov. Greg Abbott.

Illinois Democratic Gov. JB Pritzker, a possible 2028 presidential contender, and the Democratic Governors Association are each putting at least $1 million behind Hinojosa, according to sources familiar with the investments and a senior DGA official. Pritzker's contribution is actually larger — $1.2 million, according to sources familiar with the commitment. The New York Times first reported the investment.

The infusion comes at a crucial point for Hinojosa's campaign. She reported roughly $4 million in cash on hand at the end of last month, according to campaign finance filings, and her campaign said it had been outspent by Abbott by roughly 10-to-1.

In a statement, Hinojosa's campaign said her campaign has "momentum," and said "we're grateful for the support we've received in this final stretch from leaders across the country."

Last week, more than 70 Latino Democratic leaders sent a letter to Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, the chair of the DGA, urging the group to invest $10 million to help Hinojosa's campaign. A source told CBS News on Wednesday that the state's Latino leaders, including Texas congressional lawmakers, met with the DGA to increase pressure to fund Hinojosa's campaign, which was first reported by NBC News.

A source familiar with the investments tells CBS News that the DGA took action to support Hinojosa after Pritzker committed his own money to the race.

A DGA official disputed that characterization, saying that Beshear told Hinojosa in a conversation on Tuesday of last week that the DGA would spend at least $1 million on her campaign. A source close to Hinojosa's campaign confirmed the conversation between Beshear and Hinojosa took place, as well as the Kentucky governor's $1 million commitment.

Abbott's campaign said in a statement that she is "taking her campaign to out-of-state Democrat strongholds."

Abbott has significantly outraised Hinojosa, including from July to September, when his campaign said it brought in $20 million to her campaign's $13 million. But his campaign reported having $17 million cash on hand, indicating a huge amount of spending given the over $100 million on hand he reported at the beginning of the year.

A Democrat has not been elected to the governor's mansion in Texas since Ann Richards in 1990, who lost reelection to George W. Bush four years later, and President Trump won the state by more than 13 points in 2024. Abbott had not been considered vulnerable, but recent polls had shown the race tightening.

Mr. Trump is campaigning in San Antonio on Wednesday with Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton and several other GOP candidates, although Abbott is not joining the rally.

World.title: Man eyed Mall of America for attack, pledged allegiance to ISIS, FBI says
World.content:
An 18-year-old man accused of telling an FBI informant he planned to carry out an attack later this month at Mall of America was arrested at gunpoint Tuesday in Richfield, Minnesota, during an arranged meeting to buy an assault rifle, according to a federal criminal complaint filed Wednesday.

Minnesota U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen and FBI Minneapolis Special Agent in Charge Christopher Dotson discussed the case involving Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud, a Twin Cities resident and U.S. citizen, in a news conference Wednesday afternoon, where Rosen praised the FBI for its "diligence" in thwarting the attack.

"They were able to detect a threat and disrupt it before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people," Rosen said.

In the complaint, authorities say a "confidential human source" exchanged "hundreds of bi-directional messages through multiple social media and encrypted messaging applications" with Mohamud from December 2024 until Tuesday. In those exchanges, Mohamud allegedly "expressed his desire to travel to Somalia" to join al-Shabaab and "fight on its behalf and/or commit a mass casualty attack" in Minnesota.

"The messages this defendant allegedly sent to others were chilling. They document the idolization of ideologically motivated violence, a callous disregard to the sanctity of human life, a blind hatred of people of other faiths and a cold commitment to carrying out his vision of violence in our community," Dotson said. "Mohamud allegedly sought martyrdom in carrying out his plans to murder innocent civilians."

The complaint says the FBI contacted Mohamud's parents in May 2025, but they weren't cooperative.

"The FBI attempted to speak with his parents having seen that this young man was becoming radicalized, and those attempts were rebuffed by the parents," Rosen said. "I just would say to parents all over Minnesota and, for that matter all over America, if you get the indication, especially if you hear from federal law enforcement, that your son or daughter is being radicalized to the point where federal law enforcement wants to come and give you that warning, heed those warnings."

In July, Mohamud told an informant he didn't have enough money to go to Somalia, according to the complaint. He allegedly said he would attack in the United States instead, and that if he did, he wasn't doing it "for any worldly matter" but "for the sake of Allah only."

U.S. Attorney Daniel Rosen WCCO

Mohamud allegedly went on to say in a direct message to the source that he considered carrying out an attack at Mall of America in Bloomington or Valleyfair amusement park in Shakopee. An FBI affidavit says he wrote that he might buy two pistols online first.

The complaint says Mohamud said he wanted to attack the mall "because it's owned by Jewish." He said he was inspired in part by last year's deadly antisemitic attack at Bondi Beach in Sydney, Australia.

Last month, Mohamud told the source he wanted to carry out an attack at the mall during the Hmong Arts Celebration on Oct. 24, saying "it will be a lot of people," according to court documents.

In another message last month, the affidavit says Mohamud wrote that he had been watching video of the 2016 attack at the Pulse nightclub in Orlando, Florida, and thought he could do the same.

"I just walk in and shoot," Mohamud wrote, according to the complaint.

Court documents also note Mohamud sent the source a video on Discord in which he allegedly pledged allegiance to ISIS.

On Tuesday, Mohamud was arrested during an arranged meeting with the source in the parking lot of a Richfield park, according to Rosen. The affidavit says he had left an undercover employee's vehicle with the rifle, four magazines and 200 rounds of ammunition when he was arrested. The filing describes the weapon as a Norinco AK-47 assault rifle, model Mac-90 Sporter, and the ammunition as about 200 live rounds of 7.62x39-caliber.

A Richfield man says he witnessed the arrest during a visit to the dog park.

"They flew out of their vehicle and one of the FBI agents kicked my door shut," said Mike O'Brien. "I was just trying to go to the dog park"

O'Brien says he saw a swarm of up to 30 agents take down a suspect.

"They became aware that this was a radicalized young man who needed to be watched, and in fact, in this young man's case, that radicalization progressed to the point where he planned in the most serious of ways to carry out a mass casualty attack," Rosen said.

Authorities allege Mohamud "knowingly received a firearm and ammunition" with reasonable cause to believe they would be used to commit a felony and a federal crime of terrorism, including providing or conspiring to provide material support to a designated foreign terrorist organization.

Mohamud made his first court appearance Wednesday.

Simon Osamoh previously served as the head of counterterrorism for the Mall of America, now he is the CEO of Kingswood Security Consulting. Osamoh says with tens of millions of visitors each year, and its proximity to transit and the airport, the mall has been a known target in the past.

"Terrorists, or people with that sort of ideology, they favor places of mass gathering which Mall of America is," he said.

Osamoh said the mall has close connections with law enforcement and layers of security pointing to facial recognition, K9 teams and undercover officers.

"I was incredibly concerned but I wasn't surprised," Osmoh said of the alleged plot.

He referred to Minnesota cases just over a decade old, involving men inspired to join foreign terror groups.

Prosecutors accused a group of Somali Americans of plotting to join ISIS overseas. Some were caught trying to fly to Syria. Three men were later convicted at trial in Minnesota, others pleaded guilty.

"I think what Mall of America will be doing in 24, 48 hours is say did we miss anything?" said Osamoh. "Was there anything that we missed that could have identified this individual earlier?"

"We are grateful to the FBI and its law enforcement partners for their vigilance and extraordinary investigative work in identifying, disrupting and removing this threat and protecting the community we all share," the mall said in a statement. "The safety and security of everyone who visits and works at Mall of America has always been our highest priority."

World.title: Tropical Storm Isaias forms in Gulf, could reach U.S. as hurricane this weekend
World.content:
Update: Isaias became a hurricane late Wednesday night. See the latest forecast here.

Tropical Storm Isaias was "quickly intensifying" and is expected to approach the U.S. Gulf Coast on Friday after becoming a hurricane, according to the National Hurricane Center.

Currently swirling in the Gulf, Isaias would be the Atlantic basin's first hurricane of the season and is its ninth named storm. An El Niño climate pattern continues to bring a more active season in the Pacific. The storm formed with less than two months remaining in the 2026 hurricane season, which ends Nov. 30.

Maps show possible path

Tropical Storm Isaias, which grew from Tropical Depression Nine on Wednesday and is pronounced "ees-ah-EE-ahs," is expected to pass to the north of Mexico's Yucatan Peninsula on Thursday and make landfall along the northern Gulf Coast of the U.S. late Friday or early Saturday, the hurricane center said.

A hurricane warning was issued Wednesday for the northern Gulf Coast, from Ocean Springs, Mississippi, to Florida's Bay/Gulf county line, and a tropical storm warning was issued from Louisiana's Jefferson/Plaquemines Parish line to Ocean Springs, and from the Bay/Gulf county line to Florida's Aucilla River. A storm surge warning was also issued from the mouth of the Mississippi River to Yankeetown, Florida, according to the hurricane center.

Tropical storm-force winds were extending outward up to 60 miles from the storm's center on Wednesday evening. Its maximum sustained winds were 70 mph, and it was forecast to become a hurricane by Thursday morning, the hurricane center said.

A storm's maximum wind speed must rise to at least 74 mph to be considered a hurricane.

The possible path of newly formed Tropical Storm Isaias Nikki Nolan/CBS News

Isaias is forecast to bring moderate to heavy rainfall to the Gulf Coast and into the rest of the Southeast this weekend into early next week. The hurricane center forecasts 3 to 7 inches of rain and as much as 10 inches in some places on the central Gulf Coast from southeastern Louisiana to the Florida Panhandle. Much of the Southeast, and as far north as the Tennessee Valley and the Carolinas, could see rainfall ranging from 1 to 5 inches, forecasters said.

Some longer-range forecast models also see this moisture eventually reaching the Ohio Valley and Northeast by midweek next week.

Tropical Storm Isaias is expected to impact the U.S. Gulf Coast. CBS News/Nikki Nolan

The hurricane center on Thursday warned of "an increasing risk of dangerous wind and storm surge impacts" along parts of the northern Gulf Coast and urged people living in Louisiana, Alabama, Mississippi and northern Florida to "closely monitor the latest forecast updates and ensure they have their hurricane plan in place."

At high tide, the approximately 300-mile stretch between Ocean Springs, Mississippi, and Indian Pass, Florida, could see a storm surge of up to 7 feet, forecasters said, potentially causing major flooding.

In addition to rain, the hurricane center said Isaias could potentially bring urban flooding and isolated river flooding to places in its path.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis on Tuesday signed an executive order declaring a state of emergency for 25 Florida counties ahead of the storm's arrival. DeSantis said in a statement that the order "ensures communities have the time and resources necessary to prepare for potential severe weather impacts to the Panhandle and Big Bend region of Florida."

On Wednesday, Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a similar state of emergency for 40 counties, saying in a statement that it will allow Alabama officials "to take any needed steps ahead of landfall."

Beware the "I"-named storm

While tropical storm and hurricane formation and frequency vary throughout the season, the "I"-named systems tend to be the most retired names within the Atlantic basin.

The most commonly known retired "I"-named storms are Ian (2022), Ida (2021), Irma (2017) and Irene (2011).

When Ike was retired in 2008, Isaias replaced the "I" name on the Atlantic tropical cyclones list, which rotates every six years.

World.title: Obama hosts fundraiser with Senate Democrats weeks before midterms
World.content:
Washington – Former President Barack Obama headlined a fundraiser for the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Wednesday night to discuss the stakes of the upcoming midterm election.

The event featured a conversation between Obama and Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, vice chair of the DSCC, about Democrats' efforts to flip the Senate.

"I think he is just such a voice for our country, and of both realism and practical optimism, and I think we need that right now," Blunt Rochester told CBS News. "And I think he also lays the foundation for the significance of this election."

Senate Democrats have become increasingly optimistic about their prospects this fall after several races shifted toward the party in recent weeks, including in deep-red states like Texas and Ohio that are considered toss-ups, according to CBS News' battleground tracker.

"We do not want to be overconfident, but what we're seeing in state after state after state is that people are sick of Trump, they're sick of the Republican Senate going along with them, and they see the clear divisions we have drawn between what we stand for and what they stand for," Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer told CBS News last month. "That has put us on the edge of victory."

Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate. Democrats would need to pick up four seats to gain control of the upper chamber.

Meanwhile, Republicans have argued they still have a path to hold on to the Senate.

"Right now, there's a lot of noise, there always is in the political atmosphere — some of it's created by our opponents," Senate Majority Leader John Thune, a South Dakota Republican, told reporters before the body went on recess. "But if we can stay focused, talk about the future and the two paths over the course of the next several weeks, based on our record of accomplishment, things we got done, things we still need to do, we've got a great argument."

One key target for both parties is Michigan. Democrats are trying to hold the seat being vacated by retiring Sen. Gary Peters while Republicans see it as a prime pickup opportunity. An exclusive CBS Detroit poll, conducted by Mitchell Research and Communications, shows Democratic nominee Abdul El-Sayed with a narrow advantage over GOP challenger and former Rep. Mike Rogers.

Obama is expected to campaign with El-Sayed and other Democratic candidates in the Wolverine State later this month. A source familiar with the former president's thinking said his strategy this fall is "driven by where he can move the needle with Democrats and persuadable voters."

The former president has also taped two dozen ads for Senate and gubernatorial candidates around the country. Last month, he participated in the second of two fundraisers with House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries and the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee, where he pressed Democrats to do more on the issue of artificial intelligence.

"Certainly if I were running for president next year, this would be one of my central agendas, and I would have a very clear plan, and I would talk about this, and I would say, 'Here's our plan for safety, here's our plan for making sure our kids are not corrupted by this,'" Obama said. "I would be thinking about the economic impacts in very concrete ways and understanding: What does it mean if there's going to be job displacement? Where is that going to hit? How are we going to respond?"

Jeffries told CBS News he has remained in contact with Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris and expects both to be engaged through Election Day. The minority leader, who is poised to become the first Black House speaker if Democrats win control of the lower chamber, predicted that House Democrats would "take back the majority" this fall.

"It's an all-hands-on-deck effort," Jeffries said.

World.title: Newly obtained footage shows Iran attack on major U.S. post in Kuwait
World.content:
Washington — New videos obtained exclusively by CBS News show Iranian attacks on a major U.S. military base in Kuwait as the war with Iran kicked off seven months ago. American forces faced ballistic missiles, drones and what witnesses described as Iranian F-5 fighter jets.

The footage obtained by CBS News was recorded by a person stationed on the ground at Camp Buehring, and captures the moments of impact and their explosive aftermath. Damage to buildings and military equipment can also be seen in the videos.

The attacks on Camp Buehring offer a window into the strain Iranian attacks placed on American forces during the opening days of the war. CBS News has learned that soldiers defending the base ran critically low on .50-caliber ammunition as some soldiers were repositioned into the Udari Desert in Kuwait. Two soldiers were injured by lightning there in late April, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.

Contacted by CBS News, U.S. Central Command, the primary unit which oversees American military operations across the Middle East, declined to comment.

The Pentagon did not comment, but pointed back to Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth's comments on March 4 regarding the removal of U.S. troops from bases and the employment of defensive measures.

"As we built up offensive combat power, we moved the vast majority of American troops — over 90% of Americans that were on our bases — what we say off the X, out of the range of Iranian fire," Hegseth told reporters in March.

Camp Buehring, or CBKU, sits about 25 miles from the Iraqi border and has for more than two decades served as a major staging ground for American forces deploying across the Middle East.

CBS News authenticated the videos using metadata embedded in the files and compared the footage to other photographs showing damage to the base.

Ahead of the war, sources said most of the roughly 7,000 troops there were moved elsewhere — as were the majority of U.S. forces in Kuwait — as a part of the Pentagon's "get off the X" plan, military shorthand for moving away from a position vulnerable to attack.

Once the war started, Iranian attacks, some originating from Iraq, repeatedly threatened the installation. Missiles and drones forced soldiers into bunkers. Three U.S. service members told CBS News that Iranian F-5 fighter jets were also used during the attacks, a detail first reported in April by NBC News.

"They ran so close to us I could see their helmets," the eyewitness described. "They came in, they hit us, and then took off."

While most of the U.S. service members were moved off of Camp Buehring, a tranche of more than 100 soldiers stayed behind. The service members feared the isolated base was ill-equipped to handle a mass-casualty event if the attacks continued.

"They hit us bad," the source told CBS News on condition of anonymity because of the military's strict media restrictions. "It was horrible. There were a lot of brave guys who stayed to fight there — and people at home don't know what happened. We had to abandon the base."

A senior Army official working in logistics, managing operations from another post in Kuwait, confirmed to CBS News there were concerns about the availability of .50 caliber ammunition and other "exquisite" munitions like Patriot missile batteries.

The decision ultimately was to leave. Service members packed up, loading their vehicles with whatever equipment they could and drove at night deep into the Kuwaiti desert. Their remote locations would emerge as forward operating bases, or "FOBs," where the soldiers would remain indefinitely.

No one was killed by enemy fire at Camp Buehring or at the FOBs, but several were injured, including two soldiers who were struck by lightning in desert sandstorms. One soldier suffered burns after the direct strike while the other suffered a ruptured eardrum, according to U.S. officials with knowledge of the matter.

Before the lightning strike, Army leaders had been trying to move the troops out of the area, but were not able to do so quickly enough. In May, the soldiers left the FOBs for Camp Arifjan, and then relocated to other positions both in and out of the Middle East.

"CBKU got demolished," the source added. "They need to do an investigation. How come no one came to reinforce us?"

The Defense Department's inspector general last month released a report on the war with Iran that revealed "equipment losses" worth up to $3.7 billion — including nearly 60 aircraft. On Monday, the Congressional Research Service, which provides nonpartisan analysis to members of Congress, reported that 81 fixed or rotary-wing aircraft including drone assets had been lost or damaged by Iran since February, according to news reports and statements from the Defense Department.

In a first-of-its-kind mandatory report to Congress, the inspector general added that U.S. Central Command had reported Iranian strikes at U.S. bases in Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, UAE, Saudi Arabia, Iraq, Oman and Jordan.

Although strikes were mentioned in the report, pictures and videos of any impact zones have been extremely limited. Beyond Camp Buehring, CBS News earlier obtained exclusive photos of damage at Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia and Camp Arifjan in Kuwait.

CBS News has also reported extensively on the deadliest attack of the war against U.S. troops at the Port of Shuaiba, which killed six American service members.

World.title: Russia open to a Trump-Putin call as questions mount over plague lab death
World.content:
Russia's government said Wednesday that it was open to "promptly" scheduling a phone call between Presidents Trump and Vladimir Putin to discuss the still-unexplained death of a plague research center employee, but that nothing had been scheduled yet.

Mr. Trump told reporters Tuesday night that he expected to speak with Putin "very soon" about the Oct. 2 death of the Siberian lab worker, after Secretary of State Marco Rubio called on Moscow to be more transparent about the incident and to "share more information with the world."

A State Department spokesperson later told CBS News the U.S. Embassy in Moscow had "engaged Russian authorities about the reported death" and "asked for additional information," which it encouraged Russia to share "quickly and transparently."

So far, Russian authorities have only offered "pneumonia of unknown origin" as the cause of Darya Shipilova's death. Shipilova, 28, worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute, more than 2,500 miles east of Moscow, and initial Russian media reports - some of which were quickly taken down - suggested she had contracted the pneumonic plague after a lab accident and died of the disease.

The United Nations World Health Organization called Wednesday on Russia's national health watchdog agency, Rospotrebnadzor, to provide more information about Shipilova's death, and the Russian body said it had provided further details.

In a statement, Rospotrebnadzor said it was easing precautionary measures that were put in place in the Siberian region of Irkutsk, where the lab is located, after determining there was no risk of an epidemic connected to Shipilova's death. It said no cases of plague were detected among the 200 people screened after coming into contact with her, and that 90% of those who had been put under quarantine conditions for monitoring had been released.

The agency said it had conducted nearly 5,000 lab tests of those individuals and that none of them had detected dangerous pathogens.

Rospotrebnadzor's statement added that Shipilova had been vaccinated against the dangerous infections she worked with, so she had immunity to them.

But despite the reassurances from Russia's government, the lack of any clear explanation for Shiplova's death has left rumors to swirl about what might have killed her, and what work might be underway at the Russian research center.

According to its website, the Irkutsk anti-plague lab's work extends beyond research on the well-known bacteria, which is present in animal populations in the region, as it is in other parts of the world, to include planning and preparation on how to deal with incidents involving "potential agents of bioterrorism."

In other words, the center is involved in Russia's planning for how to respond to potential biological attacks. Reports in Chinese and Western media this week have noted collaboration between the facility's director - who has also visited U.S. research facilities - and Chinese authorities, including participation in a "joint emergency drill" to practice for a theoretical "cross-border infectious disease epidemic" in August.

Irkutsk lab was previously a "cover for a biological weapons facility"

Annie Jacobsen, an American journalist and author of "Biological War," a fictional story about a hypothetical engineered pathogen - a pneumonic plague - accidentally breaking out of a lab in Siberia that was published just a few months ago, said the scenario is what military experts are "most worried about."

When it comes to "the accidental release of a genetically modified pathogen from a high or maximum containment laboratory around the world," she told CBS News, "the number-one worry is Russia."

"During the 80s and before, Russia had a very robust, illegal biological weapons program," Jacobsen said. "The facility in Irkutsk, which is in question right now, was a dual use facility, meaning, yes, it was doing what it purportedly did - which was create medical countermeasures against dangerous pathogens - but it was also a cover for a biological weapons facility."

This undated photo released in 2019 by the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East, shows the institute workers in a lab. Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and Far East via AP

She told CBS News all the scrutiny Russia has drawn this week is due not only to the reports by independent media of Shipiova dying of a possible plague infection, but also to"the quarantine of some 200 people" under what she said were "draconian measures."

The real indicator, according to Jacobsen, of a serious problem in Irkutsk will be any confirmed secondary infections.

The WHO said Wednesday that it had requested more information after some media reports suggested a possible second infection in the area, but nothing has been confirmed so far.

Russians relaxed, but not their neighbors

Lyudi Baikala, an independent Russian news outlet that was among the first to break the news of Shipilova's death, and to say it could have been a plague infection, quoted a colleague of Shipilova's on Tuesday as saying her illness began with cold symptoms before worsening rapidly.

After she was hospitalized, about 200 colleagues were reportedly quarantined at the research institute for three days, and tested twice daily before being released.

Residents of her apartment building have told Russian media that a van arrived on the night she died. They said people who appeared to be from the national health agency, wearing gas masks and orange protective suits, sprayed the building's entrance with a substance residents assumed was antiseptic.

Tight controls on information in Russia make independent verification of events difficult, but reporters with the French news agency AFP visited Irkutsk on Tuesday and said residents were going about their lives, and those who agreed to be interviewed said they were not worried, "because they [authorities] said there haven't been any confirmed cases, and people who've been in contact with infected individuals have been isolated, and nothing's happened [to them]."

But until Russia offers more definitive answers about what killed Shipilova, Moscow is likely to continue facing questions - and its neighbors may not be as willing to accept its reassurances.

As of Wednesday, authorities in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan had all confirmed the implementation of additional precautionary measures at their borders with Russia, to guard against the possible spread of infectious diseases.

World.title: Trump proposes Camp David-style presidential retreat at his private Florida golf club
World.content:
Trump proposes Camp David-style presidential retreat at his private Florida golf club

toggle caption i Alex Brandon/AP

FORT LAUDERDALE, Fla. — President Donald Trump on Wednesday said he wants to develop one of his Florida golf courses into a presidential retreat where his successors can spend quiet weekends on the greens, describing it as "sort of a Camp David " that he says would already have many of the security features needed to host presidents and world leaders.

The proposal for the retreat on Trump's private golf course in West Palm Beach would comingle the presidency with Trump's business ventures beyond his time in office, and is the the latest example of Trump seeking ways to leave his imprint on the presidency.

"It's a great idea, and it'll be used a lot," Trump said, claiming it was suggested by the United States Secret Service. "It seems that all presidents play golf."

The plan has already been submitted to local officials. Trump, an avid golfer, rattled off the benefits of the property a short drive from his Mar-a-Lago home during an unrelated event in the Oval Office, noting that it's close to an airport and has some distance from residential homes and tall buildings, which pose security risks.

Sponsor Message

He did not mention that the golf course was the site of an unsuccessful attempt on his life in 2024. Trump was playing at the Trump International Golf Club during a break from the campaign trail when a Secret Service agent spotted an armed man in the trees lining the club's perimeter fence. The man was arrested after a chase and later convicted of trying to kill Trump, and was sentenced to life in prison.

Past presidents have used Camp David, a rustic compound in Maryland, as a weekend retreat and a place to host presidential meetings. Trump has spent less time there, often opting for his own properties, including golf clubs in Florida, New Jersey and Virginia.

Palm Beach County sees what it calls a 'historic opportunity'

Trump's proposal follows other projects by the lifelong real estate developer to build a White House ballroom, gild the Oval Office, erect a triumphal arch, renovate the Kennedy Center, refurbish the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool and rebuild a golf course in East Potomac Park. He has also begun planning a future presidential library in a Miami skyscraper.

In a letter to Palm Beach County commissioners last month, first reported by the Palm Beach Post, an attorney who represents the golf course said Trump is offering to designate it as a "U.S. Presidential Golf Course."

Sponsor Message

"Just as Camp David, Windsor Castle, or the Elysée Palace are known worldwide, so too will the Presidential Golf Course in Palm Beach County," Harvey Oyer said in the letter.

Palm Beach County Administrator Joseph Abruzzo said in a statement that local officials are eager to explore what this "historic opportunity" could mean to the community. "This likely would further cement Palm Beach County's place on the national and international stage for generations to come," Abruzzo said.

Oyer's letter said the West Palm Beach golf course could be used by current and former presidents, along with visiting foreign heads of state. The Trump Organization owns the golf club but leases the land from the county, which would need to approve any changes.

Under the proposal, the club would pay to build a new presidential lodging and then work with the Secret Service and other agencies to provide free access to the federal government. The retreat would have a separate entrance from the private club, which earned Trump nearly $37 million during his first year back in office, according to his financial disclosure.

"This is a gift that the President would like to share with his successors, the people of America, and his fellow Palm Beach County residents," Oyer wrote. "It should be noted that President Trump will be out of office before this proposed project could be completed so this is a gift to his successors."

Oyer highlighted past U.S. presidents who turned over land for public use. Dwight Eisenhower donated his Gettysburg Farm in Pennsylvania to the National Park Service, and Franklin D. Roosevelt donated part of his estate in Hyde Park, New York.

Years before it was bought by Trump, Mar-a-Lago itself was proposed as a "Winter White House."

Businesswoman and socialite Marjorie Merriweather Post left the home to the National Park Service when she died in 1973, but the agency returned the home to her estate in 1980 because of high maintenance costs. Trump bought the property in 1985, and it later became his primary residence.

World.title: Maricarmen, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction shook Spain, has died
World.content:
Maricarmen, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction shook Spain, has died

toggle caption i Bernat Armangue/AP

MADRID — María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old woman whose eviction from her longtime Madrid home sparked nationwide protests across Spain and unleashed a political crisis, died on Wednesday while hospitalized.

Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez led the way on social media offering his condolences after housing activists and Abascal's lawyer announced her death. Known widely as "Maricarmen," she had become a symbol for renters struggling with Spain's housing affordability crisis.

"All my love to Maricarmen's family and loved ones," Sánchez said in a post on X. "A hug as well to all of us who feel this loss as our own today. Rest in peace."

Sponsor Message

The emotions ran into anger on the street among the protesters gathered near Spain's Parliament who chanted "Maricarmen lives, the fight goes on!"

Iciar López, a 32-year-old psychologist, shared her feelings with The Associated Press at the protest in Madrid.

"A great deal of sorrow. And above all, the thought that she is the cause, the head of this whole revolution that has happened, and that she can't see it," she said. "It makes me very sad that she can't see if anything comes of it ... That's what angers me the most, honestly."

A case that captured media attention and traveled around the world

Spaniards increasingly frustrated by housing costs periodically march in major cities demanding action from lawmakers. But a fresh wave of indignation has swept Spain since Sept. 23, when Maricarmen, who used a wheelchair, was carried on a stretcher from her home of seven decades after police cordoned off the street and removed protesters. She was taken to a hospital because of her fragile health.

Televised images of the eviction prompted thousands of people to protest in Madrid and other cities across the country.

Maricarmen's lawyer, Beatriz Duro, did not disclose the cause of death when she confirmed it to Cadena Ser radio. Duro said that she and the activists were all devastated.

Sponsor Message

"Maricarmen's case, which captured media attention and traveled around the world, leaves us the image of the shameful violence of these types of evictions and the impact they can have on people's health," Duro said.

She had been expected to return home after leaving the hospital. The real estate company that evicted her in order to rent the property at a much higher price eventually caved in under immense public pressure and agreed to let her return to the apartment.

"Although a historic agreement was reached that would have allowed her to return home, this solution came too late," the Madrid Tenants' Union said in a statement Wednesday. "It was an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal."

toggle caption i Fernando Sánchez/Europa Press via AP

Maricarmen's plight galvanized a social movement

The average rent for Spain has almost doubled in the last 10 years, according to the real estate website Idealista. Spain's government said that 26% of Spaniards who rent housing spend an average of 40% of their income on rent and utilities, compared with the European Union average of 18% of renters who do so.

Protesters camped in Madrid's central Puerta del Sol square held a minute of silence after learning of her death.

Maricarmen spent almost her entire life in her apartment, where she first lived with her parents and brother. She later worked as a secretary for the board of a pharmaceutical company, Spanish daily El País reported. She said both her parents died in the apartment.

After retiring in 1998, she spent her days walking around the neighborhood, doing errands and taking care of the precious items in her home. The paper reported that black-and-white family photographs were among the only things she had brought with her to the hospital.

"Maricarmen only wanted to die in her home. She wasn't asking for anything else," Eugenio Melchor, 22, said at the protest in Madrid. "She was dying in her home and she almost did. They have killed her. I mean, there's no other word for it, and I hope those responsible for this pay and go to trial."

Sponsor Message

Maricarmen's plight galvanized a social movement, prompted Spain's unions to announce a general strike next month and intensified pressure on political leaders. Sánchez called an early election Monday after his government failed last week to push emergency housing measures through Parliament. He now hopes the issue will reinvigorate his Socialist Party and help him form a new government after the Nov. 29 election.

Housing Minister Isabel Rodríguez also expressed condolences, writing on X: "I deeply lament the death of Maricarmen. My condolences to those who accompanied her and fought by her side until the end."

Conservative opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo, who hopes to unseat Sánchez and his left-wing coalition, also offered condolences.

"I want to express my condolences to Maricarmen's family and loved ones. No campaign, no party, no use for political advantage," the Popular Party leader wrote. "When faced with the death of a person, we must only show respect."

World.title: Isaias strengthens into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season
World.content:
Isaias strengthens into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season

toggle caption i National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration/via AP

Isaias strengthened into the first hurricane of the Atlantic season late Wednesday as it surged towards the U.S. Gulf Coast, the National Hurricane Center said.

Forecasters warned that it was on track to make landfall between the Mississippi coast and the Florida Panhandle late Friday or early Saturday and was expected to bring heavy rains and potentially flash flooding.

The center of the cyclone was about 460 miles (745 kilometers) south-southwest of the Mississippi River, with maximum sustained winds around 75 mph (120 kph), according to an advisory from the Miami-based hurricane center. It was moving east-northeast at 9 mph (15 kph).

The hurricane formed late in the season

Isaias is developing more than four months into the Atlantic hurricane season, nearly tying a 121-year-old record for the area's latest-forming hurricane. According to the National Weather Service, the record dates to 1905, when the year's first Atlantic hurricane formed on Oct. 8.

Sponsor Message

The Atlantic hurricane season has been unusually quiet this year because of a strong El Niño, which disrupts storm formation over that ocean. Storm activity has been above average in the Pacific, where Tropical Storm Simon formed Wednesday off Mexico.

After Isaias (pronounced ees-ah-EE'-ahs, according to the hurricane center) became a tropical storm Wednesday in the warm waters off eastern Mexico, communities in its potential path worked quickly to prepare. Some Gulf oil wells paused production while governors in Florida and Alabama declared a state of emergency for dozens of counties.

Isaias is expected to strike along a wide swath of coastline that's very familiar with major hurricanes.

One of the 20th century's worst storms, Hurricane Camille, killed more than 250 people after hitting land near Waveland, Mississippi, in 1969. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 razed neighborhoods in Mississippi, flooded New Orleans and killed nearly 1,400 people. And Hurricane Michael leveled homes and buildings near Panama City, Florida, in 2018.

Oil production and tourism already affected

Ahead of the storm, oil and gas producers shut down a significant share of offshore production in the Gulf, which accounts for almost 15% of crude pumped annually in the U.S.

As of Wednesday about 25% of the oil production in the region was temporarily halted, taking about 511,000 barrels a day off the market, according to the Marine Minerals Administration. It said eight of the Gulf's 371 manned oil platforms were evacuated.

Sponsor Message

With oil prices already high, the production cuts are steep enough to affect markets, though other Gulf hurricanes have caused larger disruptions, said Jim Burkhard, global head of crude oil market research for S&P Global Energy. More concerning, he said, is whether Isaias strikes as a powerful storm near refineries.

"I would characterize the oil market risk as moderate, but rising," Burkhard said in an email.

In Gulf Shores, Alabama, organizers canceled the National Shrimp Festival, which had been scheduled for Thursday through the weekend. The event drew an estimated 325,000 people last year. Gulf Shores and Orange Beach issued a statement encouraging people in low-lying areas to voluntarily evacuate.

Gulf Shores resident Maranie Adams gathered water and other supplies as her family moved belongings, including a hot tub motor, to higher ground.

Adams said she, her husband and two adult sons planned to ride out the storm at home, roughly a half-mile from shore, sheltering indoors alongside their flock of chickens.

"We're having to get crates to bring them into the house so they don't blow away," Adams said. "It's going to be noisy."

Alabama Gov. Kay Ivey issued a state of emergency for 40 counties, saying on the social platform X that, "While I hope for minimal impacts, we must take preparations seriously."

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis declared one for 25 counties in the Panhandle and Big Bend regions. The declaration activates the state's emergency management plan for hurricanes, allowing officials to deploy disaster responders and equipment. The state also planned to deploy a Miami-based urban search and rescue task force.

In Pensacola, electric utilities were pre-positioning crews to quickly repair any power outages. City officials provided sand for residents to fill sandbags to protect their homes against flooding. And Mayor D.C. Reeves urged people to check on older adult neighbors and others who might need help.

Sponsor Message

"Obviously no need to panic at this point," Reeves told a news conference. "This is really about preparation."

World.title: The WHO seeks more details on the death of a plague research lab employee in Russia
World.content:
The WHO seeks more details on the death of a plague research lab employee in Russia

The World Health Organization says it wants more information on what caused the death of an employee at a Russian plague research lab. Russia says the woman died of pneumonia of unknown origin.

Transcript

SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST:

Russian authorities continue to insist there is no health emergency following the death of a 28-year-old lab technician at a plague research institute in Siberia last week. The case has created global concern over an outbreak of the plague or some other deadly pathogen. From Moscow, NPR's Charles Maynes reports.

CHARLES MAYNES, BYLINE: For nearly a week, Russia's consumer health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor has insisted the death of a female lab technician at a Siberian institute focused on combating the plague and other infectious diseases was due to pneumonia of, quote, "unknown" origin. A subsequent state investigation found no pathogens in the woman's body linked to her lab research, just as it said there was no evidence of an outbreak of the plague in the Irkutsk region of Russia where the institute is based. Yet, in a press conference Wednesday, the head of the World Health Organization, Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, said these Russian assurances were, at the very least, incomplete.

(SOUNDBITE OF PRESS CONFERENCE)

TEDROS ADHANOM GHEBREYESUS: We don't yet have the full picture of this event. And we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment. Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports.

MAYNES: Exiled Russian media with contacts on the ground in Siberia, in particular, have chronicled moments that at times seemed at odds with the official version of events. For example, reporting quarantines at some local hospitals or highlighting posts that later disappeared on social media by local government officials about health dangers. NPR has not independently confirmed the reports. The U.S., which withdrew from the WHO under the Trump administration, has also been pushing for more information.

Today, the State Department issued a formal request for Russia to provide more details on the case. And the U.S. embassy in Moscow published a health alert for Americans still in Russia to seek immediate medical assistance should they experience any adverse respiratory problems. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention also weighed in. In a statement, the CDC reminded the plague is treatable with antibiotics and said there was no indication of a broader threat to the United States. Meanwhile, President Trump played down the possibility the incident could've been a mishap involving a bioweapon.

(SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING)

PRESIDENT DONALD TRUMP: We don't think so. We're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so. And if you listen to them, it's under control.

MAYNES: Trump will have his own chance to try and learn just how much when he holds a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, expected later this week. Charles Maynes, NPR News, Moscow.

Copyright © 2026 NPR. All rights reserved. Visit our website terms of use and permissions pages at www.npr.org for further information.

Accuracy and availability of NPR transcripts may vary. Transcript text may be revised to correct errors or match updates to audio. Audio on npr.org may be edited after its original broadcast or publication. The authoritative record of NPR’s programming is the audio record.

World.title: What is the pneumonic plague?
World.content:
What is the pneumonic plague?

toggle caption i Science Source

The ancient word "plague" is back in the headlines.

NPR's Russia correspondent Charles Maynes reported this week on what we know about a Russian researcher working in a lab studying the plague who died from pneumonia of an unknown origin last week.

Maynes reports that the employee was a 28-year-old woman who worked in a lab in Siberia, some 2,500 miles from Moscow. An investigation by Russia's consumer health watchdog concluded that no pathogens in her body were connected to her work with infectious disease.

But local media have raised concerns about the spread of pneumonic plague, which NPR has not independently confirmed.

Sponsor Message

It's one of the diseases studied at the lab in Siberia. It's airborne and can be fatal.

While noting that 200 "contacts" were in quarantine, Russia has denied that there are cases of plague in the area. But questions loom. In a press conference Wednesday, the head of the World Health Organization, Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said these Russian assurances were — at the very least — incomplete: "We don't yet have the full picture of this event and we're not able to conduct a full risk assessment."

In the meantime, here's what we do know about the bacterial disease of plague — and the variant known as pneumonic plague.

Plague variations

The plague comes in several versions, depending on which body part the bacteria invade. When a flea bites a person, the individual typically develops what's called bubonic plague. In this case, the telltale sign is one or more swollen and painful lymph nodes, known as buboes. (The word "bubonic" comes from the Greek boubon, which means groin, because some people have swollen lymph nodes in their groin.) Doctors can diagnose the disease by taking a sample from the person's blood or lymph nodes and then submitting the sample to a lab for testing.

Sponsor Message

But when the bacteria spread to the lungs, this can cause what's called pneumonic plague. In this case, there's often no telltale sign of the plague, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

This version is much more dangerous, says medical entomologist Adelaide Miarinjara at Emory University. "It transmits pretty easily between people because it spreads through droplets, almost like COVID spreads."

And people can die more quickly with pneumonic plague than other forms, she adds, because the disease progresses more rapidly. "The key here is early diagnosis. If people aren't expecting it or don't seek treatment, they can die."

Treatment involves antibiotics, often administered by IV infusion.

In 2017, Madagascar suffered a large outbreak of pneumonic plague when a person from a rural part of the country brought the disease to the coastal city of Toamasina. That city hadn't seen a case of the plague in nearly a century, says Miarinjara, who was in Madagascar at the time. "A person transmitted the disease on public transportation," she says.

The country recorded more than 2,400 suspected cases, including nearly 1,900 cases of pneumonic plague. One study estimated that about 25% of people with confirmed cases died in this outbreak.

The history of quarantine

As for the reports of Russian "contacts" of the lab worker under quarantine — that reflects a long-standing response to sicknesses like the plague.

The idea of isolating, or quarantining, sick people dates back at least 3,000 years. The Book of Leviticus in the Bible mentions how to isolate people with leprosy.

The word "quarantine" itself arose during the Black Death, when the city-state of Dubrovnik, now part of the country of Croatia, enacted what is likely the first state-imposed isolation.

At the time, Dubrovnik was a wealthy merchant city along the coast of the Adriatic Sea. City leaders wanted to keep the bubonic plague out. So they began to force visitors to wait for 40 days on a remote island outside the city before coming ashore.

Sponsor Message

They called the wait quarantino, from the Italian word for "40."

"The first quarantine was pretty much improvised," Ivana Marinavić, the head of educational programs at the Lazarettos of Dubrovnik , told NPR in 2021 . The Lazarettos were the first buildings ever constructed for the sole purpose of quarantining.

If you broke the quarantine during the plague, the consequences were severe. "Torture, or cutting your nose or your ears off," Marinavić told NPR.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

World.title: This surprising mammal fossil is giving scientists something to chew on
World.content:
This surprising mammal fossil is giving scientists something to chew on

toggle caption i Chang-Fu Zhou/Shandong University of Science and Technology

Over the years, a section of the Inner Mongolia region of China has coughed up heaps of remarkable fossils, ranging from feathered dinosaurs to flying reptiles.

"To say it's [a] hot spot is actually [an] understatement," says Zhe-Xi Luo, a paleontologist at the University of Chicago.

For new discoveries, everyday mysteries, and the science behind the headlines, follow NPR’s Short Wave podcast.

Many of these fossils wind up at the nearby Paleontological Museum of Liaoning, a facility that Luo and his colleague, Thomas Martin of the University of Bonn, visit each year to examine new finds. A decade ago, a specimen in a thick slab of shale caught their eye.

It was the fossilized bones and soft tissue impressions of an ancient mammal that lived some 165 million years ago. "Early fossil mammals — in fact, they are exceedingly rare," says Luo.

Sponsor Message

This animal, which the team named Megacauda sungei and have described in the journal Nature, was a prize discovery. The remains were so intact that it was possible to determine that it was likely capable of chewing food and then swallowing it, and also suckling — traits that are shared by mammals.

Luo and his colleagues conclude that these evolutionary innovations — and their presence among our ancient mammalian relatives — extend deep into the past to at least the middle Jurassic.

"It's all there in one remarkable fossil," says Luo.

A chihuahua-sized chimera

The fossil was about the size of a chihuahua, but somewhat hard to discern from the rock surrounding it.

"The fossil itself is actually very dark," explains Luo. "The bones are black, the slab [is] dark. And it's kind of difficult to have beautiful photographs."

One of his collaborators, Chang-Fu Zhou of Shandong University of Science and Technology, snapped a different kind of vivid image using a technique called X-ray fluorescence spectroscopy. "It would make this bone pop out in different colors," says Luo.

The resulting image rendered the skeleton a bright yellow and it showcased a curious combination of characteristics. The back end, which includes the pelvis, hind limbs, and tail, resembles a modern-day platypus.

toggle caption i April Neander/University of Chicago

These features suggest that this animal was likely semi-aquatic and foraged in the water. "The big tail is good for swimming," says Luo.

"However," he continues, "its teeth and the jaw would be very different from platypus. So the head is very much of a predator." Indeed, Luo and his colleagues found a smattering of small salamander bones inside the fossil that they suspect the animal had eaten by first cutting and shearing with its sharp teeth.

A lot to swallow

There was something else that Luo instantly noticed about the fossil. "My eyes zeroed in on these tiny hyoid bones," he recalls.

Sponsor Message

The human hyoid bone sits in the throat, half an inch or so above the Adam's apple, and supports the backside of the tongue.

The team later CT scanned the fossil, including the underside of the skull, which exposed a delicate roof of the mouth as well as a series of bone hooks and ridges.

With this combination of rarely preserved features, "we are able with great confidence to reconstruct the whole muscular skeletal machinery," says Luo.

This reconstruction revealed that the animal was likely capable of doing two things that are unique to mammals.

The first is swallowing food after chewing it. Other vertebrates tend to bite and gulp. But mammals "chew down all the food with our teeth," Luo says. "And then we swallow one bolus of food down to our esophagus at a time."

Consider, for a moment, a carnivore that chews meat, an herbivore that crunches on vegetables, and an insect-eater that chomps bugs. This diverse array of foods all get chewed up and then swallowed down a mammalian throat in a similar way.

Secondly, this fossil appears to have been capable of suckling, which embodies something even more fundamental.

"That ability to suckle mother's milk literally defined our biology," says Luo. "And that's why our group is called mammals. We're named after the mammary glands."

This is some of the oldest fossil evidence of an animal with both these key mammalian abilities.

Small but varied

"It's a fascinating specimen," says Jessica Theodor, a paleontologist at the University of Calgary who wasn't involved in the research. "The whole setup looks more like what we see in modern mammals."

Theodor would like to see some of the images in greater detail, but she says a fossil like this tracks the evolution of lactation, which she likens to a kind of dietary and hormonal conversation between mother and baby.

Sponsor Message

"The conversation is beginning very far back in the Mesozoic — in the Jurassic and Cretaceous," says Theodor. "That's amazing to me that it's this old and this fundamental."

For Luo, this fossil is the latest evidence of how new ways of feeding have helped mammals and their predecessors diversify — even back when they were the little guys on the proverbial block.

"Mammals, they're never dominant in the age of dinosaurs," he says. "But nonetheless, they hold out relatively well compared to all other vertebrates."

By the time of the Jurassic period, there were already proto-mammalian gliders, swimmers, land-dwellers, tree-dwellers and diggers. Each one was making a living in its own distinct way — all united in their shared ability to chew, swallow and suckle.

World.title: Judge orders that Christa Pike execution evidence be preserved
World.content:
Judge orders that Christa Pike execution evidence be preserved

toggle caption i George Walker IV/Pool AP

The Davidson County Chancery Court in Nashville ordered Tennessee prison officials to preserve all evidence in connection with last week's botched lethal injection of Christa Pike, including log books, medical waste and all messages sent or received by officials associated with the execution attempt.

"Anything in the actual room needs to be preserved and maintained," Judge I'Ashea Myles said.

The judge also granted a request from Pike's attorneys for "liberal access" to their client, ordering that prison officials will have two hours to respond to requests from lawyers for in-person visits with Pike.

Speaking outside the courtroom, Luke P. Ihnen, an assistant federal defender in Knoxville, told reporters that this was "just a first step of many to preserve and enforce Christa's constitutional rights after this unprecedented botched execution."

Sponsor Message

The hearing came a week after Pike was left hospitalized and in critical condition following the Sept. 30 execution attempt in which she was strapped to a gurney and administered two doses of pentobarbital, a barbiturate widely used in U.S. executions. But several minutes after the first dose, she said her arm was burning and asked whether it was supposed to feel that way. She then said, "Please try up on my shoulder higher."

Pike's attorneys said that after days of unconsciousness, Pike was awake again, speaking and continuing to receive critical medical care.

Randy Spivey, a post-conviction attorney representing Pike, called his client "a survivor."

"She survived sexual abuse [and] the rapes of multiple men. She survived a suicide attempt when she was 12 and she survived the state's attempt to execute her," he said. "She deserves answers about what was done to her and the people of Tennessee deserve those answers, too."

He said of the botched execution, "all of this was foreseen," because Pike has a medical condition that would make it difficult to insert an IV to deliver the lethal doses of pentobarbital.

toggle caption i George Walker IV/AP

Spivey, who was a witness to last week's failed execution, told NPR that after a second dose, Pike fell unconscious but continued breathing and making sounds like choking. It "went on for so long," he said.

Sponsor Message

Following the failed execution, Tennessee's top prison official, Frank Strada, resigned, and the state's governor, Bill Lee, halted executions through the end of the year and ordered an independent investigation into the state's capital punishment system.

It wasn't immediately clear whether that would affect a second attempt to execute Pike, but speaking at Wednesday's hearing, Tennessee Assistant Attorney General John Ayers said the decision on when or if to schedule a new execution date was up to the state's supreme court.

Ihnen, one of the defense attorneys, said it would be "unconscionable that the state would try to execute her again."

toggle caption i Tennessee Department of Correction/via AP

Pike was on death row for a murder she committed at age 18. In 1995, she and her boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, tortured and killed 19-year-old Colleen Slemmer, a fellow classmate in the Knoxville Job Corps. Shipp, who was a minor at the time of the crime, received life in prison without parole for his part in the murder.

In a clemency petition filed last month, Pike's attorneys asked that her sentence be commuted to life in prison without the possibility of parole, citing her history of childhood trauma.

"Local and national media covered Christa's trial in the midst of the 'Satanic Panic' of the 1990s," the attorneys said. "In truth, it was Christa's abusive boyfriend and co-defendant, Tadaryl Shipp, who was fascinated by satanic imagery."

The media at the time had "focused on the salacious parts of Christa's crime, disregarding the context of her youth, trauma, and mental illness," they added.

toggle caption i George Walker IV/AP

Critics of the death penalty are outraged at what happened to Pike during the attempt to execute her.

"This failed attempt is the worst we've ever seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," Robin M. Maher, executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, said in a statement.

Sponsor Message

The Death Penalty Information Center, a nonpartisan, nonprofit organization, said Pike was the first person in the history of capital punishment to survive after being injected with lethal drugs.

World.title: Trump approved the military's 1st firing squad execution since WWII. Why now?
World.content:
Trump approved the military's 1st firing squad execution since WWII. Why now?

toggle caption i Eli Kaplan/Getty Images

President Trump has approved the execution by firing squad of Nidal Hasan, the former U.S. Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people in a shooting rampage at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.

It would be the first U.S. military execution in over six decades — and the first by firing squad since World War II.

Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell announced the news on X Monday night, writing, "Judgement day for Hasan has finally come." Secretary of the Army Adam Telle said in an order released Tuesday that Hasan's execution will take place at Fort Hood on Dec. 3.

Sponsor Message

But Hasan could delay those proceedings if he files a habeas corpus appeal in the federal courts, said Robin Maher, executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center.

"The fact that the president has approved Mr. Hasan's death sentence is another step closer to his execution," Maher said. "But that does not mean that his execution will be imminent."

For example, Ronald Gray, who committed multiple rapes and murders near Fort Bragg in the 1980s, is still on military death row despite having had his sentence approved by President George W. Bush in 2008.

It's not clear why the Pentagon is moving forward now, or why it specifically chose a firing squad as the execution method. But some death penalty experts that NPR interviewed suspect it could be connected to Tennessee's botched lethal injection of Christa Pike, which has dominated headlines and reignited debate over the past week.

"For years now, states have been pushing this rock of Sisyphus uphill … They're spending millions of dollars, and yet they're having botched executions," said Corinna Lain, whose book, Secrets of the Killing State, was published last year. "So this moment in time is one where states are really thinking about: what are we doing and what best serves the death penalty? Whether the answer to that is firing squad is another question entirely."

The White House referred NPR's questions to the Pentagon, which declined to elaborate beyond Parnell's post.

Sponsor Message

In his announcement, Parnell said Trump had acted on the recommendation of Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, who said last September that he was "100 percent committed to ensuring the death penalty is carried out for Nidal Hasan."

"This savage terrorist deserves the harshest lawful punishment for his 2009 mass shooting at Fort Hood," Hegseth told several media outlets, including The Hill, at the time. "The victims and survivors deserve justice without delays."

Hasan was working as an Army psychiatrist in Nov. 2009, when he opened fire at the Fort Hood processing center where troops were preparing to deploy to Afghanistan. He shouted "Allahu akbar" — "God is great" — before killing 13 people and injuring another 32. The attack ended when he was shot by civilian security officers at the scene, leaving him paralyzed from the waist down.

Hasan acted as his own lawyer during his 2013 trial, at which he admitted that "the evidence will clearly show that I am the shooter." The American-born Muslim said he had "switched sides" and turned against the U.S. because of its military actions in the Middle East.

The military jury found Hasan guilty on all counts. He was dismissed from the Army and sentenced to death, which triggered an automatic appeals process that ended only when the Supreme Court denied his final petition in the spring of 2025.

Hasan is one of just four people currently on military death row — all of whom were convicted of murder — according to the Death Penalty Information Center. They are all incarcerated at the United States Disciplinary Barracks at Fort Leavenworth, Kansas.

toggle caption i Uncredited/Bell County Sheriff's Department/Bell County Sheriff's Department

The military's last firing squad execution was in 1945

The first recorded execution by shooting on what would become U.S. soil happened in Jamestown, Va., in 1608, when one of the colony's early council members, Capt. George Kendall, was put to death for mutiny. Firing squads have been used relatively sparingly since, including during the Civil War.

Sponsor Message

"On the one hand, it is one of our earliest forms of execution," said Fordham Law School professor Deborah Denno, who has been studying execution methods for 36 years. "On the other hand, it's always been controversial because people associate it with extreme barbarity and … the Wild West."

The U.S. military last executed someone by firing squad in 1945: Private Eddie Slovik was shot for desertion in France, the only U.S. soldier to be executed for that reason since the Civil War.

"They didn't even tell his wife that he had been executed; they just said that he had died in Europe," journalist Charles Glass, who wrote a book about World War II deserters, told NPR in 2013. He said Slovik's case only became public knowledge about a decade later, when an investigative reporter published a book about it in the mid-'50s.

Most of the known U.S. military executions during World War II were done by hanging, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. The last time the U.S. military carried out an execution of any sort was in 1961, when Private John Bennett was hanged for the 1955 rape and attempted murder of an Austrian girl.

"We basically have gone out of the business — until now — of executing people through the military justice system," said Eugene Fidell, who teaches military justice at Yale Law School.

The military officially suspended the death penalty after a 1983 court ruling, but reinstated it the following year and specifically designated lethal injection as the standard method. Fidell says that changed with new Army regulations in 2023.

"The regulation was changed to make the choice or the method of execution a matter for the president's discretion," he said. "And obviously, the president has, in this case, approved the use of a firing squad."

Under the current rules, once the president approves an execution, the secretary of the Army decides the time, location and method, to take place within 60 to 150 days.

Sponsor Message

Fidell said he was not surprised by Trump's approval, given his administration's embrace of the death penalty overall and the severity of Hasan's offenses. But he suggested some might find the social media announcement inappropriate.

"The military has lived without executions since 1961, and yet we have here a really serious case," Fidell said. "I think it would have been a lot better had a more formal, dignified means been chosen to disseminate this information."

The Pentagon hasn't held a formal press briefing since May.

The death penalty is already under scrutiny

toggle caption i AP/South Carolina Department of Corrections

Denno, who studies the death penalty, doesn't think the timing of the Pentagon's announcement is a coincidence.

Denno says Pike's case "is probably the worst that's ever happened." But it's far from the only botched legal injection in recent years, she says, pointing to what she calls a pattern of convicts being "tortured unnecessarily" that has prompted some jurisdictions to seek out alternatives.

The Justice Department made firing squads available for federal executions earlier this year, following a directive from Trump. Seven states now have firing squads on the books as an execution method, which Denno says is the highest number ever recorded.

Denno says firing squads are "the least inhumane method of execution that we have," since, when done properly, death can occur in seconds.

But she acknowledges that those have been plagued by issues, too, including last year in South Carolina, when an autopsy revealed that the shooters may have prolonged a prisoner's death by missing his heart.
