"There is a humane way to take a life. It's called life without parole," said Lain, the author.

Lain says lethal injections, because of their relative lack of gore, have kept the death penalty "out of sight, out of mind" for many people over the last five decades.

But she sees signs of change. Data analysis by the Death Penalty Information Center shows that death sentences have declined by 90% over the past three decades. Fewer than 50 new ones have been imposed each year since 2015. A 2025 Gallup poll put public support for the death penalty at a five-decade low, with opposition highest among younger generations.

Sponsor Message

"The death penalty in this country is dying its own slow death," she said. She thinks the federal government's embrace of the firing squad, including in Hasan's case, could hasten it even more.

World.title: Don't support Trump tariffs then blame Stelco job cuts on 'act of God,' Joly warns Cleveland-Cliffs
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Canada's industry minister said Wednesday Stelco Holdings Inc. cannot use the trade war to justify cutting jobs it committed to when it bought the Hamilton-based steel plant, particularly when the head of its U.S. parent company has publicly backed steel tariffs.

Mélanie Joly told reporters that the chief executive of U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs has supported steel tariffs and therefore cannot characterize the company's plan to lay off up to 500 workers due to tariffs and market pressures as beyond its control.

"He's in favour of these U.S. tariffs against steel," she said, referring to Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves' public support of American steel tariffs.

"They cannot say that this is now an act of God or force majeure."

If the company does not respond to the federal government's demand for a plan outlining how it will meet all of its commitments, including maintaining more than 1,500 jobs, Ottawa will pursue enforcement action, Joly said.

"They need to comply," she said. "If not, we will use the full force of the law."

Canada gave U.S.-based Cleveland-Cliffs the green light to purchase Stelco back in 2024 under the Investment Canada Act.

Canada's approval of that takeover was contingent on the new owner maintaining the number of union jobs and the majority of non-union positions, Joly said.

She sent a letter to Stelco president Paul Simon on Monday demanding a plan outlining how Cleveland-Cliffs intends to comply with all of the undertakings it made to Ottawa when it acquired Stelco, including its jobs commitment.

Ottawa has not yet received a response from Stelco on the letter, Joly said.

Meanwhile, she distinguished Stelco's planned job cuts from recent layoffs and plant disruptions in the auto sector, saying Cleveland-Cliffs made legally binding employment commitments when it acquired the steelmaker.

"These obligations are binding."

World.title: 'Canada is not our enemy': Michigan Republican Senate candidate breaks with Trump on trade war
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Republican candidate in a pitched battle for Michigan's open Senate seat is calling on U.S. President Donald Trump to end the trade war with Canada.

Mike Rogers released a new 30-second ad criticizing the tariffs while sitting in a sports bar with a Labatt beer, a Canadian brand popular in border states like his.

"Here in Michigan we know that Canada is not on our enemy. We need to end this tariff war now," Rogers says in the ad, as an image of the Ambassador Bridge, which connects Windsor and Detroit, appears on screen.

"As Michigan's senator, I'll bring both parties together to lower your prices. That's job No. 1," Rogers says in the spot.

Speaking to reporters in the Oval Office later Wednesday, U.S. President Donald Trump was dismissive of the ad, recasting Rogers's trade war message.

"Well, I viewed it as though he wanted Canada to make a deal," Trump said.

"We don't want them to make cars for us.... It's a long story, but they've been ripping us off. Canada has been ripping us off for many, many years and they're not going to rip us off anymore," he said.

WATCH | Reporter asks Trump about Rogers: Trump reacts to anti-trade war ad from Republican candidate | Duration closed caption 0:45 U.S. President Donald Trump was asked by a reporter about a new ad from Michigan Republican Senate candidate Mike Rogers that called for an end to the trade war with Canada. Trump said he 'viewed it as though [Rogers] wanted Canada to make a deal' and repeated his claim that Canada has been taking advantage of the U.S. for 'many, many years.'

About-face for Rogers

This is an about-face for Rogers, who earlier had endorsed the tariffs Trump levied on Canadian goods.

In an interview with Fox News this summer, Rogers said Trump's trade policy designed to "reindustrialize" the U.S. was "huge for us ... all of these things are really positive."

He said Canada wants to sell hundreds of thousands of cars into Michigan and that should be "absolutely unacceptable" because those exports "undercut the people who build cars and car parts."

"The Canadians have not been good partners on this," he said.

WATCH | Trump adviser warns Canada against election interference: 'You will pay': Trump adviser warns Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterms | Duration closed caption 2:54 White House trade adviser Peter Navarro warned Canada not to 'interfere' with U.S. midterm elections in border states such as Maine and Michigan by lobbying against the Trump administration's tariffs. Navarro said Canada would 'pay even more dearly' for doing so.

Rogers has long been closely associated with Trump. When the U.S. president endorsed Rogers earlier this year, the candidate said he was "thrilled" to receive it.

"Together, President Trump and I will unleash a great revival in the state of Michigan," he said at the time of the endorsement.

Tariffs unpopular in U.S.: polls

Rogers's break with the president on Canadian trade policy comes as polls suggest Trump's tariffs are deeply unpopular in the U.S.

Only 26 per cent of Americans surveyed for a Politico poll late last month said levying tariffs on Canadian goods was the right thing to do.

LISTEN | Canada's choices: Front Burner 23:47 Should Canada have taken the U.S. deal?

Rogers is also trailing his Democratic opponent, Abdul El-Sayed, in most public opinion surveys. After the ad was released, El-Sayed said Rogers "must have had one too many of those Labatts."

"You cheer-led this tariff war from the beginning and you’re flip-flopping now because your poll numbers are in free fall. Donald is the reason we’re in a trade war. And he’s the reason you’re running," he wrote in a social media post.

Canada, U.S. auto industries deeply intertwined

The Canadian and U.S. auto sectors have one of the most deeply intertwined cross-border manufacturing relationships in the world.

Canada does not "undercut" the U.S. industry, as Rogers describes; rather, it supplies critical parts used in assembly plants throughout the U.S.

Some of those components cross the border a half-dozen times or more because these sectors are so integrated after decades of free trade, with Canadian plants specializing in particular parts and powertrains.

WATCH | How tariffs are affecting our auto industry: How are tariffs affecting Canada's auto industry, really? | Duration 2:28 Car parts can cross international borders six, seven or even eight times before ending up in a vehicle. But amid a trade war, as both Canada and the United States raise tariffs up to 50 per cent, it's getting more expensive — and complicated — to build cars. The CBC's Acton Clarkin breaks it down.

It's a relationship that experts say has helped the North American auto market compete against low-cost overseas manufacturers.

Plus, Canada is a huge customer for what American auto plants churn out every year. About three-quarters of all vehicles sold in Canada are imported, with the majority coming from U.S. plants in Michigan, Indiana and Texas.

Dearborn, Mich.-based Ford has been the No. 1 vehicle brand in Canada for years, with the American-made F-Series being particularly popular among Canadian consumers.

And, despite Republican claims that Trump's tariff policies are boosting industrial employment, data from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics compiled by the Economic Policy Institute shows that some 62,000 manufacturing jobs have been lost since Trump took office for his second term in January 2025.

World.title: Canada yanks sponsorship of disinformation conference discussing U.S. as a threat
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The federal government has withdrawn sponsorship of a European disinformation conference that includes panels discussing the U.S. government as a foreign interference risk.

Samantha Lafleur, a spokesperson for Global Affairs Canada (GAC), said the government took issue with the framing of some panels at the event organized by EU DisinfoLab, a non-profit based in Brussels.

The conference features panels about the U.S. as a source of "foreign information manipulation and interference (FIMI)," a phenomenon where foreign governments or actors on their behalf manipulate information to confuse, divide or mislead the public and erode confidence in institutions.

GAC — Ottawa's diplomatic arm — Lithuania's Foreign Ministry and the European External Action Service were initially listed as supporters of the annual conference largely attended by researchers and civil society organizations.

The government of Canada logo was covered up on signs spotted around the anti-disinformation conference. (Submitted)

As the gathering got underway in Vilnius, Lithuania, on Wednesday, their names were covered up on signs spotted around the conference, according to photos shared with CBC News. As of writing, the French government remains a sponsor.

In a statement to CBC News, GAC did not deny that it had concerns with describing the U.S. as a foreign interference threat.

"Following changes to the framing of several panel discussions, GAC decided to revise its participation in those sessions at the EU DisinfoLab 2026 conference," wrote Lafleur.

She did not respond to questions about particular changes GAC took issue with or whether the U.S. raised concerns.

According to the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine, the description of Wednesday's panel discussing how to push back on the U.S. as a foreign interference threat appears to have been unchanged since Sept. 9.

GAC no longer chairing Arctic panel

A GAC official also pulled out of chairing a session on disinformation in the Arctic scheduled for Thursday, said presenter Ben Shultz with the American Sunlight Project.

The panel proposes to talk about Greenland and "growing evidence that the United States has, in specific Arctic contexts, operated as a FIMI actor."

Shultz shared the initial plan for the panel from months ago, which includes talking about the U.S. as a foreign interference actor.

He called three governments withdrawing a "shock" and questioned whether they were pressured.

"Thankfully every speaker has still shown up, which is awesome, and I think a testament to the resolve of the research community. But it's definitely put a bit of a damper on the atmosphere," he said in an interview.

The European External Action Service, the EU's diplomatic service, said in a statement it asked to have its logo removed from the material associated with the conference "in view of the content of the programme."

Asked if it was related to the U.S. foreign interference panel, an EU spokesperson repeated that the EEAS logo was removed because "organizers chose to frame some of the discussions in a way which does not align with the official positions held by the EU."

Neither Lithuania's Foreign Ministry nor the conference organizers responded to a request for comment.

Canada's withdrawal comes the same week the Globe and Mail reported that some people involved in campaigning for Alberta independence had met on both sides of the border with U.S. entities.

CBC News previously reported that some of those meetings took place in U.S. State Department offices in Washington, D.C., last year.

GAC's move also comes as the country is embroiled in an often bitter and personal trade dispute with U.S. President Donald Trump's administration.

Lafleur said Canada "remains firmly committed to addressing the challenge of disinformation and misinformation" and that Global Affairs Canada officials "look forward to engaging with partners and stakeholders on efforts to counter disinformation."

World.title: 'Unimaginable loss': Horses killed on B.C. highway while travelling to championship
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The Canadian equestrian community is mourning the death of three horses after a collision in B.C.

The horses were travelling from Manitoba and Alberta to Langley on Monday, to compete in the 2026 Equestrian Canada National Dressage West championship at the Thunderbird Show Park.

At 8:45 a.m. local time on Oct. 6, officers with the B.C. Highway Patrol responded to a single-vehicle crash roughly 40 kilometres east of Revelstoke on Highway 1.

The driver was towing a trailer with four horses when she lost control and collided with a rock wall, according to Sgt. Michael McLaughlin.

Three horses died, and the fourth horse was injured.

Kate Wall seen with Rosaria, a dressage horse that died during a single vehicle collision on Highway 1 in B.C. on Oct. 6, 2026. (Shealynn Choy/S.C.apturing The Moment Photography)

Paramedics with B.C. Emergency Health Services responded to the crash with an ambulance.

"Paramedics provided emergency medical care to one patient, who was transported to hospital in stable condition," said BCEHS paramedic public information officer Brian Twaites.

Police said the driver was a 73-year-old woman from Langdon, Alta.

"The driver was issued a violation ticket for failing to keep right under the [B.C.] Motor Vehicle Act, which comes with a fine of $109," McLaughlin said.

Condolences from all over Canada are pouring in for the horses and those who knew them.

'My heart is completely shattered'

Mackenzie Abbott is a dressage rider and head trainer from Headingley, Man. She said two of the horses were ones she trained, and they were owned by Solace Stables.

"We have suffered an unimaginable loss and lost our beloved horses," Abbott said. "I loved my horses more than I could ever explain. My heart is completely shattered."

The two horses, named Fearless and Rosaria, were set to compete in Langley starting on Oct. 9.

Highway 1 near the Illecillewaet Brake Check, roughly near where the collision occurred on Oct. 6, 2026, east of Canyon Hot Springs and Revelstoke. Four horses were in the trailer and three died. (DriveBC)

"They were the top of their fields in our sport here in Manitoba, and we were looking forward to proving their capabilities to Canada," Abbott said.

The two horses were being transported with a driver, when she learned about the crash through a phone call.

"We all fundraised to get there," Abbott said. "We are just devastated to lose our best friends in the most tragic way."

The competition was being organized by Equestrian Canada, and is a major national event where athletes and their horses travel to the West Coast to compete.



It is common in the sport for athletes and owners to hire commercial drivers to transport the horses to the events.

In a statement, Equestrian Canada said it has reached out to the athletes and owners involved and extended mental health support.

"Our equestrian community functions as a close-knit family, and a sudden loss of this magnitude is felt deeply by every rider, coach, groom, and owner across the country," reads the statement

"[Equestrian Canada] extends its heartfelt sympathies to the riders, owners, families, and the entire support team surrounding these beloved horses."

James Hood, the chief of staff with Equestrian Canada, said they are organizing a fundraiser at the event to support the people impacted.



"I encourage our athletes, our coaches and our grooms and owners to lean on each other in this time of loss ... because it is a trying time and we will get through this," Hood said.

World.title: NASA's Curiosity rover takes striking image of dawn on Mars
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

NASA has released a striking image of dawn on the Martian surface taken by its Curiosity rover, showing sunlight bathing ‌jagged crags formed billions of years ago as the car-sized vehicle continues to explore Earth's planetary neighbour.

Curiosity landed in 2012 in Gale Crater near the Martian equator, and since 2014 has been climbing Mount Sharp, a five-kilometre-tall mountain rising from the crater floor.

The image was taken by the six-wheeled rover's Mastcam camera about ​an hour after the sun rose above a landscape featuring wind-carved ​cliffs in the distance.

"The bright craggy peaks in the distance are a rock layer that is quite different in appearance from all the layers the rover has driven through so far," said planetary scientist Ashwin Vasavada of NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory in California, the Curiosity project scientist.

NASA believes that some kind of wind-blown sediment landed in the crater from nearby volcanic activity. Once it hardened into rock, "eons of wind carved ‌up the rock layer into ridges called yardangs," Vasvada said.

The yardang layer most likely formed about three billion years ago, around the same time as the rest of the mountain, according to Vasavada. This layer spans about 16 ⁠kilometres across the northwestern reaches of Mount Sharp.

But the layers appears to have been added on later, he said.

"It's above what geologists call an ‌unconformity: a gap in time where previous layers eroded down before new layers were deposited on top."

Rover making gradual ascent up mountain

The rover on its gradual ascent up the mountain has gained upwards of nearly a kilometre in elevation, the most ever climbed on Mars, according to NASA.

Mount Sharp is built of layers, each recording a ​period of the planet's geological past. In studying these layers, scientists have learned more about bodies of water — lakes and streams — that long ago covered this region, at ⁠a time when Mars was wetter and warmer than the cold and desolate place it is today.

Vasavada said NASA hopes ⁠Curiosity will reach the yardang layer in 2027 or 2028, at which time it will use its instruments to ⁠scrutinize ⁠the geology there.

Curiosity has been studying the ​geology and climate of Mars and examining whether it once bore conditions conducive to harboring microbial life. It is one of two ​NASA rovers operating on Mars. The ⁠Perseverance rover is currently traversing the margins of Jezero Crater in the northern hemisphere.

Curiosity's new image of Martian dawn is certainly otherworldly.

"This scene has a wildness that reminds me of a road trip through Monument Valley, Arizona. You can almost feel the silence and the endless open space under the sky," Vasavada said.

"But as familiar as that sounds, the sky is orange and the sunrise has shades ⁠of blue. It's like Earth, but ‌it's definitely Mars."

World.title: Alberta premier says ‘ridiculous’ for separatists to offer royalties, water to Americans
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

Premier Danielle Smith says it was “absurd” and “ridiculous” for prominent separatists to offer the United States government access to fresh water and resource royalties in return for its help establishing an independent Alberta.

The information was reported by the Globe and Mail on Saturday. CBC News has not independently confirmed the details in the story.

Alberta separatists met three times with U.S. State Department officials in Washington in late 2025.

“I think it's absurd that anybody would offer something like that up that's not theirs to offer,” Smith said at an unrelated news conference in Edmonton Wednesday.

“It's a decision that Albertans would make, and I don't think Albertans would support it.”

The Washington meetings were already public knowledge, but what was offered to U.S. officials was new information.

According to the Globe and Mail, Dennis Modry, co-founder of the pro-independence Alberta Prosperity Project (APP), told the media outlet about the offer that was made.

Jeff Rath, a lawyer with the separatist movement, denied to the Globe and Mail that any of those matters were discussed.

Mitch Sylvestre is the president for the Bonnyville-Cold Lake UCP constituency association. He also heads up the APP.

In an interview with The Canadian Press on Monday, he also denied any discussion about access to water or oil taking place during the meetings in Washington, though he noted he only went to one meeting.

"We have no authority to do any of that," he said.

"We're not in government. We can't go down there and have that conversation."

Sylvestre added that he believes there's enough support in Alberta for independence that U.S. support is not needed.

Smith has been criticized for including a question on Alberta’s Oct. 19 referendum about whether the province should remain in Canada or if it should start the legal process for a binding future referendum that would provide a definitive answer on Alberta’s fate within Confederation.

Smith didn’t answer a question Wednesday about whether she believes she has encouraged U.S. involvement in the political situation by asking the question.

Instead she said she believes the people that were involved in the meetings are critics of hers because she plans to vote to stay in Canada.

“We expect that the American administration will deal with the duly elected governments,” Smith added.

“That includes mine, but it also includes the government of Canada.”

Alberta mayors voice concern ahead of fall referendum

The mayors of Calgary and Edmonton appeared on CBC News Network's Power & Politics on Monday and spoke about their concerns in light of the Globe and Mail report.

Calgary Mayor Jeromy Farkas said he believes the referendum is a distraction from other issues facing Albertans.

He said he's worried about the potential for misinformation and foreign interference, and more generally about the impact that Alberta's referendum could have on the province's future.

"My fear is regardless of the outcome, this is not going to be settled," he said.

"My fear is that we're going to continue to see continued divisive debates and potentially more referendums being called."

Edmonton Mayor Andrew Knack said the report about water and royalties being offered to the U.S. is a reminder of what's at risk, especially with U.S. President Donald Trump's past comments about his interest in potentially making Canada his country's 51st state.

"That to me has been part of the challenge of this," he said. "This is a very dangerous path."

Knack said he believes the vast majority of Edmontonians do not support a binding referendum on independence, and called on all Albertans to vote in this month's referendum.

"If there's one good thing about this ridiculous story — I can't even believe that's happening — is that hopefully it serves as a wake-up call to everyone in this province that you cannot be sleeping on Oct. 19."

World.title: Woman at centre of Cornell gang-rape case was 'misled' about investigation, lawyer says
World.content:
The audio version of this article is generated by AI-based technology. Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results.

The woman who says several men raped her at a Cornell University fraternity party was "misled" about the status of the criminal investigation in the weeks after she went to police, her lawyer said Wednesday.

Even as she took her allegations about a 2024 gang rape at the Chi Phi fraternity house through Cornell's internal disciplinary process, the university's police department gave her the impression that a criminal investigation was continuing, lawyer Thomas Giuffra told The Associated Press.

In fact, the criminal inquiry ended almost as soon as it began.

Tompkins County district attorney Matthew Van Houten, the local prosecutor, made the decision not to go forward with a criminal case within days of the woman giving her first substantial interviews to police.

Van Houten has said he asked Cornell's police department to convey the decision to the woman, who is referred to in court documents as Jane Doe, but never spoke personally to her or her lawyer.

Giuffra said the woman was told the criminal investigation was ongoing.

"I think she was misled," he said. "I was involved with this case early on. I thought they were still investigating. It was news to me that they weren't doing anything."

At the time, Giuffra added, he assumed investigators just needed more time to speak with witnesses and build a case.

"But nothing was being done, and we didn't know that," he said.

A messages seeking comment was left for Van Houten. Cornell's media relations office, citing pending litigation, declined to comment on behalf of the university's police department.

The district attorney said in a statement last week that he was confident no further investigation was necessary after prosecutors and criminal investigators from his office reviewed a six-page summary of the woman's account, written by a police officer.

WATCH | What we know about the case: 'Cornell 7' lawsuit: What we know | Duration 2:53 Alumni are threatening to pull funding, celebrities are lashing out and people are boycotting institutions associated with Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., after an alleged gang rape ignited the internet. The case came into the spotlight after the victim, known in court documents as Jane Doe, filed a civil lawsuit on Sept. 16, alleging the private Ivy League university protected the seven men, now dubbed 'the Cornell 7.' She alleges they drugged and assaulted her over several hours at a frat house in October 2024. WARNING: This video may affect those who have experienced sexual violence or know someone affected by it. It also contains vulgar language.

Different accounts

Based on that summary, Van Houten said he believed no crime had been committed, and that the woman's participation in drug use and sex was "voluntary, conscious and consensual."

That description differs sharply with what the woman told police and university investigators, and with what she alleged in a lawsuit filed against seven Chi Phi fraternity members, Cornell and others last month.

Among other things, Giuffra said, the six-page report omitted the woman telling investigators, "I can say with 100 per cent confidence I was raped," that she was subjected to physical violence, and that a fraternity brother had sent a message to a group chat using a vulgar term to advertise that a woman's body was freely available.

Last week, citing investigative records it obtained, the New York Times reported that a Cornell police investigator tried to get Van Houten's office to consider additional evidence in the weeks after the alleged rape, but was rebuffed.

"At first I thought these police were incompetent," Giuffra said. "It sounds like they were doing the right thing. And they just got shut down."

Giuffra said while he and Jane Doe have received death threats, he has been heartened by an outpouring of support — including rallies and protests on the Cornell campus and more than 1,000 women who have emailed him to share anger, frustration, solidarity and stories of their own assaults.

WATCH | Anger over Cornell's handling of the case: Cornell students protest university handling of sexual assault case | Duration closed caption 2:42 Students at Cornell are protesting their university’s handling of an alleged sexual assault case after an investigation revealed the accused faced a range of punishments from expulsion to writing papers.

Case taken away from Van Houten

Jane Doe, who was a student in 2024, alleges that Chi Phi members plied her with alcohol and drugs and several of them sexually assaulted her. One man sent others a message inviting them to participate, according to a lawsuit she filed last month.

Lawyers for two of the men have denied they participated in a sexual assault. Attempts by The Associated Press to reach the others or their representatives have been unsuccessful. Some of the men who underwent a university disciplinary hearing in 2024 told investigators that the sexual activity was consensual or said they were not involved.

The woman went to Cornell police in November 2024, though no criminal charges resulted. In the wake of her lawsuit, Van Houten said he was reopening the investigation. Days later, Gov. Kathy Hochul took the case away from him and appointed the state's attorney general, Letitia James, as a special prosecutor.

Giuffra applauded the move, saying he was troubled by Van Houten's plan for conducting the reopened investigation and "didn't think he was up to the task."

Giuffra said the district attorney wanted to take the case to a grand jury and have Jane Doe testify before the panel within two weeks.

That timeline, leaving little time to review evidence or interview witnesses, suggested Van Houten may have been trying "to go take a dive and not really give it his best effort and not do any investigation," Giuffra said.

James hasn't said how long her investigation might take, but suggested it could be months.

On Wednesday, one of the men named in Jane Doe's lawsuit filed a court petition seeking James's removal from the case, arguing she showed bias by posting on social media a few days before her appointment: "What this young woman has been forced to endure is horrific and unacceptable."

A spokesperson for James declined to comment.

Cornell closed down the Chi Phi campus chapter in 2024 and says it expelled some students and suspended others after an investigation under the federal Title IX law.

This week Cornell trustees brought in former U.S. deputy attorney general Sally Yates to review how the school investigates sexual assault and sexual harassment, how the disciplinary process works, the campus police response and more.
