World.title: World’s First All-Inclusive JW Marriott Opens in Guanacaste
World.content:
Costa Rica is now home to the world’s first all-inclusive JW Marriott. The JW Marriott Costa Elena Resort & Spa has opened at Playa El Jobo in La Cruz, Guanacaste, Marriott International announced on October 6. The opening marks the luxury brand’s entry into the all-inclusive market, and the company chose Costa Rica’s northern Pacific coast for its global debut. Advertised rates start at about $900 per person per night, based on double occupancy.

The beachfront itself is not new to resort guests. The property occupies the site of the former Dreams Las Mareas, an all-inclusive that changed hands in 2025 and was converted to the JW Marriott brand. Mullen Hospitality Management, the resort’s franchise operator, has described the project as a $60 million transformation.

The resort sits within Costa Elena, a resort-residential community that Marriott says covers about 1,200 hectares (3,000 acres) of tropical dry forest near the Nicaraguan border. The resort has 415 rooms and suites with villa-inspired designs, private terraces, and spacious interiors. Some ground-floor rooms open directly onto semi-private swim-out pools, and Presidential Suites include separate living areas.

The opening comes as Costa Rica draws growing attention from luxury travelers. Marriott recently ranked Costa Rica among the five most popular destinations for Latin American travelers looking ahead to 2027. Guanacaste’s luxury market has also expanded with properties such as Nekajui, a Ritz-Carlton Reserve, which opened on the Papagayo Peninsula in 2025.

Dining plays a central role at the property. It has 15 restaurants and bars serving Costa Rican and international cuisine, according to Marriott. Leal draws on Guanacaste’s culinary traditions and offers coffee-roasting experiences and a seven-course tasting menu inspired by Costa Rica’s seven provinces. Casado is a wood-fired coastal grill and Puerto Limón focuses on the Afro-Caribbean culinary heritage.

Other concepts include Italian, Mexican, and Japanese restaurants. There is also LaGloria, a root beer stand that honors the nine-seat Washington, D.C., business J. Willard Marriott opened in 1927, the company’s starting point. The property has its own JW Garden, which grows herbs, edible flowers, fruits, and vegetables for the kitchens and bars.

Wellness is another major focus. A wellness area of nearly 1,500 square meters (16,000 square feet) houses Spa by JW, a fitness center, and the brand’s first Mindfulness House. Treatments include hydrotherapy, sound healing, Reiki, and cacao ceremonies. Some therapies use local ingredients such as volcanic clay and native cacao.

The resort has 17 pools, including an oceanfront infinity pool. Marriott describes the complex, which covers roughly 4,090 square meters (44,000 square feet), as the largest resort pool area in Costa Rica. The resort also introduces Griffin Club, a 45-room private section for guests who want more privacy and personalized service. Members have a separate lounge, a dedicated pool, a private beach area, personal assistance, and priority reservations for restaurants and pool cabanas.

Families can use the Family by JW Club, which offers nature walks, children’s yoga, creative activities, storytelling, and movie nights. The resort’s design references Sibú, a central figure in the traditions of Costa Rica’s Bribri and Cabécar Indigenous peoples. Building materials such as wood, stone, and palm reflect traditional Costa Rican construction.

Weekly night markets bring local artisans, food, music and dance to the property. Excursions include kayaking, fishing, scuba diving, sunset hikes, and private yacht charters. The project may not be Marriott’s last on the site. When the deal was first announced in 2025, the company said JW Marriott-branded residences could follow on adjacent land. That is another sign of the large-scale luxury investment still flowing to Guanacaste’s coast.

World.title: Liberation Party Will Vote Against Costa Rica Joining Trans-Pacific Trade Pact
World.content:
Costa Rica’s largest opposition party said it will vote against entry into the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership (CPTPP), complicating the outlook for an accord the government has not yet decided to sign. National Liberation Party (PLN) faction leader Álvaro Ramírez Bogantes announced the position on behalf of the party’s legislative caucus, which holds 17 of the 57 seats in the Legislative Assembly.

Ramírez said Costa Rica does not lack consumers but rather support for its own producers and described the caucus’s position as firm. The CPTPP’s 12 members are Australia, Brunei, Canada, Chile, Japan, Malaysia, Mexico, New Zealand, Peru, Singapore, the United Kingdom and Vietnam. Together they account for roughly 15% of global GDP and about 600 million consumers.

Costa Rica already has trade agreements with six of those countries. The main gain from membership would be preferential access to the other six, Japan, Australia, New Zealand, Malaysia, Vietnam and Brunei. Karen Alfaro Jiménez, who chairs the Assembly’s Agriculture Committee, identified rice, coffee, palm oil, sugarcane, cattle and dairy as the most exposed sectors.

Deputies Salvador Padilla Villanueva and Ronald Campos Villegas pointed to the gap in production scale between Costa Rican farms and those in member countries such as Vietnam and Malaysia. The caucus cited projections attributed to the Ministry of Foreign Trade (Comex) of a 3.3% drop in dairy production and a 3.7% decline in agricultural employment.

Deputy Diana Murillo Murillo called the treaty harmful and said producers and business chambers had not been adequately consulted. The party also said 18 municipalities have declared their opposition. Farm groups have raised similar objections. The National Chamber of Agriculture and Agroindustry (CNAA) has questioned whether small producers can compete with larger, better-capitalized operations abroad.

Dairy producers have said milk costs 72 to 80 cents per kilogram to produce in Costa Rica (about 33 to 36 cents per pound), compared with 46 cents per kilogram (about 21 cents per pound) in New Zealand. The livestock corporation Corfoga has sought to have beef excluded from the deal.

Costa Rica formally requested to join the bloc in August 2022. The 12 members and Costa Rica announced the substantial conclusion of accession negotiations in May, but the accession protocol remains under legal review and has not been signed. President Laura Fernández said on Sept. 24 that she had not endorsed the agreement and would consult productive sectors before deciding. That meeting is scheduled for Friday, at Casa Presidencial, with free-trade-zone companies, agricultural producers and meat and dairy producers invited.

Fernández has said that if the analysis shows certain sectors would be harmed, the government would consider compensation mechanisms. If she signs the protocol, the text is expected to reach the Assembly in November. The PLN’s position carries weight because of how the vote may be counted. The ruling Pueblo Soberano party holds 31 seats, enough for a simple majority of 29 but short of the 38 votes, a two-thirds majority, required for some international agreements.

The Assembly’s Technical Services department will determine which threshold applies once the text is formally submitted. If 38 votes are needed, the government would have to secure at least seven of the nine opposition votes outside the PLN, a group that includes the Broad Front’s seven deputies.

Domestic objections also have limited room to change the deal itself. Costa Rica cannot alter terms already agreed with the 12 member states on its own, and any substantive change would require their consent. The debate comes as foreign investment rises and some major employers cut staff. Foreign direct investment grew 23.4% in the first half of the year, driven by free-trade zones, while several multinationals have announced layoffs.

Whether the accord reaches a vote at all now depends on the decision Fernández makes after Friday’s meeting with the areas that stand to gain or lose the most.

World.title: Costa Rica Suspends Investigation Into Who Ordered Roberto Samcam’s Murder
World.content:
Costa Rica’s prosecutor’s office has suspended its investigation into who ordered the 2025 killing of retired Nicaraguan military officer Roberto Samcam, an outspoken critic of Nicaragua’s government who was living in exile in San José, according to a resolution made public Tuesday.

Costa Rican authorities pointed to “ideological” motives for the killing six months ago, but an assistant prosecutor concluded there was “insufficient” evidence to identify who ordered it, according to a recent document. “It is unacceptable,” Samcam’s widow, Claudia Vargas, told AFP in San José.

The United States has accused the government of married co-presidents Daniel Ortega and Rosario Murillo of carrying out “transnational repression” and has called for those responsible for the killing to be brought to justice. The resolution issued by assistant prosecutor Karla Chaves states that the investigation into who ordered the killing may be reopened if new information emerges.

The decision does not affect the case against five Costa Ricans arrested and accused of carrying out the murder. Prosecutors requested in June that their case proceed to trial. Samcam, a 66-year-old retired Nicaraguan army major, was shot dead on June 19, 2025, in his apartment in northern San José. He had fled to Costa Rica following the 2018 protests against Ortega.

Samcam denounced the army’s role in the crackdown on those demonstrations, which left more than 300 people dead, according to the United Nations, and triggered a political crisis that has driven hundreds of thousands of Nicaraguans into exile. In 2023, he was stripped of his Nicaraguan citizenship along with dozens of opponents and critics of Ortega and Murillo, who have ruled Nicaragua for nearly two decades and now wield absolute power.

The Samcam family’s lawyer, Almudena Bernabéu of Spain, expressed her “dissatisfaction” with the prosecutor’s decision. “It is surprising that they decided to close it when little or very little has actually been done on that front,” Bernabéu said. She stressed the need to “get to the bottom of who is behind” the killing.

A United Nations expert group that has documented surveillance, threats and attacks against Nicaraguan exiles in several countries maintains that Samcam’s killing was carefully planned as “a contract killing.”

World.title: Dollar Holds as Central Bank Warns US Rates Could Push It Higher
World.content:
The U.S. dollar has given back part of its early-October rebound against the Costa Rican colón, but the head of the Central Bank of Costa Rica (BCCR) has warned that a widening gap between Costa Rican and U.S. interest rates could push the exchange rate higher again. The rate for today was ₡454.50 to buy and ₡460.35 to sell, down from ₡455.71 and ₡462.08 yesterday.

On the Foreign Currency Market (Monex), the dollar eached ₡460.45 on Oct. 1, up ₡13.65, or 3.1%, from the record low of ₡446.80 set on Sept. 17. It then eased to ₡458.67 on Friday, Oct. 2, ending a run of five consecutive daily gains, and averaged ₡457.03 on Monday, Oct. 5, in a session with about $68.7 million traded.

In real terms, $1,000 exchanged at yesterday’s Monex average was worth about ₡457,030, roughly ₡10,230 more than at the September low. The gains extended a dollar rebound from its record low that began in the second half of September. BCCR President Róger Madrigal has identified the interest rate differential with the United States as the main risk.

The Central Bank lowered its monetary policy rate from 3.25% to 3% in July and has held it there since July 24, while the U.S. Federal Reserve raised its benchmark rate in September to a range of 3.75% to 4%. Madrigal said the gap between the two had widened to between 75 and 100 basis points.

Madrigal explained that when the financial return favors one currency, demand for it rises while demand for others falls. If dollar-denominated assets continue to offer better returns, savers and investors could move money out of colones, adding to dollar demand and putting upward pressure on the exchange rate.

He said such a shift had not yet occurred on a significant scale but described the widening differential as a genuine risk. The BCCR’s next scheduled monetary policy review is on Nov. 26.

Economists do not all read the situation the same way. Fernando Rodríguez, an economist at the National University (UNA), said after Friday’s session that keeping the policy rate at 3% would continue to make Costa Rica attractive to investors seeking yield, sustaining the flow of dollars into the country.

Seasonal factors could also pull in the other direction. Federico Quesada Chaves, director of the School of Administrative Sciences at the State Distance University (UNED), has said the extra foreign currency that typically enters the market with aguinaldo payments, bonuses and holiday spending from late October could renew downward pressure on the dollar.

Even after the rebound, the dollar remains well below where it began the year. Monex averaged ₡497.07 on Jan. 2, meaning the dollar has lost about 8% of its value against the colón in 2026. It also sits roughly 34% below its June 2022 peak of ₡696.76.

The colón’s strength has squeezed exporters and tourism businesses that earn in dollars but pay salaries and other costs in colones, and it has coincided with a wave of job cuts at major employers. For households, the rate determines what dollar-denominated rents, loans and imported goods cost in local currency.

Whether the October rebound resumes may depend less on local dollar supply than on the direction of U.S. rates in the weeks before the Central Bank’s November meeting.

World.title: Bukele and Colombia’s President Expected at Costa Rica Prison Opening
World.content:
Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele and Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella are expected to attend the Oct. 14 inauguration of Costa Rica’s new maximum-security prison, according to reports in Costa Rican media late Monday. The presidency had not publicly confirmed the foreign guest list as of Tuesday morning.

The High Containment Center Against Organized Crime (CACCO) is scheduled to open at 12:30 p.m. on Oct. 14, the presidency announced Sunday night. The facility sits on the grounds of the La Reforma penitentiary complex in San Rafael de Alajuela and was built from plans donated by the government of El Salvador, as detailed when the Oct. 14 opening date was announced.

The presence of both leaders would turn the ceremony into a regional showcase for the hard-line prison model Bukele built in El Salvador. Governments in Honduras and Panama have announced El Salvador-style prison measures this year.

President Laura Fernández invited De la Espriella to the opening during a visit to Colombia in September. She said at the time that she had asked him and his security teams to join the October ceremony, and that sharing intelligence with Colombia would strengthen Costa Rica’s fight against drug trafficking networks.

De la Espriella took office Aug. 7 after a campaign that drew on Bukele’s security message. Salvadoran Vice President Félix Ulloa said around the inauguration that his government was ready to advise Colombia on building large prisons.

Justice Minister Gabriel Aguilar declined last week to say whether either leader would attend, saying the question should be answered by the presidency. If Bukele attends, it would be at least his third visit to Costa Rica tied to the prison system. In November 2024 he toured La Reforma and warned that Costa Rica showed symptoms of criminality similar to those El Salvador faced with its gangs.

In January, he returned for a ceremony marking the start of CACCO construction alongside then-President Rodrigo Chaves.That January visit came less than three weeks before Costa Rica’s presidential election and drew criticism from opposition parties, which described it as foreign interference. The Supreme Elections Tribunal allowed the visit to proceed but warned that foreign delegations must not intervene in domestic politics. Fernández won the Feb. 1 election and took office May 8.

The Justice Ministry has said the prison will hold about 5,100 inmates in five modules. It is intended for leaders of criminal organizations, inmates considered violent, people facing extradition and prisoners who require special protection. Inmates will wear orange uniforms and will not be allowed clothing from outside.

The opening also faces a legal challenge. Ricardo Zeledón, a University of Costa Rica professor, filed an amparo appeal on Oct. 1 seeking to block the inauguration and any transfer of inmates to the facility. He argues the center copies El Salvador’s model and would violate human rights. The appeal names Fernández, Chaves and Aguilar.

The government presents the CACCO as the centerpiece of its response to organized crime, which authorities blame for most of the homicides. The Judicial Investigation Agency (OIJ) recorded 873 homicides in 2025. Whether the new prison will change that trend remains an open question.

The Oct. 14 ceremony will be broadcast live on YouTube, according to the presidency.

World.title: Costa Rica Opens Probe Into Political Ties of Man Wanted by US DEA
World.content:
Costa Rica’s attorney general will investigate whether a naturalized Costa Rican detained for extradition to the United States had political ties or helped finance last February’s presidential campaign, after he was photographed at President Laura Fernández’s election-night celebration.

Guobin Tam Zhang, 54, who also uses the name Juan Carlos Tam Cheong, was detained Oct. 2 in Granadilla de Curridabat at the request of the U.S. government. He is sought by the United States in connection with alleged international drug trafficking, and Costa Rican prosecutors say he also faces a local investigation for alleged money laundering.

The Ministry of Public Security described Tam as one of the main launderers of drug-trafficking proceeds here. According to the ministry, he allegedly coordinated cocaine shipments bound for the United States and then handled payments for those shipments on behalf of the cartels involved.

The arrest was carried out jointly by the Public Prosecutor’s Office, the Drug Control Police, the Fuerza Pública, the U.S. Drug Enforcement Administration (DEA) and the U.S. Treasury Department.

On Monday, the San José Criminal Court ordered two months of provisional detention while the extradition request proceeds, according to Tam’s lawyer, Moisés Chinchilla. Chinchilla said the court informed his client of the DEA file during the hearing, and that the United States must still submit formal documentation and the evidence supporting its request.

The same day, the Ministry of Justice and Peace ordered Tam into the prison system’s high-containment circuit. The ministry said he met the criteria because of his alleged links to criminal structures, and that he will be held in an individual cell with controls on his visits, calls, contacts and personal belongings.

Attorney General Carlo Díaz said Monday that prosecutors will open an investigation on their own initiative into any political relationships Tam may have had, with a focus on money laundering and possible illegal campaign financing. Díaz said prosecutors will first await a report from the Supreme Elections Tribunal’s department that oversees political party financing.

Díaz said Costa Rica will prioritize sending Tam to the United States, applying a prosecutorial discretion rule that suspends local cases against an extraditable defendant. He said, however, that anyone found to have assisted Tam, including front men, corrupt officials or party representatives who knowingly accepted illegal money, would face investigation.

The attorney general also said a judge has authorized prosecutors to open five electronic devices seized from Tam, four of them cellphones, and that any evidence of crimes by other people would lead to new cases. Díaz linked the arrest to the second phase of a joint strategy with the DEA aimed at what he calls invisible narcos, people who would not be identified as possible traffickers without an investigation.

The case turned political after a photograph circulated showing Tam beside Pilar Cisneros, a former lawmaker who now advises the presidency on communications, at the Feb. 1 event at the Aurola hotel in San José where Fernández received the election results. Local reports say Tam was inside rooms reserved for campaign staff, party leaders and invited guests. The mother of two of Tam’s children also attended and was photographed with Fernández, according to those reports.

Fernández said Monday that she does not know Tam, has never met with him and does not know what he does for a living. Cisneros said she does not know him either and that many people approached her for photographs that night.

The two have given differing accounts of the photograph itself. Speaking yesterday in Mora, Fernández said she did not know whether the image circulating of Tam with Cisneros was authentic, adding that about 2,000 people attended the celebration and she did not know all of them. Cisneros, however, has confirmed that the photograph is genuine and was taken that night at the Aurola, while maintaining that she has never spoken with Tam.

The ruling Pueblo Soberano party issued a certification from its treasurer, Raúl Zamora, stating that party records show no donations, contracts, transfers or other transactions involving Tam under any of the names he uses. Party president Mayuli Ortega said neither she nor the party has any relationship with him, and secretary general Freddy González said Tam was not on the party’s guest list for the celebration.

Opposition lawmakers have demanded further explanations. Liberación Nacional legislator Marco Badilla said the Legislative Assembly’s Security and Drug Trafficking Commission will examine the case, and fellow party legislator Víctor Hidalgo formally asked the presidency whether Tam was invited to the May 8 transfer of power or has visited executive branch offices.

Frente Amplio leader José María Villalta called on the government and the party to explain Tam’s presence at official events, while Claudia Dobles, head of the Coalición Agenda Ciudadana caucus, asked the Supreme Elections Tribunal to examine campaign financing. Pueblo Soberano caucus leader Nogui Acosta questioned whether the Legislative Assembly should investigate, saying the faction has no relationship with Tam.

In a sworn statement dated Aug. 4, 2025, Tam declared that all his income came from lawful activities, mainly the rental of commercial premises and homes on properties he represents or manages. Public records reviewed by local media show no properties registered in his name or in companies where he sits on the board.

Tam has not been convicted of any crime. His case is one of a series of U.S. extradition requests Costa Rica has handled this year in connection with drug investigations, including the 24 requests under review as of August and the prosecution of former magistrate Celso Gamboa in Texas.

World.title: Mile 8 man accused of assaulting police inspector granted bail as daughter alleges harassment
World.content:
Mile 8 man accused of assaulting police inspector granted bail as daughter alleges harassment

By Breaking Belize News Staff: A 47-year-old maintenance worker from Mile 8 has been granted bail after pleading not guilty to aggravated assault and threat of death charges involving a police inspector, while his daughter has accused the officer of repeatedly harassing her father.

David Funes, also known as “Bonna,” appeared unrepresented before the Chief Magistrate in Belize City on Wednesday, charged in connection with an October 1 incident involving a police inspector who is attached to the Mahogany Heights Sub-Police Station.

According to court allegations, the inspector was performing special duties at CK’s Shop in the Mile 8 community around 7 p.m. when he encountered Funes, who was reportedly drinking a beer outside the establishment.

The inspector alleges that after telling Funes he could not remain at the location, Funes threatened him, saying, “Nuh because you dah police I fraid feh you. You wah dead.”

A physical confrontation reportedly followed, during which Funes allegedly pushed the officer in the chest. The inspector said he grabbed Funes, and a struggle ensued before Funes fell, got up and walked away.

During Wednesday’s arraignment, Funes’ daughter addressed the court, alleging that the inspector had been harassing her father following a previous court case that was dismissed. She claimed the officer had even attempted to prevent her father from visiting the neighbourhood shop, despite the shopkeeper having no objection to his presence.

She also informed the court that her father has a history of mental health difficulties and had previously been prescribed medication. She said she had requested his medical records but was advised they would take approximately one week to obtain.

The Chief Magistrate urged her to secure those records as soon as possible to help the court understand Funes’ condition and determine how to proceed with his case.

Funes was offered bail of $800 plus one surety of the same amount, with no additional conditions imposed. His daughter was advised that she could sign as his surety but would be responsible for ensuring his attendance at subsequent court hearings.

The matter was adjourned until December 14, 2026.

World.title: No more Area Rep visits: New portal opens online access to Education assistance
World.content:
No more Area Rep visits: New portal opens online access to Education assistance

By Zoila Palma: On October 6, 2026, Prime Minister John Briceño said that the government has introduced a new online portal for educational assistance, allowing students and families to apply for support based on need without having to visit their Area Representative.

The PM said that this is part of his administration’s efforts to put more money in the pockets of Belizean families through measures including free education and education assistance programmes.

Briceño said approximately 80 percent of students at the high school and University of Belize levels receive some form of assistance.

“Minister Fonseca set up a portal for educational assistance so you can apply and get assistance through that portal based on need. So, now you don’t have to go to your area rep for assistance,” Briceño said.

The new system represents a shift from a longstanding practice in which families would visit the offices of their respective Area Representatives to request educational assistance.

Through the portal, families can instead submit applications directly for consideration based on their needs.

World.title: World Food Programme concerned that record-strong El Niño could push millions deeper into hunger
World.content:
World Food Programme concerned that record-strong El Niño could push millions deeper into hunger

By Zoila Palma: The World Food Programme (WFP) is warning that the intensifying 2026-27 El Niño could worsen global hunger and food insecurity, with as many as 49 million people potentially pushed into acute hunger.

WFP climate expert Richard Choularton said the current forecasts suggest the El Niño could become the strongest on record, bringing more intense and widespread droughts, floods and storms.

Choularton said initial impacts have already been seen in Central America and Africa’s Sahel region.

In Central America, severe drought during the early growing season caused farmers to lose crops or experience lower yields, with the effects extending beyond agriculture as farmers reduce planting, investment and labour hiring.

WFP estimates that Latin America and the Caribbean, along with large parts of Africa and Asia and the Pacific, could face some of the greatest impacts.

Choularton said he is particularly concerned about countries already facing severe hunger crises, such as Somalia, as well as vulnerable countries in Southern Africa that are still recovering from previous El Niño-related droughts.

He also warned that disruptions to major global trade routes, including the Strait of Hormuz, Red Sea and Black Sea, are contributing to higher food, fuel and fertilizer prices, potentially worsening the effects of drought and reducing agricultural production and incomes.

The WFP is using anticipatory action to help communities prepare before extreme weather strikes, including early warnings, disaster risk financing and community preparedness programmes.

World.title: Stakeholders review proposal to strengthen Belize’s Climate Resilience
World.content:
Stakeholders review proposal to strengthen Belize’s Climate Resilience

By Zoila Palma: The Protected Areas Conservation Trust (PACT), Belize’s accredited entity for the Green Climate Fund, brought together key stakeholders in Belmopan on October 6, 2026, for a Review and Validation Workshop on a proposed project aimed at strengthening Belize’s climate resilience.

The workshop focused on reviewing and validating the first draft of a funding proposal titled “Strengthening the Belize National Protected Area System (BNPAS) to Provide Resilience and Reduce Vulnerability of Communities against Climate Change.”

Participants examined the proposed project components, outputs and activities as part of the ongoing project development process.

The session included representatives from the Association of Protected Areas Management Organizations, the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management, and the Ministry of Blue Economy and Marine Conservation.

World.title: Team Belize to compete at Dakar 2026 Summer Youth Olympic Games
World.content:
Team Belize to compete at Dakar 2026 Summer Youth Olympic Games

By Zoila Palma: The Belize Olympic and Commonwealth Games Association (BOCGA) has announced the athletes and officials who will represent Belize at the 4th Summer Youth Olympic Games in Dakar, Senegal, in 2026.

The Games will bring together young athletes from around the world for a celebration of sport, culture, friendship and the Olympic spirit.

Belize’s delegation will feature two young athletes: Melody Gabourel of Corozalito Village, who will compete in the women’s shot put, and Jaaden Williams of Punta Gorda, who will compete in the men’s triple jump.

The delegation will be led by Chef de Mission Herman Pastor Jr., with Shelmadine Carr serving as Team Official.

Gabourel and Williams were selected by the Belize Athletic Association (BAA) in accordance with the International Olympic Committee’s participation criteria for Belize. The criteria require athletes to meet the under-18 age requirement, include one male and one female athlete in the delegation, and compete in the disciplines allocated to Belize.

Team Belize is scheduled to depart Belize on October 29, 2026, and return on November 14, 2026.

World.title: Time to grow more food and to eat more of what we grow
World.content:
Time to grow more food and to eat more of what we grow

By Hugh O’Brien: The issue with ANY PROBLEM WE HAVE IN BELIZE, including INFLATION and the COST OF LIVING, amongst others, is that our culture is to look outside for solutions and not to marvel enough at our individual resilience. As a people, we look 1st to the International Community for solutions, 2nd to the Government, 3rd to our Area Representatives, City or Town Councils, 4th to our community, friends and neighbours, 5th to our family, and last to each of OURSELVES.

Within ourselves lie the solutions, as when we change and make decisions, we influence our family and friends, then we influence our community, then eventually our approach to local government and national government and ultimately the international way of life.

‘WE CANNOT EXPECT THE CHANGE IN OTHERS THAT WE OURSELVES ARE UNWILLING TO MAKE AND LIVE BY.”

Food prices have risen sharply over the last 5-10 years, and the sad news is that food prices are expected to continue to increase in the next 5 to 10 years – Let’s begin to plant and eat a little more healthy callaloo, chaya, okra, spinach, sweet potato, habanero pepper, leafy onion or chives, cilantro etc in our backyard, and for those living in the villages, let’s plant and consume more coconuts, papaya, banana, plantains, limes, avocado, breadfruit, golden plum, bluggoe, cocoyams, cassava, etc. and grow more local chickens, eggs, a lil sheep or goat here and there etc.

The photo below shows a health patch of callaloo being grown in the yard of a villager in the Cayo District.

World.title: International News: World Health Organization says it cannot conduct full risk assessment on Russia plague reports
World.content:
International News: World Health Organization says it cannot conduct full risk assessment on Russia plague reports

By Zoila Palma: Today, the World Health Organization (WHO) said it cannot conduct a full risk assessment into reports surrounding the suspected plague death of a laboratory technician in Russia because it has not received complete information from Moscow. The 28-year-old woman worked at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia and died after being hospitalized with severe pneumonia.

WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said initial media reports suggested pneumonic plague following an accidental laboratory exposure.

The WHO requested more information from Russia on Saturday under the International Health Regulations, but Moscow responded Tuesday that no plague case had been reported in the Irkutsk region and that about 200 contacts had been quarantined.

The WHO is seeking details on the laboratory tests conducted on the woman, the results, and the health status of those placed under quarantine or follow-up. Tedros said the agency does not yet have the full picture and therefore cannot complete a risk assessment, stressing that timely, complete and transparent information is needed to clarify conflicting reports and assess potential public health risks.

Russia has said the woman died from community-acquired severe pneumonia of unknown origin and has warned against false information following reports of a second suspected plague case.

World.title: Osmond Martinez sworn in as Minister of Economic Transformation
World.content:
Osmond Martinez sworn in as Minister of Economic Transformation

By Zoila Palma: Today, Osmond Martinez took the oath of office in a swearing-in ceremony before Governor-General Dame Froyla Tzalam at the Belize House in Belmopan.

Martinez, former Minister of State in the Ministry of Economic Transformation, is now appointed Minister of Economic Transformation.

He now assumes responsibility for the ministry.

World.title: ‘DISGRACEFUL’
World.content:
A motorist navigates a pothole-riddled road.

ROADS dug up by the National Water Commission (NWC) and left with massive ditches for months, and even years, took centre stage at Tuesday’s sitting of Parliament’s Public Accounts Committee (PAC), as Government and Opposition members turned their fire on the agency.

The grilling came as the NWC appeared before the PAC for a review of the Auditor General’s Performance Audit Report on its effectiveness in managing capital projects and the credibility of its budgets at the entry level.

The appearance also came as Jamaicans continue to grapple with drought conditions linked to El Niño, with the NWC expected to face questions about water resources for communities severely affected by the dry spell.

But while the committee addressed the country’s water challenges, it was the NWC’s long-standing road-reinstatement arrangement with the National Works Agency (NWA) that drew some of the sharpest criticisms, with committee Chairman Julian Robinson declaring that the system “doesn’t work” and recounting instances in which roads remained unrepaired for weeks, months and years.

At the heart of Tuesday’s road discussion was a memorandum of understanding (MOU) between the NWC and the NWA under which the works agency is responsible for repairing roads dug up by the commission, with the NWC reimbursing the agency for the work.

NWC vice-president responsible for engineering and capital projects Garth Jackson confirmed that the MOU remains in effect and said it covers roads under the NWA’s portfolio across the country.

Jackson explained that under the arrangement, the NWA carries out the road repairs while the NWC provides the funds, reimbursing the agency for the cost of repairing road cuts.

But when Robinson asked whether the NWC owed the NWA money for road reinstatement, Chief Financial Officer Fabian Christie said the commission did not currently have any outstanding debt to the works agency for that purpose.

“We have some other disputes pertaining to some other projects.

But not for reinstatement of roadworks,” Christie said.

That answer prompted Robinson to question how the two agencies communicate when the NWC excavates a road to repair a leak or replace a pipe.

Christie said there are coordinators between the agencies to deal with such matters, but Robinson rejected the explanation, saying the experience of motorists and Members of Parliament suggested otherwise.

“It doesn’t work… let’s just be plain.

It doesn’t work, and…I understand reinstatement can’t take place the following day because you want to ensure the thing is fixed properly before you reinstate.

But I can tell you about weeks, months, and years where there is no reinstatement.

“So I don’t know that protocol.

You tell me about communication…I don’t know where that exists, and the MP is the one who gets the cussing and the MP then has to call somebody at Water Commission or NWA to say, ‘Listen, this part of Anderson Road, which I paved like a carpet, you dig it up a year ago and it’s still not fixed’.

So there is no protocol there,” lamented Robinson.

The exchange led permanent secretary in the Ministry of Water, Environment and Climate Change Wayne Robertson to acknowledge that the agreement needs to be reviewed.

The committee also heard that the problem may stem from the difficulty of mobilising equipment and asphalt for small sections of road.

Member of Parliament for St James Central, the Government’s Heroy Clarke, said he had been told by NWA officials and contractors that small road cuts are sometimes allowed to accumulate before repairs are carried out.

“They give you this argument, and I want NWC to verify… that they are unable to do one square metre each time.

So they allow it to pile up to a certain amount, and that’s where the six months and the one year come in.

Because, for example, if they only have one leak in Montego Bay, and it is just one square metre, then they’re not going to fix it until they get some more, which may never happen,” Clarke said.

Clarke also questioned who checks the quality of work carried out by contractors after the NWA is engaged to repair NWC road cuts.

He pointed to Salt Spring in St James, where he said the Government had spent $237 million on a pipeline from Quarry to Meggie Top, only for sections of the rehabilitated road to develop potholes after rainfall.

The NWC told the committee that responsibility for road reinstatement varies depending on the type of work being done.

“We handle roadway reinstatement on a number of different bases.

So, for our capital projects, where we have third-party contractors, they are responsible for doing the roadway reinstatement, and that we incorporate the road authority [NWA] to ensure, one, that the compaction is to their satisfaction, and two, that the roadway reinstatement meets their requirements at the end,” he said.

For routine road cuts, Jackson said the NWC sometimes engages contractors directly, particularly in emergency situations, although the commission prefers to use the NWA arrangement.

He explained that the entity relies on the NWA because of its expertise in road work.

Opposition spokesman on land and works Lothan Cousins, contributing to the discussion, questioned whether the arrangement was working equally well outside the Corporate Area.

He said rural MPs often had difficulty getting information about when road cuts would be repaired and suggested that Kingston received more attention under the MOU.

Cousins also asked for a system that would allow MPs and other officials to track road cuts from the time they are made until they are permanently repaired.

His concern was that limited NWA resources could leave roads patched temporarily while communities waited for proper reinstatement.

Cousins also raised concerns about sections of Retreat Avenue, Seymour Avenue and Wellington Drive in St Andrew, where he said repeated patching and rehabilitation had failed to stop significant settlement and deterioration.

He described the situation on Retreat Avenue as a “disaster” and questioned the NWC about the contractors involved, the amount spent and whether the commission or contractors were paying for repeated rehabilitation.

“When you drive on these roads, they are worse than they were before you started to cut them, and these are roads that were completely rehabilitated, but now it is a disaster.

So, who is the contractor? How much money was spent on these roads? And in reality, is it that the NWC is paying for these continuous rehabilitations or is this at the expense of the contractor? “Because it goes back to this audit report in terms of proper planning, accountability, these are serious issues and nobody can deny them.

They are there before the eye, especially on Retreat avenue, and it is disgraceful, I can tell you that much,” said Cousins.

Jackson attributed some of the problems to the difficult conditions under which the NWC is installing new water and sewer infrastructure.

“The challenge that that particular project raises, there are a myriad of challenges it’s experiencing.

We’re…in the process of installing large diameter sewers, large diameter potable water pipe, distribution pipes, property laterals for the water and waste water.

“And we are doing that where there is an existing aged infrastructure.

The problems we have encountered there are in terms of subsidence, settlement subsidence is largely as a result of the breaks on the old pipes, the existing pipes.

So that is what happened on Retreat, a few weeks ago,” Jackson said.

As the committee pressed the NWC on its road-reinstatement arrangements, Christie disclosed that the commission spends approximately $200 million annually on reinstating roads through contractors it engages directly.

The committee did not complete its examination of the report and Robinson instructed NWC officials to prepare responses to outstanding questions for a future sitting.

Among the unanswered questions was how much the NWC owes contractors overall, separate from its road-reinstatement payments to the NWA.

Christie said that figure would have to be broken down before being provided to the committee.

World.title: Chang: Lower murder rate will lead to fewer fatal police shootings
World.content:
Dr Horace Chang (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

Police fatal shootings will likely be reduced as Jamaica’s homicide rate gets lower, National Security Minister Dr Horace Chang argued on Tuesday.

Chang was responding to a question posed by Opposition Leader Mark Golding, during the sitting of the House of Representatives.

The national security minister and deputy prime minister had earlier made a statement in which he pointed to the historic gains that have led to a sustained reduction in murders over the past two years.

He said that to sustain the numbers and further reduce them, there will be no complacency on the part of the security forces in going after criminals.

The security minister shared that, as at October 6, there were 407 murders recorded across the country.

This represents a 24 per decrease when compared to the 534 homicides during the similar period in 2025.

While Opposition members welcomed the sustained reduction in murders and lauded the security forces for their accomplishment, they nevertheless raised questions about alleged extra- judicial killings by the security forces.

A total of 311 people were killed by the police in 2025 and at least 231 so far this year.

“I want to know whether, in the context of the very elevated, high level of police fatal shootings in our society today and over the last two years, whether you regard that as problematic, and whether you are in favour of the rapid implementation of a policy of body-worn cameras, especially for targeted or planned, special operations?” Golding asked Chang.

In response, Chang said, “Fatal shootings have remained a concern but we’re convinced that the fatal shootings are a result of the circumstances under which [the security forces operate]”.

“As I’ve said, the police are on the road, [if] their lives are at risk then they have to respond,” Chang added.

The security minister pointed to a September 9 incident in which three policemen were shot and injured by a gunman in Mount Salem, St James.

The gunman, a known violence producer, had reportedly returned to the community which is under a zone of special operations (ZOSO), and declared that he would “not be leaving again.

He also reportedly threatened to kill members of the security forces.

According to Chang, the gunman had publicly stated that “while he expected the police to come for him, he was going to make sure to take three with him”.

“He shot three police officers; none died, thankfully.

He, of course, was fatally shot by the police,” Chang noted, while reiterating that “fatal shootings [by the police] will always cause concern”.

Continuing, he said, “Any loss of any Jamaican life is a concern, it’s a question of the circumstances…

My understanding, and I will say it again, as the homicide rate gets lower, the likelihood is that fatal shootings [by the police] will go lower.” Chang insisted that the police are not impetuous in their actions but rather act on information and intelligence.

He said while one or two incidents may be considered questionable, “the police at all times, in my opinion, operate professionally”.

The security minister told the Parliament that the reduction in homicides over the past two years “is a result of the significant number of known killers who have left the space”.

He cited that many are in jail, some have migrated to North and Central America, as well as to Caribbean neighbours such as Haiti.

“The police activity and pressure have successfully disrupted criminally violent individuals,” he said.

In response to a question posed by MP for Portland Eastern Isat Buchanan about two men being fatally shot by the police on the day they were to report to the police while on bail, Chang said he was willing to brief Buchanan “off the air”.

He said in at least one of those cases, the police, in seeking to find an individual, would have issued a statement asking the individual to turn himself in.

“If they don’t come in and they’re known to be involved in violent activity, the police, of course, have an obligation to track and find them.

And if they engage the police, then the police will, of course, have to protect themselves by returning fire.” Chang pointed to statistics that showed that between July and September, Jamaica recorded 123 murders, the lowest quarterly figure in more than three decades.

September, with 36, recorded the lowest monthly total in more than 30 years.

Chang emphasised that it was the fourth month this year in which Jamaica recorded 40 or fewer murders.

“Five of the first nine months of 2026 are among the lowest monthly murder totals recorded in more than three decades.

Additionally, the first three quarters of 2026 are the lowest quarterly murder totals recorded over that period,” Chang said.

He further highlighted, “Just a few years ago, 123 murders was a figure Jamaica could record in a single month.

In May 2024, Jamaica recorded 134 murders.

In 2017, the monthly average was 137 murders.

Today, 123 murders represent an entire quarter.”

World.title: Jamaicans increasingly afraid of the police, says Jackson
World.content:
Opposition Spokesperson on National Security, Fitz Jackson

OPPOSITION spokesman on national security Fitz Jackson says there is a growing number of Jamaicans who are afraid of the security forces.

He made the assertion in the House of Representatives on Tuesday while posing questions to Dr Horace Chang, the minister of national security and peace.

Chang had earlier presented a statement to the Parliament in which he pointed to the historic gains being made by the Jamaica Constabulary Force in reducing murders.

He provided statistics that showed that, as of Tuesday, October 6, Jamaica had recorded 407 murders, compared with 534 during the corresponding period in 2025.

This represents a reduction of 24 per cent.

The statistics also showed that between July and September, Jamaica recorded 123 murders, the lowest quarterly figure recorded in more than three decades.

September recorded 36 murders, the lowest monthly total in more than 30 years.

It was the fourth month this year in which the country recorded 40 or fewer murders.

When he rose to ask questions, Jackson, the Member of Parliament for St Catherine Southern, welcomed the sustained reductions in murders and lauded the security forces.

“The reduction of murders, and the reduction of crime generally, is the desire and expectation of all Jamaicans and all well-thinking people generally,” said Jackson.

“The reduction is what we on the Opposition have always called for, yearned for, and pushed the Government towards achieving,” he added to snickers from the Government benches.

Jackson argued that these numbers “didn’t just fall out of the sky”.

He said the numbers evolved from an extended period of high murder rates under the current Government which has been in office since 2016.

“While we welcome the reduction, 407 murders to date, what is also of concern is that as of today, there are 231 deaths at the hands of the security forces.

That’s more than 50 per cent of the murders reported by criminals,” said Jackson.

He said the high level of police killings should concern all Jamaicans.

He quoted from a section of the statement made by Chang, telling the Parliament that he endorsed it.

The security minister had remarked, “As we continue to reduce murders and other serious crimes, greater attention must now be placed on public order.

We must ensure that the way in which the police engage citizens is professional, proportionate and respectful.

We want effective enforcement while maintaining a strong relationship between the police and the public.” “That is most welcome,” said Jackson.

But he expressed concern that “when the occasions of interaction between citizens and the police result in 231 [fatal shootings] over the same period, it defies this statement”.

Said Jackson, “We want a Jamaica where everyone, regardless of where you live, can see the police as your partner in security.

We do not want a situation as is evidenced by the records, that there are growing numbers of Jamaicans who are afraid of the police.” Jackson told Government members that it is not convenient for them to look at the numbers on one side of the picture.

“We have to look at the complete picture,” he insisted.

He told Chang that when history is written, it should state that “crime reduction in this country occurred in an environment where all Jamaicans felt safe and not afraid of our security forces”.

The Opposition spokesman told the House that one way of achieving a balanced approach to crime-fighting and having all of Jamaica embracing the security forces is the policy enactment of body-worn cameras by the security forces, particularly when they embark on planned operations.

“[In] every incident of police fatality you can write what the script is going to be and just put in the [new] name and the address,” Jackson stated.

He said the only difference was the shooting death of Latoya “Buju” Bulgin in Montego Bay, St James, by the police.

In that case, the incident was captured on surveillance cameras and contradicted aspects of the statement issued by the police.

Following an investigation by the Independent Commission of Investigations (Indecom), Police Constable Andrew Wilson was charged with murder.

World.title: R&B singer Freddie Jackson dies at 70
World.content:
Freddie Jackson, the smooth balladeer who rocked local airwaves and charts with songs including Rock Me Tonight (For Old Times Sake); Tasty Love; You Are My Lady; A Little Bit More featuring Melba Moore; Nice and Slow; and All I Ever Ask featuring Najee, has died.

Jackson’s death on Monday, October 5 was confirmed by his family in a statement posted on his official Instagram account.

“Freddie was more than a legendary voice.

He was a kind, generous soul who loved his fans, his family, his friends and his music with everything he had,” the post read.

“For decades he gave us the songs that became the soundtrack to our love stories, our celebrations, and our most treasured memories.

That gift will live on forever.

To everyone who ever sang along, danced, or felt something when Freddie took the stage: Thank you.

You were family to him, and he carried your love with him always.” The cause of Jackson’s death was not stated; however, two years ago, he revealed in published reports, that he had been diagnosed with kidney disease.

Jackson topped the Billboard Hot R&B Singles chart 10 times during his career, with seven of his songs made the Billboard Hot 100, with You Are My Lady being the biggest hit, reaching #12 in 1985.

He released 13 studio albums with 2023’s My First Love being his last release.

He was nominated for a Grammy Best New Artiste Award as well as for Best Rhythm and Blues Vocal Performance – Male for the song You Are My Lady.

The singer, who was born Frederick Anthony Jackson, performed in Jamaica on several occasions.

His last performance here was at the pre-Valentine show Love in the Gardens, which took place on February 11, 2024 at Hope Gardens, which also featured Alaine, Island Kings, Digicel Rising Star winner Remone Watson, and Sanchez.

Emcee for the event, Heather Cummings- Williams shared her recollection of their meeting.

“Freddie was awesome energy the moment I met him! One of the humblest superstars I’ve ever come across.

The other was Peabo Bryson.

Two pioneers… gone leaving behind unmatched legacy,” Cummings-Williams told the Jamaica Observer on Tuesday.

“His performance was satisfactory; however, we assumed at the time that the reason for that was the fact that he was unwell.

The promoters were unaware at the time of booking him.

I interacted with him at the media launch as well as onstage at the Love in the Gardens show.

Sleep well, Freddie.

Your impact and contribution of endless love songs will never be forgotten,” said Cummings-Williams.

In a joint statement shared with the Jamaica Observer, Maya Sewell and Tara Johnson, from the Love in the Gardens production team, said: “We are deeply saddened by the news of Freddie Jackson’s passing.

His music brought immense joy to lovers of R&B and soul across generations, particularly here in Jamaica.

It was an honour to present his final concert performance on the island.” Reflecting on what it was like working with Jackson, Sewell said: “Freddie was an absolute gentleman — warm, gracious, and extraordinarily pleasant to work with throughout the entire production.

It was a genuine honour for our entire team and local crew to accommodate him.” Sewell continued: “Freddie was a consummate professional and successfully delivered his entire scheduled set.

While there was a noticeable, subtle shift when he landed and onstage, on a few of the audience’s favourite anthems, the energy in the space was magic.

The crowd was so thrilled to share that nostalgic moment with him that the performance quickly transformed into a unified, heart-warming sing-along.” Jackson was a back-up singer for R&B singer Melba Moore before he got his big break.

Her publicist shared a statement with the Observer, commenting on Jackson’s passing.

“My heart is broken over the loss of a great singer and even a greater friend, Freddie Jackson.

When we worked together on songs such as our hit, A Little Bit More, his sense of humour had me laughing during the sessions.

We had such a special relationship.

I will forever miss my dear friend.

Rest peacefully, Freddie,” shared Melba Moore.

World.title: LANCO PAINTS BIGGER FUTURE
World.content:
PEREZ… the commencement of manufacturing locally is also critical to sustaining sales growth, especially as the company looks to grow revenues beyond the domestic market.

PAINT and coatings manufacturer Lanco Jamaica Limited is targeting annual sales growth of between 20 per cent and 30 per cent as it moves to deepen its presence in the local market, expand its product offering, and position Jamaica as a manufacturing base for the wider Caribbean.

The company expects its planned build-out of a US$25million manufacturing plant in Caymanas, St Catherine, to play a key role in achieving that growth target by improving product availability, expanding production capacity, and supporting its push into new market segments.

Speaking with the Jamaica Observer in a recent interview, Lanco Jamaica Managing Director Alberto Perez said the company expects to significantly increase its customer base as the expansion takes shape.

“We would like to grow our sales by about 20 to 30 per cent a year,” Perez told the Business Observer, while noting that the expansion would provide the capacity needed to support that objective.

“We currently serve hundreds of customers but we are also looking to grow our customer base in a much larger way,” he added.

Construction of the new plant is expected to begin before the end of this year, with completion timed for as early as 2028.

“We are now waiting on the contractors to get started with construction activities. The new Jamaica outlet will be our 14th factory, so we have some experience, and we also have the machinery and all the other equipment needed so the build-out, I think, should take between a year and a half or two years,” Perez said.

Indicating that the plant will incorporate newer and more energy-efficient production technology, Perez said this should help to improve manufacturing efficiency as it strengthens Lanco’s competitiveness in Jamaica’s paints and coatings market, which now includes other players such as Berger, BH Paints, Edgechem, and Sherwin Williams.

Lanco, in looking beyond conventional paint products, is also seeking to capture a greater portion of current market share. To this end, Perez said the company is focusing on specialised products and formulations that can perform multiple functions, including one that combines paint, primer and sealer in a single application.

“We are concentrating right now on identifying things that others don’t do,” he said, while declining to disclose full details of the products being developed ahead of their official market roll-out.

Lanco’s portfolio currently includes architectural and industrial coatings, wood finishes, adhesives, sealants, solvents and removers, as well as a range of caulks and silicone products used in construction and plumbing applications. In addition to Lanco Paints, its major brands include Harris Paints, Crossco, Enco, Weco and Corona Corlanc.

Perez said the commencement of manufacturing locally, in giving Lanco greater control over its product mix and availability, is also critical to sustaining sales growth, especially as the company looks to grow revenues beyond the domestic market.

The company’s longer-term objective, he said, is to manufacture products in Jamaica for distribution throughout the Caribbean, with formulations designed specifically for the region’s climate and operating conditions.

“Our idea is to put our products made in Jamaica all over the Caribbean,” Perez further noted.

Lanco Jamaica forms part of the Puerto Rico-based Blanco Group, which operates across several markets in the Americas and Caribbean.

The group reported coatings sales of approximately US$748 million last year, up 15 per cent from US$650 million in 2024. Architectural and decorative coatings accounted for 84 per cent of sales, while general industrial and industrial maintenance products contributed 15 per cent, and automotive finishes the remaining one per cent.

In addition to its five manufacturing operations in Puerto Rico, the group also has production facilities in Orlando, Florida; Costa Rica; Nicaragua; Santo Domingo; Colombia; Jamaica; Guatemala; and Chile. The company employs more than 2,800 people across its operations.

Given Jamaica’s geographic position, infrastructure and access to regional market, Perez said this makes the country well suited to serve as a manufacturing base for Lanco’s Caribbean expansion.

“The new factory is therefore expected to serve as both a growth engine for Lanco Jamaica and a potential manufacturing hub for the company’s expansion across the region,” he said.

State minister in the Ministry of Industry, Investment, and Commerce Delano Seiveright, recently commenting on the planned expansion, underscored the factory’s potential to create opportunities for Jamaica to increase its exports to the wider Caribbean.

“This factory that they are building in Jamaica is the only one that will be built specifically for the Caricom region. It will bring dozens of jobs and indirect opportunities for Jamaica, and we are very excited about that. As a country we want the growth and the development, and our productive sector continues to carry a lot of great opportunities,” Seiveright said.

World.title: Crisis-stricken Haiti postpones elections
World.content:
A woman reacts during a collective funeral service for more than 20 people killed by armed gangs in Kenscoff, a neighbourhood near Port-au-Prince, Haiti. Gang members attacked displaced people huddling inside a church near Haiti’s capital, killing around 40, some of them execution-style, the mayor told AFP on August 24. (Photo: AFP)

PORT-AU-PRINCE, Haiti (AFP) — Haiti, which has been engulfed by years of gang violence and political chaos, has indefinitely postponed elections due to be held later this year, officials said Tuesday.

Haiti has not held elections since 2016, and its last president, assassinated in 2021, has not been replaced.

The first round of presidential and legislative elections was set for December 13, and the second round for February 21, 2027.

“The period originally scheduled for the electoral campaign has been postponed,” the Provisional Electoral Council’s statement said, omitting any mention of a new election date and adding that the timetable “will be made public as soon as possible.”

The council says the schedule will be updated to take into account the “technical and operational requirements of the process, as well as the conditions necessary for the proper conduct of the various stages.” It adds, however, that voter registration is continuing.

A member of the electoral council, speaking to AFP on the condition of anonymity, confirmed that “the December 13 date no longer stands,” adding that “we are working on a new timetable.” As of Tuesday, only 769,000 voters had been registered since the process began on July 20.

Holding elections has been seen as a crucial step to stabilizing the Haitian government and tackling rampant gang crime.

“I didn’t have high hopes about going to vote this year,” Davidson Jean Baptiste, a taxi driver in the capital Port-au- Prince, told AFP.

“Who can claim to hold elections in a country where the citizens are more concerned about insecurity and the abuses by armed groups?” Some Haitians hope their country can get back on the path to democracy as soon as possible.

“The people have been long kept out of the political debate,” said Claudette Piard at a voter registration center in Delmas.

“We finally want to vote for a government that will bring solutions to the masses,” she added.

The Caribbean country, the poorest in the Americas, has long faced a political, economic and security crisis, but the situation has deteriorated in recent years as gangs step up killings, kidnappings, rape and child recruitment.

Of its approximately 11 million inhabitants, nearly 1.5 million are internally displaced by violence, according to the International Organization for Migration, which stressed that attacks were not confined to the capital.

The security crisis has also presented challenges to organizers hoping to coordinate a vote across the country.

Several municipalities under gang control did not have registration centers, and the closure of roads from gang threats have prevented the delivery of electoral materials to several parts of the island nation.

The country’s gang violence crisis has left at least 5,700 people dead or wounded this year while more than 1,000 women and girls have been raped, UN human rights chief Volker Turk said last week.

The figures, compiled by the UN mission in Haiti up to September 11, also include 230 kidnappings, though Turk said “the real figures are likely much higher.” A UN-backed Gang Suppression Force (GSF) is being slowly deployed to assist overwhelmed local police.

The mission is intended to reach 5,500 personnel but currently only has about 1,500 so far.

The GSF replaced the Kenyaled Multinational Security Support mission, which was seen as under-equipped and underfunded.

The UN Security Council late last month approved a six-month extension of the mandate for the GSF with the resolution authorizing it, emphasizing “the importance of ensuring security conditions conducive to holding free and fair elections.”

World.title: Specialised land court needed
World.content:
Attorney-at-law Gloria Brown, speaking with reporters after Monday’s presentation at the World Habitat Day Conference, held at S Hotel Montego Bay. (Photo: Anthony Lewis)

MONTEGO BAY, St James — An attorney- at-law whose background includes a stint at the Titles Office and the role of a land tenure specialist has called for a court dedicated to land matters, pointing to severe judicial backlog and a critical lack of specialised expertise among judges handling property disputes.

“The reality is that a lot of our judges are not well-versed in land law. Many of them have come out of the DPP’s (Director of Public Prosecution’s) office; they have a criminal background. We find that the land matters are taking too long, and there are just too many land matters. Land is crucial to Jamaicans. So we need to do something. I think a specialist land court, like how we have a traffic court, a gun court — we need a land court,” said Gloria Brown, a senior partner in the firm Brown, Finlay and Company.

She was speaking with reporters after Monday’s presentation at the World Habitat Day Conference, held at S Hotel Montego Bay under the theme ‘The Struggle for Land, Shelter and Sustainable Communities’.

Land matters are now spread across the parish and supreme courts as well as the National Land Agency (NLA).

Issues such as disputes over ownership, disagreements over boundaries, ejection of squatters and easements are handled at the parish court level.

The civil division of the Supreme Court is where litigation in high-value property cases, complex vesting orders and major amendments of cancellations to titles are done.

Meanwhile, the National Land Agency manages registration and titling. This is not the first time a call has been made for a change in this approach.

In October 2010, while providing an update in the House of Representatives on the progress of land titling and registration under the Land Administration and Management Programme (LAMP), then Prime Minister Bruce Golding pointed to delays in the courts, noting that it takes close to a year to resolve matters dealing with the probate of Letters of Administration, or boundary or ownership disputes.

Golding said, then, that as part of the solution to address the backlog, the NLA had recommended the establishment of a land court for each county.

Golding also expressed a willingness to consider the appointment of a full-time paralegal and deputy registrar in the Supreme Court to deal with LAMP matters. There has been little reported on the issue since then.

Brown is a former project director at LAMP where she spearheaded the drafting and eventual passing of the Land Tenure Clarification Act, which sets the legal framework for the programme’s operations.

She left LAMP in 2010 to start her own law firm. On Monday, Brown said she and her team frequently encounter significant knowledge gaps when dealing with property litigation.

“It’s one of the most ignorant sets of individuals I’ve had to deal with in terms of the lack of knowledge in relation to land,” argued Brown.

One critical area to which she wants more Jamaicans to pay attention is the historical naming of locations and the associated environmental risks. “When you go into a community and somebody tells you that’s ‘Big Pond’, ask why it’s called that name.

Look at the places where we have had problems — Black River, Harbour View, Big Pond, Great Pond — those names were not just given by coincidence; they were given because of the history of the property,” warned Brown.

“We need to look at the history, because many of us have known the folklore. My parents always said, ‘The river will come back to take its course’.

We need to look at some of these areas, because we have the technology now where we know places that are not environmentally [friendly], competent to house persons’ dwellings, etc.

“We should learn from [Hurricane] Melissa. Melissa has taught us quite a bit… Look at Harbour View. We’ve had so many problems there whenever there’s a hurricane,” argued the attorney-at-law. Turning her attention to the issue of informal settlements, Brown warned that piecemeal approaches will only worsen the crisis.

“There are many, many solutions that we can look at. We can look at what was there for Operation Pride; we can look at the sites and services situation; we can look at the LAMP programme. But we need to bring all these things together. We have been too piecemeal in our approach to land, and this cannot continue. We have to solve this situation or else we’re going to have a Cooper’s Pen [Trelawny] multiplying all over Jamaica, because there’s something that God is not making any more of, and that is land,” argued Brown.

Her Cooper’s Pen reference was to a decades-old land dispute that culminated in roughly 20 houses in Trelawny being demolished in a pre-dawn operation on August 11.

Fresh eviction and cease-and-desist notices have since sparked days of protests.

Noting that illegal construction does not happen overnight, Brown highlighted the crucial role of local authorities in enforcement.

“Where are the planners? Where are the people whose job it is to go and enforce? Why is it that we only enforce when there is a problem? Because a man did not put up a three-storey building overnight, the people who work at the parish council (municipal corporation), many of them live in the same communities. I’ve seen so many clients who have gone to the parish council to say: ‘Somebody is building on my land’ they go and nothing is done. We need to know what exactly the parish councils are doing in terms of enforcement,” the attorney urged.

While acknowledging that squatting will persist, Brown warned that systemic failures could lead to civil unrest.

“When you have these problems like this, you’re going to have another Morant Bay Rebellion, maybe in another 10, 20 years, because Jamaicans are not going to continue where we see a lot of persons — the big hotels are coming to take away the beach properties, while the marginalised — we don’t have even marginal lands again,” she said.

Brown predicted that the construction of highways will open up interior sections of the country for those seeking to own land.

“It’s not the needy who are going to be succeeding; it’s going to be the greedy,” she argued.

World.title: ‘OBJECTIVES MET’
World.content:
Honduras midfielder Kervin Arriaga slide-tackles Jamaica’s defender Ronaldo Webster during the Concacaf Nations League Cup football match at the Nacional Chelato Ucles stadium in Tegucigalpa on October 5, 2026.

AFTER Jamaica’s Reggae Boyz booked their spot in the Concacaf Nations League quarter-finals against Mexico, interim Head Coach Rudolph Speid believes a solid foundation has been laid for future success.

The national senior men’s team drew 1-1 away to Honduras at the Chelato Uclés National Stadium, which was enough to secure second place in Group B with seven points and a spot in the next round of the competition.

With Guatemala beating Suriname (seven points each) and Martinique and El Salvador (four points each) drawing minutes before the game, Jamaica only needed a point to advance as they would have a better goal difference than Suriname.

They looked set to top the group after Tyreece Campbell’s 27th-minute strike but Luis Palma’s stunning long-range effort earned the Hondurans a point.

Speid was pleased to move on the knockout stages and gave Honduras credit for their performance.

“We did what we set out to do, which was qualify for the next round. I think both Jamaica and Honduras are very happy tonight,” he said.

“Honduras were very brave tonight. They had players who were making their debut in such an important game. They had to get a positive result not to be relegated, and they made a lot of changes and brought on some young players, and I think that is the way going forward. That’s really a good move by them.”

Throughout the four group games which began at the end of September, Speid dealt with a number of injuries and withdrawals, but this also afforded him the opportunity to see several players making their competitive debuts, including teenagers Jahmarie Nolan and Jamone Lyle.

He believes this window has given him optimism that Jamaica can compete with the best, going forward.

“Jamaica is in a rebuilding phase. We carried some really young players here — a lot of them played their first game for Jamaica in this series — so I think one of our objectives has been met,” he said.

“We were able to look at about 25 players over the four matches, and it will form the basis of our squad going forward. We have been able to see all the players play in top-level competition games and, based on that, we are better prepared to pick players going forward.”

Honduras Head Coach Jose Molina believes his team has a bright future, despite not qualifying for the next round, after going unbeaten against Jamaica over two matches, having last done so in 2013.

“If you want to achieve something you have to follow a path, and that path is the process; and what we want to achieve is qualifying for the 2030 World Cup, which is the main objective. We remain convinced that at some point the criticism will turn into something else,” he said.

The Reggae Boyz will now meet Concacaf’s number oneranked team and last summer’s FIFA World Cup hosts, Mexico, in the two-legged quarter-finals next month.

Jamaica will host the first leg at the National Stadium, on either November 13 or November 14, before travelling to Mexico on November 17 for the second leg.

The other quarter-final matchups will see USA take on Haiti, Canada battling Guatemala, and Curacao taking on Panama.

The winners will not only book their spot in the Nations League Finals in March but the Concacaf Gold Cup next summer.

World.title: Can Europe finally get tough on China?
World.content:
Trade Commissioner Maroš Šefčovič is kicking off his visit to China today — and the stakes are high.

On today’s show, Zoya Sheftalovich and Sarah Wheaton discuss the most important topic on the agenda: Europe’s trade deficit with China. France and Germany are finally on the same page and want Brussels to get tougher on unfair trade. So can we expect results from the meeting?
