World.title: Polanski’s final pitch in Holborn by-election: I’ll keep Burnham honest
World.content:
Zack Polanski leverages ex-Labour voters — and his barber — in his bid to snatch a seat from the governing party in Thursday’s by-election.

LONDON — Zack Polanski promised to smash Britain’s two-party political system — but his campaign for a U.K. parliamentary seat has leaned heavily on the idea that he can keep the existing prime minister honest.

POLITICO analysis of the online battleground in the Holborn and St. Pancras by-election – which takes place Thursday — shows the Green leader has been pitching himself as a protest vote for Labour-backing constituents in the London seat, which has been held by Labour since its creation in 1983.

The party has spent nearly £5,000 pushing ads on Meta’s platforms, which include Facebook and Instagram, promising that a Green win would help “keep the government in check.”



In one campaign video, Polanski takes credit for a series of Labour U-turns on their “most unpopular policies” over the last 12 months. A victory in the seat, he claims, would add further pressure on Prime Minister Andy Burnham to listen to the Greens, rather than “Nigel Farage, Donald Trump, or their corporate donors.”

An additional £7,000 has been spent by the party promoting graphics of recent newspaper headlines it thinks demonstrate the influence it holds over Burnham’s Labour government — including a Guardian story flagging a possible delay on North Sea gas field decisions until after the by-election.

“When Zack Polanski speaks, Labour listens. That is the power of the leader of the Green Party,” the accompanying ad copy states.

Building Brand Zack

The by-election marks Polanski’s first attempt to win a seat in the House of Commons.

The left-wing leader oversaw a rapid polling increase for the Greens after taking charge in September 2025, snatching a Labour safe seat in Gorton and Denton under former Labour Prime Minister Keir Starmer the following February.

But its polling momentum appears to have stalled since Labour switched to Burnham, and the party has also faced internal rows over anti-semitism.



The party has spent around £8,000 on targeted ads highlighting endorsements for Polanski from local residents, including former independent candidates and NHS workers.

And at least £500 of that has been spent promoting effusive praise of the Green leader from his own local hairdresser.

Alongside a picture of the pair hugging, barber Rami is quoted saying: “I’ve been cutting Zack’s hair for years. When you chat to him you can tell how much he really cares.”

A significant number of the showcased endorsements come from former Labour backers and members as Polanski seeks to convince voters that Burnham’s majority — and the mid-term timing of the contest — means they can register a protest vote in the symbolic seat previously held by Starmer.

One standalone advert features former Labour member Gopa, who says: “We all know there will still be a Labour government whoever wins, so I’m excited for a Green candidate who will listen to us and help push Labour to do better.”

Other endorsements include a Labour member of three decades who says she is now backing Polanski after her former party “lost its way and let me down.” Ex-Labour councillor Naser says he’s switched his allegiance to “keep the pressure on, and keep Labour in check.”

The Labour pitch

By contrast, Labour candidate Sagal Abdi-Wali has kept her campaign local.

She has spent more than £21,000 with Meta promoting dozens of slick cinematic clips and polished graphics pitching herself as a “local champion.”

Supported by Labour’s well-oiled digital team, Abdi-Wali’s online campaign focuses heavily on her experience of arriving in the area as a child refugee, and her subsequent career as a local councillor.

Labour has also pumped more than £20,000 into Google’s ad program. The majority of that sum was spent on bitesize YouTube ads, with the remainder spent on buying up sponsored Google search results in an attempt to grab the attention of voters hunting for information about the contest.

Also running

Britain’s hard-right Restore Britain has also been making a pitch to voters in Holborn and St Pancras — while openly admitting it has no chance of winning in “one of the most left-wing seats in Britain.”

Rupert Lowe’s party has spent around £30,000 on Meta ads positioning itself as a “genuine patriotic alternative” to Nigel Farage’s Reform UK — which has not spent significant cash in the contest.

Restore’s spending included £1,500 promoting a “quiz” comparing comments from Reform politicians with Restore’s more hard-line agenda. A further £2,000 went on promoting a graphic of the “ten reasons” why voters should support it.



That list includes removing “millions of foreign nationals who hate who we are,” a promise to “reverse the Islamification” of London, deport “foreign tramps who ruin our city” and force “healthy” benefit claimants to clean graffiti and pick litter.

In a further attempt to present his insurgent party as a credible alternative to Reform or the Conservatives, Lowe’s paid online content repeatedly describes the by-election as a “free hit” for right-wing voters to “vote with your heart.”

“They don’t want the capital reformed, or conserved,” one paid ad states. “They want London restored.”

World.title: Far-right Vox sees election as its big chance to reshape Spain
World.content:
While the center-right People’s Party is expected to come first — with about 33% of the vote, according to POLITICO’s Poll of Polls — it will almost certainly have to team up with Vox, which commands support of about 18%, to build a stable coalition.

Abascal will then be able to demand the inclusion of key elements of Vox’s agenda as its price for that partnership. Its goals include deportations of undocumented migrants, a benefits preference for Spaniards over foreign nationals, slashing EU health and safety rules in the farming sector and rolling back support for gender equality and the LGBTQ+ community.

Vox secured 33 of the 350 seats in Congress in 2023, but is now set to double that. Under the PP’s coalition leadership, it should be able to form part of a comfortable majority.

“This time round, Vox is much stronger,” José Antonio Fúster, spokesperson for the party and a member of the Madrid regional parliament, said. “We are going into a very important election, not so much for us, as for Spaniards … This is the last hope for Spain to be Spain again.”

Fúster would not be drawn on which ministries his party has set its sights on, warning against “selling the bearskin before it has been hunted.”

Pointing to talks with the PP in recent months in four regions where the two parties now govern in coalition, he said the shaping of policy was being prioritized ahead of institutional power. “That is the last thing we negotiate because it is the least important,” he said.

World.title: French PM tries to defuse anger over schools, fuel and agriculture in sweeping speech
World.content:
On Tuesday, between 256,000 people, according to police, and 450,000, according to organizers, joined demonstrations across France. Unions, teachers and left-wing political parties took to the streets in solidarity with high school students.

But discontent in France extends beyond schools. A surge in fuel prices, triggered by the U.S.-led war in Iran, has added to concerns about the cost of living.

Online calls for a Yellow Jackets-style protest on Oct. 17 have emerged in response to rising fuel prices.

"Last Friday, [the G7] decided to release strategic [fuel] reserves... As part of this effort, we will make 10 million barrels of diesel from our reserves available to distributors in France," Lecornu announced, claiming that the supply increase would lower diesel prices by €0.12 to €0.18 per liter.

France still has 8 million barrels of oil products to release under a wider deal brokered in March after the outbreak of the war in Iran, and had privately signaled Wednesday morning that it might release an additional 2 million barrels of diesel on top of that, as POLITICO reported earlier on Wednesday. It's unclear whether the 10 million figure includes that earlier commitment.

The French energy ministry did not immediately reply to a request for comment.

World.title: EU Parliament defends secret ballots that kept far right out of top committee jobs
World.content:
Specifically, the Patriots are contesting elections in which the chairs and vice-chairs of parliamentary committees were selected after the 2024 EU election. Those jobs were filled through voting in secret ballots. The group is also questioning the composition of the Parliament’s international delegations, saying its lawmakers were kept away from key roles.

Lawyers for the Patriots — home of France’s National Rally, Spain’s Vox and Hungary’s Fidesz, among others — said its MEPs being kept from top committee jobs was a “categorical exclusion” and it was “not acceptable” for the Parliament’s third-largest party to be locked out of these positions.

The Patriots have 85 lawmakers in the 720-strong chamber. Top jobs in Parliament come up for grabs again in January 2027, giving the Patriots another chance to try to get into powerful positions.

Hungarian lawmaker Kinga Gál, the Patriots’ first vice-president, has previously called the mainstream parties’ actions “outrageous” and “against the rule of law.”

The Patriots’ lawyer, Azelio Fulmini, referred to the EU institution’s own description of representation.

“This proportional distribution of leadership positions within Parliament prevents the dominance of political life by just one or two large political groups, ensuring that smaller political groups also have a say in setting the political agenda,” he read.

World.title: German stock exchange tussle leaves EU supercop deal at risk
World.content:
But a push by Germany to exclude one of Europe’s biggest stock exchanges from central EU oversight could turn dinner into a food fight.

This exemption remains in the current compromise position among EU capitals after Berlin refused to give up local supervision of its stock exchange behemoth Deutsche Börse over fears of job losses and ceding power to a bloc-wide entity, despite central supervision being one of the key tenets of the MISP package.

It's sparked protests from smaller countries, which feel the compromise would disproportionately benefit their larger neighbors — and could scupper the entire deal.

The carveout is “polluting the whole debate” by giving a “huge gift to Germany” while other countries receive nothing in return for their support, one diplomat said.

Another went further. "No deal is better than a bad deal," a senior EU official said ahead of Friday's meeting.

One market

Securing a deal on MISP this year is central to the "One Europe, One Market" plan that the EU’s three political leaders in Brussels agreed to in April. EU governments have invested significant political capital into MISP in a bid to turn the bloc into an investment hub where innovative companies can find investors without having to leave for deeper pockets on Wall Street.

World.title: EU-Länder wollen erst nach Prüfung durch die IEA neue Ölvorräte freigeben
World.content:
Bei einem Treffen am Mittwochnachmittag bezogen auch EU-Vertreter diese Position und kündigten an, künftige Entnahmen „bis zu einer klareren Einschätzung der Marktbedingungen und der Risiken für die Versorgungssicherheit durch die IEA“ auszusetzen, so einer der Diplomaten. Die Länder müssten wissen, „wie weit wir gehen können“, sagte ein anderer.

Mit Blick auf die aktuell hohen Dieselpreise warnten einige EU-Länder, dass eine Freigabe der Vorräte zum jetzigen Zeitpunkt sie im Falle einer Versorgungskrise verwundbar machen könnte. Unter den IEA-Mitgliedern gibt es noch genügend ungenutzte Vorräte, um die Zusage zur Freigabe von 100 Millionen Barrel zu erfüllen.

Von den im März zugesagten 400 Millionen Barrel wurden 325 Millionen freigegeben, wobei einige Länder „größere Mengen als ursprünglich zugesagt“ freigegeben haben, teilte die IEA in einer Erklärung im Anschluss an eine außerordentliche Ministerkonferenz mit. Damit verbleiben noch rund 100 Millionen Barrel, die die Länder im Rahmen dieser Vereinbarung noch freigeben können, fügte sie hinzu.

In der Erklärung der IEA heißt es, die neue Zusage stelle eine „Vollendung“ der Vereinbarung vom März dar. Zu den 32 Mitgliedern der IEA zählen wohlhabende Länder aus Europa, Nordamerika und Ostasien.

POLITICO hatte bereits berichtet, dass Frankreich und Deutschland – die über einige der bedeutendsten Vorräte in Europa verfügen – signalisiert hätten, dass sie über die bereits zugesagten Mengen hinaus keine oder nur minimale Mengen freigeben würden.

Es bleibt unklar, welchen Anteil der jetzigen Freigabe die Nicht-EU-Mitglieder der IEA übernehmen werden, nachdem zum Beispiel Japan jegliche weiteren Freigaben ausgeschlossen hat.

Weitere Einzelheiten zur Ölfreigabe durch die G7 sollen nächste Woche bei einer Sitzung des IEA-Verwaltungsrats erörtert werden, sagte der zweite Diplomat.

Dieser Artikel erschien zuerst auf Englisch bei POLITICO.

World.title: EU countries will release fresh oil stocks only after top agency assessment
World.content:
In a meeting Wednesday afternoon, EU officials endorsed the position, pledging to defer any future drawdowns "pending a clearer IEA assessment of market conditions and security-of-supply risks," said one of the diplomats. Countries need to know "how low we can go," said another.

While diesel prices are high as a result of airstrikes on energy infrastructure in Russia and the Middle East, some EU countries warned that releasing stocks now could leave them vulnerable in the event of a supply crisis.

There remain enough untapped stocks among IEA members to satisfy the pledge to release 100 million barrels.

Of the 400 million barrels pledged in March, 325 million have been released, with some countries releasing "greater volumes than they initially pledged," the IEA said in a statement following an emergency ministerial meeting. That leaves around 100 million left that countries can still release under that agreement, it added.

It said the fresh commitment would represent a "completion" of that March agreement. The IEA's 32 members include wealthy European, North American and East Asian countries.

POLITICO reported earlier Wednesday that France and Germany — which hold some of Europe's most significant stockpiles — had signalled they would release no or minimal supplies on top of those already pledged.

It remains unclear what share of the releases non-EU members of the IEA will accept, after Japan, another member, ruled out any further releases.

Further details on the breakdown of the G7 release will be discussed at a meeting of the IEA's governing board next week, the second diplomat said.

World.title: Oil prices are climbing on concerns about an escalating Iran war
World.content:
Asian shares fell, and oil prices surged on Thursday after Wall Street's S&P 500 and Nasdaq retreated from record highs.

 

Oil prices rebounded amid uncertainty over global crude supplies. The US and Iran have yet to reach a deal to end their war.

Crude prices had fallen earlier in the week amid signs that exports from the Middle East were heading back towards pre-war levels and that G7 nations had agreed to tap their stockpiles.

But anxiety returned as data showed Tehran had stepped up attacks on tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, the Houthis denied claims they had lost key territory and senior oil officials warned that global reserves were running worryingly low.

On Wednesday, The Atlantic reported that the White House had asked the Pentagon to draw up options for strikes on Iranian targets ahead of next month's US midterm elections, with Trump's Republicans at risk of losing control of both chambers of Congress.

The report said the scale of the potential strikes and their targets were still being discussed, but added that a wider operation could follow the 3 November vote.

Even supporters of the proposed strikes did not expect them to bring Iran to the negotiating table or restore safe passage through the Strait of Hormuz, according to the report. However, they hoped military action would help Trump project strength before the election.

Both main crude benchmarks rose more than 2% on Thursday, with supplies also hit by the loss of more than 500,000 barrels a day of Gulf of Mexico output as producers shut down operations ahead of Hurricane Isaias.

Early on Thursday, Brent crude, the international benchmark, was up 2.4% at $102.68 per barrel. US benchmark West Texas Intermediate rose more than 2.2% to above $90.20 a barrel.

The International Energy Agency said on Wednesday that its members supported accelerating oil stock releases already pledged in March, prioritising diesel where possible.

The rise in oil prices revived inflation fears and added to upward pressure on government bond yields, which have reached multi-year highs.

France's 10-year government bond yield stood at 4.89%, while Germany's was 3.48%.

The yield on the 10-year US Treasury remained near a multi-decade high, trading at 5.32%. Minutes of the US Federal Reserve's September meeting, released on Wednesday, showed that most officials considered another interest rate rise likely to be appropriate before the end of the year.

Inflation in the US remains above the Fed's 2% target. In September, the Fed raised rates for the first time since July 2023, by a quarter of a percentage point to a range of 3.75% to 4%.

Rising bond yields have also put pressure on stocks, as higher borrowing costs can weigh on company profits and make bonds more attractive to investors.

Markets across Asia fell, including Tokyo, Hong Kong, Sydney, Shanghai, Singapore, Seoul, Wellington, Taipei and Manila.

On Wednesday, Wall Street's benchmark S&P 500 dropped 0.2% a day after reaching an all-time high. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 0.7%, while the technology-heavy Nasdaq Composite declined 0.2% from its record.

Tech shares pulled back from recent gains as investors prepared for earnings season, with high valuations and vast spending on artificial intelligence putting profits under scrutiny.

Samsung shares fell despite the company estimating a 782.5% rise in third-quarter operating profit to 107.4 trillion won (about €71.8 billion), supported by higher memory chip prices.

Meanwhile, the euro remained near its lowest level since June 2025, weighed down by concerns over France's high debt levels.

On Thursday morning, the euro traded at $1.12, the pound at $1.32 and the dollar at ¥158.13. Gold edged higher to $4,143.90 an ounce.

World.title: Portuguese hospital lets pets visit owners in wards: a paradigm shift?
World.content:
Since 9 July, São João, one of the leading public university hospitals in Portugal’s health system, has been opening its wards to visits from pets.

 

The "Pets and Company" project brings together different professionals from the One Health São João (source in Portuguese) programme, as well as from the Unit for Infection Prevention and Control and Antimicrobial Resistance and the hospital’s Humanisation service. The initiative forms part of a strategy designed to break isolation and ease the exhaustion caused by prolonged hospital stays.

The therapeutic potential of animals is far from a recent discovery. Countries such as the United Kingdom and Germany have been using them in psychiatric treatment and for human physical conditions since the 19th century. The term "pet therapy" (animal-assisted therapy) was scientifically defined in the 1960s by an American psychologist, who discovered the healing qualities of these interventions by chance.

In Portugal, dogs trained and certified for emotional-support sessions have been working in hospitals for several years, including at São João, in partnership with handlers from associations.

On 30 May 2023, a 77-year-old patient admitted to Cascais Hospital while recovering from a haemorrhagic stroke (cerebrovascular accident) received a visit from her own dog, in a reunion that took place in the outdoor area of the facility.

This unprecedented experience is now being expanded by São João through a comprehensive protocol, created from scratch, which goes a step further and normalises the practice of taking pets into inpatient areas, recognising them as part of the patient’s family circle and providing people who have long been away from home with moments of comfort under safe public-health conditions.

What does the protocol say?

Visits are requested by the healthcare professional (doctor or nurse) who is following the patient and responsible for flagging the case; they are not available to everyone who is in hospital. An individual assessment of risks and benefits is always carried out.

Once informed, the team responsible for the programme assesses whether there is a clinical need and whether there are conditions to proceed with the visit in terms of infection control at the chosen location. Other patients are also asked whether they feel comfortable with the presence of animals.

Once approval is given, the patient’s family must provide a veterinary certificate proving that the animal’s vaccinations and deworming are up to date, and that it has behaviour compatible with the requirements associated with staying in hospital premises.

Dog in the lift at São João Hospital before visiting its owner, Porto, 2 October 2026 Bruno Figueiredo/Euronews

"Any professional, from security staff to doctors or nurses, who sees that something is not in line with the protocol can interrupt the visit," Filipa Ceia, spokesperson for the One Health São João Group, tells Euronews.

If the animal is "anxious" because of the "noise of the ward", appears "aggressive" or is "visibly dirty", the visit is "immediately called off", the infectious-disease specialist and vet warns.

Dogs, cats and even "more exotic species" are allowed, provided that "all the conditions are met", adds Filipa Ceia. While in hospital areas, the animal must be accompanied by an adult.

Each patient can enjoy these meetings, lasting half an hour, once every seven days. The project gives priority to people who are in a terminal phase or undergoing prolonged hospitalisation.

To the surprise of those in charge, it is male patients who have most often requested the presence of their pets in hospital, although the small sample does not allow definitive conclusions. "Men may be more fragile when they are ill. They realise there are things of great importance in life and want to have them close during their stay," says Ceia.

Visit of a pet to its owner in a ward at São João Hospital, Porto, 2 September 2026 Bruno Figueiredo/Euronews

Benefits for the patient and for the animal

Studies carried out on interventions assisted by trained animals show clear improvements in patients’ clinical condition: blood pressure drops and the production of hormones linked to stress and anxiety is inhibited. When the household pet is involved, there is "a greater benefit", highlights Filipa Ceia.

Euronews accompanied the visit of Princesa, who went to São João for the second time in 15 days to ease the longing for her owner, António, who has been in hospital for three months. The dog was taken to the hospital by the patient’s wife, who led her on a lead to the ward.

As soon as the lift doors opened, Princesa could not contain her excitement, and António felt the same.

Dog visits owner in a ward at São João Hospital, Porto, 2 October 2026 Bruno Figueiredo/Euronews

"My heart beat wildly with joy. It is like having family here. She is a daughter to me," confessed the 65-year-old man, who is in rehabilitation because of balance and walking difficulties.

The diagnosis has not yet been confirmed, but it is suspected that he suffers from a rare blood disease. The reunion with the dog, which was given to him five years ago after being rescued from the street, is a balm for the soul.

"It feels as if I want to walk better and everything. This is the joy a person has," he said. These reunions bring "smiles, engagement with treatment and an incentive to leave hospital", notes Filipa Ceia, pointing out further benefits for the animal itself and even for healthcare professionals.

"Residual risk"

This initiative began at the start of July and, so far, there have been no recorded infections.

The team behind the project wants to review the protocol at a later stage to correct any possible flaws. Given the procedures adopted, a scenario involving "incidents" is, however, "highly unlikely", stresses Filipa Ceia.

In northern and central Europe, infection-control and public-health rules are stricter. Assistance dogs are prioritised and, when visits by privately owned animals are authorised (normally for patients in palliative care), they take place in isolated facilities, namely open courtyards or gardens attached to the main structure.

Take the example of Sint-Trudo Hospital in Sint-Truiden, Belgium. In July 2023, this health facility opened an independent pavilion (source in Portuguese), separate from the main building but connected to the hospital, so that terminal patients or those in long-term stays could interact with their pets. The access (source in Portuguese) for pets is via an outside courtyard, and they are strictly forbidden, under any circumstances, from passing through the interior of the hospital grounds.

Instead of erecting physical barriers by building secondary structures, São João has drawn up a set of rules which, while maintaining clinical rigour, are integrated into a flexible protocol shaped by scientific evidence.

"There is an excessive fear of transmitting zoonoses that is not borne out by studies," says Filipa Ceia. In fact, the infectious-disease doctor notes, "it is easier for most diseases to be transmitted from human to human than from an animal to a human".

"As we try as much as possible to preserve safety and, since the patient, when they go home, will be living with their animal, the risk really is residual. We have to understand whether, in trying to mitigate the risk, we are not preventing patients from enjoying the benefit," she adds.

São João’s boldness lies not only in the balance between empathy and sanitary control, but also in its autonomy and ability to humanise care without waiting for legislators, unlike Italy, for example, where progress has come through decrees issued by regional governments.

World.title: Can Europe's return hubs work without breaking its own human rights rules?
World.content:
EU home affairs ministers gave their final approval to a new Return Regulation in Luxembourg on October 1. The regulation replaces the 2008 Return Directive and includes a legal framework for "return hubs" in non-EU countries.

 

What governments say

The Council of the EU presents the rules as a way to make returns work. Ireland's Minister for Justice, Home Affairs and Migration, Jim O'Callaghan, whose country holds the presidency, pointed to the gap between decisions and departures. "Around two in three people ordered to leave the EU do not actually leave. The revised return rules adopted today will help member states implement swift returns effectively."

The Council says the rules complement the Migration and Asylum Pact and that all return measures must respect fundamental rights. They set obligations on people with no right to stay, who must leave and cooperate with authorities. Non-compliance can bring sanctions from reduced benefits to financial penalties.

People posing a security risk can face an indefinite entry ban or detention beyond 24 months, where justified and proportionate. A European Return Order lets states recognise one another's return decisions, voluntarily at first, with a reassessment after three years.

Hubs require an agreement or arrangement with a non-EU country that respects international human rights standards and the principle of non-refoulement. Unaccompanied minors are excluded. Separately, Germany, Austria, Denmark, Greece, and the Netherlands are pursuing a joint hub in Africa. Greece's migration minister, Thanos Plevris, said the aim is to open a facility in 2027. Rwanda is reported as a possible frontrunner.

A promise on paper

Human rights NGOs worry whether the rights guaranteed in the EU can be enforced once a person has left the bloc’s territory.

Marta Welander, EU Advocacy Director at the International Rescue Committee (IRC), has no doubts. "The proposed idea of return hubs is cruel, costly and counterproductive,” she told Euronews. "No amount of additional funding, training or monitoring design changes the fact that a transferred person's protection would depend entirely on a state outside the EU's legal reach, so proper oversight, rights to appeal and protection from refoulement cannot be guaranteed the way they can be inside EU jurisdiction," Welander continued.

Chiara Catelli, Advocacy Officer at PICUM, said that "no safeguard can make deportation centres a legitimate tool to manage migration." She argues that the transfer itself is a rights issue. "The very fact of sending people to places they don't even know, far from the life they were trying to build, goes against the right to private and family life."

The gaps in the text

Catelli points to what the regulation doesn’t include. "The Return Regulation doesn't say anything about living conditions or timeframes for detention in the return hubs, nor who will monitor the respect of and enforce any safeguards."

The Council's description confirms that details are left to individual deals, like an "agreement or arrangement." This is where the Council of Europe's human rights commissioner, Michael O'Flaherty, objected. In letters published in July to the five countries pursuing the joint initiative, he called for four guardrails.

These include a risk assessment before any hub opens, independent and continuous monitoring with the power to suspend cooperation, legally binding agreements with enforceable human rights clauses, and publication of agreements and findings so parliaments and courts can scrutinise them. These are his recommendations, not clauses of the regulation.

Welander doubts that monitoring is realistic. "It is hard to see how effective monitoring could work in a third country where the EU has no courts, no jurisdiction and no enforcement power at all."

The IRC points to Italy's detention centres in Albania, often described as a blueprint for return hubs, which it has visited twice. "What has been witnessed in Albania includes widespread psychological distress among those detained without proper mental health care, including extremely troubling reports of self-harm."

Who is responsible?

Catelli says responsibility cannot be handed over along with the detainees. "What is clear is that the EU and its member states cannot just outsource their responsibility to protect people's fundamental rights, or to prevent and address violations, especially when those violations are a direct consequence of policies they have put in place."

UN human rights chief Volker Türk made the same point after Parliament adopted the text in June. "EU States cannot simply outsource their human rights obligations to third States in this context."

Welander argues the real bottleneck lies elsewhere. "A major factor behind slow returns is third countries' willingness to cooperate on readmission and document verification - this is widely cited as a bigger constraint than coordination at EU level."

Rights groups do not dispute that the rules apply. They dispute if the new powers can uphold them in practice. With no host country confirmed, the answer will emerge from the agreements governments sign, and from whether those agreements are made public.

The "safe third country" label carries much of the weight, and Catelli says it should not. "A country could be considered safe by the EU and still be unsafe for certain people, depending on their individual circumstances."

World.title: Texas execution first in US since Christa Pike survived botched lethal injection
World.content:
Texas has carried out the first execution in the US since Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike survived a failed lethal injection last week.

 

Jamaal Howard, 46, received a fatal dose of pentobarbital at the state prison in Huntsville and was pronounced dead at 8:03 pm. Howard had been convicted of shooting and killing 42-year-old clerk Vickie Swartout in a convenience store robbery in Silsbee, Texas, in 2000.

Howard is said to have gasped and taken a few breaths as the drug took effect, before making snoring sounds and coughing. All movement stopped within around 30 seconds, and he was pronounced dead 19 minutes later.

Before the execution took place, Howard addressed some members of Swartout's family, apologising and asking for forgiveness.

"I wish that you accept my apology and I wish for your forgiveness," he said. "I'm sorry for what happened. I wish you can learn to forgive me one of these days."

He added that he was "in a good state of mind to find peace and the Lord, so I thank y’all."

"Hey, enjoy life, and peace to y’all."

Howard's attorneys had unsuccessfully attempted to halt the execution, filing a motion before the Texas Court of Criminal Appeals questioning the quality of Texas' execution drugs. They also argued to the Supreme Court that the execution should not go ahead because Howard was intellectually disabled.

The Texas court denied the request relating to the drugs and a second filing without comment.

The Supreme Court has barred the execution of intellectually disabled people, but it has given states some discretion in determining such disabilities. The state told the court that Howard's attorneys did not provide evidence that would show he met the requirements to claim intellectual disability.

The high court also declined to intervene without comment late on Wednesday, clearing the way for the execution to go ahead.

The Texas Coalition to Abolish the Death Penalty, an advocacy organisation campaigning to end the death penalty in Texas, had called on people to urge Texas Governor Greg Abbott to insist on a reprieve for Howard, so that his lawyers could "obtain critical records from the Texas Department of Criminal Justice about when the drug was bought, how it was stored, and what testing was done and when."

Including Howard, Texas has executed seven people so far this year, up from five in both 2025 and 2024. A further two executions are scheduled to take place in November - death row inmates John Rubio and Reinaldo Dennes.

World.title: Monte Carlo added to glamorous Venice Simplon-Orient-Express rail itinerary for 2027
World.content:
The Venice Simplon-Orient-Express is adding a glamorous new stop to its European routes in 2027, with Monte Carlo joining the itinerary for the first time.

 

From May, the legendary train operated by Belmond will travel from Paris along the Côte d’Azur before arriving in Monaco on its onward journey to Venice.

It’s set to become an annual addition to the iconic rail company’s schedule and will allow guests to explore the famously glitzy city, world-renowned for landmarks including the Casino de Monte-Carlo and the star-studded Formula One Grand Prix.

Travellers will start their journey in the French capital, boarding the train’s midnight-blue carriages, all decked out in Art Deco style.

On offer are historic cabins, grand suites, as well as the L'Observatoire carriage, designed by French artist JR. The suite comes complete with a bedroom and en suite bathroom with a freestanding bathtub as well as a spacious living area, library and secret tearoom.

No matter which level of accommodation guests stay in, they can opt to eat dinner in one of the train's two restaurant cars, Étoile du Nord or L'Oriental, before moving onto the Bar Car '3674', where cocktails are accompanied by live music at the piano.

The next morning, guests will enjoy a breakfast of fresh pastries and pressed fruit juices, while taking in views of the beautiful Côte d'Azur.

The route takes passengers along the dramatic red cliffs of the Massif de l'Estérel and winds through Saint-Raphaël towards Cannes and Nice, offering sweeping views across the French Riviera.

Guests can spend their evenings in the luxury train’s Bar Car '3674' Belmond

Closer to Monaco, the railway cuts into the mountainside before arriving at Monte Carlo station, deep beneath the rock.

According to the company, the decision to add Monte Carlo to the route was an easy one.

“Monaco has long held a special place in the story of European travel, with generations drawn to the Côte d'Azur by its distinctive sense of style, culture, and occasion,” said Pascal Deyrolle, Area Managing Director for Trains – Continental Europe.

“Introducing the destination feels like a natural continuation for the Venice Simplon-Orient-Express, bringing the romance of luxury rail travel to a locale that has always understood the art of arrival.”

With a slated price starting at €4,870 per person based on two guests sharing a historic cabin, with 24-hour steward service, all meals with the sommelier's choice of wine and unlimited soft drinks, and transfers, many of us might need to start saving ahead of May’s launch.

World.title: Europe Today: Rubio urges Europe to wake up as EU trade chief begins key China trip
World.content:
Water Matters

Europe's water is under increasing pressure. Pollution, droughts, floods are taking their toll on our drinking water, lakes, rivers and coastlines. Join us on a journey around Europe to see why protecting ecosystems matters, how our wastewater can be better managed, and to discover some of the best water solutions. Video reports, an animated explainer series and live debate - find out why Water Matters, from Euronews.

World.title: Menopause patients left without treatment: what is happening in Spain?
World.content:
Hundreds of thousands of Spanish women have spent months encountering problems getting hold of some of the hormone treatments used to relieve menopausal symptoms.

 

What began as an issue with a single medicine — Lenzetto, a transdermal estradiol spray — has finally triggered a domino effect in the market for hormone replacement therapies (HRT).

The shortage of Lenzetto drove up demand for other estradiol formulations, such as patches and gels, which were not prepared to absorb it. Over recent months, Aemps has recorded supply issues affecting medicines such as Evopad, Estradot and Bijuva.

The result has been months of supply problems, patients searching for their medication from pharmacy to pharmacy, and authorities trying to find alternatives.

November could mark the start of an improvement, although there are still doubts about when supply will truly return to normal.

The Secretary of State for Health, Javier Padilla, told Euronews on the sidelines of the European Health Forum Gastein in Austria that the situation should start to ease from next month.

Spain's Medicines and Medical Devices Agency (Aemps), however, warns that the forecasts communicated by Lenzetto's manufacturer, Gedeon Richter, "have not always been accurate".

Related Spanish Nutrition Agency issues menopause guidelines based on male studies

Gedeon Richter confirmed to Euronews that it expects Lenzetto to be available again in Spanish pharmacies starting in the second half of November. However, the company acknowledges it may not be able to fully meet demand throughout 2027 due to global supply constraints, though it expects to gradually meet demand starting in the second half of 2027.

European issue

The problem is not confined to Spain. According to Padilla, a sharp surge in demand has outstripped manufacturers' production capacity in several European countries. Aemps also considers this to be an international supply issue affecting, to varying degrees, different European Union member states.

The European Medicines Agency (EMA) has confirmed to Euronews that it has been informed of the supply issues regarding Lenzetto and is considering possible coordinated measures at the EU level to mitigate the impact. The matter will be addressed in upcoming meetings of the European group responsible for medicine supply issues.

The EMA further notes that it is aware of recent supply problems involving other estradiol-based medicines in the EU. However, these cases have not been deemed critical at the European level and are being managed by national authorities.

The crisis mainly affects women who use these therapies to alleviate symptoms associated with the menopause, although estradiol is also used in other clinical situations, including the prevention of osteoporosis and gender-affirming hormone treatments for trans women.

From Lenzetto to a domino effect

The crisis was brewing for months. Aemps began receiving reports from users about difficulties in finding Lenzetto in February and contacted pharmaceutical company Gedeon Richter at that point. Initially, the company insisted it was meeting demand as normal.

The situation changed soon afterwards. The laboratory reported that it was facing a surge in demand it could not meet immediately and problems with the device used to administer the medicine. Weeks later it announced that it had run out of stock and that the issue was affecting all its markets throughout 2026.

Aemps also maintains that the company failed to meet its obligation to notify in advance of incidents that could disrupt the continuous supply of the medicine. Consumption of Lenzetto had risen very rapidly. In Spain, distributed units rose from around 13,000 in 2018 to about 123,000 in 2024.

Gedeon Richter explained to Euronews that demand had outstripped its manufacturing capacity and that the availability of the applicator used to administer the medication could not keep pace with the growth. The company emphasises that the shortage is unrelated to any quality or safety issues with the medication.

To increase supply, the company states that it is maximising its current capacity and developing new manufacturing options and suppliers. Furthermore, it is establishing a new plant and a new production line.

Spain raised the price, but it was not enough

The government has tried various ways to increase the availability of these medicines. Among them, as Padilla explained, raising the regulated price in an attempt to attract more supply to the Spanish market. But the measure failed to resolve the problem. The Secretary of State stressed that the difficulty goes beyond price: manufacturers do not have sufficient capacity to cope with the sharp rise in demand.

The Health Ministry then explored another option. It contacted manufacturers of alternative treatments that are not reimbursed by the National Health System and signalled its willingness to consider funding them in order to widen the options available to patients.

According to Padilla, this route has also not delivered the expected results so far. The companies told the government that they did not have enough production capacity to increase supply, even if their products were to be publicly funded. Aemps confirms that the Health Ministry has held talks with the holders of these alternatives, although no reimbursement requests have yet been formalised.

More than 25,000 signatures reach the Health Ministry

While the authorities look for solutions, patients have begun to mobilise. More than 25,000 people have supported, in barely three weeks, a petition calling on the government to take urgent action over the supply problems. Its organiser, 49-year-old Rebeca Marín, who uses hormone replacement therapy, is due to submit the signatures this Tuesday, 6 October, at the Health Ministry.

The petition calls on the authorities to act preventively in the face of future supply problems and to ensure that when a medicine is unavailable, there are accessible alternatives for patients regardless of where they live. The financial aspect is particularly important. Some of the existing alternatives are not covered by the public system, forcing patients to bear the full cost.

The Institute of Women demands "urgent" action

The issue has also reached the Institute of Women, which has asked the Health Ministry and Aemps to tackle "as a priority and urgently" the supply problems. The body acted after receiving complaints from individuals and women's associations concerned both about the difficulty of maintaining their treatments and about the price of some of the available alternatives.

Catalonia turns to pharmacies

In view of the prolonged shortage, Catalonia has decided to prepare an alternative solution. The regional government plans to allow pharmacies to prepare magistral estradiol formulas if supply problems persist.

The measure would allow individualised treatments to be made up from the active ingredient and on the basis of a medical prescription. Compounding pharmacies have estradiol in stock as a raw material, so this route could serve as an alternative when industrially produced medicines are unavailable.

The proposal has, however, opened up a divide between health authorities and pharmacists. Aemps believes magistral formulas should be used only as a last resort, as their absorption can be more variable than that of authorised medicines. The General Council of Official Pharmacists' Associations, by contrast, advocates their use in the current shortage.

The Health Ministry is also studying, together with scientific societies and laboratories, other measures to tackle the shortage, including the possibility of setting criteria to prioritise certain patients if necessary.

When will the shortage end?

For now there is no definitive answer. The situation differs from one medicine to another. For some Evopad presentations, Aemps expects new batches in October and a return to normal from November.

The outlook for Lenzetto is more uncertain. Gedeon Richter has informed Aemps that it will distribute new units over the course of November and will gradually resume supply from that month and throughout 2027.

It is precisely this uncertainty that qualifies the forecast passed on by Padilla to Euronews. November may mark the beginning of recovery, but not necessarily the end of the crisis.

World.title: Aegean, Ryanair and Austrian ranked highest in new 10-year European Airline Safety Index
World.content:
Aegean Airlines, Ryanair and Austrian Airlines have been ranked in the top three positions of a new 10-year safety index of 20 major European airlines.

 

Released by AirAdvisor, the 2026 European Airline Safety Index assessed the 10 largest eligible low-cost and 10 largest eligible mainline carriers operating in Europe, based on 2025 flight volumes reported by EUROCONTROL.

Each airline was scored out of 100 across six weighted categories:

40%: safety record, based on accidents published in the IATA Safety Report between 2016 and 2025 inclusive

20%: certification and audit, including audit history and International Civil Aviation Organization (ICAO) data on the effectiveness of national aviation oversight

15%: operational safety systems

10%: fleet age and technical profile

10%: pilot training

5%: financial stability

Scores for operational safety, fleet, training and financial stability were based on publicly available regulatory and company information, AirAdvisor said, adding that the index is “comparative and should not be read as a measure of whether any individual airline is safe or unsafe”.

In the final rankings, Greek flag carrier Aegean scored 89/100 with no qualifying accidents in the 10-year period, ahead of Ryanair (86/100) and Austrian Airlines (85.5/100).

Aegean achieved a perfect 40/40 for its safety record and also scored highly on operational safety (13/15), fleet (9/10) and financial stability (5/5).

A perfect safety record alone “was not enough to reach the top”, said AirAdvisor. “British Airways, SAS and Eurowings also scored 40/40 in that category but finished outside the top five, because the index weighs six factors together.”

Low-cost carriers rank high

Three of the top five airlines in the 10-year safety index were low-cost carriers: Ryanair (second), Norwegian (fourth) and SunExpress (fifth). Across the full study, low-cost airlines averaged a score of 79.2/100, compared with 82.8/100 for mainline carriers – a gap of 3.6 points.

"Many travellers assume that a cheaper ticket means accepting more safety risk, but the data doesn't support this," Anton Radchenko, CEO of AirAdvisor, said to Euronews Travel.

"Low-cost and mainline airlines have very similar accident records, and their safety management systems scored the same on average. In other words, the price of a ticket tells you very little about how safe an airline is.”

Low-cost carriers outranked mainline airlines on their fleet age and technical profile, with the former scoring 7.8/10, while the latter scored 7.1/10. Low-cost carriers tend to have a younger fleet, with Wizz Air and Pegasus scoring 10/10 in this category.

"A young fleet can bring technological and efficiency advantages, but aircraft age should never be treated as a safety rating on its own," Radchenko said in the report. "An older aircraft that is properly maintained can continue operating safely for decades."

World.title: US to lay fresh torture charges against Venezuela's Maduro and wife
World.content:
Prosecutors are considering charges over the alleged torture of more than a dozen Americans detained in Venezuela. Meanwhile, Cilia Flores is seeking release from jail on health grounds.

US prosecutors are expected to bring new charges against ousted Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro and his wife Cilia Flores over the alleged torture of Americans held in Venezuela, a US official said late on Wednesday.

The charges could be announced as soon as Thursday and reportedly concern the alleged wrongful detention of more than a dozen US citizens during Maduro's 13-year rule.

Prosecutors are also considering charges against others allegedly involved in the torture.

Details of the potential new charges and the alleged victims were not immediately available.

Maduro's wife seeks release

Meanwhile, the 69-year-old Flores is due in Manhattan federal court on Thursday where she is expected to ask a judge to release her from jail and place her under house arrest, citing health problems.

Her lawyers say she has lost 25 pounds in custody, suffers from dizziness and shortness of breath and may have suffered a minor heart attack in July.

They have proposed that she live at a New York residence under 24-hour security.

Media reports said prosecutors are also considering charging several other people for their alleged role in torturing Americans [FILE: March 26, 2026] Image: Jane Rosenberg/REUTERS

Prosecutors, however, oppose the request, arguing that Flores poses an "extreme risk of flight and danger to the public” if released.

They said she has received hospital treatment when necessary, while in custody.

Trump vs Maduro

Maduro, 63, and Flores are being held at a federal detention center in Brooklyn as they await their trial in June next year.

The couple was captured during an unprecedented middle-of-the-night raid on their Caracas home on January 3, which was hailed by US President Donald Trump as a "surgical law enforcement operation."

Critics have accused Trump of operating outside international law.

They were subsequently brought to New York, where they face existing drug trafficking and firearms charges.

Maduro has maintained his innocence, calling himself a prisoner of war and referring to his capture as a kidnapping.

Meanwhile, in August, Trump announced that the US had reached a deal to take control of part of Venezuela's vast oil reserves, which Venezuelan Interim President Delcy Rodriguez also termed "historic."

World.title: Germany news: UK's Burnham, Merz to talk security in Berlin
World.content:
Steinmeier and his wife, Elke Büdenbender, arrived in Paris on Wednesday evening Image: Bernd von Jutrczenka/dpa/picture alliance

German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier is to be welcomed by French President Emmanuel Macron on Thursday with military honors at one of the French capital's best-known landmarks, the Arc de Triomphe, at the start of a state visit.

Following the ceremony, the German head of state is to hold talks with Macron at the Elysee Palace, with an ensuing joint press statement.

Steinmeier will then be received for a state banquet at the palace, the official residence of the French president.

On Friday, Steinmeier is to travel with Macron to the southwestern city of Bordeaux, where the two will visit two facilities connected with atomic deterrence.

Before leaving for France, Steinmeier said he saw the trip as a kind of farewell visit to Macron, whom he described as a "committed European and a good friend."

Both men took office in 2017 and both will be stepping down early next year.

However, their roles are very different despite their having the same title: The German president has, in the main, ceremonial duties, while Macron is the head of government and holds executive power.

World.title: Yemen's Houthis claim strike on Riyadh airport, three killed
World.content:
A Houthi missile strike on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport killed three people and disrupted operations, the rebels said, as Yemen's conflict continues to escalate beyond its borders.

Yemen's Houthi rebels say they struck Saudi Arabia's main international airport in the capital, Riyadh, with a missile attack on Thursday.

They said the strike killed three people and injured several others. It was the third time this week that the armed group claimed to have targeted the airport.

"Our armed forces successfully targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with a ballistic missile, which accurately struck its target and disrupted airport operations," Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said on X.

The conflict in Yemen has increasingly spilled across the country's borders since reigniting in July.

A day earlier, the Saudi-backed and internationally recognized Yemeni government announced a major counteroffensive against the Houthis, who are fighting government forces for control of additional territory.

At the same time, the rebels also warned passenger airlines to stop flying through Saudi airspace.

"We reiterate our call and warning, for the last time, to all international airlines against continuing to operate flights through Saudi airspace," Saree said.

Can Yemen's government turn the tide against the Houthis? To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

What is the status of the conflict?

According to the United Nations (UN), the conflict has displaced more than 200,000 people within Yemen.

This week, the Yemeni government claimed to have pushed Houthi fighters out of strategic areas along the Red Sea coast and around the port city of Mocha.

Coalition forces spokesperson Turki al-Maliki said 82 Houthi military targets had been destroyed in the Yemeni provinces of Saada, Marib, Al Jawf, and Al Hudaydah. Al-Maliki did not provide details about casualties or damage, and his claims could not be independently verified.

The targets reportedly included missile launch sites, command centers, and missile and weapons depots.

World.title: Why music in Iran is more than just entertainment
World.content:
Iranian authorities are trying to persuade prominent singers in exile to return home. While the state seeks to harness music as a political tool, music has also become a powerful expression of dissent and resistance.

After spending 47 years abroad, Iranian musician Bijan Mortazavi returned to his homeland at the end of September.

Mortazavi is one of Iran's most renowned violinists, singers, and composers.

In July 2026, he performed with his famous white violin at the closing ceremony of the FIFA World Cup alongside the New York Philharmonic Orchestra.

In the videos that he and his wife have now posted on social media, the couple can be seen taking walks through the city of the Iranian capital, Tehran, while passersby greet the musician warmly and welcome him.

Singer Mohsen Namjoo also recently returned to Iran after about 20 years in exile.

Internationally renowned for his experimental Persian music, he blends traditional Persian singing and poetic lyrics with elements of blues, rock, jazz, and folk.

In 2009, Namjoo was sentenced in absentia by a court in Tehran to five years in prison.

He was accused of insulting holy sites and mocking verses from the Quran, among other things.

In a video posted online after his return to Iran, Namjoo said he had returned to the country to spend more time with his family and friends.

Women are prohibited from singing solo in Ira, but many young female musicians play and sing on the street without headscarves, defying the existing ban Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

Return as a political tool

On August 27, Abbas Salehi, Iran's minister of culture and Islamic guidance, said in an interview with the prominent Iranian media outlet Farhikhtegan that his ministry had compiled a list containing the names of more than 100 distinguished Iranians living abroad.

The goal, he said, was to remove obstacles to their travel or return to Iran.

Salehi stressed that even "critics of the Islamic Republic" could return at any time. He added, however, that the return of artists does not necessarily mean they would perform in Iran. Instead, they could simply visit the country, the minister said.

Sina Yousefi, a human rights lawyer, pointed to international law, specifically Article 12 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which Iran is also a signatory.

According to this provision, no one may be arbitrarily prevented from entering their own country. This right cannot be made contingent on a citizen's level of loyalty to the government, he told DW.

"The idea of seeking out certain well-known figures — who the reformists, in particular, believe are less likely to cross the red lines — and winning them over to collaborate or bringing them back to the country is not new," said Sepideh Raissadat, an ethnomusicologist who has been studying the history and development of Persian music for years.

As an internationally renowned performer of classical Persian music, she combines her artistic work with scholarly research, with her dissertation focusing on the lives of Iranian female singers since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

Iran uprising seen through the eyes of Iranian women To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Between control and resistance

"The 1979 revolution in Iran was a revolution against music. Music was one of the red lines," said Raissadat, referring to statements by the leader of the revolution, Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini, who as early as July 1979 had publicly described music as harmful to society and called for its complete abolition.

In a speech to employees of Radio Darya on July 21, 1979, Khomeini is said to have described music as "a betrayal of the country" and "a betrayal of the youth." A few days later, the Iranian newspaper Keyhan quoted him as saying that music was "like a drug” and must be completely eradicated.

During the Iran-Iraq War from 1980 to 1988, however, music made a comeback in the form of revolutionary and religious songs. It was also used to stir up feelings of national pride and a sense of belonging.

The regime also failed to completely banish the female voice from the public sphere. "They couldn't completely eliminate the voice of women. The female voice returned through choral singing," said Raissadat.

But the conflict between the state and music continued.

For years, musical instruments were not allowed to be shown on Iranian television. Instruments were confiscated or destroyed on the streets. Fearing repercussions, musicians did not carry their instruments in public, while some hid them in their cars.

"Listening to banned music at home was a political act. And when women began to sing, that, too, became a political act," Raissadat noted. The development of Iranian pop music was also part of this political and cultural tension, she underscored. "People began producing new domestic pop music to compete with music from Los Angeles."

Over the past ten years, social media — which is not entirely under government control — has become increasingly important and now wields considerable influence.

This change is particularly evident among young people, with young women now even playing the guitar without headscarves and performing in public.

Iranian singer finds voice in Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Music as an expression of protest

Raissadat observes a particular trend among the families of the young people who were killed during the nationwide mass protests in late December 2025 and January 2026.

The demonstrations began on December 28, 2025, and were violently suppressed by security forces.

Human rights organizations report that thousands of protesters were killed, but the exact figures are unknown due to the extensive information blackout imposed by the regime.

"The most important thing we've seen in recent years has been the use of music by the bereaved families of those killed in the protests. This stands in complete contrast to Shiite tradition and our history," said Raissadat.

At some funerals, families turned the memorial service for their loved ones into a new form of protest.

Instead of religious hymns, music played, and the mourners sang and danced along to it. In doing so, they created a deliberate contrast to traditional religious mourning rituals, the musician said.

"Music became a weapon. Those who were mourning were able to connect with it on their own, and at the same time, it stood in opposition to what the political system stands for," Raissadat pointed out, adding, "Dancing in white clothing also became an expression of this resistance."

This article was originally written in German.

World.title: India news: Opposition doubles down against poll chief after detentions
World.content:
Skip next section Indian workers who built US consulate in Milan agree to record payout

10/08/2026 October 8, 2026 Indian workers who built US consulate in Milan agree to record payout

In all, nearly 480 workers can expect payouts with some 300 still working on the site Image: Luca Bruno/AP Photo/picture alliance

Foreign workers, mostly Indian, building a vast new US consulate compound in Milan, Italy, signed agreements on Wednesday securing payouts averaging tens of thousands of euros each.

The payout is over alleged labor abuses while working for an American construction company.

Over 60 laborers signed the deal to receive their share of a €31 million (nearly $35 million) settlement with Alabama-based Caddell Construction. Prosecutors say this is the largest-ever settlement over labor exploitation in Europe.

The payouts include unpaid overtime, reimbursement for housing illegally deducted from their pay and other hefty damages sought by the prosecutors.

Dilip Ram, a 43-year-old mason from India who worked at the Milan site for over two years, said that the money would go a long way to help his family of five in the Indian state of Bihar.

The settlement is not an admission of liability, the construction company said Image: Antonio Calanni/AP Photo/picture alliance

"Things are better now than before …we get more rest now," Ram said, after signing the deal. "This has led to a lot of change. This settlement will be good. Because the workers had troubles, that’s why this settlement has been applied."

Prosecutors alleged that workers were paid less than $2 (€1.8) an hour, were illegally docked money for housing and denied overtime for working up to 10 hours a day, six days a week. They were reportedly also subjected to threats and not given proper medical care when injured on the job.

While most of the workers were from India, others were from Nigeria, Kenya and Bangladesh.

The Indian workers reported having to pay €5,000 ($5,600) to recruiters to get the jobs. However, the current settlement could not address abuses in India as that is out of its jurisdiction.

World.title: South Sudan's road to elections remains uncertain
World.content:
South Sudan's first general election is set for December 22. Insecurity, political tensions and the failure to begin voter registration have raised doubts over whether a credible poll can be held.

South Sudan has scheduled a general election for December 22, the first since the country gained independence from Sudan in 2011.

But, as preparations lag, political tensions are high and the debate has intensified since President Salva Kiir dissolved the transitional unity government on September 22 to form a caretaker administration.

Denis Logonyi, a journalist based in the capital of South Sudan Juba, said that many in the country, which has seen violent power struggles and political instability, were not only concerned about the logistics of the polls.

Will elections happen in South Sudan? To play this audio please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 audio

"People have different views on these elections," he told DW. "You hear discussions in political circles and on social media, but ordinary people are not talking much about them."

One voter complained that "there has been no voter education, no voter registration, and only a few months remain." Another told DW that while South Sudanese citizens were eager for a credible election process, the country was not adequately prepared.

Food prices are rising, civil servants are not being paid, and displaced people are struggling, they said.

Politicians admit to 'obstacles' but agree to adhere to election timeline

Political parties have until October 22 to present their manifestos and register.

On October 7, South Sudan concluded a two-week Inter-Party Dialogue, in which 39 parties participated, discussing key issues ahead of the election.

Logonyi said that some civil society groups had been left out of the dialogue, which was initiated by President Kiir.

Minister of Cabinet Affairs Martin Elia Lomuro outlined a few of the challenges: "Delayed funding could severely affect civic education and election infrastructure. There is a need for a clear legal framework to govern the participation of the country's administrative areas. The three administrative areas are not clearly reflected in the National Election Act, which is necessary for the election outcomes to be accepted."

He added that "a credible election requires security readiness throughout the entire cycle — including campaign rallies, polling stations, voting, counting, and results transmission. The unified security forces have not yet been fully deployed."

According to Albino Akol Atak, the deputy rapporteur of the Inter-Party Dialogue and minister of humanitarian affairs and disaster management, the parties unanimously agreed to adhere to the election timeline. "The election train has left the station, and it has no reverse gear," he said. "We are trying to smooth the pathway for this train to arrive on December 22, 2026, without obstacles."

Meanwhile, Changkuoth Bichok Reath, the secretary general of the South Sudan Opposition Alliance (SSOA), said he strongly believed "that successfully conducting the election on December 22 requires coordinated, inclusive action from all national institutions, political parties, security actors, civil society, and other stakeholders."

He added that "given the limited time remaining, priority should be placed on resolving outstanding legal issues and ensuring constructive dialogue among political actors. Furthermore, political parties must be funded to meet key requirements, because a lack of funding will only draw us backward."

South Sudan's checkered election history

South Sudan has endured decades of conflict, from long wars that preceded independence to a devastating civil war that erupted just two years after it became a sovereign state.

Power-sharing transitional governments have been in place under fragile peace deals, including the Revitalized Peace Agreement of September 2018. Elections have repeatedly been planned then put off.

South Sudanese President Salva Kiir is set to contest the December election Image: Brian Inganga/AP Photo/picture alliance

Armed opposition groups remain active, and many citizens fear political tensions could trigger renewed violence.

"The absence of [former Vice President] Riek Machar from the political process is a major concern," Logonyi said. "If there is to be an election or a meaningful political dialogue, many believe he has to be part of it."

In 2018, a power-sharing deal that saw Kiir become president and Machar — his long-time rival and main opposition leader — vice president briefly stabilized the country.

However, tensions between the two men persisted and in March 2025, Machar was placed under house arrest. He was later put on trial for offences that include treason and murder.

South Sudan's former vice president, Riek Machar, pictured in court in Juba in September 2025 Image: Peter Louis Gume/AFP

Key conditions for elections not fulfilled yet

"The government has demonstrated that it is keen for the election to happen," said Wambui Njehu Nzigo, an analyst with Control Risks, a global consulting firm. "But there are important processes that have not yet taken place."

The lack of voter registration is among the biggest concerns. "If elections are to take place soon, you would expect there already to be a voter register," Nzigo said. "There is very little time for that to happen."

Security reforms required under the 2018 peace deal have not yet been finished. These include the unification of armed groups to create the conditions for a stable transition.

Analysts have long warned that if these key issues are not addressed the legitimacy of any election would be undermined.

"The elections would be taking place in an environment where there is still active fighting in some parts of the country," Nzigo said. "The fact that the main opposition leader is under house arrest raises questions about whether this will be a true competition."

According to Logonyi, civil society groups are calling for greater dialogue, political inclusion and protections for journalists and activists before the vote is held.

How instability persists in South Sudan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Ongoing flooding could interfere with the vote

Futhermore, South Sudan faces severe flooding, a displacement crisis and food insecurity. This could make it difficult for some citizens to reach polling stations, Nzigo said.

For those displaced by conflict, there's uncertainty over how they can register and cast their ballots.

Floodwaters, oil and health fears in South Sudan To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Experts warn that a vote without broad participation could lead to a disputed outcome and instensify conflict.

Regional organizations such as the African Union and international partners are expected to continue encouraging an inclusive political process.

Analysts argue that the focus should be not only on ensuring elections take place, but also on creating conditions that make them credible.

For many South Sudanese, the choice is clear: elections alone won't guarantee stability.

This article contains material generated by artificial intelligence (AI) from the AfricaLink podcast.

Edited by: Benita van Eyssen

World.title: US: Award-winning Kashmiri filmmaker detained
World.content:
Arfat Sheikh was detained by ICE agents in Washington on September 24, it was confirmed on Wednesday. Officials say he "illegally overstayed his lawful admittance" as US President Trump pursues an immigration clampdown.

A filmmaker whose award-winning work has explored conflict in his native Kashmir has been detained by United States immigration officials on suspicion of residing and working in the country illegally.

Arfat Sheikh was detained by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) after disembarking a flight from California at Washington Dulles International Airport on September 24, according to a statement from friends and relatives who labeled his detention "unlawful" and are calling for his release.

The Department of Homeland Security (DHS), which oversees ICE, confirmed to the Reuters news agency on Wednesday that Sheikh had "legally entered the US on a temporary basis and illegally overstayed his lawful admittance."

Sheikh, 42, entered the US in 2019 on a student visa and enrolled on a graduate course in film studies at Georgia State University, according to the statement from friends and family.

Having applied for asylum in 2020, the statement said he had a ​pending immigration application and was authorized to work and live in the US. It did not mention the ground for asylum.

The DHS said Sheikh would receive due process but that a pending ​application does not confer legal residency status.

ICE arrests up amid Trump immigration crackdown

US President Donald Trump has been pursuing an immigration crackdown and deportation drive that he claims is aimed at improving domestic security.

His administration said in August it was to "identify ⁠and revoke the non-immigrant visas of foreigners who have come to the US claiming to be short-term visitors, but then file for asylum to stay here permanently."

The number of ICE arrests hit record levels this summer, with about 51,000 recorded across August.

Critics say the crackdown has violated due process and ​free speech rights and ​has created an unsafe ⁠environment, particularly for ethnic minorities, who have raised concerns about racial profiling.

ICE targets South Asians for removal from United States To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Sheikh, who hails from India-administered Kashmir, won the Emerging Filmmaker Activist Award at the Teaneck International Film Festival in 2025.

His first feature film, 2024's "Saffron Kingdom," won Best Feature Film at the Chicago Filmmakers Awards, ​the LA Film and Documentary Awards, the Melbourne Independent Film Festival and the ​Wake Forest ⁠Film Festival.

The film explored conflict in Kashmir, a disputed Muslim-majority region claimed by both Hindu-majority India and Islamic Pakistan, which each control only part of it and have fought wars over it.

World.title: IMF reaches tentative $1.21 billion bailout deal with Pakistan
World.content:
Pakistan's dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and regional financing has left the economy exposed to the fallout from the Middle East conflict.

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) has reached a staff-level agreement with Pakistan that could unlock about $1.21 billion (roughly €1 billion) in financing, the lender said on Wednesday , as the South Asian country grapples with spiking food and fuel prices, and high unemployment.

The bailout deal still needs to be approved by the IMF Executive Board.

IMF negotiator Iva Petrova said Pakistan had successfully navigated the impact of the Middle East conflict, with strong policies helping preserve macroeconomic stability.

How does the Middle East conflict impact Pakistan?

Pakistan's economy grew 4% in the first three quarters of fiscal 2026 with full-year growth estimated at 3.6%, the IMF said.

Petrova attributed the weakened momentum to "higher energy prices and supply disruptions."

Inflation eased to about 10.3% in September after peaking in May, while core inflation remained contained, Petrova said.

Pakistan remains dependent on external financing to shore up foreign exchange reserves and meet debt repayments.

A prolonged Middle East conflict makes it particularly vulnerable due to its dependence on Gulf energy imports, remittances and financing from the region, according to S&P Global Market Intelligence economist Ahmad Mobeen earlier this year.

In the recent past, Pakistan has had to turn to the IMF to tackle Islamabad's acute balance-of-payments crisis.
