World.title: Poland detains senior managers from state oil giant Orlen over pre-election fuel price cuts
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland has detained and charged five current and former senior managers at state energy giant Orlen as part of an investigation into allegations that the company artificially lowered fuel prices in the run-up to the 2023 parliamentary election. At the time, many experts and the then-opposition – which won that election and is now in power – accused Orlen of cutting prices to help the then-ruling national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party’s re-election campaign. Prosecutors say that the decisions made by the executives constituted “a gross violation of procedures” and caused “over 4.1 billion zloty” (€938 million) of financial damage to the company. If found guilty, the accused could face up to 25 years in prison. Prokurator przedstawił pięciu menadżerom Orlen S.A. zarzuty wyrządzenia spółce szkody w wysokości ponad 4,1 mld zł w związku z nierynkowym kształtowaniem cen paliw w 2023 r. ⬇️https://t.co/yjiaX0ehHu — Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) October 6, 2026 At the end of August 2023, just over a month before the elections, Orlen, which controls around 60% of Poland’s fuel market, began sharply cutting its wholesale petrol prices as well as the prices at the large network of petrol stations it runs. By early October, the wholesale price of unleaded petrol had fallen by nearly 12.7%, while average prices at petrol stations had dropped by about 10%. The price cuts, however, puzzled experts because oil prices on international markets were rising and the zloty was weakening, both of which would normally push fuel prices higher. The relatively low prices in Poland encouraged some motorists from neighbouring countries to travel to Poland to tank up, while some Polish drivers began stockpiling fuel. Just days after the election, held on 15 October, fuel prices began to rise. State oil firm Orlen's wholesale petrol prices have risen this week after falling in the leadup to Sunday’s elections Some had accused Orlen of artificially lowering prices to help the ruling party’s election campaign and warned they would rise afterwards https://t.co/FLUs1n8EA9 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 19, 2023 Figures from the then-opposition accused Orlen of lowering prices to win popularity for the government ahead of the elections. Under the leadership of its then-CEO, Daniel Obajtek, the company had regularly carried out actions seen as beneficial for the ruling PiS party. Obajtek is now a PiS MEP. In October 2023, Krzysztof Brejza, a lawmaker from the centrist Civic Coalition (KO) – which was then in opposition and is now Poland’s main ruling party – notified prosecutors of a potential crime. He claimed that strategic fuel reserves had been emptied as part of Orlen’s price-cutting move. Now, after a lengthy investigation, prosecutors have announced that five current and former managers have been detained. One, named only as Michał R. under Polish privacy law, served as a member of Orlen’s board from 2018 to 2024. The others are identified as an executive director, two office directors, and the head of a department responsible for pricing. The National Prosecutor’s Office said that all five had been charged with causing large-scale economic damage, which carries a prison sentence of between five and 25 years. “The charges concern abuse of power and failure to fulfil managerial duties, causing damage to Orlen in the amount of over 4.1 billion złoty in connection with the implemented pricing policy,” wrote prosecutors. They said that the main aim of that pricing policy was to keep the price of fuels below the psychological threshold of 6 zloty per litre, and that this was carried out “in a manner detached from market realities…in gross violation of numerous formal and informal procedures applicable to the managerial staff at Orlen”. Prime Minister @donaldtusk says that Poland has been “disgraced in front of the entire world” by a new @FT report on how state energy firm Orlen lost $230 million through a botched effort to buy Venezuelan oil under the former government https://t.co/LlGcgXOvGG — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 15, 2026 Speaking anonymously to broadcaster TVN, one of the prosecutors involved in the case said that the executives’ actions had implications not only for Orlen’s finances, but also Poland’s national security, given that strategic reserves are meant to be saved for emergency situation. “State security was jeopardised for the sake of politics,” they said. “These reserves are intended, at a time of war, to ensure there is fuel for tanks, to put it simply.” Meanwhile, justice minister Waldemar Żurek, who also serves as prosecutor general, wrote on social media that Orlen and Obajtek had, by “manually controlling prices”, “acted to the detriment of national assets in order to save the party’s [grip on] power”. Na polecenie łódzkiego wydziału ds. Jesienią 2023 roku Daniel „wszystko mogę” Obajtek ręcznie… https://t.co/qV9qroeBu0 — Waldemar Żurek (@w_zurek) October 6, 2026 Obajtek today rejected the allegations and defended Orlen’s actions under his leadership. World.title: Poland and Lithuania prepare to evacuate one million Baltic residents to Poland in event of war
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Poland and Lithuania are jointly preparing plans for the evacuation of one million or more residents of the Baltic states into Poland in the event of a war or other major crisis, amid growing concern in the region over potential Russian aggression. On Monday, the two countries’ interior ministers met to discuss the issue following a recent large-scale Lithuanian mobilisation exercise that also involved Polish officials. The pair also addressed their joint response to the migration crisis on the borders orchestrated by Russia’s ally Belarus. “In crisis situations, it is best to cooperate. It is best to prepare such plans through mutual understanding, thus attempting to address potential situations,” said Lithuanian interior minister Martynas Katelynas, speaking alongside his Polish counterpart, Marcin Kierwiński, at the Budzisko-Kalvarija border crossing. “As for this crossing here, this place that connects us with Poland, this plan foresees approximately one million, and perhaps even more, refugees who will be able to be evacuated from our countries in the event of war,” he added. The three Baltic states – Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia – are seen as a primary potential target for Russian aggression. NATO states, including Poland, have in recent months warned of the growing possibility of Moscow conducting some form of “provocation” against the alliance’s eastern members. Lithuania last week finished a major exercise testing its national mobilisation system in the event of war or other crises. For the first time, it included elements relating to cross-border evacuation of civilians from the Baltic states to Poland. Alongside thousands of Lithuanian officials, a 20-person Polish team, led by representatives of the interior ministry, took part in the exercise. This has allowed Poland to develop “an agenda and action plan for what must be adjusted very quickly: cross-border evacuation plans, infrastructure and alternative border crossings in an emergency, as well as reception points”, said Kierwiński, adding that “we will begin intensive work” on implementation. Poland already has extensive recent experience in receiving civilians fleeing conflict. In 2022, it became the primary destination for the millions of refugees fleeing Ukraine following Russia’s full-scale invasion. Poland’s government and civil society quickly implemented measures to support the refugees, almost one million of whom remain in the country. Almost 80% of Poles say they would want Poland to come to the aid of the Baltic states if they were attacked by Russia The poll follows controversy over comments by a senior opposition figure casting doubt as to whether Poland should come to their defence https://t.co/l3dj02ETZ5 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) September 10, 2026 The two ministers also used their meeting to discuss their joint response to illegal migration. Both countries have been the target of a crisis engineered by Russia’s ally Belarus, which has encouraged and assisted tens of thousands of migrants – mainly from Asia and Africa – to try to cross into Poland, Lithuania and Latvia. In response, Poland last year introduced checks on its borders with Lithuania and Germany. Those measures have been repeatedly extended, including last week, when Poland announced that they would remain in force until at least March 2027. “Border controls with Germany and Lithuania allow us to catch people illegally crossing the border from the Baltic states,” said Kierwiński on Monday. “As soon as there are grounds to end these controls, we will discontinue them. But for now, we have decided that they will remain in place for at least another six months.” Poland is reintroducing controls on its borders with Germany and Lithuania to prevent the “uncontrolled flow of migrants”, in particular those returned by Germany after entering illegally "Poland’s patience is running out," says Prime Minister @donaldtusk https://t.co/Pttd3FvpHA — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 1, 2025 Katelynas emphasised that “Lithuania and Poland share a common goal: to ensure the protection of our borders and effectively prevent irregular migrants from moving through our countries and across the Schengen area”. He also noted that an agreement between the two countries on cooperation between police, border guard and customs services is currently being finalised. “Poland and Lithuania are like brothers and sisters who support each other and will continue to do so,” said Katelynas. Kierwiński likewise expressed his satisfaction that the two countries “speak with one voice…because this part of Europe, the eastern flank of NATO and the EU, must speak with one voice to address and counter the threats posed by Russian imperialism and the difficult situation beyond our eastern border”. EU chief @vonderleyen has thanked Poland for defending Europe from “cynical hybrid attacks” during a visit with PM @donaldtusk to the border with Belarus. She emphasised the “urgency” of protecting the EU’s frontier from the “predator” Vladimir Putin https://t.co/O9bhmLha44 — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 31, 2025 Last month, Poland’s prime minister, Donald Tusk, warned that, according to intelligence sources, Russia is planning drone and missile strikes on eastern NATO countries, which it would present as accidental. Poland has already recently suffered airspace violations by Russian drones, a missile and a helicopter. It has also been the primary target for Russian sabotage operations in Europe. In response, the Polish government has moved to expand the network of warning sirens along the Ukrainian border, launched a campaign informing the public how to respond to aerial threats, and started more clearly marking bomb shelters. The Polish-Lithuanian border area, which sits between Belarus and the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad and is known as the Suwałki Gap, is seen as a potential target for Russia in the event of war. Poland and Lithuania held joint military exercises there in 2024 to test their defensive capabilities. World.title: Reports claim Trump tried to change Poland’s government. What do we know?
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Media reports claim that US President Donald Trump, during a previously unreported meeting earlier this year with Poland’s defence minister, Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz, suggested that he leave Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s ruling coalition and form a new government with the right-wing opposition. Kosiniak-Kamysz has confirmed that the meeting took place, but has not commented on what was discussed. Meanwhile, Tusk himself has said that, while he wants to “maintain discretion”, the information he received from Kosiniak-Kamysz indicates that Trump was interested in discussing the “internal situation in Poland”. Foreign minister Radosław Sikorski has even more bluntly suggested that the meeting may have served as “an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics”. Below, we outline how the controversy unfolded, what we know so far, and how senior political figures have commented on the issue. The context Poland’s government is a broad coalition that ranges from left to centre right. Although Tusk’s centrist Civic Platform (KO) dominates, it would not have the parliamentary majority necessary to rule if it lost any of its junior coalition partners. One of those partners is the Polish People’s Party (PSL), which is the most conservative element of the coalition. It has clashed with its partners over issues such as abortion and LGBT+ rights. PSL is led by Kosiniak-Kamysz, who serves as both deputy prime minister and defence minister. Some elements of the right-wing opposition have suggested that PSL could break with Tusk to form an alternative government, perhaps even with Kosiniak-Kamysz as prime minister. Last year, PSL controversially polled its members on whether they would want to do so. However, PSL and its leader have repeatedly insisted that they remain loyal to Tusk’s coalition. The Polish People's Party's parliamentary survival is on a knife edge, and could determine whether @donaldtusk's coalition remains in power after next year's elections.@AleksSzczerbiak looks at the challenges facing PSL and how it may respond to them https://t.co/MmswSLNWJE — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) June 30, 2026 Meanwhile, the government is in constant conflict with President Karol Nawrocki, who is aligned with the opposition. Nawrocki is also a close ally of Trump, who endorsed him during last year’s presidential election. By contrast, Tusk and his government have clashed with the Trump administration, though they also seek to maintain close relations with the US as Poland’s most important security partner. The meeting The news that Kosiniak-Kamysz had met with Trump in March this year came to light in a rather roundabout way. On 21 September, Poland’s defence ministry announced that a planned meeting at the Pentagon between Kosiniak-Kamysz and his US counterpart, Pete Hegseth, planned for 23 September, had been cancelled “at the urgent request of the American side”. The official reason for the change of plans was Chinese President Xi Jinping’s visit to the US at the same time. However, some commentators in Poland claimed that Hegseth had actually cancelled the meeting at the behest of figures close to Nawrocki. In an effort to debunk those claims, Adam Bielan, a senior PiS figure from the opposition Law and Justice (PiS) party, claimed that he and Nikodem Rachoń, a presidential advisor, had helped to arrange a meeting earlier this year between Kosiniak-Kamysz and a US figure “much more important than Hegseth”. Rachoń later confirmed this, but said that the meeting had been secret and he was unable to reveal the identity of the US official. He urged Kosiniak-Kamysz to do so. The defence minister obliged, confirming that the meeting had been with Trump himself and had taken place at the White House on 2 March, alongside a ceremony at which a US army officer, Michael Ollis, was posthumously awarded the Medal of Honour for giving his own life to save that of a Polish officer, Karol Cierpica, in Afghanistan. “I had the opportunity to talk to President Trump for a moment, for which I am very grateful,” said Kosiniak-Kamysz, who noted the role of Nawrocki’s office in arranging the conversation. What did Trump say to Kosiniak-Kamysz? Neither Rachoń nor Kosiniak-Kamysz indicated what had been discussed at the meeting. However, last Friday, Dominika Wielowieyska, a leading Polish journalist, claimed that her conversations with various sources, who she did not name, had indicated that Trump used the meeting to encourage Kosiniak-Kamysz to split with Tusk and form a new government with the right-wing opposition. “Trump suggested to Kosiniak-Kamysz that it would be best if he formed a coalition with the right, and that then they would have 100% support from the United States and the presidential administration, and the door would essentially be open to achieving great success for many Poles,” said Wielowieyska, who writes for Gazeta Wyborcza, a leading liberal daily that is hostile towards Nawrocki and sympathetic towards Tusk. She added that Kosiniak-Kamysz had immediately shared information about the meeting with the government but that Rachoń had failed to submit a note about it to the foreign ministry, despite that being normal practice and despite a request for a note from foreign minister Radosław Sikorski. Today, Republika, a right-wing broadcaster with close ties to Nawrocki and the opposition, likewise reported, based on unnamed sources, that, “during the conversation with Kosiniak-Kamysz, there were indications that the Americans were interested in a change of prime minister in Poland”. What has Poland’s government said? On Friday, Sikorski took to social media to respond to a claim by Bielan that the Trump-Kosiniak-Kamysz meeting was intended to “unblock” negotiations regarding Poland’s desire to host a new permanent US military base. “In the case of such an important conversation, the organiser [Rachoń] had an obligation to prepare a note,” wrote Sikorski, adding that such a document never reached the foreign ministry. “Could that be because the meeting also served as an attempt to involve a foreign state in our internal politics?” Z tak ważnej rozmowy organizator miał obowiązek sporządzić notatkę. Do @MSZ_RP ona nie dotarła. Czyżby dlatego, że spotkanie służyło też próbie zaangażowania obcego państwa w naszą wewnętrzną politykę? https://t.co/0wL0QZBxPv — Radosław Sikorski 🇵🇱🇪🇺 (@sikorskiradek) October 2, 2026 On Monday, Tusk himself told broadcaster TVN that Kosiniak-Kamysz had informed him about his meeting with Trump immediately after it took place. He added that the subject of the meeting “is too interesting to talk about publicly”, but that military “bases were not the topic of the conversation”. “The conversation was of a confidential nature, and therefore I feel obliged to maintain discretion. It was more about the internal situation in Poland, that’s how I would put it most delicately,” said Tusk. Kosiniak-Kamysz himself also confirmed on Monday that the question of a permanent US base in Poland had not been discussed at the meeting. He noted that, in March, that issue was not even seriously on the table, because it was only two months later that Trump announced he intended to send additional troops to Poland The defence minister did not give any further details about the content of the meeting, which he described as “informal”. World.title: Thousands of protesters trap Polish bishop in church amid anger over dismissal of local priest
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. Thousands of protesters blockaded a bishop inside a church in a Polish village on Sunday – and some even physically attacked him – amid anger over the dismissal of a popular long-serving local Catholic priest. As a result, police were called in and, after efforts by negotiators to calm the crowd failed, officers escorted the bishop away from the premises after midnight. „Kościół w Grojcu otoczyło kilka tysięcy osób, parafian i uczęszczających do grojeckiej świątyni. #Aktualnie Okrzyki „jesteśmy z Tobą” dla księdza Józefa Zborka." Materiał od @FaktyOswiecim pic.twitter.com/3zaqlBCDF6 — Sebastian Kościelnik (@S_Koscielnik) October 4, 2026 The incident took place in the village of Grojec, near the city of Oświęcim in southern Poland. The municipality has an official population of around 3,200, but local media – including the Gazeta Krakowska newspaper and Fakty Oświęcim website – report that around 3,000 people gathered on Sunday evening to protest. They were angered by the decision to remove local priest Józef Zborek, who has served in the parish for almost 30 years, from his position. The diocese of Bielsko-Żywiec says the priest was found in church proceedings to have been guilty of “serious and proven irregularities in the performance of his duties”. However, the actual nature of his offences has not been publicly revealed, with the church noting that, under canon law, only Zborek himself can do so. The case against him was initially reported in 2024. The priest repeatedly appealed against the decision, taking the case to the Vatican. However, the decision to remove him was upheld, with Zborek removed from his position on Saturday. On Sunday, Roman Pindel, the bishop of Bielsko-Żywiec, visited Grojec to meet with the parish council and discuss the situation. Afterwards, he proceeded to the local church to attend the Eucharist. However, before his arrival, thousands of people had gathered around the church, holding signs saying “Don’t take away our parish priest”. Some burst inside and disrupted the ceremony. Asked about the reasons for Zborek’s popularity, one woman told Gazeta Krakowska that he had accepted children who had been turned away by other priests for first communion and had “no problem baptising illegitimate children”. News website Onet reports that one local theory is that the priest was removed from his position because he had not charged parishioners for sacraments. Churches in Poland generally expect people to make payments in return for sacraments such as baptism, confirmation and marriage. 🔴Sceny pod kościołem. Biskup w eskorcie policji. Jest nagranie Nocna interwencja policji przed kościołem w Grojcu w Małopolsce. Biskup bielsko-żywiecki Roman Pindel wraz z towarzyszącymi mu księżmi został wyprowadzony ze świątyni pod eskortą funkcjonariuszy. Wszystko po… pic.twitter.com/XEXU3LOMXm — Wirtualna Polska (@wirtualnapolska) October 5, 2026 After the church service had been disrupted, Pindel and several other priests retreated to the sacristy. Social media videos show protesters shouting angrily at the bishop. Some even physically assailed him and had to be pulled away. Once inside, the bishop faced continued verbal aggression. Shortly afterwards, the police arrived, including specialist negotiators. Pindel spoke to the crowd, explaining that the decision to dismiss Zborek had been confirmed by the Vatican and was final. The bishop reiterated that only Zborek himself was authorised to disclose the reasons for his dismissal. But, with a large, angry crowd still gathered outside and blocking all exits, the bishop was evacuated under the protection of officers at around 1 a.m. Hundreds of people have protested in Kraków’s Kazimierz district against plans to evict residents and businesses – including some of the area's famous bars and galleries – from historic church-owned buildings that will be redeveloped into a luxury hotel https://t.co/Xo3SmkWc9g — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 24, 2026 Subsequently, the Bielsko-Żywiec diocese issued a statement saying that the “aggressive crowd” had “threatened the health and lives of the priests”. It also noted that Zborek had been dismissed after a full canon law process in which he had been able to defend himself and appeal. “We know that many people, especially his parishioners, are experiencing this pain,” they wrote. “However, we ask that you accept this decision in a spirit of faith and in unity with the church.” Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. World.title: Poland updates nuclear strategy with delays to launch of first two plants
World.content: Keep our news free from ads and paywalls by making a donation to support our work! Notes from Poland is run by a small editorial team and is published by an independent, non-profit foundation that is funded through donations from our readers. We cannot do what we do without your support. The government has updated Poland’s nuclear strategy for the first time in six years, with the new document acknowledging that the country’s first-ever nuclear plant will go online in 2036, three years later than previously planned, and the second in 2040, one year behind schedule. The delays were widely anticipated, as Poland is already behind the schedule set out in the previous nuclear programme, adopted under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government in 2020. However, the current administration says the country is still on track for nuclear to become a major part of a more diversified energy mix, providing around 15-16% of electricity generation by 2040. “This is not just a plan to develop new capacity, but also to build a strong Polish nuclear industry,” energy minister Miłosz Motyka wrote on social media. “We are building a nuclear sector that will drive the Polish economy and serve our security for decades to come.” Rząd przyjął aktualizację Programu polskiej energetyki jądrowej 🇵🇱 To nie tylko plan rozwoju nowych mocy, ale także budowy silnego polskiego przemysłu jądrowego ⚡️ ✅ W sumie do 9 GWe nowych mocy jądrowych; ✅ coraz większy udział polskich firm – docelowo nawet 70 proc. przy… pic.twitter.com/8DorRLUWUj — Miłosz Motyka (@motykamilosz) September 29, 2026 Under the updated Polish Nuclear Power Programme (PPEJ), Poland plans to develop two nuclear power plants with a combined capacity of around 6 GW to 9 GW, using large-scale Generation III+ reactors. The first plant, which will have a total capacity of about 3.75 GW, is being built in partnership with an American consortium made up of Westinghouse and Bechtel in the municipality of Choczewo on the Baltic coast. Preparatory work at the site is already underway. The European Commission last year approved Polish state aid for the project, which is set to receive 60.2 billion zloty (€13.8 billion) in public support between 2025 and 2030 In March 2026, the investor submitted an application to the president of the National Atomic Energy Agency for a permit to construct the plant, with the pouring of the first nuclear concrete scheduled for 2028. The first reactor is now expected to enter commercial operation in 2036, three years later than previously planned. Construction of Poland’s first nuclear power plant is now set to begin after the @EU_Commission approved Warsaw’s request to allocate 60 billion zloty (€14.2 billion) in state aid for the project https://t.co/Z7BJpRRKnq — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) December 9, 2025 Plans are already underway for a second nuclear power plant, with construction scheduled to begin in 2032 and the first unit expected to come online around 2040, one year later than previously planned. Bełchatów and Konin in central Poland remain the preferred locations for that plant, with both areas offering existing energy infrastructure and extensive experience in electricity generation. Companies from the United States, France and Canada are currently competing to supply the technology and build it, with Poland to choose its partner next year. Alongside expanding nuclear capacity, the programme aims to increase the role of Polish companies in the sector. Domestic firms are expected to account for about 40% of the value of the first reactor project, according to the government. That share could rise to as much as 70% for subsequent units as Polish companies build up expertise, experience and the necessary certifications. The government also plans to develop the broader skills base needed to support the nuclear industry, involving universities, research institutes, technical schools and businesses. A group of prominent Polish businesspeople – including @RBrzoska of @InPostPL and @mati Staniszewski of @ElevenLabs – are investing in a project to develop small modular nuclear reactors being led by Poland's richest man, Michał Sołowow https://t.co/NFoCh9JmYz — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 1, 2026 The expansion of nuclear power is part of a broader effort to reduce Poland’s traditional reliance on coal, which currently generates around half of the country’s electricity. That is by far the highest figure in the EU. Poland has already been diversifying its energy mix. Coal has declined from supplying 87% of power a decade ago. Meanwhile, the share of renewables has risen from 9% to 29% over the same period. Under a national energy and climate plan approved in June, Poland aims by 2040 for coal to account for only 0-5% of the energy mix. Around 15-16% will come from nuclear, 7-8% from gas, with most of the rest from renewables: onshore wind (22-27%), offshore wind (18-21%) and solar (14-18%). Poland’s first offshore wind farm has begun to deliver electricity, with Prime Minister @donaldtusk celebrating the development as a "key element of our energy security and sovereignty". The government wants 20% of power to come from offshore wind by 2040 https://t.co/EodvInFmrn — Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 10, 2026 As well as traditional large-scale nuclear power plants, Poland is also pursuing small modular reactor (SMR) projects. SMRs, which are prefabricated in factories before being installed onsite, are much smaller than traditional reactors, and proponents say they provide a faster and more cost-effective way of adding nuclear capacity. World.title: Prague 7 Turns Streets Into Outdoor Art With Designs by Local Children
World.content:
Prague 7 has transformed several streets around local schools with large-scale colorful paintings created with the help of local schoolchildren.

The new artwork can be seen on Rajská, Plynární, Jablonského and Antonínská streets, as well as part of Bubenská Street. The municipality placed the designs mainly near schools and along busy pedestrian routes.



On Antonínská Street, students from grades five through eight at Strossmayerovo Square Elementary School helped create the artwork. They produced the original drawings, which artist Jakub Karlík then combined into the final design.

Several other educational institutions are located close to the painted streets, including Bratrská Elementary School, the Holešovice Business Academy, the Higher Vocational School of Fashion Design and the Secondary Industrial School of Fashion Design.

The new designs have received mostly positive reactions from local residents. Comments on Prague 7’s Facebook page described the streets as more cheerful and said the artwork had made the area more interesting.

There has also been criticism, particularly over the cost and the practical impact of painting the asphalt. Some residents questioned whether the project was necessary and raised concerns about the roughness of the surface, pedestrian movement and whether the paint could become slippery.

Prague 7 said anti-slip paint was used, similar to materials applied to cycle paths and sports surfaces.

The project cost 755,000 CZK, covering the designs, preparation, materials and application. According to Prague 7 spokesperson Martin Vokuš, each of the two phases took around 20 days.

The municipality awarded the contract directly to Karlík. Before selecting his proposal for the Antonínská and Bubenská sections, Prague 7 compared three offers and chose his as the most advantageous.

World.title: Beer Consumption in Czech Republic Falls to Lowest Level on Record
World.content:
Czech beer consumption fell to its lowest level on record in 2025, with the average resident drinking 121 liters during the year, according to data from the Czech Association of Breweries and Malt Houses (ČSPS).

Total domestic consumption reached 14.86 million hectoliters, down 3.2% from 2024. The figure is the lowest recorded since nationwide beer consumption statistics began.

Overall beer production in the Czech Republic also declined last year. Breweries produced 19.96 million hectoliters of alcoholic and non-alcoholic beer, 4.3% less than in 2024.



The decline affected nearly every category, with non-alcoholic beer the main exception. Production of non-alcoholic and flavored non-alcoholic beer increased by 4% to 1.68 million hectoliters.

Demand for non-alcoholic beer has been rising steadily for more than a decade. Between 2019 and 2024 alone, production increased by around 50%.

Pubs lose ground as more Czechs drink at home

The shift in drinking habits is particularly visible in restaurants and pubs. Draft beer accounted for 28% of beer sold on the Czech market in 2025, down one percentage point from the previous year.

The longer-term decline is more significant. Draft beer represented 35% of sales in 2019 and 51% in 2008.

The ČSPS said the figures reflect changes in consumer behavior, including greater interest in moderation and healthier lifestyles. When Czechs do go out for beer, they are increasingly looking for quality and variety rather than simply drinking larger quantities.

Czech beer exports also decline

Exports followed the domestic market downward. Czech breweries exported 5.48 million hectoliters of beer in 2025, an 8.2% decrease compared with the previous year.

European Union countries accounted for around 90% of Czech beer exports, with Germany and Slovakia among the largest buyers.

Imports also declined, falling by 18.3% year on year. Foreign beer accounted for only 2.5% of total beer consumption in the Czech Republic, down 0.5 percentage points from 2024.

World.title: Nearly Half of Czechs Spend More Than 30% of Their Income on Housing
World.content:
Nearly half of people in the Czech Republic spend more than 30% of their net income on housing, while around one in 10 spends more than half.

Housing is generally considered financially burdensome when rent, utilities and other related costs exceed 30–40% of household income. The EU average is around 24%.



The findings come from a survey by Česká spořitelna and Evropa v datech, conducted with Ipsos among 1,000 respondents in February.

Housing affordability remains particularly difficult for young Czechs. Among people aged 18 to 29, 58% live with their parents at least part of the time, while 29% live with friends or a partner.

The survey found that 60% of people under 30 who are dissatisfied with their housing situation have postponed a major life decision because of it. For around one-third, this has happened repeatedly. Starting a family is among the decisions affected by housing conditions.

Homeowners were considerably more likely to be very satisfied than renters, with 41% of owners describing themselves as very satisfied compared with 18% of renters.

Czechia still has the least affordable housing in the EU

The Czech Republic improved by six places in this year’s housing conditions ranking, reaching 17th among the 27 EU member states. The improvement was linked to increased investment in residential construction, fewer households facing excessive housing costs or difficulties paying for heating, and relatively favorable rental conditions.

Buying a home, however, remains more difficult than elsewhere in the EU.

An average-sized Czech apartment costs 13.3 average annual gross salaries, compared with 13.6 a year earlier. The figure has improved only slightly, while other countries have made faster progress. In Hungary, the ratio fell from 13.6 to 11.9 annual salaries, while Slovakia improved from 13.2 to 11.7 and Slovenia from 13.4 to 11.4.

Ireland has the most affordable housing by this measure, with an average home costing 6.2 annual salaries, followed by Belgium and Finland.

An average apartment in Czechia costs roughly the equivalent of 29 years of average rent. In city centers, the figure is close to 31 years, compared with less than 13 years in Ireland.

High housing costs are changing household decisions

Housing expenses are also forcing some households to reduce other spending. Last year, 40% cut their budgets because of housing costs. Nearly one-quarter reduced spending on holidays, hobbies and entertainment, while 16% cut spending on essentials such as food, clothing and personal-care products.

Around 38% of Czechs see living with parents as an economic necessity caused by high property prices. Another 26% consider it a reasonable temporary solution, while 9.4% see multigenerational living as a viable long-term model.

At the same time, 46% of young people expect to inherit property from their families.

World.title: Famous Dancing House Photo Spot in Prague Is Set for a Major Makeover
World.content:
Jiráskovo Square in Prague is set for a major redesign that will change one of the city’s best-known photo spots near the Dancing House.

The project, estimated to cost around CZK 35 million, will replace part of the damaged lawn with paving, restore a historic fountain and move the monument to writer Alois Jirásek.



The Prague 2 district plans to carry out the transformation over the next two years. The redesign is based on a 2022 study prepared by archiF studio.

The square’s lawn has long been a problem. Its location directly opposite the Dancing House makes it a popular stopping point for tourists, many of whom step onto the grass to take photographs with the distinctive building in the background.

One of the most common poses involves visitors appearing to support the Dancing House with their foot or kick it. The repeated foot traffic has left the grass heavily damaged, despite attempts to restore it.

Under the new plans, part of the lawn will be replaced with a paved surface. This will create a more durable area for visitors to take photographs while reducing pressure on the remaining greenery.

Historic fountain to return to operation

The redesign will also restore the Cubist fountain created by architect Vlastislav Hofman. The area around the fountain will be repaved, while the fountain itself will be returned to its original appearance and function.

Water is expected to flow through the fountain again after decades.

Architect Soňa Formanová, one of the project’s authors, said the team was able to locate Hofman’s original documentation, including plans covering the fountain and the approaches to the nearby bridge.

The project will also introduce a raised edge around the lawn that can be used for seating. New flowerbeds and trees are planned for the northern part of the square, while existing shrubs considered unsuitable for the area will be removed.

The monument to Alois Jirásek, the Czech writer after whom the square is named, will be relocated to the center of the small park.

World.title: Queer Arts Festival PINKBUS Returns With New Performances and International Guests
World.content:
The PINKBUS Festival will return to Prague on November 3-14 with several days of theatre, dance, drag, music, visual art and performance.

This year’s edition, titled Forward March!, will focus on the need to keep moving forward amid an uncertain social and political climate.

Organised by the PINKBUS queer arts platform, the festival aims to create a space for artists and audiences to meet, experiment and share experiences. The programme combines established artists with new projects and will also mark the beginning of a new season for the platform.



One of the highlights of this year’s festival will be the premiere of two original works developed through the PINKBUS open call First Ride.

Richard Eliáš, an Academy of Arts, Architecture and Design in Prague (AVU) student, will present the interdisciplinary drag fantasy I Guess It’s Kind of My Fault, or What?. The second project, by the performative art collective Izbová teplota & Alejandra, is Štúrovci Went to Devín and Had Some Fun, offering a new and unconventional take on the group of Slovak national revival figures known as the Štúrovci.

The festival will also feature international guests. French artists Nicolas Poggi and Giselle Hauscarriaga will present SUDOR (Sweat), a Czech premiere performed with a local cast. The post-performative work explores physical exhaustion, sweat and the limits of the body.

Another premiere, Lipsync Her Name… Because It’s Precious, is being created in collaboration with the Italian festival RAINBOW.IT and Slovak organisation DRAMA QUEER. The performance focuses on three figures from European LGBTQIA+ history: Lucy Salani, Romina Cecconi and Ota Tasinata.

Directed by Tomáš “Grófka” Procházka, the production combines three monodramatic sketches exploring identity and the determination to remain true to oneself. The cast includes Italian actor Antonello Foddis and his drag alter ego La Trave Nell’Okkio, as well as Czech performer Venice, also known as Martin Talaga.

The programme will also include the PINKPANEL discussion series. This year’s edition, titled (The Tinsmith’s) Hammer Against Queerness, will examine the potential impact of current cultural policy on LGBTQIA+ artistic production and discuss possible forms of resistance.

The festival will conclude with a special BEST OF edition of the PINKBUS variety show, featuring Venice, Just Karen, La Cuntessa, Tonic Garbáge, Helena Araujo and other performers, alongside special guests.

World.title: Roger Waters Brings New Pink Floyd Show to Prague in June 2027
World.content:
Roger Waters will bring a new Pink Floyd concert production to Prague next year, with LEGACY – A Pink Floyd Show scheduled for June 8, 2027, at O2 universum.

The new production has been created under Waters’ direction and will feature a ten-piece band led by his son, Harry Waters. The Prague show will focus on music from what is widely regarded as Pink Floyd’s most influential period, spanning 1971 to 1979.



The setlist will draw from four of the band’s best-known albums: The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

The music will be accompanied by a new visual production featuring high-resolution LED screens and imagery inspired by Pink Floyd’s original artwork and stage concepts.

Harry Waters will serve as the show’s musical director, performing on Hammond B3 organ and piano while also contributing vocals. He has a long history with the band’s music and spent more than 15 years performing alongside his father on major tours, including The Dark Side of the Moon and The Wall.

His connection to Pink Floyd goes back even further. As a child, Harry’s voice appeared on “Goodbye Blue Sky” from The Wall. He also saw the original The Wall concert production at a young age.

The band includes drummer Graham Broad, guitarist Edo Scordo, bassist and backing vocalist Dahniel Knight, saxophonist and multi-instrumentalist Ryan Saranich, keyboardist Matt Riddle, lead vocalist Clifton David Broadbridge and backing vocalists Eva Avila and Genevieve Little.

Roger Waters co-founded Pink Floyd in 1965 and became the band’s principal lyricist and conceptual leader following Syd Barrett’s departure. He played a central role in the creation of albums including The Dark Side of the Moon, Wish You Were Here, Animals and The Wall.

Ticket prices start at 1,600 CZK

Live Nation Club and O2 presale starts October 8, 2026, at 10:00 AM

Tickets on sale via Ticketmaster and Ticketportal starting October 9, 2026, at 10:00 AM

World.title: GALLERY: Vltava Philharmonic Reveals Its Interiors for the First Time
World.content:
Prague’s planned Vltava Philharmonic has offered the first detailed look inside the building, releasing visualizations of its main foyer and the spaces serving its three principal concert halls.

The interior design will combine wood, glass and stone, with flowing shapes inspired by the Vltava River and the building’s distinctive sloping roof. The plans also emphasize open public spaces designed to connect the concert halls with the rest of the building.



The main foyer will be dominated by a large glass wall extending across several floors. Its curved geometry is intended to echo the movement of the Vltava and will separate the open foyer from other areas of the building.

Light-colored solid wood panels will cover the ceilings, following the contours of the roof above. Stone elements will be used in areas connecting the public foyer with the foyer of the main concert hall, including spaces designed for both seating and standing around bar counters.

´

The project has become significantly more expensive

The cost of the Vltava Philharmonic has increased sharply since the project was first estimated.

In 2021, the projected construction cost was CZK 6.1 billion. After the Danish architecture studio Bjarke Ingels Group (BIG) won the international competition in 2022, the estimate rose to CZK 9.4 billion.

A more detailed architectural study completed in 2024 put the figure at CZK 11.65 billion. The latest estimate is CZK 11.98 billion for the building itself.

Once improvements to the surrounding area are included, the overall project is expected to cost almost CZK 17 billion.

Construction could begin in 2028

The city expects to obtain the permit in the first quarter of 2027. A general contractor would then be selected, with construction currently scheduled to start in the first quarter of 2028.

Trial operations are planned to begin in 2033.

The Vltava Philharmonic will occupy three underground and six above-ground floors. In addition to five concert halls, the complex will include facilities for the Czech Philharmonic and the Prague Symphony Orchestra (FOK), a music department operated by the Municipal Library of Prague, a creative hub, a restaurant and publicly accessible terraces.

The building is being designed by Bjarke Ingels Group, whose proposal was selected in the international architectural competition in 2022.

World.title: Up to 80 Startups to Pitch Investors at Prague’s Engaged Investments Conference
World.content:
The international Engaged Investments conference, taking place on October 21 and 22, 2026, is significantly expanding its scope this year.

The event, which brings hundreds of startup investors from all over Europe to Prague, is now fully opening its doors to tech founders and the broader innovation ecosystem.



Alongside the main program, the two-day event will feature two specialized industry tracks focusing on fintech and defense, pitches from up to 80 startups, and an extended accompanying program.

Real defense instead of geopolitical theories

The defense track is being organized in collaboration with the Invest in Bravery initiative, which is deeply involved in the Ukrainian ecosystem, alongside the European EUDIS Matchmaking program for defense and Cassini Matchmaking for space technologies.

A special guest will be Senior Lieutenant Mykyta Puz, Defense Industry Liaison Officer of the Azov Brigade of the National Guard of Ukraine. He previously worked in business and AI product management before volunteering for the front lines in 2024.

He will shed light on what a modern army truly and urgently needs from the defense industry. Alongside him, speakers will include Erin Hallock, Managing Partner of the NATO Innovation Fund, a representative of the renowned Ukrainian fund Brave1, and others.

Fintech that solves business, not theory

The UnBundled Fintech track, which will run throughout the second day of the conference, is being prepared by The FinTechers in collaboration with Mastercard. The goal is to connect the traditional banking sector with technology companies and investors. The program will focus on stablecoins and tokenization, operational resilience of banks, liability for fraudulent payments, and the deployment of artificial intelligence in financial services.

In addition to new technologies, it will address what European companies need to grow into global players without relying on American capital and infrastructure.

Speakers will include Michal Vodrážka, Director of the Payment Systems Regulation Division at the Czech National Bank. In a debate with Jiří Raška, Chief Technology Officer of Partners Banka, he’ll raise the question of who takes the hit when a payment ends up in a fraudster’s hands. It’s a timely topic, with mandatory payee verification coming in 2027.

The block dedicated to stablecoins and new financial infrastructure will be opened by Dorothea Ysenburg, Vice President of Global Partnerships for Digital Assets and Blockchain at Mastercard. Maryna Muntian from J.P. Morgan will also present, discussing why Central European banks and investors still lack mutual trust when looking at the same deals.

A place where startups find real investors

Closing investments is one of the core components of the conference, which last year attracted investors from more than 20 countries. Up to 80 selected startups, ranging from early-stage to Series A, will have the opportunity to pitch their companies in three minutes to investors actively investing in their respective segments. This year will introduce new dedicated pitching blocks for startups in the fields of financial technology, defense, and space.

On October 22, the best fintech projects from the two-day “Coding the Future of Finance” hackathon—organized on October 19 and 20 by The FinTechers together with Deloitte, AWS, and other partners—will also be presented to investors.

World.title: Pneumonic plague fears grip Russia after lab worker dies, quarantine measures imposed
World.content:
Local authorities in Russia’s Siberian region of Irkutsk have imposed quarantine measures on people and several hospital departments amid reports of a possible “plague” outbreak.

Russia’s consumer and health watchdog, Rospotrebnadzor, said an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East was diagnosed with “pneumonia of unknown etiology.” The employee died from her illness, according to numerous media reports and official statements, while authorities placed those who had contact with her under medical observation.

Rospotrebnadzor later said the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region was “calm.” The developments, however, have raised concerns and public health fears on social media.

Here is what is known about the reported outbreak, according to Anadolu Agency.

Reported outbreak

On Friday, Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev said that he convened an extraordinary meeting of the regional sanitary and anti-epidemic commission following reports of a suspected “highly dangerous infectious disease” in a local resident.

Kobzev said Rospotrebnadzor organized and was implementing a comprehensive set of anti-epidemic measures, adding that the watchdog and regional government were closely monitoring the situation.

“I would like to inform you that all identified contacts have been placed under medical observation. As of today, none of the contacts show any signs of illness, and laboratory test results have come back negative,” Kobzev said.

Maxim Modin, mayor of Irkutsk’s Shelekhovsky district, said the same day that several departments of the district hospital in Shelekhov suspended patient discharges and admissions.

Alexey Tsydenov, head of the neighboring Russian Republic of Buryatia, said the woman who died in Irkutsk “possibly from the plague” had not visited his region. Tsydenov said there were no “plague” outbreaks in Buryatia, including in areas bordering Mongolia.

Two days later, Rospotrebnadzor said no emergencies had been reported while working with pathogenic microorganisms at the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Institute. It said the sanitary and epidemiological situation in the Irkutsk region and the cities of Irkutsk and Shelekhov was “stable.”

The watchdog added that no cases of infectious disease had been reported among employees of the institute over the previous 10 days. Rospotrebnadzor said Monday that the sanitary and epidemiological situation in Irkutsk was “calm.”

Media attention intensified after local outlet People of Baikal on Friday reported that the institute employee, identified as 28-year-old Darya Shipilova, allegedly broke a test tube containing “pneumonic plague.”

The outlet reported that she became ill after allegedly breaking the test tube late last month and was hospitalized in Shelekhov, where she died Friday evening.

High-level reactions

Several high-level officials have commented on the situation, urging people to rely on official assessments from relevant authorities. “Rospotrebnadzor is the lead agency with competence in this area,” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told a news conference in Moscow on Monday.

“It is precisely Rospotrebnadzor’s official statements that should be heeded, rather than listening to various rumors or speculations,” Peskov said. He added that the watchdog employs top-tier professionals in the field and again urged people to “heed their official statements.”

US President Donald Trump said Monday that Washington was closely monitoring the reported case of “pneumonic plague” in Russia and pledged assistance. “Years ago you could treat pneumonia easier, and the microbes and the germs have gotten stronger,” Trump told reporters at the White House before departing for a campaign rally in Nebraska.

“But we’ll help them. We’ll help them,” he added.

Responding to Trump’s comments, Peskov said it is “always good when mutual assistance is offered.”

The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention said Tuesday that it was closely monitoring reports of a “suspected case of pneumonic plague” in Russia that resulted in one death. US Secretary of State Marco Rubio urged Russia the same day to provide full transparency and share detailed information about the incident with the international community.

The World Health Organization told Russian state news agency Tass that it was maintaining contact with local health authorities over the incident. The WHO said that, based on “available unofficial information,” it assessed the public health risk in the region as low.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

What is plague?

While the exact cause of the reported illness remains unclear, official statements have raised questions about plague. Plague is an infectious illness caused by the Yersinia pestis bacterium, which spreads through small wild mammals and their fleas, according to the WHO.

The WHO said bubonic plague is the most common form, while pneumonic and septicemic forms are invariably fatal unless treated early. According to the WHO, pneumonic plague is the most virulent form, with an incubation period potentially as short as 24 hours.

Plague was historically responsible for the “Black Death,” a pandemic in Europe in the 14th century that resulted in more than 50 million deaths, according to the WHO.

World.title: Hungarian transport minister announces Budapest’s long-delayed Student City project restart
World.content:
Hungary’s Transport and Investment Minister Dávid Vitézy has announced the restart of Budapest’s long-delayed Student City (Diákváros) project, which aims to create new student accommodation and affordable housing in the capital.

Vitézy said the decision was made at a meeting of the re-established Budapest Public Development Council, with EU funding set to contribute to the project. The development has been stalled for years due to the former government’s plans to build a Chinese Fudan University campus on the same site.

Student City project to be revived after years of delay

Budapest has long struggled with a shortage of university accommodation, while the city’s housing crisis has made finding affordable housing particularly difficult for students. According to Vitézy, the Student City project could help address both problems while making higher education more accessible.

The minister said final plans supported by the capital and the affected districts had already been prepared before the project was put on hold.

“The goal is to give the brownfield site in Ferencváros new, valuable functions: we will create new student accommodation places with affordable housing in a liveable urban environment that is easy to reach,” Vitézy said.

He added that the next step would be to further develop the existing plans, with more details to be discussed by the Budapest Public Development Council.

Fudan plans put the project on hold

The Student City project was originally intended to provide a major expansion of student accommodation in the capital. However, the previous Fidesz government put the development on hold as plans emerged for a campus of China’s Fudan University on the site.

The proposed Fudan campus became a major political issue in Budapest, with the project facing strong opposition from the city leadership.

Former Budapest mayoral candidate and former Fidesz group leader Alexandra Szentkirályi announced in autumn 2024 that the Student City would nevertheless be built, presenting the project as a response to the capital’s housing crisis.

The original Snøhetta plan for the project. Photo: Karácsony Gergely

Earlier plans envisaged around 12,000 places at the Student City.

Mayor Gergely Karácsony had also repeatedly called for the project to be built. In 2021, he even warned that Budapest could refuse to host the 2023 World Athletics Championships if the government did not proceed with the Student City.

Budapest ultimately hosted the championships, but the Student City project did not materialise.

If you missed it: Good news for homebuyers and students: vast student city and residential district could rise on Budapest’s derelict waterfront

Site is now back in state ownership

Under the previous government, the state expropriated the land needed for the development. The Ferencváros local council had been set to receive HUF 3.5 billion in compensation for the property.

Vitézy said the site has now returned to state ownership, meaning the conditions are in place for the long-awaited project to move forward. He also said funding would be provided from EU resources brought back to Hungary.

The government now plans to revise and develop the existing plans before moving ahead with the project, which could eventually provide thousands of students with more affordable accommodation in Budapest.

World.title: PM Magyar questioned over 2024 phone incident after Parliament lifts immunity
World.content:
Hungarian Prime Minister Péter Magyar has been questioned by the Central Investigating Chief Prosecutor’s Office over a 2024 incident in which he is accused of taking a man’s mobile phone and throwing it into the Danube.

Magyar said on Wednesday evening that he had been questioned at a pre-arranged time and had given a brief statement, but did not admit to the offence he is accused of committing.

“I was questioned this evening, at a pre-arranged time, by the Central Investigating Chief Prosecutor’s Office regarding what happened on 21 June 2024. I gave a brief statement and did not admit to the crime I am accused of. I will provide information on all further developments,” Magyar wrote on Facebook.

He added a brief comment underneath his post: “Back to work.”

Magyar questioned after immunity was lifted

The questioning comes shortly after Parliament suspended Magyar’s parliamentary immunity on 28 September in an extraordinary session. The immunity suspension was requested by Deputy Chief Prosecutor István Lajtár in connection with a suspected theft case.

Magyar had previously asked Parliament to lift his immunity himself.

The same parliamentary vote also concerned Fidesz MP Balázs Hankó and KDNP MP Miklós Seszták, whose immunity was also suspended.

What happened at the Budapest nightclub?

The case dates back to the early hours of 21 June 2024, when Magyar was at Budapest nightclub Ötkert.

According to the prosecution, Magyar took a mobile phone from a man who had been filming him. The authorities allege that he subsequently left the venue with the phone and deliberately dropped it into the Danube.

The prosecution said in September 2024 that Magyar’s conduct was capable of fulfilling the legal definition of theft. Magyar has rejected the accusation and previously described the proceedings against him as a political attempt to damage his reputation.

Investigation moves forward

The questioning shows a new stage in the case following Parliament’s decision to suspend Magyar’s immunity. The Tisza Party leader has said he will provide further information as the proceedings develop. Right now, the allegations are still disputed: the prosecution says Magyar’s actions constituted suspected theft, while the prime minister has denied committing the offence.

World.title: Tax-free savings at risk? Hungary reviews future of retail government bonds after EU procedure launched
World.content:
Hungary’s Finance Ministry is examining whether changes may be needed to the tax treatment of retail government bonds after the European Commission launched an infringement procedure over their tax advantage compared with securities issued by other EU countries.

EU raises concerns over tax advantage

The dispute concerns one of the key attractions of Hungarian government bonds for private investors: the interest earned on most Hungarian retail government securities is currently exempt from tax. The European Commission objects to the fact that interest from Hungarian government securities issued specifically for retail investors is tax-free, while similar income from government bonds issued by another EU or European Economic Area country is generally subject to Hungarian tax rules.

Foreign government bond returns can normally be subject to 15 per cent personal income tax, with an additional 13 per cent social contribution tax applying in certain circumstances. Meanwhile, interest on Hungarian retail government securities issued after June 2019 is exempt from these taxes.

According to the argument behind the EU procedure, the difference in taxation can financially encourage Hungarian savers to invest in domestic government securities rather than bonds issued elsewhere in the EU, potentially restricting the free movement of capital within the bloc. The financial impact for individual investors could be significant. On a HUF 10 million (around EUR 27,350) investment, as much as HUF 154,000 (EUR 421) a year could depend on whether the interest remains tax-free.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Ministry examining more than taxation

The Finance Ministry has now confirmed that it is reviewing possible responses to the European Commission’s action. In a statement to Hungarian financial news outlet Portfolio, the ministry said it was examining “all possible solutions” and that the review extended beyond taxation.

It is also looking at capital-market and government-financing considerations, although the ministry has not explained what specific measures these areas of review could involve. This has raised questions about whether the government could eventually change the pricing or other conditions attached to retail government securities, although no such decision has been announced.

More on the economy: An exact date of Hungary adopting the euro emerged with new roadmap proposed

No decision has been made yet

The Finance Ministry said it would inform the public once a final government decision had been reached. For now, the tax exemption remains in place, and the government has not indicated precisely how it intends to respond to the infringement procedure.

The issue could nevertheless have important implications for Hungary’s retail government bond market. The securities have been an important way for the government to attract household savings and domestic financing, while the tax-free interest has been a significant incentive for individual investors. Any changes could therefore affect both the attractiveness of government securities for Hungarian savers and the government’s approach to financing through the domestic retail market.

World.title: Ukraine thanks Hungary for ‘green light’ on key EU accession talks
World.content:
Ukraine’s Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha has thanked Hungary for reportedly giving the “green light” to the opening of two more clusters in Ukraine’s European Union accession negotiations.

Sybiha said on Wednesday that Hungary had supported further steps concerning the second and third negotiating clusters at the level of the EU’s Committee of Permanent Representatives (COREPER).

“Ukraine’s EU accession is moving forward step by step. Ukraine and Hungary are taking steps together towards each other and towards European unity,” Sybiha said.

Ukraine’s EU accession is moving forward step by step. Ukraine and Hungary are taking steps towards each other and towards European unity together. These days, a bill aimed at regulating the educational rights of national communities was registered in the Ukrainian Parliament and approved by the relevant parliamentary committee. Today, at the COREPER level, the Hungarian side gave the “green light” to the negotiating positions on Cluster 2 “Internal Market,” and Cluster 3, “Competitiveness and Inclusive Growth”. Thank you, @_OrbanAnita, for the teamwork, which is at once in the interests of our friendly nations and of a strong Europe. 🇺🇦🇪🇺 — Andrii Sybiha 🇺🇦 (@andrii_sybiha) October 7, 2026

Ukraine thanks Hungary for support

The two clusters concern important areas of Ukraine’s EU accession process. The second cluster covers the internal market, while the third focuses on competitiveness and inclusive growth. Sybiha also specifically thanked Hungary’s Foreign Minister Anita Orbán for her cooperation.

“Thank you, Anita Orbán, for the teamwork, which serves the interests of both our friendly peoples and a strong Europe,” the Ukrainian foreign minister wrote.

The announcement comes amid signs of improving relations between Budapest and Kyiv following a period of particularly tense exchanges between the two countries.

Minority education rights also in focus

Sybiha linked the latest development to a bill recently submitted to the Ukrainian parliament concerning the educational rights of national minorities, including the Hungarian community in Ukraine.

The proposal has already received unanimous support from the relevant parliamentary committee. Ukraine’s parliament is expected to discuss several bills related to European integration and the advancement of the country’s EU accession process on 12 October.

The issue of minority rights, particularly those of the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia, has long been a sensitive point in relations between Budapest and Kyiv. According to Sybiha, these developments demonstrate that Ukraine and Hungary are taking reciprocal steps towards each other while also supporting Ukraine’s European integration.

Hungary has not yet officially confirmed the move

There is, however, an important caveat to the Ukrainian announcement: Hungary has not yet officially confirmed that it gave the green light to the two negotiating clusters. For the time being, therefore, the information is based on the Ukrainian foreign minister’s statement and an earlier Financial Times report.

World.title: The EU had enough of Viktor Orbán, proposes long probation period for new member states
World.content:
The European Commission has proposed a 15-year probation period for future EU member states, with countries potentially facing the loss of voting rights or funding if they breach democratic standards.

The plan, outlined by European Commissioner for Enlargement Marta Kos, is designed to give the bloc faster tools to respond if a newly admitted country undermines the rule of law, democracy or the EU’s principle of sincere cooperation. Kos explicitly invoked the former Hungarian prime minister, saying:

“No more Viktor Orbán.”

The proposals would still require approval from the member states before they could take effect.

Faster sanctions than Article 7

Under the current system, Article 7 of the EU treaties can ultimately suspend a member state’s voting rights following a serious and persistent breach of the bloc’s fundamental values. However, the procedure has never reached that ultimate sanction. Previous efforts to address democratic backsliding in Hungary and Poland were complicated by the countries’ ability to support one another politically.

Kos said the European Union therefore needs quicker mechanisms to deal with potential violations by future members. Under her proposal, the threshold for imposing measures such as suspending voting rights would be lower. The safeguards could also involve withholding funds from a country that breaches democratic principles or fails to uphold its obligations to the bloc.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Why is the EU considering the change?

The proposal comes as EU enlargement gains new momentum, particularly in eastern Europe and the western Balkans. Montenegro, Albania, Moldova and Ukraine are among the countries regarded as frontrunners in the current enlargement process. Ukraine and Moldova applied for membership shortly after Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, giving fresh impetus to a process that had previously stalled.

As The Guardian reported, he Commission sees enlargement not only as an institutional project but also as a strategic issue. Kos has pointed to competition for influence from Russia and China in countries seeking closer ties with the bloc.

Stay up-to-date: Prime Minister Péter Magyar says Hungary can only be a truly European country if it remains itself and is not sent out for coffee break

Safeguards would not be permanent

Kos acknowledged that the proposed probation system would eventually expire. She argued that making the restrictions permanent could create a situation in which some countries were effectively treated as second-class members. The proposed 15-year period would therefore be intended as a temporary safeguard while new members establish themselves within the bloc.

The debate comes as the European Union also considers other ways of preventing future enlargement from creating institutional gridlock, including temporary restrictions on new members’ veto powers. For the proposal to become reality, all existing member states would ultimately have to agree to the changes, meaning the safeguards themselves are likely to become part of the wider political debate over the bloc’s next phase of enlargement.

World.title: Baffling: disabled parking space in the middle of the road in Budapest
World.content:
A disabled parking space has been painted directly in the middle of a busy road in Budapest’s Újpest district, prompting questions over how the unusual arrangement was approved.

The space appeared on István Road following renovation works. It sits between a lane used by motor vehicles and a newly designated cycle lane, meaning a disabled driver using the bay would have to leave their car in an area surrounded by moving traffic. The unusual layout was highlighted by Zsolt Wintermantel, a former mayor of Újpest and a qualified transport engineer, who shared a photograph of the parking space on social media.

Disabled drivers face difficult exit

Wintermantel argued that the design could create serious difficulties for the very people the parking bay is intended to assist. A disabled parking space should allow its users to leave their vehicle safely and, where possible, independently. However, in this case, a driver would apparently have to open the car door towards the road, retrieve any walking aids from inside the vehicle and then make their way across the cycle lane to reach the pavement.

The former mayor questioned how safe such a manoeuvre could be with both motor vehicles and cyclists passing nearby. He also pointed out that the parking space is not protected from behind by a pedestrian island or similar physical barrier.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

Concerns reportedly raised before completion

According to information cited by Blikk, the project was approved by the Municipality of Budapest. Újpest’s local authority reportedly only became aware of the final arrangement after the markings had been painted, as the district was not responsible for carrying out the work. Wintermantel said district representatives are normally involved in consultations over similar developments.

He claimed that Újpest representatives had taken part in earlier discussions about the project. He also said that concerns about the design had already been raised at a public forum attended by representatives of the district and the project’s designers. According to the second source, Wintermantel and a former deputy mayor had pointed out the problem during the consultation and were reportedly told that the arrangement would be reviewed.

More on Budapest traffic: Busy road section in the Hungarian capital renewal finally completed

Residents question the road design

Despite those concerns, the project was completed according to the original plans, Wintermantel said. The unusual parking bay has since prompted strong reactions from local residents. One resident questioned where a disabled person would be expected to go after getting out of the vehicle, given the traffic on either side and the cycle lane beside the parking space.

The reports do not include a response from the Municipality of Budapest explaining why the bay was designed in its current position or whether changes are planned. For now, the unusual marking on István Road has raised a broader question about accessibility and road safety: can a parking space intended for disabled motorists really serve its purpose if reaching the pavement means crossing active traffic lanes?

Read also: Budapest Assembly ends free parking for electric cars

World.title: Important Budapest road section’s renewal finally completed
World.content:
The structural refurbishment of the Flórián Square flyovers in Budapest was completed at the end of August, and all associated reinstatement and defect rectification works have now also been completed.

The worksite has been cleared, equipment and materials have been removed, and the surface-level junction has been restored, meaning that all works related to the project have now been completed. The technical handover and acceptance procedure was concluded on 7 October.

Flórián Square flyovers finally complete

The works, commissioned by BKK and carried out by KM Építő Kft. as the general contractor, were limited in September to minor defect rectification, aesthetic reinstatement and road construction works. These included the repair, replacement and reinstatement of the existing stone cladding on the bridge abutments, as well as the necessary minor road construction works.

The restoration of the surface-level junction was completed with the removal of temporary traffic management measures and diversions. Temporary arrangements – such as the U-turn facility on Pacsirtamező Street – helped maintain traffic during the refurbishment, but have now been removed following completion of the works. The final technical handover and acceptance procedure has been concluded.

The bus priority measures introduced as part of the refurbishment will, however, remain in place on Szentendrei Road and Pacsirtamező Street after the completion of the works. BKK thanks road users and local residents for their patience, cooperation and understanding throughout the works.

Never miss a headline: join our Messenger group!

A vital transport link in Budapest has been renewed

The refurbishment of the Flórián Square flyovers became necessary due to their significant deterioration. The bridges play a key role in transport between Budapest and the surrounding agglomeration. The works began on the southern flyover in March 2025 and continued with the northern flyover in November 2025. The southern flyover was reopened to motor traffic in November 2025, while the northern flyover reopened on 30 August 2026.

This marked the completion of the structural refurbishment of both flyovers. With the subsequent reinstatement, defect rectification and road construction works now also complete, the entire project has been brought to a close. BKK provided continuous updates on the progress of the works on their website, while details of the refurbishment and its key milestones were outlined in the press release issued when the northern flyover reopened.
