World.title: Russian supplier reportedly dropped from EU sanctions package at Estonia's request
World.content:
A Russian company supplying rare earths to Estonia's Silmet was reportedly removed from the European Union's proposed 22nd sanctions package at Estonia's request.

Radio Free Europe journalist Rikard Jozwiak said one company and one individual were dropped from the proposal following Estonia's intervention. Neither was named. ERR has not independently verified the claim.

1 company & 1 person was actually removed from the original proposal on request by . its a company providing rare earths to the firm Silmet that processes the material for wind turbines etc in . Company looking for alternative sources — Rikard Jozwiak (@RikardJozwiak) October 7, 2026

Silmet processes the materials for use in wind turbines and other products in the EU. According to Jozwiak, the company is seeking alternative suppliers.

EU ambassadors agreed October 7 to sanctions targeting 743 individuals and 826 companies linked to Russia's military-industrial complex. The package awaits final approval by member states' foreign ministers and is expected to take effect in the coming days.

World.title: Political ad ban on social media sends Estonian politicians writing their own posts
World.content:
As restrictions on purchasing political advertising on social media will be in place for this year's Riigikogu elections, political parties are putting more effort than before into creating their own posts.

Political advertising has been banned on Meta and Google's social media platforms since last fall.

Isamaa betting on organic spread

Isamaa Secretary General Andres Metsoja said political content itself has not been banned on social media, only its promotion through paid advertising. "This means that content needs to be engaging and resonate with people and then it will spread on its own," Metsoja said.

He noted that outdoor advertising is certain to reach everyone in Estonia.

Metsoja added that organic reach is always better than paid advertising when it comes to how social media works. "Ahead of elections, paid advertising becomes 'wallpaper' because all parties would be using it extensively. In other words, if the content doesn't have a 'hook' that makes readers or viewers stop scrolling, its impact won't be particularly significant anyway," Metsoja said.

"Isamaa has people who are very good at capturing viewers' attention on social media. Sandra Laur and Jüri Ratas are certainly the best-known examples, but Aivar Kokk's gardening and cooking videos are also very popular. As a party, we will certainly invest in producing quality content over the coming months to ensure it spreads and that the positions we are campaigning on reach as many people as possible," he added.

Metsoja said that, according to publicly available data, Isamaa and its affiliated candidates spent a total of €35,000 on paid advertising on Meta platforms during the final month before the 2023 Riigikogu elections. This was €20,000 less than both the Reform Party and the Social Democrats spent and €40,000 less than EKRE.

"The cost of living in Estonia has risen significantly over the past four years, including a substantial increase in value-added tax. This means the overall cost of campaigning ahead of the elections will rise by a much greater amount than the so-called 'extra money' freed up by the ban on social media advertising," Metsoja said.

Metsoja said an election campaign should be viewed as a whole, with everything starting from the party platform. Advertising, whether on the streets, on television, on the radio or on online news portals, serves to reinforce the messages of that platform.

SDE's hopes on active posting

Social Democratic Party Secretary General Piret Hartman acknowledged that the inability to advertise on Facebook and Instagram will certainly affect the party's ability to reach voters. "That's why we're putting even more effort into actively posting content ourselves and sharing and amplifying each other's posts. We've also started producing more video content," Hartman said.

"We also need to make our activities more appealing and find ways to improve the organic reach of our posts. We're also trying to increase the number of party members who actively use social media. To support our members, we're organizing training sessions for this purpose," she added.

"We're also trying to have more direct contact with our voters, both on the streets and at various events. We've also launched a poster campaign in different counties to increase our visibility," Hartman said.

According to Hartman, the loss of social media advertising will not have a major impact on the party's campaign budget, as it did not account for a particularly large share of spending in the previous elections. "We'll redirect those resources toward advertising in other channels," she said.

Eesti 200 prioritizing constant visibility

Eesti 200 Executive Director Anneli Kannus said restrictions on political advertising on social media took effect just before last year's local elections, meaning parties have already had to rethink their campaign strategies.

"Parties also generally know the profiles of their potential voters and the ways they are likely to reach them with their messages. We're also running our campaign a little differently this time than in previous elections. The fact that social media is no longer flooded with different parties' colors and slogans immediately before elections is probably a positive development for most people," Kannus said.

She pointed out that Eesti 200 and its members maintain a constant presence on social media. "For politicians, communicating with people or explaining their plans and decisions isn't something that should be limited to the campaign period. Political activity needs to be approached more comprehensively and deliberately because without an established reputation and a track record, no poster or banner will bring in enough votes at election time," Kannus said.

According to Kannus, it would be an oversimplification to suggest that young voters can only be reached through social media. "People who are interested in politics and social issues get the information they need to make their voting decisions from a variety of sources throughout the year, not just from social media ads during election campaigns. We believe younger voters are well-informed and can find information both on party websites and through party members' social media accounts. It would be truly sad if elections were won through paid advertising," Kannus said.

Center sees no great tragedy in the political ads ban

Center Party Secretary General Anneli Ott also said the ban had been known about in advance and that Center Party members are active on social media.

"The Center Party has invested heavily in social media in recent years and because our posts also spread organically, the advertising ban doesn't affect us very much," Ott said.

According to Ott, the ban poses a problem for parties and politicians who only become active immediately before elections and have so far relied on expensive outdoor advertising to gain support.

Ott said the Center Party's strengths have been its campaign tents and direct communication with people. "We do this year-round, although naturally more intensively during election campaigns," Ott said.

"The last local elections showed that people dislike enormous election posters and parties that spent more than €1 million on their campaigns ended up shooting themselves in the foot. The Center Party, which took a more frugal approach, emerged as the most popular party. People appreciate clear solutions to pressing problems and in Tallinn, we've already delivered on several of our promises," Ott said.

"As for younger people, whose voter turnout has been lower, all parties need to take a hard look at themselves and ask whether they've paid enough attention to young people's proposals and tried to address their concerns. The Center Party's election platform will certainly include measures concerning quality, accessible education and homeownership," Ott added.

Reform Party channeling ad money into direct contact and content creation

Reform Party Secretary General Kristo Enn Vaga said what matters most in elections is the future that parties offer Estonia, not how much they spend on advertising on Facebook or Instagram.

"Direct contact with voters remains the most effective campaign method and that's what we'll focus on in these elections as well. This will be supported by outdoor advertising, radio, print media and television. Good content can reach people on social media even without paid advertising. Young people are no exception. Content matters," Vaga said.

"We'll redirect the money previously spent on Meta platforms toward meetings with voters, content creation and increasing our visibility in public spaces, on radio and on television. It's also still possible to post political content and videos on social media," he noted.

According to Vaga, the party plans to focus on more modern and engaging content on the Reform Party's social media channels to increase its organic reach.

"The Reform Party's strength has always been its substantive platform and strong team. The central question in the upcoming parliamentary elections is how to keep Estonia secure and its economy growing. Electoral success will depend largely on how specifically and credibly parties can answer that question," he added.

EKRE refuses to divulge campaign details

Aarne Mäe, an adviser to EKRE's Riigikogu parliamentary group, said the party does not disclose details of its campaign in this way.

World.title: Authorities alarmed as Estonian teens climb restricted buildings
World.content:
Young people are competing for attention by slipping into abandoned buildings and infrastructure sites, prompting concerns that the urban‑exploring craze may pose real security risks.

In recent years, social‑media content has sharply increased in which youngsters outdo one another, breaking into empty buildings and poorly guarded sites and performing feats there. One thing is adrenaline hunting and chasing fame, on the other hand it is often vandalism and theft, and according to experts hotheads may in extreme cases even be used in hybrid warfare.

The former Harju District Court building in Tallinn, the emptied Swedbank headquarters, Viimsi winter garden, but also the Paldiski nuclear site or Levira's television and communication mast at Valgjärve. These are only a few examples of startling videos shared in communities dedicated to the subject.

"Above all, attempts are made to find such places where people have no access. Then it is filmed, it is especially cool if in that video there is some kind of entry method that could be especially complicated," described Anders Allandi, head of the Ida‑Harju proceedings unit of the Northern Prefecture.

One of the most popular places where sometimes neck‑breaking tricks are done is the gigantic elevator in Hiiu, Tallinn, which has stood empty for almost 20 years and whose tower rises far above the surrounding buildings.

Jan‑Erik Moon, with an IT background, has been mapping old buildings for 20 years already, and Raigo Kotkas, who earns a living project‑based, got hooked six years ago and today even run a corresponding YouTube channel. The hobby carries internationally the name urban exploring or briefly urbex, which can be translated as discovering the urban environment. In Estonia it originally meant mainly exploring old military installations or shelters. Jan and Raigo call themselves rather hobby historians and photographers and emphasize that they try to visit sites correctly. Jan has even conducted official tours in the Hiiu elevator with the owners' agreement.

What bothers Jan and Raigo is that when for a long time the circle of enthusiasts in Estonia was quite small, then in the last couple of years an explosion occurred. If earlier enthusiasts were motivated by history, architecture and the joy of discovery, then now the average age has come down a lot and there is outdoing one another.

Let's be clear — urbex is not fundamentally a negative phenomenon and there are also more correct practitioners, but lately in TikTok alone there are in Estonia about 500 accounts connected with the urbex topic, where thousands and thousands of clips have been uploaded, a large part of which is clearly the illegal activity of rascals.

Separate sub‑types are roofing, that is, climbing in high places, and diggers, who explore tunnels and other underground structures.

Anders Allandi. Source: ERR

The police have also noticed a clear rise, confirms Anders Allandi, head of the Ida‑Harju proceedings unit.

"Everything starts with simple and accessible buildings, like the music high school, the Liivalaia courthouse, some other abandoned building that is visible and known to everyone. From there it moves to more extreme. For example some kinds of masts, excavators, building roofs," he said.

According to Marko Künnapas, sales manager of the Riigi Kinnisvara (RKAS), their portfolio contains across Estonia about 600 properties with altogether around a thousand buildings. Among them is the music high school complex in Kivimäe, Tallinn, which has stood mostly empty for about ten years and consists of five buildings. A large number of break‑in and rampage videos have been recorded there. RKAS has indeed made efforts to protect the buildings, and at the dormitory one can even read young people's "feedback."

"The headache is that this involves resources that are spent on it, and it involves costs, and these costs per site can reach tens of thousands," said Künnapas.

The videos show a clear dynamic: when the first break‑in has occurred and becomes known, a mass invasion and decline follows. For example the former Viisnurk factory in Pärnu, where skis were once produced.

"At some point all the security systems were broken there and basically the entire archive contents were thrown down from the fourth floor into the stairwell," said Jan.

Or the once popular Mereranna sanatorium in Narva‑Jõesuu. "Where actually at the beginning of this year everything was still quite in order, they broke in, smashed all the security there and in just the past summer there were a whole 14 fires," said Raigo.

Because social media requires public sharing, paradoxically the pranksters themselves document their crimes. There are videos where a crowbar, an angle grinder is used or a hole is smashed in a stone wall with a hammer. A vivid example is the Soviet‑era shelter in Õismäe. In the end the owner had no choice but to place multi‑ton concrete elements in front.

In the videos there is also quite a bit of teasing owners, security firms and even the police.

"In places where there is security, they have a so‑called five‑minute rule, meaning within five minutes you basically have to be gone from the site. You have to be able to run through the building with sirens blaring," said Raigo.

Allandi admits that probably only a fraction of cases reach the police, but when they do, it is formally a break‑in, which is a misdemeanor and may involve a fine. If the break‑in perpetrator is under 14, the matter usually ends with a conversation with the culprit and their parents.

A separate issue is that for damaged property a civil claim may also threaten. One thing is financial damage, but everyone highlights the physical dangers, which begin with mold, inhaling which is harmful, up to the possibility of falling to one's death. In one music school video, for example, a boy trips and flies through a door glass.

One thing is young people's risk behavior, but lately more and more videos have come from sites that can be called vital infrastructure. For example a clip from the end of August, where a masked group breaks into the Valgjärve television and communication mast.

It is still light outside and one worker's car stands in front of the building, but at the same time the guys stroll on the roof. In the end the intruders admire the sunset 350 meters above ground at the top of the mast, through which among other things ETV's picture is transmitted into many homes.

It is also noticeable that urbex enthusiasts have clearly climbed, without owners' knowledge, for example to the top of the chimney of the Iru thermal power plant, accessed the Paldiski nuclear storage, Tallinna Vesi and several Eesti Raudtee sites, which should be quite well guarded.

Just last week a video was posted of how a stranger climbed in the dark into the crane cabin at the Rail Baltic terminal construction in Ülemiste. Experts warn that on the one hand in the current era of hybrid war videos may provide information, on the other hand hotheads may be used for some mischief.

"I think that danger may be great, we actually see in the context of hybrid war very many acts that we could not yet yesterday think of in hybrid war. These acts develop at tremendous speed and all the more we ourselves must be careful how or what we do," said Allandi.

World.title: Estonia aims to teach air‑gun shooting to 14‑year‑old students
World.content:
The Defense Resources Agency wants as many eighth‑grade students as possible to be able, if they wish, to shoot an air gun. This school year, about 20 schools are offered in‑depth national defense instruction at the end of basic school.

The Defense Resources Agency began this year with a so‑called national defense year project, with which it wishes to bring national‑defense‑related instruction also into the 8th grades of basic school.

At present, national defense instruction is compulsory in high school. The head of the Defense Resources Agency's national defense education bureau, Aare Jamnes, said that in eighth grade it may not be a separate subject. "Basically, in every subject there is something that can be used in national defense or discussed from national defense," he said.

Jamnes said that this school year 23 schools expressed interest in the national defense year, and in the coming years it is hoped that the number of interested schools will keep growing. The goal, however, is that all Estonian schools would implement integrated national defense instruction in eighth grades.

The programme of these roughly 23 schools' eighth grades includes, among other things, national‑defense‑themed quizzes, excursions to Defense Forces units, and also shooting instruction with air guns.

Jamnes noted that in this way Estonia can get more good shooting athletes, but at the same time young people would be somewhat earlier ready also for national defense.

He explained that there are two different ways to organize shooting in schools. One possibility is when the school itself is active and expresses the wish that they would have such an opportunity. For such schools, the state also offers separate shooting‑trainer instruction.

"The other possibility is that when a physical education teacher wishes to go with their group somewhere to a shooting range. Let's take, for example, Elva school, which contacts the sports center, goes a couple of kilometers from the school to the shooting range, there are trainers, equipment, and shooting is done in a safe environment," Jamnes explained.

Jamnes said that in the case of air pistols it would be entirely feasible also for schools to have a separate shooting range. "A safe shooting lane for an air pistol can be set up in any sports hall. Even now there are still very many schools where shooting ranges are in working order or repairable," he said.

Teenage years are turbulent and young people also have more and more mental health problems. Jamnes said that giving young people an air gun, however, rather reduces any danger situations connected with shooting.

"The more physically active young people are and the more they do joint activities with others, learn and gain new experiences, the more anxiety and various mental problems come down. They are not so withdrawn and they have more opportunities to do things together. I find that this does not increase danger situations, but rather in the broad picture does only good for the mental side, when young people can do sports together and learn new things," he said.

And ultimately shooting an air gun is not compulsory for young people. That is, whoever does not wish to, does not have to shoot, Jamnes noted. "If a young person does not wish it or parents do not wish that their child would get experience in a shooting range, then of course no one is forced," he said.

World.title: Justice minister vows new gender equality bill will reach vote before elections
World.content:
Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta says the long‑stalled gender equality and equal opportunities bill will be passed during the current Riigikogu term, though she has not yet explained the draft's contents or the timeline for its processing.

"We hope to complete the processing of the equal opportunities bill by the end of this Riigikogu term," Pakosta said.

She is not worried that time may be tight — under normal procedure, the bill should reach the Riigikogu by November at the latest.

"There is nothing unusual about this. It is completely normal that things are in progress and some take a bit longer. That is the case with many bills," she said.

Pakosta said it is not actually a problem that the gender equality and equal opportunities bill has remained unpassed for so long. She said the Constitution already provides protection that covers the bill's provisions.

"This bill changes almost nothing in people's lives because paragraph 12 of the Constitution is directly applicable," she said.

"Courts, the chancellor of justice and everyone else work on the basis of that constitutional paragraph, which guarantees protection for all people across all characteristics in all areas of life. Estonians are very well protected against discrimination because we have a very good Constitution. The changes achieved with this bill are extremely nuanced," Pakosta said.

She did not agree to discuss the content of the bill, including how the current draft differs from the version she withdrew from the process in 2024.

"Once again, the bill is still being drafted," she said.

When Pakosta halted the processing of the gender equality and equal opportunities bill prepared at the Ministry of Economic Affairs in May 2024, the Ministry of Justice commissioned a new perspective from the private sector — from the law firm Sorainen — without informing the NGOs and the office of the equal treatment commissioner who had worked on the earlier draft.

Although Pakosta insisted Sorainen was not commissioned to write a bill, as media reported at the time based on ministry information, but only preparatory materials, she still chose to keep those materials from the public. She also did not show the newly completed analysis to equal treatment commissioner Christian Veske, who requested it, or to the equality policy department at the Ministry of Economic Affairs.

As before, Pakosta justified the secrecy by citing the need to avoid confusion. "There was just a major public confusion over the statute of limitations for sexual crimes against children, which shows how easily confusion can arise. That is exactly why the law states that preparatory materials are not always public. In this case, the Data Protection Inspectorate has confirmed that," Pakosta said.

Gender Equality and Equal Treatment Commissioner Christian Veske. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Commissioner skeptical about timeline

Although Pakosta said Estonians are currently well protected against discrimination, equal opportunities commissioner Christian Veske wrote to the minister in summer with a series of proposals, including a recommendation to complete the processing of the equal opportunities bill and ensure equal legal protection for everyone.

In her autumn response, Pakosta wrote that the ministry considers the issues addressed in the bill very important and added that the bill concerns socially significant and sensitive matters that require thorough consideration of different rights, interests and positions. "We consider it important that these positions be taken into account in shaping equal opportunities policy," she wrote.

Commenting on Pakosta's response to ERR, Veske said it seemed rather vague. Based on it, he finds it hard to believe the bill will be processed during the current Riigikogu term. "Especially considering that none of the relevant parties have received any substantive information about the bill," Veske said.

Because withdrawing the earlier bill angered the NGOs and the equal treatment commissioner's office that had worked on it, Pakosta repeatedly promised at the time that she would definitely submit the new bill for consultation, where all stakeholders could give feedback. "I confirm that we are ready for full cooperation with the relevant state agencies and advocacy organizations," Pakosta said.

Veske, who has had no information about the bill for the past two years, also has no knowledge of any planned stakeholder consultation. He hopes it will still happen. "It would be very poor legislative practice if the ministry wanted to skip the consultation round. There may be some legal obstacles to skipping it, but since this is a Ministry of Justice bill, they likely know that better," Veske said.

In response to ERR's question about whether consultation will take place, Pakosta said it is still planned. She did not say when.

Justice Minister Liisa Pakosta decided at the end of 2024 to halt and not send for official government coordination the gender equality and equal opportunities bill prepared at the Ministry of Economic Affairs.

The bill aimed to merge two existing laws — the Gender Equality Act and the Equal Treatment Act — into one comprehensive legal act. It sought to resolve a long‑standing legal gap in Estonia where protection against discrimination is not equal across all characteristics. Pakosta said she halted the bill because of extensive legal criticism and conflicting feedback.

World.title: Iraqi dinar’s exchange rate slightly rises following sharp decline
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The exchange rate for the Iraqi dinar compared to the US dollar slightly declined on Wednesday evening in the Iraqi capital, Baghdad, and the capital of the Kurdistan region of Iraq, Erbil, following a sharp rise earlier in the morning.

The US dollar exchange rate declined in Baghdad’s al-Kifah and al-Harithiya stock exchanges, reaching 1,670 Iraqi dinars compared to 1,685 Iraqi dinars on Wednesday morning.

The exchange rate in currency exchange shops in Baghdad ranged between 1,675 Iraqi dinars and 1,665 Iraqi dinars, Shafaq News reported.

In Erbil, the US dollar exchange rate also declined, fluctuating between 1,667 and 1,666 Iraqi dinars.

US dollar exchange rates rose noticeably in the Baghdad and Erbil markets on Wednesday morning, following the cabinet’s decision to revalue the official rate of the local currency, causing turbulence and instability in the parallel market.

Iraq officially depreciated its national currency, with the baseline dropping from about 1,300 Iraqi dinars to 1,500 dinars per US dollar.

The Iraqi cabinet approved on Tuesday the structural adjustment, which marks a 14.5 percent decline compared to the previous official framework that had been in place since early 2023.

Following the announcement, parallel market rates in Baghdad and Erbil soared, with exchange shops reporting market gains of more than 1,700 Iraqi dinars per US dollar.

World.title: Iraq’s foreign reserves may fall to $60 billion by end of 2026
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – A Standard Chartered economist said on Wednesday that Iraq may resort to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) if oil revenues continue to fall and the currency’s devaluation fails to boost state finances as intended.

Standard Chartered chief economist for the Middle East and Pakistan Carla Slim said that any potential program with the IMF could entail structural reforms, particularly regarding the public sector wage bill, to enhance fiscal sustainability, Bloomberg reported.

If the current pace of depletion continues, Iraq’s foreign reserves might fall to roughly $60 billion by the end of the year, down from over $100 billion at the beginning of the year, according to Slim.

The economist indicated that the local currency’s exchange rate may be adjusted again in the future months, based on changes in oil earnings and foreign reserves.

According to IMF data, Iraq’s foreign currency reserves currently stand at approximately $85 billion.

Standard Chartered is a leading British multinational banking and financial services company headquartered in London.

World.title: Iraq to ban Israeli-developed GPS navigation app Waze
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq has formally banned the Waze navigation application, pushing the effective date until the end of December 2026.

Iraqi Communications Minister Mustafa Sanad originally planned to start the block in early 2027. However, the government recently changed the timeframe, pushing the restriction ahead to late December 2026.

Waze’s Israeli roots influenced the decision, which aligns with Iraq’s strict 2022 legislation criminalizing rapprochement with Israel.

The Iraqi government raises security, data privacy, and geopolitical concerns over geographic tracking data.

While it is unclear how the Iraqi government would restrict access to the application, technology analysts expect local telecommunication providers to block Waze servers or ban the program outright from regional app stores.

The step triggered rapid online discussion among Iraqis. Drivers expressed disappointment at losing Waze’s extremely accurate, real-time traffic updates, which are critical for navigating crowded cities like Baghdad.

The Communication Ministry suggested using Google Maps as a primary legal alternative, even though Google owns both Google Maps and Waze.

World.title: Iraq lowers currency exchange rate to 1,500 dinars per US dollar
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq has officially depreciated its national currency, with the baseline dropping from about 1,300 Iraqi dinars to 1,500 dinars per US dollar.

The Iraqi cabinet approved on Tuesday the structural adjustment, which marks a 14.5 percent decline compared to the previous official framework that had been in place since early 2023.

The Central Bank of Iraq (CBI) established a multi-tiered exchange framework to facilitate the transition across commercial and banking channels.

An exchange rate of 1,500 Iraqi dinars per US dollar is now used for government purchases from the Finance Ministry, 1,510 Iraqi dinars for official sales to commercial banking institutions, and 1,520 Iraqi dinars for public consumers who buy foreign currency directly from banks.

The forceful monetary policy shift acts as a direct fiscal stabilization mechanism in response to significant macroeconomic shocks.

The regional conflict has severely affected important marine trade routes, including partial closures and interruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Since oil exports account for about 90 percent of Iraq’s national finances, transportation delays reduced real export capacity to around 2.34 million barrels per day compared to 3.6 million.

The Finance Ministry informed the Iraqi parliament that it would be unable to cover the domestic budget for 2026 unless the dinar was revalued.

By demanding more local dinars for every US dollar of incoming oil revenue, the Iraqi government generates artificial liquidity to meet rising public expenditure, local deficits, and civil service salaries.

The depreciation is intended to reduce the disparity between the government’s stated measurements and parallel market realities.

Following the announcement, parallel market rates in Baghdad and Erbil soared, with exchange shops reporting market gains of more than 1,700 Iraqi dinars per US dollar.

The Iraqi cabinet also prohibited the collection of advance customs duties on foreign imports to reduce unexpected operational disruptions within business supply chains.

World.title: Iraq’s trade exchange with China surpass $51 billion in 2025
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – The Chinese Ambassador to Iraq, Xiang Bo, revealed on Tuesday that the trade exchange between Iraq and China exceeded $51 billion in 2025.

In a statement to the state-run Iraqi News Agency (INA), Bo noted that relations between China and Iraq are continually improving. He emphasized that Iraq is a crucial partner for China in the Belt and Road Initiative, which has yielded positive outcomes.

Major Chinese firms are involved in the construction and development of several industries in Iraq, such as oil, energy, and infrastructure, according to Bo.

Bo emphasized that the cooperation between the two countries is based on shared interests and is continuously developing.

The Chinese diplomat expressed his hope that this collaboration will continue and grow into other sectors, contributing to the development of a complete partnership between Iraq and China.

The two countries’ strong economic interdependence assures a bright future and enormous possibilities for collaboration, according to Bo.

Chinese companies have been heavily involved in the oil industry and in significant infrastructure projects, such as the construction of major bridges and schools, with more than 600 schools completed in various Iraqi provinces.

China’s investments in Iraq are also rapidly rising, notably in infrastructure and energy.

World.title: Iraq advances as Gulf-Europe data hub with iQ Networks, Ooredoo fibre deal
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraq’s iQ Networks and OFN, the international connectivity arm of Qatar’s Ooredoo Group, have agreed to build a high-capacity fibre connection across Iraq, furthering ambitions to connect the Gulf and Asia to Turkey and Europe via Iraqi territory.

According to the arrangement, OFN will buy numerous dark fibre pairs from iQ Networks for international transit throughout Iraq.

The terrestrial network will link to Ooredoo’s proposed Fibre in Gulf (FIG) subsea cable infrastructure, creating a single route for international data traffic.

The project might boost Iraq’s position as a regional digital transit center, using the country’s geographical location between the Arabian Gulf, Turkey, and Europe to transport increasing quantities of international data.

FIG is intended to link Qatar, Oman, the UAE, Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, and Iraq with a capacity of up to 720 terabits per second across 24 fibre pairs.

OFN has also struck a landing agreement with the state-owned Iraqi Telecommunications and Post Company (ITPC) to send the undersea cable into Iraq.

From there, iQ Networks’ terrestrial infrastructure will transport connections north across the nation to Turkey and European markets.

According to the firms, the new corridor will serve as an extra route between the Gulf and Europe while also increasing network resilience and capacity.

The need for such infrastructure is fast expanding as artificial intelligence, cloud computing, data centers, telecom operators, and big technology businesses require increasing quantities of international bandwidth.

The deal was signed at the Ooredoo Group’s headquarters in Doha by top Iraqi communications authorities as well as executives from Ooredoo, OFN, ITPC, and iQ Networks.

For Iraq, the initiative is part of a larger attempt to transform its position into an economic benefit by attracting international data traffic that would otherwise utilize other regional routes.

The infrastructure might also help Iraq’s developing digital economy and data center industry, as well as provide new possibilities for foreign traffic passing through the country.

Implementation will continue in accordance with the agreed-upon plan, subject to regulatory and government approval.

The initiative is another step toward establishing Iraq as a digital bridge between Asia, the Arabian Gulf, and Europe, broadening the country’s significance beyond conventional energy and commercial channels.

World.title: US dollar surges past 180,000 IQD amid parallel market disruption
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Parallel currency exchanges across Iraq experienced severe disruption and sharp price swings on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, after the federal government abruptly modified the official exchange rate benchmark to 1,500 dinars per dollar for purchases and 1,520 dinars for retail sales to citizens.

The unexpected regulatory shift sent shockwaves through cash trading floors, propelling parallel dollar prices past the 170,000-dinar threshold per $100 and triggering deep regional rate discrepancies across major commercial centers.

Trading data collated across provincial exchanges reflected widespread variance as exchange desks struggled with price discovery. In Baghdad, cash selling rates settled at 170,000 dinars per $100 against purchase bids of 168,250 dinars. In Erbil, the commercial hub of the Kurdistan Region, prices surged even higher, with sales touching 180,000 dinars alongside a wide bid-ask spread anchored by buying offers at 166,500 dinars.

In the southern port city of Basra, trading desks quoted selling rates at 179,000 dinars per $100 against buying bids of 178,000 dinars, reflecting intense localized demand for physical greenbacks.

The rapid escalation in currency volatility coincided with growing legislative mobilization inside parliament, where lawmakers have begun organizing appeals for an emergency parliamentary session.

Proponents of the emergency hearing aim to legally compel the executive branch to reverse the sudden exchange rate hike and assess the broader economic and living strains imposed on households, warning that runaway parallel spreads risk amplifying retail inflation and destabilizing domestic supply chains.

World.title: Iraqi MP demands emergency session as official dollar hike paralyzes markets
World.content:
Baghdad (IraqiNews.com) – Iraqi Member of Parliament Miqdad Al-Khafaji called on the Council of Representatives on Wednesday, October 7, 2026, to convene an immediate emergency session to compel the federal government to reverse its decision devaluing the Iraqi dinar against the U.S. dollar.

The legislative push comes as the official adjustment to 1,500 dinars per dollar triggers immediate price shocks, widespread commercial freezes, and severe market gridlock across Iraqi wholesale hubs.

In a formal statement, Al-Khafaji criticized the government’s fiscal priorities, pointing out that political factions continue to expand administrative overhead and create patronized public positions that bloat state expenditures, while forcing ordinary citizens to absorb the financial fallout of structural deficits.

Al-Khafaji warned that devaluing the currency directly erodes the real purchasing power of fixed-income public servants, daily wage laborers, and low-income families, emphasizing that a public already strained by regional tensions cannot endure additional economic shocks.

Currency analysts and market participants anticipate that parallel exchange desks will soon test psychological highs of 180,000 dinars per $100 as greenback liquidity tightens.

The rapid depreciation of the dinar in real terms has triggered public frustration across Iraqi cities, where consumer earnings and local commerce remain heavily denominated in local currency.

On the commercial front, the devaluation has delivered immediate ripple effects to retail and wholesale food supply networks:

Retail Food Surges: Nabhan Al-Ahmad, a commercial market owner in Saladin Governorate, reported that consumer food staples experienced an immediate price hike of roughly 25 percent within hours of the cabinet announcement. A standard sack of rice that previously retailed for 45,000 dinars spiked to 50,000 dinars, with proportional increases hitting sugar, cooking oil, and packaged goods.

Distribution Freezes: Yousef Al-Rubaie, a sales agent for food distributor Altunsa, confirmed that major regional food supply and FMCG distribution firms have suspended shipments and wholesale deliveries until further notice to protect operational capital against volatile replacement costs.

Shorja Commercial Stagnation: In Baghdad’s central commercial district of Al-Shorja, wholesale centers have ground to an effective standstill. Abu Ahmed Al-Asadi, a prominent commercial center owner in Shorja, described the wholesale sector as completely paralyzed. Al-Asadi explained that activity had already begun stalling two weeks earlier amid regional geopolitical tensions and rising exchange rates, adding that the official devaluation has shut down the market entirely, forcing most wholesale merchants to shutter storefronts and suspend trade until currency volatility stabilizes.

As legislative calls grow for parliamentary intervention, commercial friction and consumer uncertainty continue to mount, presenting the administration with significant economic headwinds following its statutory rate revision.

World.title: NTPC identifies 3 locations for nuclear power projects
World.content:
NEW DELHI: Public sector NTPC has identified three locations, one each in Madhya Pradesh, Bihar and Odisha, to set up nuclear power plants as it aims to add 30GW of nuclear capacity across 14 states by 2047.

The company has submitted detailed feasibility reports for each site to the Atomic Energy Commission for approval. NTPC is also exploring technology collaborations with global players such as Holtec International and Westinghouse of the US, Rosatom of Russia and EDF of France for pressurised water reactor projects to be deployed at these locations, said an official aware of the development.

With an installed power generation capacity of 89GW, including thermal, hydro and renewable capacity, the company is targeting 149GW by 2032 and 244GW by 2037, besides adding significant battery and pumped storage capacity.

It has set up NTPC Parmanu Urja Nigam Ltd as its wholly owned nuclear subsidiary to foray into nuclear power. Its first nuclear project in Rajasthanâs Mahi Banswara, comprising four 700-MW units, however, is being developed through Anushakti Vidhyut Nigam Ltd, a joint venture with Nuclear Power Corporation of India.

World.title: Rupee may be undervalued, markets can be irrational: RBI governor Sanjay Malhotra
World.content:
MUMBAI: Reserve Bank of India governor Sanjay Malhotra said the rupee was undervalued and the central bank would intervene to ensure orderly movement in the currency market even as it closed at 96.78 on Wednesday, down 36 paise from its previous close, after falling to a five-month low of 96.85 during the day.

"By a number of estimates, including the real effective exchange rate, the rupee is not overvalued. It may be undervalued," Malhotra said at a press conference after the MPC meeting. He was responding to a question on whether the rupee market was irrational.

"Markets can be quite irrational in the short run. It's only in the long run that they are able to find the right value," he said.

The governor said RBI would support the rupee's orderly movement and help it find its "correct value", while ensuring there was no excessive volatility.

Malhotra also said a correction in the valuation of global AI stocks could redirect foreign capital to emerging markets such as India. He said a correction in AI stocks would not have a major negative impact on India and "if at all, there may be" a positive impact.

Malhotra said that US tariffs and the absence of a trade deal would be a negative but could be offset by a trade deal with other countries.

Despite a robust services trade surplus and strong net remittance receipts, the current account deficit widened in July because of a higher merchandise trade deficit, Malhotra said.





The merchandise trade deficit rose to $58.7 billion in July and Aug from $55.1 billion in the same period a year earlier, mainly because of higher imports of electronic goods and crude oil. On external financing, Malhotra said net FDI had shown sustained improvement, with inflows rising to $13.8 billion in the first four months of the year from $9.6 billion in the corresponding period a year earlier.

The increase was driven by higher gross inflows and a slowdown in the growth of outward FDI.

"Robust gross FDI reflects the strong interest of global investors in India," he said. FPI recorded net outflows of $10.3 billion during the period up to Oct 5. However, capital-flow measures announced in the June policy had supported inflows, he said. The balance of payments is consequently expected to record a healthy surplus this year.

World.title: Doctors, hospitals can't use AI to create testimonials: National Medical Commission
World.content:
Representative image

Join conversation View All Comments â Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful Â· TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Doctors and hospitals cannot use AI to create patient testimonials, clinical outcomes or promotional content, nor can they pay to manipulate rankings like those on search engines and apps, under new ethical advertising guidelines issued by National Medical Commission Tuesday, effective immediately.NMC has barred registered medical practitioners and hospitals from using AI-generated content to advertise their services, solicit patients or disseminate unverifiable information about diagnoses, treatments or outcomes. AI cannot be used to create synthetic patient testimonials, voices, clinical outcomes or fake endorsements, or misrepresent the nature or quality of medical services.Doctors can't pay for manipulate search rankings. They also can't make unverified claims such as "best", "number one", "most trusted", "guaranteed cures" or "100% success".Doctors cannot engage influencers, advertising agencies or online platforms in arrangements involving payment linked to procuring patients. Doctors and hospitals cannot offer limited-period discounts, coupons, gift packages or referral benefits if these are likely to encourage unnecessary consultations. However, NMC allows doctors to use social media for factual, non-promotional health education. Hospitals can similarly share objective details.The guidelines restrict the use of patient photographs without valid consent and safeguards. Patient testimonials, before-and-after images and treatment-success claims that could create unrealistic expectations or mislead are also prohibited.NMC has prescribed a warning and mandatory ethics training for a first violation, censure and monetary penalty for a second, suspension for three to six months for a third, and six to 12 months for serious violations. Repeated violations can lead to removal from the medical register for one to three years.

World.content:
Actor Nana Patekar was known for his versatility and powerful screen presence. He was 75 years old.

Patekar was known for his roles in several Hindi and Marathi films. His notable Hindi movies include “Parinda”, “Prahaar: The Final Act”, “Tirangaa”, “Krantiveer” and “Khamoshi: The Musical”.

Patekar was a recipient of three National Film Awards, several Filmfare Awards, the Maharashtra State Film Award and Filmfare Awards Marathi. He had also received Padma Shri, the country’s fourth-highest civilian honour.
