World.title: Nobel winner Kenso Soai says he understood the significance of his research
World.content:
Japanese scientist Kenso Soai, one of two winners of Wednesday’s Nobel Prize in Chemistry , knew the significance of his research all along — though he had not expected that he would ever get the coveted prize, let alone this year.

When he received a phone call from the Nobel Foundation in Sweden notifying him of the prize a few hours before the announcement, he was out shopping for groceries at a supermarket near his home in Shiki, Saitama Prefecture.

“I may sound arrogant, but I had thought I would not get complaints if I won,” Soai, 76, told a news conference on Wednesday night at the Tokyo University of Science, where he taught and researched until he retired in 2016.

World.title: Corridor named after late PM Abe completed in India
World.content:
A corridor named after the late former Prime Minister Shinzo Abe has been completed at an international convention center built with Japanese grant aid in the Hindu holy city of Varanasi in the northern Indian state of Uttar Pradesh.

Attending a ceremony Wednesday to mark the completion, Abe’s widow, Akie, said that if her husband were alive, he would have been moved by the creation of a corridor bearing his name and would have come to see it firsthand, according to local media reports.

Photos displayed on the wall of the Abe Memorial Corridor include one showing the former prime minister holding a meeting with Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi.

In a post on social media platform X, Uttar Pradesh Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath said that the corridor symbolizes Abe’s contributions to strengthening historical, cultural and diplomatic ties between India and Japan.

Abe visited Varanasi in 2015 while serving as prime minister.

World.title: AI data-center boom ignites bidding war for critical TDK unit
World.content:
A bidding war for TDK’s hard-disk drive parts business could determine the prospects of Japanese corporate icon Toshiba as well as who controls an increasingly lucrative artificial intelligence data-center storage market.

Seagate Technology Holdings and delisted Toshiba are vying for TDK’s magnetic-heads business in a deal that could be worth several billion dollars. The winning bidder would be able to expand in-house capabilities in the $23 billion hard-drive market that’s been transformed by voracious AI data-center demand.

Fast-moving AI data-center operators now are demanding hard-drive suppliers pack ever more storage into limited spaces. Prices are climbing and net income at Seagate and Western Digital — which together control more than 90% of the global HDD market, according to research firm TrendForce — has grown by multiples in recent quarters.

World.title: EU takes firmer stance on China’s trade practices as Beijing talks begin
World.content:
The European Union is striking a more assertive approach to China as it heads into two days of negotiations in Beijing aimed at avoiding an economically damaging trade war.

The EU’s trade chief, Maros Sefcovic, is set to meet with Chinese Commerce Minister Wang Wentao this week to address a trade deficit that exceeds $1 billion a day. The meeting comes as the EU prepares what are described as safeguard measures that would limit imports of Chinese hybrid vehicles — a move that may be seen as an escalation.

Germany and France this week called on the EU to adopt stronger tools — including an instrument that could cut off China from the bloc’s massive single market — in order to defend European sectors that have fallen prey to surging Chinese imports. But the EU wants to moderate its action to try to avoid retaliation from Beijing.

World.title: Populations of wild species fell by an average of 73% from 1970 to 2022, WWF says
World.content:
Nearly 6,000 monitored vertebrate species across more than 35,000 populations declined by an average of 73% from 1970 to 2022, the World Wide Fund for Nature (WWF) said in its latest Living Planet Report published on Thursday.

The Living Planet Index, managed by the Zoological Society of London (ZSL) and WWF, monitored a total of 35,803 populations covering 5,790 different species of mammals, birds, reptiles, amphibians and fish over the 52-year period.

The 2026 Living Planet Report estimates that overall populations fell by an average of around 2.5% per year over the period.

“Monitored global populations continue to decline on average with no evidence yet of that global recovery,” said Andrew Terry, chief conservation officer at ZSL.

The average rate of decline across the monitored populations does not represent a headcount of the total number of animals lost from 1970 to 2022, and the number is especially sensitive to changes in already small populations.

Monitored freshwater species saw an average decline of 85%, while terrestrial species fell 69% and marine species 59%, the index showed.

The steepest average population declines were in South America, at 95%, with Africa also experiencing losses of 80%.

The 2026 Living Planet report incorporated an additional 295 species and 967 populations across a longer time series compared to the last report in 2024.

The additional data “reinforces our confidence in the continued decline in biodiversity,” Terry told a briefing.

Habitat loss and degradation were the most frequently reported threat, but wildlife populations are also at risk from overexploitation, climate change, pollution, invasive species and disease, the report said.

“Amid these steep declines, there are grounds for hope, rooted in evidence. Wildlife populations are under pressure but recovery is in reach,” said Kirsten Schuijt, WWF’s director general.

Targeted conservation efforts have enabled populations of some species to recover, including tigers, Atlantic and Pacific bluefin tuna, southern African elephants and green sea turtles.

Alongside conservation efforts, changes in the energy, food and finance systems are required to halt nature loss, Schuijt said.

World.title: Dodgers get past Braves in Game 4 to reach NLCS
World.content:
Andy Pages’ two-run single in the seventh inning broke open a pitchers’ duel and helped the Los Angeles Dodgers close out their NL Division Series against the Atlanta Braves with a 4-1 win in Game 4 on Wednesday.

“I’ve been preparing myself all series for a moment like that, give myself an opportunity, get a good pitch to hit,” Pages said. “And luckily I was able to put a good swing on a pitch.”

The Dodgers, who won the series 3-1 and are looking to be the first National League team to win three straight World Series, will open the NL Championship Series on the road against the Milwaukee Brewers on Sunday.

World.title: Japan ranked best country in the world for fourth straight year
World.content:
Japan was named the world’s most attractive country for the fourth consecutive year, according to survey results released Wednesday, extending a winning streak as record numbers of overseas visitors continue to flock to the country.

Japan took the top spot in the U.S. edition of the magazine Conde Nast Traveler’s Readers’ Choice Awards for “Best Countries in the World.”

Italy ranked second, followed by Ireland, Cambodia and Spain.

The results demonstrate the country’s enduring appeal among international travelers as inbound tourism continues to surge . A record 42.7 million overseas visitors came to Japan in 2025, according to Justice Ministry figures.

Tokyo’s Haneda Airport was ranked the sixth best in the world, with Singapore’s Changi Airport taking the top place.

In a news release Wednesday, the Japan National Tourism Organization (JNTO) said Japan’s strong showing reflected not only the appeal of its tourism resources, but also qualities distinctive to Japan, such as its hospitality and safety.

“We hope that this continued international recognition will generate even greater interest in Japan and encourage more people to visit,” the organization wrote.

Conde Nast Traveler readers cast 798,867 votes in this year’s awards, the magazine’s 39th edition. The awards, held annually since 1988, rank destinations and travel experiences based on readers’ overall evaluations, with voting across categories including countries, hotels and cruises.

In the magazine’s U.K. edition of the rankings, Japan placed second behind Greece, with Italy, Turkey and Portugal completing the top five. The magazine highlighted the country’s restaurants, hot springs, cherry blossoms and high-speed rail network, as well as its mix of traditional culture, design and technological innovation.

“We will continue to showcase the unique attractions of regions across Japan, including their nature, culture, and cuisine, to audiences around the world, while encouraging travel to regional destinations and working toward sustainable tourism,” JNTO wrote.

World.title: Move quickly and bravely in the Okinawa killing case — or else
World.content:
Like many readers, this writer was shocked by the news this past weekend of the alleged murder of a Japanese woman in Okinawa by a U.S. Marine.

While the investigation is still ongoing, the Japanese government has lodged a protest with the United States. On social media, the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo released a comment to the effect that it “extend(s) our sincere condolences to the victim’s family,” and acknowledged that “an investigation is under way to determine the facts of the case (in which) the United States is communicating and cooperating with the government of Japan and local authorities.”

It is unlikely that tensions will easily dissipate, however. The timing of the heinous tragedy was particularly unfortunate. An extraordinary session of the national parliament was set to begin on Oct. 5, only days after the incident, and the new administration of Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja had just assumed office shortly before, on Sept. 30.

World.title: Man arrested after red paint splashed at joint office of ‘unhelpful’ lawmakers
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested a man for allegedly splashing red paint at the joint office of two lawmakers, accusing them of being unhelpful.

A source said on Thursday that police arrested a 66-year-old man over the incident at the shared office of Kowloon East lawmaker Bill Tang Ka-piu and insurance-sector legislator Chan Pui-leung.

The force said it received a report at 6.40am from a security guard at Sau Mau Ping Estate that red paint had been splashed at an office in the estate’s Sau Chi House.

Officers made the arrest after reviewing surveillance footage that captured the act.

World.title: Helper arrested for allegedly slapping 5-year-old boy after he refuses to eat
World.content:
Hong Kong police have arrested a foreign domestic helper for allegedly slapping a five-year-old boy who refused to eat his meal at a Kowloon City flat.

Police received a report at about 11.57pm on Wednesday from the boy’s mother, who said her son had been ill-treated by her 37-year-old Filipino helper at their home at 97 Hau Wong Road.

Police said the woman checked the flat’s CCTV footage after her son told her he had been slapped by the helper when she returned home.

The footage showed the helper hitting the boy with her hand at around 9pm on Wednesday while feeding him, after he refused to eat his meal.

World.title: Will Huanggang Port opening boost spending at Shenzhen’s border retail shops?
World.content:
Retail businesses in Shenzhen are gearing up for the imminent opening of the revamped Huanggang Port at the border Hong Kong shares with mainland China, but some fear the area still lacks commercial appeal to make travellers stay.

After six years of redevelopment, the expanded checkpoint is due to open on October 12, according to a source. It will adopt the “joint inspection” model for immigration clearance, which is expected to cut the previous clearance time from about 30 minutes to five minutes.

Authorities have said the port will initially be able to handle 100,000 passenger trips a day, with capacity potentially rising to 300,000 in the future.

The Bosen Dental clinic opened a new branch across from the new facility in August. Its other branches are also located near border crossings such as Futian and Liantang, as well as one near Shenzhen North railway station.

World.title: Boy, 13, rescued after climbing onto air-conditioning unit to escape fire in flat
World.content:
Hong Kong firefighters have rescued a 13-year-old boy who climbed out a window onto the air-conditioning unit to escape a fire that broke out in his flat, while his mother has been arrested on suspicion of child neglect.

Police received reports at 7.54pm on Wednesday that a fire had broken out in a flat at Tsui To House, one of the blocks of Tsui Ping (North) Estate in Kwun Tong.

Online footage showed the boy, wearing only his underwear, climbing out of a window and onto the condenser unit as thick black smoke filled the flat.

Firefighters deployed a ladder to reach the boy and pulled him to safety. Around 70 residents were evacuated. The blaze was extinguished at about 8.25pm.

World.title: Mainland Chinese arrivals beat last year’s ‘golden week’ figures despite shorter holiday
World.content:
Mainland Chinese visitor arrivals in Hong Kong during the entire National Day “golden week” holiday exceeded the government’s forecast and surpassed last year’s total despite the break being one day shorter, with major mall and hotel operators also reporting brisk business.

The city recorded more than 1.42 million mainland visitor arrivals during the seven-day holiday, exceeding the government’s forecast of 1.29 million, according to Immigration Department figures.

More than 1.4 million mainland visitors arrived during the same holiday last year, when the break lasted eight days, from October 1 to 8.

Echo Huang Shaomei, executive director and CEO of New World Development, said footfall at the group’s flagship K11 Musea mall reached a record for a National Day golden week holiday, while tourist spending rose by 26 per cent year on year.

World.title: 24 luxury houses at One Stanley sold amid probe into alleged construction defects
World.content:
Two dozen luxury houses at One Stanley have been sold since Hong Kong authorities launched an investigation into alleged structural defects in March, with buyers including local and international businesspeople.

The transactions have prompted experts to call for stronger homebuyer protections, including implementing a mandatory period for buyers to rescind contracts when statutory violations are discovered.

The South China Morning Post learned that 24 transactions were recorded at One Stanley between March and September. The government launched a probe into construction quality at the development in March.

Lingnan University Professor Yau Yung, a surveyor who researches building illegality, urged stronger consumer protections for first-hand property buyers.

World.title: More than 300 hopefuls sign up for Hong Kong’s Election Committee poll
World.content:
More than 300 people signed up for Hong Kong’s Election Committee poll as the nomination period opened on Wednesday, vying for seats on the body that chooses the city’s leader.

The nomination period for committee subsectors for the November 22 election will run until October 20. The 1,500-member body will select Hong Kong’s next chief executive in March next year.

The Registration and Electoral Office received 305 nominations for candidacy on Wednesday. It also received two nominations from designated bodies proposing members for the Election Committee.

Registered subsector voters will elect up to 982 representatives to the committee. They will join 362 ex officio members and 156 members nominated by designated bodies.

World.title: Hong Kong and Indonesia can deepen green finance ties, Jakarta envoy says
World.content:
Hong Kong and Indonesia can deepen cooperation in green finance as their ties strengthen, the country’s special envoy for international trade has said, adding that the city’s common law expertise can support the nation’s efforts to attract family offices.

Hong Kong also played a vital role as a conduit channelling mainland China investments to Asean, Mari Elka Pangestu told reporters before delivering a lecture at the University of Hong Kong on Wednesday.

Pangestu is the Indonesian president’s special envoy for international trade and multilateral cooperation, as well as vice-chairwoman of the country’s National Economic Council.

Following efforts by the Hong Kong government to tap the Asean market, ties between the city and the bloc had prospered, she said, noting the region was the city’s second-largest trading partner.

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.title: The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019096/The New Upgrade for Concert Fans in China: Rent More Zoom
World.content:
With hundreds of concerts scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, some fans found the cheapest way to upgrade a seat was to rent a better camera phone.

For about 100 to 200 yuan ($15 to $30) a day, concertgoers can rent flagship smartphones with powerful telephoto cameras that pull distant performers into clearer view, a useful option when high demand leaves fans seated far from the stage and professional cameras and long lenses are often barred from venues.

On Chinese rental platform Renrenzu and Xianyu, a secondhand marketplace owned by Chinese tech giant Alibaba, some flagship phones are listed as “concert essentials.”

One Renrenzu ad touted a “200-megapixel telephoto, crystal clear — even the nosebleed seats feel VIP,” while the platform has also offered concert ticket reimbursements through prize draws.

The phones on offer are among the latest flagships from Chinese smartphone makers such as vivo and OPPO, with high-resolution telephoto cameras, image stabilization, and, in some cases, detachable lens kits that extend their reach.

A vivo X300 Ultra bundled with a telephoto lens, for example, rents for about 215 yuan for one day, while a two-day rental brings the average daily cost down to about 125 yuan. Other popular models include OPPO’s Find X10 Pro Max, which packs three 200-megapixel rear cameras and is advertised as supporting up to “20x lossless zoom” with its official telephoto kit.

Such high-end models typically sell for about 5,000 to 8,000 yuan, while official telephoto lens kits can add another 1,000 to 2,000 yuan, making a short rental far cheaper for fans who only want the extra reach for one concert.

Online, concertgoers are comparing phones and lens attachments, posting photos from the stands, and swapping tips on which setups work best from distant seats.

Liu Hang, who attended Taiwan singer Steve Chou’s concert at Beijing Workers’ Stadium, told Time Finance that he brought a Ruiying Z10 camera module and telephoto attachment made by Chinese tech giant Huawei into the venue. “I had a 580-yuan ticket, but with the ‘Huawei cannon,’ it felt like a 1,680-yuan seat,” he said.

Another social media user, who said he had attended nearly 100 concerts, compared several phones and camera setups for live shows. He said such phones were easy to carry, worked well for close-up shots, and had a dedicated stage mode that automatically adjusted exposure, though adding a telephoto attachment made it tiring to hold through an entire concert.

Renrenzu said orders for concert-related equipment jumped 388% year on year over the summer, far outpacing a 67% rise in short-term rentals overall. A total of 257 concerts were scheduled across China during the National Day holiday, according to Alibaba’s entertainment data platform Lighthouse.

Chen Shenyu, a manager at consulting firm China Insights Consultancy, told Time Finance that smartphone photography was becoming less about simply recording daily life and more about performing well in specific situations. Concerts are especially challenging because fans may be seated far from the stage, lighting changes constantly, and they are often shooting handheld photos and video.

That also makes concerts a natural showcase for smartphone makers, Chen said. If consumers increasingly reach for telephoto cameras at sporting events, on trips, and during family activities, demand for the same high-end imaging features could extend well beyond concerts.

(Header image: Posts show concertgoers using flagship camera phones with telephoto attachments to capture performers from the stands. From Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.title: China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019095/China’s Golden Week Crowds Reach Smaller Cities and Counties
World.content:
Chinese travelers are increasingly stringing together multiple destinations during the weeklong National Day holiday, boosting mid-holiday air travel and drawing more visitors to smaller cities and counties.

More than 20% of air travelers booked flights to two or more destinations during the holiday, which runs from Oct. 1 to Oct. 7, according to online travel platform Tongcheng Travel. Demand for flights in the middle of the holiday rose 35% from a year earlier.

Smaller destinations were among the biggest beneficiaries of the holiday travel boom, with data from travel platform Qunar showing that its 10 top trending scenic spots were all in county-level destinations.

In Qilian County in northwestern Qinghai province, which has a population of about 50,000, more than 100,000 tourists arrived on Oct. 3, filling local hotels and prompting authorities to house nearly 500 stranded visitors in school dormitories as temperatures fell to minus 4 degrees Celsius and snow covered nearby mountaintops.

The county’s culture and tourism department received more than 400 calls for help in seven hours, according to local authorities. Posts on Xiaohongshu, the lifestyle app also known as RedNote, showed tourists searching for rooms as hotels across the county filled up.

One traveler told domestic outlet Jimu News that he spent the afternoon and evening searching major booking platforms after arriving in Qilian from Xi’an but could not find a room. After seeing a notice from local tourism authorities, he called for help and was assigned a school dormitory room shared by four people, with new bedding provided.

Wansui Mountain Martial Arts City in central Henan province also struggled with heavy crowds, repeatedly capping admissions and suspending same-day ticket sales after interest surged 22-fold from a year earlier.

Many travelers were also going farther and staying away longer. According to Tongcheng Travel, people on multi-city trips visited an average of 1.2 more cities than in 2025, with Chengdu, Suzhou, and Wuhan among the busiest transfer hubs.

More than 70% of multi-city travelers booked both natural and cultural attractions, suggesting that many were combining different types of destinations within a single itinerary.

Interest in six- to 10-day groups and customized tours to destinations including Xinjiang, Sichuan, Yunnan, and Guizhou rose more than 60% on Tongcheng from a year earlier. Couples and families accounted for more than half of those bookings.

(Header image: Tourists visit the Zhuo’er Mountain Scenic Area in Qilian County, Qinghai province, Oct. 1, 2026. VCG)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.title: Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019094/Feathered Dinosaur From China Points to Another Path to Flight
World.content:
Researchers have identified a new species of feathered dinosaur from northeastern China whose anatomy suggests that birds and their close dinosaur relatives developed flight-related features along separate evolutionary paths.

The fossil — a nearly complete 57-centimeter skeleton with some feathers preserved — dates to the Early Cretaceous, more than 100 million years ago. Discovered by a local farmer in Liaoning province’s Jianchang County, it was donated to Hebei Geo University’s museum in 2023.

Researchers from the Chinese Academy of Geological Sciences and Hebei Geo University, working with colleagues from around the world, named the species Norellraptor barsboldi in a study published Sept. 29 in the journal Nature Communications.

The fossil adds evidence to a long-running debate over whether birds and their close dinosaur relatives inherited flight-related anatomy from a common ancestor or developed it separately.

Norellraptor belongs to the microraptorines, a group of small, feathered predators closely related to birds. Fossils of some members show long feathers on both their forelimbs and hindlimbs, suggesting they were adapted to move through the air.

The researchers compared Norellraptor with other fossils and found that roughly 30% of the anatomical changes they traced through microraptorine evolution also appeared in the bird lineage. In microraptorines, finger bones shortened before wrist and hand bones fused and the breastbone lengthened. In the bird lineage, those changes appeared in the opposite order.

Growth marks in Norellraptor’s forearm bone suggest it was at least 3 years old and still growing when it died, an age estimate the researchers factored into their comparisons with other fossils.

The different sequences challenge the idea that microraptorines and birds inherited the same flight apparatus or followed a shared pattern of development, the researchers said. They argue that the similar features arose independently in the two lineages.

(Header image: Left and right: Fossilized limb bones of Norellraptor barsboldi. Center: An artist’s reconstruction of the species by Zhang Chuang. From Nature)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.title: The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019069/The Transsion Story: How a Chinese Firm Conquered Africa’s Tech Market
World.content:
Few people in China have heard of Transsion Holdings, but hundreds of millions of people across the Global South use its phones.

The firm, headquartered in China’s southern tech hub of Shenzhen, has risen from obscurity to become a dominant player in Africa, where it makes nearly half of all phones bought on the continent every year, beating competition from Samsung, Apple, and domestic Chinese giants like Xiaomi and Huawei Technologies. It also holds more than a 10% share of the Southeast Asian and Middle Eastern markets.

Transsion’s rise has been all the more impressive given its humble origins: unlike many of its rivals, it hasn’t benefited from massive funding or market-leading technology.

Instead, it has built a global business almost from scratch — a decades-long journey spanning Shenzhen’s knock-off electronics markets, scrappy networks of African “suitcase entrepreneurs,” and years of careful, locally targeted innovation.

Lu Miao, a media anthropologist and assistant professor at Hong Kong’s Lingnan University, charts this fascinating tale in her book “The Transsion Approach: Translating Chinese Mobile Technology in Africa.”

Based on years of research, it explores the secrets to the company’s success in the Global South — and how its strategy offers an alternative to the “blitzscaling” model favored by many tech startups in both Silicon Valley and China.

In this interview, Lu talks to Sixth Tone and Zhang Lin, an associate professor at the University of New Hampshire whose research focuses on tech innovation, about the Transsion story and what it teaches us about global technology flows. The interview has been edited for brevity and clarity.

Sixth Tone: Your book explores how Transsion grew from the informal global phone market that emerged during the 1990s and early 2000s, when African and Arab traders began traveling to southern China to buy cheap knock-off — or shanzhai — handsets. What is the company’s connection to that era?

Lu Miao: Shanzhai phones were extremely common in the early 2000s. The Huaqiangbei electronics market in Shenzhen was a major hub, while Chungking Mansions in Hong Kong was an important gateway for knock-off phones going overseas.

The main buyers were small traders from Africa, the Middle East, and Southeast Asia. Some scholars call them “suitcase entrepreneurs” because they would arrive with a few suitcases, buy phones, take them home, and distribute them to smaller towns.

By the time Transsion was founded in 2006, shanzhai phones had already swept through many African countries. On the one hand, they met the basic communication needs of many low-income users; on the other, they damaged the reputation of Chinese phones, which African consumers came to associate with cheapness and poor quality.

When I went to Ghana in 2019, I found that many of Transsion’s national distributors had started out-selling secondhand and shanzhai phones bought from traders in Chungking Mansions. After partnering with Transsion, they gradually became formal agents for a multinational company.

These local African distributors linked the shanzhai era to the Transsion era. The personal connections and distribution networks they had built up played a major role in helping Transsion establish itself.

There is also continuity in design. Features such as dual-SIM support and large batteries originated in the shanzhai phone ecosystem and were later adapted for African markets. Dual SIMs, for example, help users avoid costly cross-network calls in countries with patchy network coverage.

But Transsion also represented a break from that era. First, the phone business became more formalized and institutionalized. These distributors set up trading companies of their own, and their relationships with Transsion became governed by more formal contracts.

Second, Transsion did not want to make quick money and leave, as sellers had done in the shanzhai era; it wanted to build a brand and stay for the long term. That is why it invested heavily in its after-sales service network.

Shanzhai wasn’t simply about one manufacturer producing copycat phones. It was an ecosystem: factories, supply chains, designers, distributors ... Transsion grew out of that ecosystem, but also moved beyond the shanzhai model of the time.

Sixth Tone: Looking at the bigger picture, how has Africa’s digital communications sector evolved over time, and how has that affected Chinese companies like Transsion?

Lu: Take Ghana as an example. The country’s telecommunications companies were originally state-owned. But in the 1980s and 1990s, the country had to turn to the World Bank and International Monetary Fund for loans to deal with ongoing economic and debt crises. One condition of these loans was structural adjustment, which meant privatizing the telecom sector.

After the reforms, one common outcome was a widening urban-rural gap. Commercial operators were reluctant to serve low-margin rural areas, where costs were high and consumer spending was low, so infrastructure such as base stations remained concentrated in cities.

The needs of rural and low-income communities were overlooked during the reforms, and after the state retreated, it did not step back in to meet those needs. That meant many people could only afford cheap Chinese shanzhai phones.

Transsion stepped into this market, offering affordable feature — or “dumb” — phones that were tailored to African users’ needs. It optimized its models for areas with sparse base-station coverage, making them better at picking up weak signals than many other phones. Electricity supply could also be unreliable in rural areas, so the long battery life of both shanzhai and Transsion phones was another important advantage.

Zhang Lin: Against this backdrop, you argue that we should understand global technology flows in terms of “technology translation” rather than “technology transfer.” What does this framework help us understand about how technology moves between countries?

Lu: I don’t really like the concept of “technology transfer” because it frames the process as one-way: advanced Western societies export technology to less-developed non-Western societies in order to help them develop. But the endpoint of development in this model is always Western modernity.

It also assumes that technology is neutral and fixed, as if transferring technology alone will solve social problems and generate economic growth. Yet many aid projects failed precisely because they transferred equipment without transferring the knowledge, skills, and institutional environment around it.

That is why I used the concept of “technology translation.” When a technology enters a new context, it is often reinterpreted, adjusted, and transformed. Examining the context and process of how technology is translated allows us to see how knowledge moves, and the politics embedded in the process.

Transsion did not simply take phones made in China and move them unchanged to Africa; its products were continually redesigned through their encounter with local markets. Chinese engineers and product managers, Ghanaian promoters, distributors, and repair workers all became “translators” in this process.

For example, Transsion’s dual- and multi-SIM functions were not simply extra hardware features; they responded to high communications costs, uneven network coverage, and users’ need to switch between operators. Cameras optimized for darker skin tones respond to the fact that imaging technologies have historically treated white skin as the default.

These features were not simply invented by an individual designer. They emerged through interactions among the company, users, distribution channels, and repair networks.

Zhang: You describe Transsion’s business strategy as “deep plowing” and contrast it with Silicon Valley’s “blitzscaling” model. How are they different?

Lu: “Blitzscaling” was a widely celebrated model in Silicon Valley from the mid-2010s onward. Popularized by (American internet entrepreneur) Reid Hoffman, it relies on large amounts of capital to expand rapidly, prioritizing speed over efficiency.

The idea is to capture the market first and then achieve winner-takes-all dominance. Facebook, Uber, and Airbnb are typical examples, as are Chinese companies such as ride-hailing firm Didi.

At its core, blitzscaling involves a deliberately inefficient use of capital. Companies sustain themselves through venture capital, and much of that money is wasted. It is a game only a small number of players can afford. Most fail; the few that survive can end up monopolizing the market.

“Deep plowing” is more commonly seen in the Global South. It is slower and depends much more on local knowledge and relationship networks. The term originally comes from agriculture, referring to a labor-intensive mode of production that requires long-term investment and continual care.

In business and technology, I use it to describe a market-driven, labor-intensive approach in which a company continuously interacts with local markets and adjusts its products and business strategies in response to feedback.

In many cases, this model is adopted out of necessity. Transsion chose to work deeply in rural markets overlooked by Western capital largely because it lacked large pools of capital and core technologies. It often had to create room for itself by understanding markets in much finer detail.

(Header image: An entrance to the Circle Market in Accra, Ghana, 2019. Courtesy of Lu Miao)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.title: China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019093/China’s Esports Haul Includes an Asian Games First for Women
World.content:
As the esports competition at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, came to a close Friday, China finished atop the medal table with three golds and one silver after entering four of the 11 events. Its final gold came in Identity V, where victory over host Japan made 20-year-old Mu Xinyue the first woman to win an Asian Games esports title.

China won gold in Naraka: Bladepoint and Honor of Kings, took silver in Game for Peace, the Chinese version of PUBG Mobile, and closed its campaign with the Identity V gold. All four games were developed by Chinese companies.

Mu was one of only 14 women among more than 500 esports athletes registered for the Games, where competitions are not divided by gender. She was the only woman on China’s 23-member esports squad.

Mu competes under the name Tao Wan’an as a survivor in Identity V, an asymmetrical multiplayer game developed by Chinese tech giant NetEase that made its Asian Games debut this year. In each round, teams play two halves, taking turns as four survivors trying to escape and one hunter trying to catch them. Points are awarded based on how many survivors escape or are caught.

China and Japan were level after the first two rounds. China pulled ahead in the third and, after another draw in the fourth, secured the title during the first half of the fifth round.

Mu joined professional esports club Beijing Weibo Gaming at 18 and is now the only woman with a starting role in Identity V’s professional league.

According to domestic media reports, she decided to pursue professional gaming at 16 but could not win her family’s support. She moved out of her family home in the eastern province of Shandong and supported herself while practicing with Mechanic, her signature character, eventually becoming the server’s top-ranked player in that role.

“I had never even dared to imagine this scene,” Mu wrote on the Chinese microblogging platform Weibo on Oct. 1, after winning gold.

South Korea won the final esports gold Friday by defeating Chinese Taipei in League of Legends. Japan and South Korea each finished with two golds, with Japan taking second place in the esports medal table because it won more silvers.

Esports first appeared at the Asian Games as a demonstration sport in Jakarta in 2018, then became a medal sport in Hangzhou in 2023. China won four golds and one bronze at those Games, which featured seven esports events.

China had collected 155 golds, 71 silvers, and 64 bronzes across the Games by the end of Oct. 1, with three days of competition remaining. It led both the gold-medal and overall medal counts and was on course to top the standings for the 12th consecutive edition, extending a run that began in 1982.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Mu Xinyue at the 2026 Asian Games in Nagoya, Japan, Sept. 30, 2026. From Weibo)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.title: When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019082/When China’s Family Heirlooms Need More Than Tape, Glue, or Luck
World.content:
SHANGHAI — “Great-grandma, your head seems to be a little loose,” Yu Mingrui jokes as he examines an ancestral portrait depicting nine members of a family across three generations.

The 28-year-old Shanghai restorer was commissioned to repair the Qing dynasty (1644–1911) portrait by a descendant of the family in Ningbo, in eastern China’s Zhejiang province, which had been passed down through generations. Yu filmed the process and posted it on Douyin, China’s version of TikTok.

Amid the portrait’s cracks and damage, Yu found clean, deliberate cuts around one woman’s painted head, suggesting the section was once removed and replaced.

Yu commented that the painter might have added the faces after painting the bodies. But viewers offered their own explanations. Some hypothesized the painter had covered up a mistake and repainted the face. Others suggested that descendants of a male ancestor’s concubine had altered the portrait to replace his wife’s image.

The answer may never be known. But the mystery drew widespread attention online, with videos about the painting receiving more than 100 million views and likes across Chinese social media platforms.

On Chinese social media, independent restorers like Yu are demonstrating how damaged paintings, old books, and family records are taken apart, repaired, and preserved.

“A lot of people told me that they simply didn’t know that something damaged could actually be restored before watching my videos,” Yu told Sixth Tone.

The objects brought to independent restorers include ancestral portraits, genealogies, old books, and calligraphy passed down through families and kept in homes rather than institutions.

Often made from paper or silk, these objects are vulnerable to moisture, insects, light, and age. Even when damaged, they can retain names, images, and other details about the families that preserved them.

For restorers like Yu, the videos can also connect that work with owners who might otherwise have left such objects damaged at home. Those commissions provide restorers with work and, in some cases, allow families to recover information from records that had become too fragile or damaged to read.

Face value

When the Qing-era ancestral portrait arrived at Yu’s studio, its ink had faded, its paper had become brittle, and its edges were torn. A patchwork of old advertising flyers held it together, promoting everything from cakes to real estate.

At 3.4 meters long and 1.2 meters wide, the portrait barely fits into the worktable at the center of Yu’s roughly 40-square-meter studio in Shanghai’s rural Songjiang District.

Yu turned the makeshift repairs into another joke for his viewers. Families in China traditionally honor deceased relatives with food and other offerings. The flyers, Yu joked, had given the painted ancestors a modern assortment of their own.

“Whatever the ancestors are missing, they can just take it from behind the painting,” he said.

Repairing the portrait, however, was a more exacting process. Yu said the restoration is divided into four broad stages: washing away dust and stains, removing the backing paper and remnants of earlier repairs, patching tears and holes with paper matching the original, and retouching missing colors and lines.

Each stage depends on the painting’s condition. Even washing it requires the restorer to decide whether to use hot or cold water, whether mold and stains require chemical treatment, and how much the paper can withstand. Chemicals can remove stains quickly, but excessive treatment can damage the paper or alter the painting itself.

“The real difficulty lies in the uncertainty,” Yu said. “A restorer’s experience gives you certainty at the beginning, serving as a safety net to deal with the uncertainty that appears in the process.”

The portrait took around three months to restore. Before treatment, Yu said, face-detection software picked up only three of the nine painted faces. Afterward, when he photographed the restored portrait, the software marked all nine faces on screen. Yu charges around 10,000 yuan ($1,493) for a painting of this size and complexity.

Yu began posting restoration videos while studying Chinese antique restoration in college. After graduating in 2021, he opened his own studio. His videos often begin with an unusual detail, a question about an object’s history, or a joke designed to catch attention.

“History isn’t only made up of famous paintings or nationally protected cultural relics,” he said. “It is also made up of these seemingly insignificant objects. As I restore them, I’m also helping to pass that culture on.”

Genealogies, ancestral portraits, and other family documents offer a view of the past that differs from official histories and local gazetteers, Zhang Yi, a historian at Shanghai Jiao Tong University, told Sixth Tone. Genealogies, for example, can record more than 1,000 people, while larger volumes can include tens of thousands, sometimes with birth and death dates.

“These materials greatly enrich our understanding of the lives and personal histories of ordinary people in Chinese history,” Zhang said.

The videos have also helped Yu turn restoration into a livelihood. His online following attracts commercial sponsorships, which now account for roughly half his income, he said. Many clients bring him just one family object in need of repair, but together, those individual commissions have allowed him to build his own customer base.

Paper trail

Beijing restorer Lian Chengchun also works mainly for private owners, from collectors to families preserving books passed down through generations.

Her videos offer them a first lesson in how to handle and preserve those objects at home, and can prompt people to take a second look at old records before the stories they carry disappear.

“I see little distinction between collections held by organizations and individuals,” Lian said. “Whether a book is restored by a public institution, an independent restorer or a private collector, the goal is the same: to preserve it for future generations.”

Books kept in private hands can arrive in almost any condition. Some have been patched with tape, glue, calendars, or whatever paper was available, repairs that may hold them together temporarily but can cause further and sometimes irreversible damage.

“Others were stored in plastic bags, where trapped moisture can encourage mold and decay,” said Lian, 38, who’s spent 18 years restoring old books by hand.

Before starting such work, Lian studies a book’s age and history, along with its paper, printing style, and other materials, which can vary across periods.

“Only then can I decide how best to repair it,” she said.

Cai Yadong came across Lian’s videos just when members of his clan in Jiaozhu Village, in southern China’s Guangdong province, needed help repairing a badly damaged genealogy.

In 2023, two elderly clan members handed Cai a 111-page genealogy dating to 1920. The wider Huazhou Cai clan today numbers about 20,000 descendants across roughly 110 villages, but Jiaozhu’s own records had almost completely disappeared, leaving residents unsure how their branch fit into the family or even who its founding ancestor was.

“When I first saw it, it was barely recognizable,” Cai, secretary of the Huazhou Cai clan association, said. “The pages were mixed together. Some had been burned, and years of damage had left the book extremely fragile.”

After contacting Lian, Cai flew to Beijing to deliver it himself rather than risk shipping it. “It was simply too valuable to risk any accidents,” he said.

Restoring the genealogy took Lian nearly a year and a half. Because of the genealogy’s age and poor condition, the restoration required careful, piece-by-piece work, Lian said.

“We try to repair it in a way that preserves its original appearance, while retaining as much of the surviving text as possible,” she said.

Lian compared numerous samples before selecting restoration paper that matched the original pages in color and texture. She repaired torn fragments and holes one by one, reinforcing sections where the original characters remained legible.

“Saving each character felt like picking up the brush where the Cai ancestors had left off,” Lian said. “Each page I uncovered felt like a dialogue with people from hundreds of years ago.”

When the work was completed, the volume showed that more than 30 pages were devoted to Jiaozhu, detailing family members and major events.

One entry showed how Jiaozhu’s branch fit into the wider Huazhou Cai clan and identified its founding ancestor as Cai Wende. The restored volume also helped three other villages establish their own connections to the clan.

“If our generation does not do this, the family memory may be gone after another one or two generations,” Cai said. “Once it is lost, it will be very difficult to recover.”

Just weeks before the genealogy surfaced, Jiaozhu had held a ceremony to renovate an ancestral tomb. Villagers knew it as the tomb of their founding ancestor but no longer knew his identity. Once the book was restored, they added Cai Wende’s name to the tomb’s inscription.

Cai described the timing as uncanny. “Whenever we talk about it, we all get goosebumps,” he said.

Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: Yu Mingrui at his studio in Shanghai, August 2026. Lü Xiao/Sixth Tone)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019092/Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.title: Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019092/Bug Bounty: Beijing Park Recruits Visitors Against Invasive Moth
World.content:
Beijing Wildlife Park has turned its fight against a surge of invasive caterpillars into a public contest, offering up to 10 park tickets to visitors who collect the heaviest haul each day. From Sept. 28 to 30, participants caught an estimated 120,000 larvae weighing a combined 18.5 kilograms.

The safari-style zoo on the capital’s southern outskirts announced the event with a call for “warriors” to battle a leaf-eating pest it dubbed the “forest food monster.” Initially scheduled for two days, the contest was extended through Oct. 7 after drawing strong interest and now runs throughout the weeklong National Day holiday.

Participants first register and receive a brief lesson on identifying the pest before staff hand out disposable gloves, food containers, and chopsticks. They search the park for larvae and submit their catches by 2:50 p.m., when staff weigh them and determine the day’s rankings. The captured caterpillars are destroyed rather than fed to the park’s animals.

Prizes are awarded each day based on the total weight collected. The first-place entry receives 10 park tickets, with five for second place and two for third. Everyone who participates receives a commemorative pin, while those finishing fourth through 10th also receive a themed headband.

Competition was stiff from the opening day. A visitor surnamed Liang collected about 4,000 caterpillars weighing 596.3 grams, filling six containers but finishing second. The winning entry came from a five-person team that brought in 1,069.5 grams, while third place went to a catch weighing 391.4 grams.

“The winners were a team of five and caught nearly twice as many as I did,” Liang, a pianist who has visited the park for a decade, told Beijing Daily. “I couldn’t keep up.”

Liang said there was no particular trick to catching the caterpillars, though she found more in less crowded parts of the park and in the shade beneath taller trees. “I brought my own plastic bottles and tweezers, which I found more convenient,” she said.

The winner on the second day, Zhang Hanfang, 18, collected 1.3 kilograms with a six-person team. A taxidermist who runs a studio specializing in insect, reptile, and bird specimens, he made the two-hour drive from neighboring Hebei province with a friend’s family the day after seeing the park’s announcement. The group shares an interest in natural science.

“There’s no secret,” Zhang told Sixth Tone. “Just keep your eyes on the trees and keep at it. It was intense and thrilling. The contest also satisfied our October itch to go bug hunting.”

A video about the contest posted on the lifestyle app Xiaohongshu, known in English as RedNote, received more than 31,000 likes and 1,400 comments. One commenter described the initiative as “crowdsourced debugging,” while a related hashtag on Weibo attracted nearly 3 million views.

In recent weeks, residents across Beijing have reported seeing fall webworm caterpillars — the larvae of an invasive moth native to North America — on sidewalks, balconies, and even people’s shoulders.

The city is experiencing the peak larval period of the pest’s third generation this year, with mature larvae descending from trees in search of sheltered places to pupate and survive the winter.

Yang Zhongqi, chief scientist at the Chinese Academy of Forestry, said the species is a major invasive pest that threatens more than 300 plant species, including forest and fruit trees, flowers, and crops.

“During severe infestations, the caterpillars can strip a tree of every leaf, damaging urban greenery and hindering the tree’s growth,” Yang said. “But they do not kill the tree.”

Beijing had released nearly 700 million parasitic wasps this year before beginning the release of another 400 million on Sept. 28. Harmless to people and pets, the wasps lay their eggs inside fall webworm pupae, preventing adult moths from emerging.

Yang Sihan, head of monitoring and forecasting at the Beijing Gardening and Greening Resources Protection Center, attributed this year’s surge to a cyclical pattern of severe outbreaks, warmer winters, and frequent summer rain that disrupted spraying.

At sites monitored over five consecutive years, the survival rate of overwintering pupae rose from 65.3% in 2023 to 84.2% this year, Yang Sihan said. Heavy rain also left fewer clear days for spraying and washed away pesticides after they were applied. A single female moth can lay 300 to 600 eggs and sometimes as many as 2,000.



Editor: Apurva.

(Header image: A participant tries to catch a caterpillar at Beijing Wildlife Park, September 2026. From @北京野生动物园 on Xiaohongshu)

World.id: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019091/In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.title: In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.link: https://www.sixthtone.com/news/1019091/In Photos: China Begins Its Weeklong National Day Holiday
World.content:
China’s weeklong National Day holiday began Thursday, extending a travel period that started with the Mid-Autumn Festival less than a week earlier and fueling demand for long-distance trips at home and abroad.

The Mid-Autumn Festival, traditionally an occasion for family reunions, fell on Sept. 25 this year. National Day, which marks the founding of the People’s Republic of China in 1949, followed on Oct. 1 and began a weeklong public holiday. With only three working days between them, people who took those days off could combine the two breaks into a 13-day holiday ending Oct. 7.

Chinese airlines are expected to carry 31.19 million passengers from Sept. 25 to Oct. 7, up 3.6% from the same period last year, according to the Civil Aviation Administration of China. Bookings for domestic flights covering more than 2,000 kilometers rose about 14%, according to aviation data provider Umetrip.

International flight bookings for the period were up 22.5% year on year as of Sept. 24, the CAAC said. Flights to Thailand, Malaysia, Vietnam, and Laos increased by about 20%, while those to Britain, Germany, and Spain rose by about 15%.

Here are snapshots from the extended holiday period across China.

World.title: Mark Villar joins Senate majority bloc
World.content:
(1st UPDATE) Mark Villar’s move comes as the Office of the Ombudsman announced graft complaints against his family over PrimeWater contracts, and amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte before senator-judges

MANILA, Philippines — Senator Mark Villar has joined the Senate majority bloc, Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente “Tito” Sotto III confirmed Thursday, October 8.

“Well, apparently,” Sotto told reporters in an ambush interview when asked about Villar’s transfer.

“We’re glad because we’re all loaded with work… We have the impeachment, legislative [duties], and budget [deliberations], so it would be better if we have more members,” he said.

Sotto said he was informed of the change only earlier in the day and that Senate Majority Floor Leader Juan Miguel “Migz” Zubiri coordinated Villar’s transfer.

The Senate held its final plenary session on Thursday before going on a break from October 9 to November 9.

During the session, Zubiri moved for the election of Villar as a member of the Commission on Appointments (CA) under the majority bloc. Villar was also elected chairperson of the Senate committee on public works and highways, replacing Sotto.

Asked if Villar had formally joined the majority, Zubiri said: “Yes, we just elected him to the CA and public works committee as part of the majority.”

With Villar’s transfer, the majority bloc now has 14 members, while the minority has 10. His sister, Senator Camille Villar, remains with the minority bloc.

Villar’s move came as the Office of the Ombudsman announced graft complaints against members of the Villar family over contracts involving their firm, PrimeWater. It also comes amid the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, which will be decided by senator-judges.

Asked about the decision of Villar to jump ship to the majority bloc, Senator Bong Go, a member of the minority bloc, said in a media interview that they respect his decision.

Responding to questions, Go said that they remain on good terms with Villar. “We respect each other,” he said. – Rappler.com

World.title: Why does affordable connectivity modernization matter for integrated resorts (IRs)?
World.content:
Editor’s note: This press release is sponsored by Trends and Technologies and was handled by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the publishing of this piece.

Technology-enabled business services and solutions provider Trends & Technologies, Inc. (Trends), together with global connectivity technology leader ReadyLinks, recently hosted a joint event, “Modernizing Networks Without Rebuilding Infrastructure: Smarter Connectivity for High-Demand Environments,” held last September 10 at Solaire in Parañaque City.

The forum introduced Trends and ReadyLinks’s Smart Integrated Resort Solution, an integrated methodology toward modernizing network capabilities for integrated resorts (IRs) and hospitality businesses with a strong emphasis on connectivity, visibility and management, and operational intelligence, and without the need for expensive overhauls.

The Smart Integrated Resort Solution instead focuses on building around existing infrastructure investments, on long-term scalability and ease of deployment with minimal disruption for accommodating growing connectivity requirements.

“The underlying outcome s we’re trying to achieve for IR organizations, in this modernization thrust [with Smart Integrated Resort], is stronger connectivity, more manageable operations, and of course, serviceability for future technologies, without the need overhauls that clients may not be ready for, currently,” said ReadyLinks CEO Larry Synstelien. Synstelien added that IR organizations often move toward having these key improvements:

Better visibility across properties

More consistent connectivity across environments, including gaming environments

Simplified management and operations

Support for future technologies and services

And all the above modernization goals should be achieved with reduced disruption during transformation. According to Trends’ converged access infrastructure group head Mark Anthony Castillo, disruption is a key consideration in the Smart Integrated Resort approach.

“Disruption and downtime are crucial consideration s in this approach, as an organization could lose up to $15,000 a minute – that is the average in 2026 for the Global 2000, but the loss is much greater for integrated resorts, especially during peak operational windows. With this threat in mind, our approach should be subtle and most cost-effective,” said Castillo.

“We’re glad we’ve found a strong partner in Trends for the implementation of this approach, which we have developed for the unique needs of the sector, zeroing in on their networks. With our technology, experience in this sector, along with the breadth of expertise of Trends, we’re confident we could achieve these goals for our clients, while also achieving lower costs,” Synstelien said.

The joint forum attests to Trends and ReadyLinks’ commitment to bringing stronger network capabilities to IR operators in the country. In an environment where connectivity is supporting more needs, modernization is crucial for improving hotel and guest services, surveillance and security, retail, dining and event spaces, and gaming and facility operations. – Rappler.com

World.title: ‘Floating’ money: Did the Dutertes use manager’s checks to hide wealth off bank balances?
World.content:
IN AND OUT. Boxes containing evidences lie on the floor before the start of Day 24 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte on September 14, 2026.

'Repeatedly issuing and cancelling manager’s checks around year-end could therefore raise red flags of reverse window dressing, making bank balances appear smaller without actually reducing wealth,' says global tax policy expert Mon Abrea

A mischievously simple theory put forward by the prosecution: Could you move tens of millions of pesos out of a bank account through manager’s checks before year-end, leave the checks unused, and make the account balance look smaller without actually letting go of your wealth?

That is why P96 million in “floating” manager’s checks drew so much attention during the lengthy examination of Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI) records involving Vice President Sara Duterte and her father, former president Rodrigo Duterte, on Wednesday, October 7.

BPI division head for central Metro Manila branches Marwin Galvez confirmed that two joint time deposits worth around P41 million and P55 million were later converted into manager’s checks.

“A similar time deposit that became a manager’s check in the amount of P55 million was also running during the same years, simultaneously with this P41 million. It’s a total of P96 million,” private prosecutor James Bryan Ibrahim Alih said.

Manager’s checks for ‘reverse window dressing’

A quick refresher on how manager’s checks (MCs) work. Once a manager’s check is issued, the amount is taken out of the customer’s deposit account and moved to the bank’s settlement account to ensure the check is funded. While that check remains outstanding, the money won’t be reflected in the customer’s bank balance anymore. If it goes unused, the purchaser may later return the unutilized check and get the money back.

Alih called the money “floating,” and when asked by Senator-judge Panfilo Lacson if the prosection was trying to establish a “pattern aimed at proving concealment,” Alih said yes.

Senator-judge Tito Sotto even had a more colorful name for the financial sleight of hand. Citing a banker friend, he said the supposed scheme was called “tinikling” a Philippine folk dance where a dancer goes in and out of moving bamboo poles, although the BPI division head himself said he had never heard the term used in banking.

Play Video

But is it actually normal for wealthy clients to buy large manager’s checks and then leave them unused?

Reverse window dressing?

Rappler asked a senior executive in the wealth management sector about the practice generally. The executive said clients have different reasons for getting manager’s checks, but “usually it’s deposited or paid immediately.”

Rappler has also asked a high-ranking Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas official about safeguards for manager’s checks that remain outstanding for long periods. The official said they were willing to comment, but Rappler had not received a response as of writing.

Global tax policy expert Mon Abrea was even clearer.

“No, it is not common practice. Manager’s checks are generally issued for specific payments, not to temporarily park funds,” he told Rappler.

From an accounting perspective, if an outstanding check has not actually paid anyone and the purchaser still retains ownership or a recoverable claim, Abrea said the amount remains an asset even though the deposit account has already been debited.

“Repeatedly issuing and cancelling manager’s checks around year-end could therefore raise red flags of reverse window dressing, making bank balances appear smaller without actually reducing wealth,” he said.

If a manager’s check paid a loan, it should reflect in the reduced amount of liability. If it bought an investment, the asset changes form. So what happens if a manager’s check remains unencashed?

“Substance over form – it is still cash to be added back to bank balance so sa (in the) total cash, it should still be there,” he told Rappler.

All this goes back to the discussion of the Vice President’s Statements of Assets, Liabilities and Net Worth (SALN).

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said he checked Sara Duterte’s 2010 and 2011 SALNs – back when she was still vice mayor and then mayor of Davao City – and could not find the P96 million in joint time deposits reflected there.

Play Video

The defense, however, stressed that the documents presented in court carried Rodrigo Duterte’s signature, not Sara’s. Her lawyer Michael Poa said the Vice President did not recall the account, while BPI testimony showed her father could transact on the joint account without her participation. (READ: Is Sara Duterte unaware of BPI accounts with father Rodrigo?)

This was actually not the first time manager’s checks came up in the BPI money trail. Several MCs also appeared in records tied to a separate controversy involving BPI’s request for the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC) to delete 13 transaction reports after what the bank called a “system bug” inflated transaction records involving Sara Duterte’s husband, Manases Carpio. The inaccurate amounts triggered covered transaction reports. – Rappler.com

World.title: At least 32 killed in Ukraine, Zelenskyy condemns one of Russia’s most ‘vile strikes’
World.content:
DESTRUCTION. A resident reacts, at the site of an apartment building damaged during a Russian drone strike, amid Russia's attack on Ukraine, in Kyiv, Ukraine October 7, 2026.

'This is the kind of birthday present that Putin gave himself: the killing of children, the killing of people,' says Ukraine President Zelenskyy, noting that the attacks coincided with the Russian leader's birthday

KYIV, Ukraine – Russia pounded Ukraine with waves of missiles and drones in one of its most “vile strikes” on Wednesday, October 7, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said, killing at least 32 people, including children, and damaging industrial facilities and energy infrastructure.

The heaviest losses were in Pryluky in Ukraine’s northern Chernihiv region, where a Russian missile destroyed a five-story residential building.

Ukraine’s emergency service said on Telegram that the death toll in Pryluky has risen to 22 as of Thursday morning and two more bodies were discovered following a Russian air strike on an apartment building in the capital Kyiv, taking the toll there to four dead.

Interior Minister Ivan Vyhivskyi has earlier put the country-wide death toll at 28, including 20 people who died in the Pryluky attack, including five children.

On Wednesday evening, prosecutors in Kyiv said falling debris from a drone killed two people in a suburb.

Zelenskyy said that 100 people had been injured throughout the country.

The President noted that the attacks coincided with Russian President Vladimir Putin‘s birthday.

“This is the kind of birthday present that Putin gave himself: the killing of children, the killing of people,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly video address.

In earlier online comments, Zelenskyy said civilians had also been killed in the capital Kyiv and in the central cities of Oleksandria and Kremenchuk during the massive attack.

In total, Russia fired 70 missiles at Ukraine overnight — many of them high-velocity ballistic munitions — and dozens of Shahed attack drones, he said.

“The Russians wanted to strike painfully and demonstratively. This was one of the most vile strikes.”

In Pryluky, an excavator and dozens of rescuers with shovels sifted through rubble at the site where several sections of the apartment block had collapsed.

Emergency workers used ladders to get to the upper floors of what remained of the building, and brought out 15 survivors as they worked their way down through the rubble. Around 55 people were wounded in the town, regional officials said.

“There’s a lot of destruction, especially in the town center,” said Danylo Savenko, deputy mayor of Pryluky, who said he had run to an air raid shelter with his wife as soon as he heard the missiles flying.

Big jump in reported drone interceptions

Russia’s defense ministry said its forces had carried out a “massive strike” on military-industrial facilities in Kyiv and other Ukrainian regions, using high-precision land-, sea- and air-launched weapons, as well as drones.

Ukraine’s air force said it had downed just over 80% of the 46 jet-powered drones launched by Russia — an increase from recent weeks when air defenses took down 50% to 60%.

Since the summer, Russia has used increasing numbers of the new high-velocity drones in round-the-clock attacks on Kyiv and other cities, with Ukraine’s air defenses struggling to cope.

The air force did not explain the jump in the interception rate and did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

Zelenskyy said the Russian ballistic missiles remained the major challenge for Ukraine, adding that he and his team were “every day looking for Patriot (missile interception) systems that can and must protect people’s lives.”

Ukraine received a new €1.2 billion ($1.34 billion) tranche from the European Union on Wednesday and will channel the funds towards defense needs, Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi said.

The US-made Patriot system is the only weapon in Ukraine’s arsenal capable of stopping high-velocity ballistic missiles. Global supplies have been drained by the Iran war and the Ukraine conflict.

Russia’s defense ministry said its targets included sites where Ukrainian defense company Fire Point manufactures and stores its Flamingo cruise missiles and medium- and long-range drones in Kyiv as well as regions of Kyiv, Chernihiv, Kirovohrad, Dnipropetrovsk, Poltava and Kharkiv.

Last week Zelenskyy said Ukraine had fired its first domestically made ballistic missile in combat, produced by Fire Point. In an interview with Reuters, he said he expected the company to have a longer-range FP-9 missile ready by the autumn. Fire Point has said that weapon will be able to reach Moscow.

People shelter overnight in Kyiv metro

Zelenskyy said Ukrainian troops hit four targets in Russia over the past 24 hours, including two Russian oil facilities and a training ground in the Perm, Samara and Astrakhan regions.

In the Reuters interview, Zelenskyy said Ukraine would hit Russia’s energy assets in response to Moscow’s escalating strikes on civilian infrastructure.

Ukrainian officials and military intelligence shared warnings of the upcoming attacks on Wednesday, and many Kyiv residents took shelter in the city’s underground metro stations.

Several loud explosions reverberated through the capital during the night.

In the part of Ukraine’s southern Kherson region under Russian control, the regional Russia-installed governor said a Ukrainian drone killed two civilians in a car. And Russia-installed officials in Moscow-held parts of eastern Donetsk Region said three people died in Ukrainian attacks. – Rappler.com

($1 = 0.8947 euros)

World.title: Attacks on Saudi airports kill 3 people, as fighting escalates in Yemen
World.content:
HOUTHI SUPPORTERS. Houthi supporters carry weapons as they gather in solidarity with the movement as fighting intensifies across several fronts, in Sanaa, Yemen, October 7, 2026.

One person was killed and eight wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, and two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on facilities at Abha airport, Saudi civil aviation authorities say

Three people have been killed in attacks on Saudi airports, the country’s civil aviation authorities said on Wednesday, October 7, as fighting intensified in Yemen between the Iran-aligned Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces.

One person was killed and eight wounded in an attack on King Khalid International Airport in the Saudi capital Riyadh, and two were killed and 28 wounded in an attack on facilities at Abha airport, it said in a statement.

One of the attacks was on Wednesday and the other on Tuesday, the civil aviation authorities said, without saying which attack had occurred on which day.

A Saudi-led coalition fighting the Houthis vowed retaliation, saying the attacks “will not go unpunished”. In a statement issued late on Wednesday, the coalition said it had attacked more than 80 Houthi military sites across the governorates of Saada, Hodeidah, Jawf and Marib.

The Saudi airport attacks were among a series of strikes targeting aviation infrastructure on Wednesday.

The Houthis attacked Aden’s international airport with ballistic missiles and explosive-laden drones earlier on Wednesday, the country’s Transport Ministry said.

One missile landed near the runway minutes before a flight from Cairo was due to land, the ministry said. The airport is the main international gateway for parts of Yemen outside Houthi control.

Battles in Yemen have focused in recent days on areas around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a shipping route that has become more crucial for energy exports since the conflict between the US and Iran restricted trade through the Strait of Hormuz.

This week, Yemeni government forces with Saudi-led coalition air support launched a counteroffensive to recapture strategic territory near the strait and around the town of Mocha that the Houthis had captured in September, but it is unclear if their advance will hold.

The fighting, a spillover from the wider US-Iran conflict, has revived a complex 12-year war in Yemen that led to one of the worst humanitarian crises globally and fragmented the Arab world’s most impoverished country. The number of people displaced since the latest round of fighting began has risen to more than 200,000, the International Organization for Migration (IOM) said on Wednesday.

“People are running for their lives and finding nowhere safe to go,” said IOM Director General Amy Pope, who called for more funding amid rising needs for food and shelter. Both sides allege that hundreds of people have been killed in fighting, without providing details. The UN says three in four families are going hungry in parts of Yemen.

The Houthis have repeatedly ​targeted infrastructure including airports, oil refineries and pipelines in Saudi Arabia, a US ally.

On Wednesday, the Saudi-led coalition said it had intercepted and destroyed a Houthi ballistic missile north of the Saudi capital Riyadh. It said it was tracking the launch platform over Houthi-controlled Sanaa and would destroy it, but gave no details of casualties or damage.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said in a statement that the group had targeted King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh with several drones.

Battles over the strait

Any Houthi control of the strait could threaten shipping or global oil flows, and Saudi Arabia has been seeking international assistance to repel the Houthis. Turkey is sending mainly defensive and technical support, two officials said on Wednesday, after the NATO member and Pakistan pledged to implement a collective defence commitment under their newly formed alliance.

Syria is carefully considering providing military assistance to ally Saudi Arabia amid the escalating war against the Houthis, a US official and a Syrian military official briefed on the matter said.

Options being considered include defensive aid to protect the kingdom from attacks, or deployment of forces in an offensive capacity to help Saudi-backed Yemeni troops fight the Houthis, the officials said.

The US official said Saudi Arabia had requested that Syria deploy forces to fight the Houthis.

In response to a request for comment from the Syrian foreign ministry, a Syrian diplomat said Syria stood firmly with Saudi Arabia in the face of Houthi attacks but that the government’s primary focus was on domestic priorities such as recovery from the country’s civil war.

Fighting on the western front remains concentrated in the Dhubab district overlooking Bab el-Mandeb, with pro-government forces attempting an advance in the strategic hills to the east of that coastal plain, Yemeni military and government sources said.

On Monday, the Yemeni government said it had reached Mocha, which sits at a junction with a supply route to the critical battleground of Taiz, but the claim had been premature, according to Yemeni military officials on the ground and analysts.

The Houthis, who control much of Yemen’s north, seized the capital Sanaa in 2014, prompting a military coalition led by Saudi Arabia, fearful of rival Iran’s influence in Yemen and chaos on its borders, to intervene.

The Saudi-led coalition accuses Iran of arming, training and funding the Houthis. The group, mountain fighters who have emerged as a force of tens of thousands with missiles and drones that threatens the region, denies being part of Iran’s Middle East proxy network, and says it develops its own weapons. Tehran also rejects the allegations. – Rappler.com

World.title: Poland’s Nawrocki meets Pacman: In Manila, diplomacy in boxing
World.content:
STATE VISIT. Polish President Karol Nawrocki trains with Filipino boxing icon Manny Pacquiao on the sidelines of a state visit to the Philippines on October 7, 2026. Pacquiao is head of the National Anti-Poverty Commission.

What happens when two government officials — an amateur boxer and a world champion — meet in Manila? Boxing pad work, of course.

Wearing leather shoes, slacks, and a shirt that bore the flags of his country and his host, Polish President Karol Nawrocki﻿ stepped into a boxing ring.

His trainer? No less than Philippine boxing icon Manny Pacquiao. Video from the session shows both Pacquiao and Nawrocki beaming before, during, and after a few drills.

It was a novel and literal action-packed side quest in Nawrocki’s 4-day state visit to the Philippines from October 5 to 8. He’s the first Polish head of state to make such a visit.

Pacquiao, in a post on his official Facebook page, said it was an “honor” to train Nawrocki.

The day of his Pacquiao training session, Nawrocki had spoken at the University of Sto Tomas. The day before that, he was received in Malacañang for a bilateral meeting and a state dinner hosted by President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.

During that visit to Malacañang, Nawrocki﻿ was also gifted a pair of boxing gloves signed by Pacquiao, a boxing legend worldwide.

BOXER. Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. gifts Polish President Karol Nawrocki a pair of boxing gloves signed by Filipino boxing legend Manny Pacquiao, in Malacañang, on October 6, 2026. Courtesy of Bongbong Marcos Facebook

EVERLAST. A pair of boxing gloves autographed by Filipino boxing legend plus other items are among the gifts of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. for visiting Polish President Karol Nawrocki, on October 6, 2026. Courtesy of Bongbong Marcos Facebook

The visit to an Elorde gym (a franchise founded by another Filipino boxing champ, Gabriel Elorde) and Marcos’ choice of gift were not random, of course.

Nawrocki is known for his athleticism. His experience as an amateur boxer is part of his public image, particularly in his successful 2025 campaign.
