World.title: Kazakhstan plans $134m glass plant in Aktobe
World.content:
BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. The Kazakh government has approved the signing of an investment agreement between the Ministry of Industry and Construction of Kazakhstan and Aktobe Steklo LLP for the construction of a glass container plant in Aktobe city, with total investment in the project estimated at 60 billion tenge ($134.2 million).

According to the government, the relevant resolution was signed by Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov.

Construction of the plant is scheduled to begin in the fourth quarter of 2026, with commissioning planned for 2029. The facility will have a production capacity of 256 million glass containers per year.

“Currently, there is no domestic production of glass products in the Aktobe region. The new plant will increase domestic glass container production and expand its supply on the domestic market. Up to 80% of the plant’s products are planned to be sold in Kazakhstan, with the remainder supplied to Central Asian markets,” the government said.

The plant will be equipped with automated systems for raw material sorting, process management and quality control. Production will use domestic natural mineral raw materials, as well as goods, works and services provided by Kazakh producers.

The project also envisages gradually increasing the use of recycled materials. More than 245,000 tons of glass waste is expected to be processed and reused in production over the project financing period.

The plant is expected to create about 300 permanent jobs. Continuous training and professional development will be provided for Kazakh specialists.

The project is also expected to generate additional demand from the food and processing industries. Increased domestic glass container supplies are expected to shorten delivery times and improve supply stability for related industries.

The project is also expected to support the secondary resources sector, particularly the collection, sorting and consolidation of waste glass for further processing and reuse in production.

The exchange rate used is the official rate of the National Bank of Kazakhstan: $1 = 447.14 tenge as of October 8, 2026.

World.title: Another NASA crew is coming home. Here's what to expect from their splashdown
World.content:
NASA's Crew-12 astronauts are set to parachute back to Earth in a SpaceX capsule after 237 days of orbital research and lab maintenance on the International Space Station.

The four crew members launched into space on February 13 to oversee scientific investigations to help prepare humans for future Moon and Mars exploration, the US space agency said.

NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts have spent their final day aboard the International Space Station and are in transit back towards Earth. (Supplied: Instagram/NASA)

Preparations for their return have been underway for several weeks, and the astronauts' SpaceX Dragon capsule undocked from the ISS on Wednesday evening, Australian time.

Here is what to know about their expected splashdown voyage.

When will NASA SpaceX Crew-12 return to Earth?

The astronauts have already started their 27-hour voyage home and are currently in orbital transit.

NASA said the quartet's return began with the closure of the Dragon capsule's hatch at 6:05am US Eastern time (8:05pm AEST) on Wednesday, followed by a final undocking from the ISS at 8:05am (10:05pm AEST).

The International Space Station, as seen by NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 astronauts from their Dragon capsule spacecraft moments after undocking from the global orbital base. (Supplied: YouTube/NASA)

The timeline of their expected descent and splashdown into the Pacific Ocean off the coast of California is:

10:20am EDT Thursday (12:20am AEST Friday): NASA begins voyage live coverage;

NASA begins voyage live coverage; 10:46am EDT Thursday (12:46am AEST Friday): SpaceX Dragon capsule begins deorbit burn and controlled descent;

SpaceX Dragon capsule begins deorbit burn and controlled descent; 11:34am EDT Thursday (1:34am AEST Friday): Splashdown, followed by a NASA and SpaceX crew retrieval.

The US space agency said the crew have spent weeks packing items to return with them to Earth, including personal belongings, cargo and scientific samples.

During their descent to Earth, the astronauts will need to drink fluids from bags containing salt tablets to maintain hydration and help their bodies adjust to a return to gravity, NASA said.

Who are the Crew-12 astronauts?

The astronaut crew consists of NASA's Jessica Meir and Jack Hathaway, serving as the mission's commander and pilot respectively, as well as French engineer and specialist helicopter pilot Sophie Adenot and Russian military pilot and cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev.

NASA's SpaceX Crew-12 consisted of Commander Jessica Meir, pilot Jack Hathaway, France's Sophie Adenot and Roscosmos cosmonaut Andrey Fedyaev. (Supplied: NASA/SpaceX)

This latest mission was Commander Meir's second in space since being selected as a NASA astronaut in 2013.

During her first voyage, she spent 205 days in orbit as a flight engineer and took part in NASA's first three all-woman spacewalks outside the ISS.

US Navy Commander Hathaway became a NASA astronaut in 2021 and this year's mission was his first in space.

The Crew-12 astronauts launched into orbit in February. (Supplied: NASA/SpaceX)

Beforehand, he was deployed aboard the USS Harry S Truman aircraft carrier and accumulated more than 2,500 flight hours in 30 different aircraft, including 39 combat missions.

This mission was also the first for French Air Force Colonel Adenot, who previously worked as an Airbus helicopter cockpit design engineer, search and rescue pilot and formation flight leader.

Roscosmos cosmonaut and Air Force Major Fedyaev was previously deployed to the ISS for 186 days in 2023 as a mission specialist for NASA's SpaceX Crew-6.

Before that, he was a military pilot engineer and served in the Russian Ilyushin-38 aircraft unit in the Kamchatka Region.

What did Crew-12 work on?

The 12th SpaceX rotation voyage to the ISS was aimed at research and technology advancements "for future Moon and Mars missions and [to] benefit humanity back on Earth", NASA said.

The astronauts spent 237 days — more than seven months — aboard the International Space Station to conduct biological and food production studies. (NASA/Roscosmos/Handout via Reuters)

The astronauts' research included:

Studies of pneumonia-causing bacteria to improve potential treatments;

to improve potential treatments; On-demand intravenous fluid generation for future missions;

for future missions; The monitoring of plant health and enhanced microbe food production in space, and;

and in space, and; Examinations of how a person's physical characteristics could affect blood flow during spaceflight.

Support teams aboard the ISS also helped Crew-12 prepare a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket booster for a second flight.

Who replaced Crew-12 in space?

The four astronauts taking the place of Crew-12 aboard the ISS arrived in space on October 1 after an eight-hour express rocket launch into orbit that set a US speed record.

Crew-13 is being led by NASA flight engineer Jessica Watkins — a geologist and the first Black woman to command a crew into orbit.

NASA's SpaceX Crew 13 consists of Commander Jessica Watkins, and astronauts Luke Delaney, Canada's Joshua Kutryk and Russian cosmonaut Sergey Teteryatnikov. (Reuters: Joe Skipper)

She will be joined by NASA’s Luke Delaney, who is a retired Marine; Canada’s Joshua Kutryk, a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force; and Russia’s Sergey Teteryatnikov, a former submariner.

Colonel Kutryk will become the fourth man to become a father while orbiting Earth, with his wife Heather due to give birth to their third child in late November.

Their stay on the ISS will last six months, but the four astronauts have already begun their work.

Crew-12 launched into orbit and arrived on the ISS on October 1 in the fastest voyage to the space base from Earth ever overseen by NASA. (Reuters: Joe Skipper)

NASA said in their first days in space, Commander Watkins collected and analysed her own blood samples for a risk assessment study of space-caused blood clots, while Major Delaney logged his sleep patterns to monitor his health data.

Colonel Kutryk had his veins scanned by a device used on the ISS to monitor cardiovascular health, and cosmonaut Teteryatnikov wore an acoustic sensor around his neck to record his breathing for a respiratory study.

What is the ISS?

First launched in November 1988, the ISS became a continuous, inhabitable space base for humanity in the year 2000.

NASA describes it as "the most enduring platform for international cooperation in orbit", and the temporary home of flight crews from various nations, inter-orbital missions, launch vehicles, training and engineering facilities and communications networks.

Its primary use is for research on living and working in space, with the ultimate goal of allowing humans to be sent further into space than ever before.

The International Space Station took decades to construct, and consists of several separate modules maintained by various global space agencies. (Supplied: NASA)

The ISS orbits Earth at a speed of about 28,163km/h, meaning it laps the planet roughly every 90 minutes.

The main ground control centres that oversee operations aboard the ISS are located in the US and Russia, however there are also additional support centres in Canada, Japan and Europe.

While the expected life span of the ISS has been extended multiple times, the entire base exists as separate, connected modules — meaning when one part wears out or becomes unusable, it can be replaced.

NASA says the station should be able to remain a working laboratory until at least 2030.

ABC/AP

World.title: Kai Allen shines as Ford gets engine change for Bathurst
World.content:
Kai Allen has fired the first warning shot ahead of Sunday's Bathurst 1000 with the fastest time across today's two practice sessions.

In perfect conditions at Mount Panorama, Allen topped the time sheets in the first practice session of the weekend with a time of 2:05.5460, more than three-tenths better than the next fastest.

The blistering time for Allen, who drives a Ford for Grove Racing, comes after Supercars confirmed the engine in all Ford competitors would be changed for this weekend.

Bathurst 1000: How to watch, race start time and weather forecast Here is what you need to know about this weekend's Bathurst 1000, including when the race begins and how you can follow the action.

Barometric pressure testing before last year's Bathurst 1000, and again before this weekend, found the Ford engine lost power at high altitude.

A change to the engine, developed by Triple Eight Race Engineering, which is Ford's homologation team, has been approved by Supercars to level the playing field this weekend.

There will be no change to the Toyota or GM (Chevrolet) engines.

"As you're aware, Supercars have conducted Barometric engine testing over the last 12 months and recently completed a further test," a note to teams read.

"The results of this test have been provided to the Homologation Teams following which consultation has taken place.

"The testing has identified a power loss on the Ford at lower Barometric pressure and as such Supercars have approved a change of ESD developed by the Ford Homologation team to correct this for the Bathurst event only."

Six of the top 10 cars from Thursday's first session were Fords, with Chevrolets making up the other four spots, including PremiAir's Jayden Ojeda who was second fastest with a 2:05.8737.

The fastest Toyota belonged to reigning Supercars champion Chaz Mostert who was 17th fastest for the number 1 Walkinshaw TWG Racing.

While Allen shone, it was not all smooth sailing for Grove Racing with Matthew Payne, last year's Bathurst 1000 winner, being called in early after his team found power steering fluid on the garage floor.

Lochie Dalton, driving for the Chevrolet number 99 Erebus Motorsport, topped the co-drivers practice session later on Thursday with a 2:05.874.

Again, only Fords and Chevrolets were in the top 10. Again, Walkinshaw TWG Racing's number 1 was the fastest Toyota, with co-driver Fabian Coulthard at the wheel.

There will be two more practice sessions on Friday ahead of qualifying.

World.title: Melbourne man accused of spreading Islamic State material granted bail
World.content:
A Melbourne man accused of spreading extremist material for the Islamic State terror group has been granted bail, with a magistrate citing his significant health issues.

Mohamed Bakit, 65, was arrested by counterterrorism police at his Carlton home on September 23.

He has been in custody since he was charged with multiple offences including using a carriage service to transmit violent extremist material, possessing violent extremist material and being a member of a terrorist organisation.

He appeared via video link at a hearing on Thursday in the Melbourne Magistrates' Court.

Deputy Chief Magistrate Gerard Lethbridge granted bail, saying Mr Bakit suffered significant health issues including the effects of a stroke in 2023 and a permanent and significant neurological disability.

He said the accused received support and care at home seven days a week and was at risk of "adverse health" outcomes in custody.

"[Prison] simply cannot provide the same levels of support or care without hospitalisation," Magistrate Lethbridge said.

The magistrate said any risks could be ameliorated with strict bail conditions, including that Mr Bakit reside only at his apartment in Carlton, report regularly to police and surrender any passports.

He was also barred from leaving the state.

The 65-year-old was arrested during a raid on his home in Carlton in September. (Supplied: Australian Federal Police)

At a previous hearing, the court heard Mr Bakit was a member of a WhatsApp group chat which was initially used to discuss religion but soon became a space to access and distribute extremist material.

While giving evidence, police informant Katherine Dillon described Mr Bakit as an "influential participant" in the group and the "most active" member, sending close to 10,000 messages.

Those messages allegedly included images, audio files, videos of beheadings and suicide bombings and propaganda documentation as well as other extremist material promoting or glorifying the terrorist group.

"His communication demonstrates strong support to Islamic State," Ms Dillon said.

"The distribution of these materials shows active participation in the propagation of Islamic State."

Defence lawyer Michael McGrath previously argued that if the recipients of the material did not find it offensive, then no crime had been committed.

"The intention of the [legislation] is to stop the material from being distributed to people who don't want to receive it," Mr McGrath said.

Mr Bakit's case was adjourned until March.

World.title: Angus Taylor tries to find his place on the migration middle road
World.content:
Welcome back to your weekly federal politics update, where Courtney Gould gets you up to speed on the happenings from Parliament House.

Angus Taylor arrived at the three-corned migration battle this week with a plan aimed at the middle road between One Nation and the government.

Vowing to slash Australia's temporary workforce by 650,000 people over four years, the opposition leader was trying to land the twin objectives of bringing the fight to One Nation while also presenting an economically sound policy.

With a top line designed to grab headlines — "the largest cut to immigration in Australia's history" — the opposition has pledged deep cuts to graduate, refugee and bridging visas should Taylor get handed the keys to the Lodge.

The opposition is the last to join the migration debate. Labor released its own policy several weeks ago, forging ahead with changes to reduce the Net Overseas Migration figure to its Treasury forecasted cap of 225,000 people. One Nation got out of the blocks first, though, flagging a period of negative migration before its policy settles at 130,000 people per year.

The Coalition hit the middle: two years at 100,000 before rising to 160,000 in the fourth year.

Angus Taylor arrived late to the migration debate. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

That's a deeper cut than Peter Dutton proposed ahead of the last election. So far, Taylor has done a better job at selling the plan than his predecessor. Dutton's pitch was mired in confusion as he struggled to explain which visa categories would be targeted.

But time will tell if the Coalition's revamped policy stacks up. Business groups claimed the plan would harm economic growth, concerns dismissed by Taylor as being made by "vested interests". The aged care sector also raised the alarm.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

"I think the problem is that whenever any party talks about immigration they use these sort of flashy headline numbers that … appeal hugely to people who want less immigration, terrify everybody who relies on immigration, and we get this sort of big swirling debate and we need to stop doing that," Aging Australia chief Tom Symondson told ABC's Radio National this morning.

The policy wasn't formally costed by the Parliamentary Budget Office (PBO), despite senior figures insisting they worked closely with the independent watchdog. Taylor's office modelled the policy and asked the PBO to confirm if it was budget neutral.

The Australian Financial Review reported that Taylor's team had told MPs not to say the migration policy was officially costed. Of course, the PBO can't discuss what it's working on. It declined to comment when asked on Wednesday.

Loading...

It's a far cry from Shadow Home Affairs Minister Jonno Duniam's declaration last month that the Coalition would do the work One Nation failed to do.

He argued this morning that it would be done. Just not right now. That job will be completed closer to election day and by that time Duniam will be well out of the political fray, having confirmed he'll be exiting politics by the end of the year.

The shadow of One Nation looms large over the policy. Both the Coalition and One Nation have used the term "breathing space" to describe why Australia requires the cuts. The blueprint was also released just days before Taylor is scheduled to headline the Conservative Political Action Conference (CPAC) in Brisbane.

He's the first Liberal leader to attend. Flyers promoting CPAC placed the opposition leader in a trio alongside Pauline Hanson and Nationals leader Matt Canavan.

A storm in a coffee cup

While the government largely stayed out of the migration debate this week, it was facing another storm over a decision to wind back surcharges.

A ban on additional card payment fees, announced earlier this year by the Reserve Bank, came into effect last week. The move was originally championed by Labor MP Jerome Laxale before the RBA even started looking at the issue.

The central bank expanded it beyond Laxale's original focus on debit cards, arguing the change was a win for consumers. As such, the government started selling it as a cost-of-living measure, with Anthony Albanese and other MPs taking to social media to herald the change.

Labor split on ATO credit card ban The federal government is facing growing pressure over the ATO'S decision to stop accepting credit cards.

But within days the sentiment began to shift — turbocharged by the Australian Tax Office's decision to jump on board and ban credit card payments on tax bills. That opened another can of worms.

The business backlash was fierce. The ATO refused to budge, despite holding a crisis meeting about the issue on Wednesday. It argued that only 2.3 per cent of payments to the ATO are via credit.

So far, the government has shown little interest in helping the ATO solve the problem. Labor may be a little relieved that it's the tax office that's become the focus of the story, rather than the additional 50 cents many people are paying for their coffee. At least for now.

Loading

COP that

So, where has the prime minister been this week? He's been off in Fiji and the low-lying atolls of Tuvalu where Australia had organised an international conference to highlight the impact of climate change on the Pacific.

Albanese made the promise way back when climate change was front of mind for the public and Australia's relationship with Pacific neighbours was lagging. The idea was to bring world leaders to the region to see what's going on for themselves.

But the years have chipped away at that promise. First, Australia wasn't able to secure the right to host the UN climate summit, known as COP, in its own right. Albanese and minister Chris Bowen had to settle for a precursor to the main event in Türkiye in November.

Anthony Albanese and Chris Bowen had big hopes for pre-COP. (ABC News: David Sciasci)

One by one, world leaders declined the invitation to come and, as time went on, the government had to accept that mostly ministers and other officials would visit Tuvalu.

In all, 36 people boarded the plane to Tuvalu. Mauritius's Prime Minister Navin Ramgoolam and East Timor President José Ramos-Horta were the sole leaders from outside of the Pacific to attend.

Both Albanese and Bowen have defended the poor showing, arguing world leaders don't typically attend pre-COP, which is hardly the main event.

So, was it a flop? That was the question foreign affairs reporter Stephen Dziedzic tackled this morning — a recommended read if you have a spare moment this afternoon.

He argues that it's hard to say for certain just yet. We'll have to wait to see if there are concrete outcomes from COP31 held next month. But the gap between what the government hoped the event would be and what was delivered is hard to ignore.

World.title: Charges dropped against 12yo after alleged bashing of Sunshine shopkeeper
World.content:
Prosecutors have dropped the case against a 12-year-old boy who was charged after the alleged fatal bashing of Sunshine shopkeeper Van Viet Truong.

Mr Truong, 60, was allegedly attacked by a group of youths on August 2 after coming to the aid of a fellow retail worker. He died in hospital days later.

Mr Truong ran the Hong Hung Asian Grocery for nearly three decades, and was a well-known figure in his local business community.

Five children were initially arrested, however charges only remain against three.

Community members have laid flowers outside Van Viet Truong's store in Sunshine. (ABC News)

Today, prosecutors withdrew charges of violent disorder, affray and two assault-related charges against the 12-year-old boy, conceding they could not prove he was criminally liable.

The doli incapax legal principles presumes children younger than 14 are incapable of criminal intent.

In order for the case to have continued, prosecutors would have needed to prove the boy knew his alleged actions were morally wrong.

A prosecutor told the Children's Court that the case had been reviewed and the Crown would not be able to successfully rebut the Doli Incapax presumption.

"The prosecution will have to withdraw the charges," she said.

In a statement, Victoria Police said advice from the Director of Public Prosecutions confirmed there were "no reasonable prospects of conviction" in relation to the boy due to the presumption at law that a child who is 12 or 13 is not criminally responsible for their actions.

"The family of the victim has been notified and we will continue to support them throughout this process. Our thoughts are with them today," a Victoria Police spokesperson said.

Three other teenagers to face court over alleged assault

The case against the other teenagers will continue.

A 15-year-old is accused of manslaughter, while two 14-year-old girls are charged with violent disorder, affray and assault-related offences.

Last month, a police officer told the court the alleged attack on Mr Troung was captured on security cameras.

"The entire incident goes for approximately one minute so it's quite chaotic," she said.

The lawyer for the 12-year-old said his involvement was "secondary".

He said the education department had blocked the Year 6 student from returning to school while the case was before the courts.

"It is having an enormous impact on him," he said.

The 15-year-old charged with manslaughter is due to face court next on October 21.

The 14-year-old girls remain on bail after being released in August.

World.title: Breaking: Sam Wood denied bail on DV charges after allegedly choking wife
World.content:
Prominent fitness influencer and reality TV personality Sam Wood has been denied bail on domestic violence charges.

Police allege Mr Wood, who is from Melbourne, became involved in a family argument in Noosa on Saturday night before he assaulted and choked his wife, Snezana Wood.

"The victim refers to she thought she was going to die, and she was in fear of her safety," prosecutor Sergeant Jeanette Grigoris told the court on Thursday afternoon.

Sergeant Grigoris told the court the complainant's video recorded statement was "strong evidence".

"She does articulate there's choking … banging of her head on the floor, she couldn't breathe. The defendant only stopped when one of the children called out," Sergeant Grigoris said.

Sam Wood appeared via video link. (Supplied: @scottbreton)

Complainant 'in support of criminal charges'

Mr Wood's adult stepdaughter made a Triple Zero call to police to report the alleged incident, the prosecution told the court.

"He essentially agrees with the prosecution's case but minimises the offending … He's essentially victim-blamed."

In opposing bail, the prosecution tended photographs of the victim's injuries as evidence, as well as a statement from a responding paramedic.

Sergeant Grigoris said the complainant is "in support of the criminal charges".

Snezana Wood and her daughter Eve Markoski-Wood, either side of Sam Wood. (Supplied)

"[Mr Wood] was here on holidays … there is that risk he will not return to face the charges before the court," she told the court.

"He does have the resources to essentially flee the jurisdiction."

His lawyer told the Maroochydore Magistrates Court today Mr Wood "may be entitled to the self defence argument".

"Mr Wood's depression is regarded as extremely severe," Mathew Cuskelly told the court, citing an affidavit by Professor Ian Coyle, a forensic psychologist.

"He ought to be given the chance to engage with mental health professionals to try to salvage something of his professional reputation and career, which is taking a hell of a beating at the moment."

Sam Wood's father Andrew Wood (left) arrived with his legal team. (ABC News: Nykayla Dux)

Mr Cuskelly said his client has "no prior criminal offending".

"At 46 years old, this is his first interaction with the criminal justice system."

Mr Wood appeared via video link from custody.

He was unshaven and wearing a dark green long sleeve shirt with his sleeves rolled up.

He sat quietly with a neutral expression throughout the hearing, before sitting with his head bowed while the magistrate spoke.

When the decision was delivered, Mr Wood put his head in his hands.

He was remanded in custody until November 23.

World.title: An average of 17 older Australians died each day last year waiting for home care
World.content:
An average of 17 older Australians died while waiting to receive necessary home care each day last year, according to the latest official figures — an increase of more than a third on the previous year.

New data published by the health department revealed 6,436 older Australians approved for Support at Home, but in the queue for funding, died in 2025-26.

The figure is an almost 34 per cent increase from the 4,812 people who died while waiting under the former National Priority System for home care packages in the previous year.

However, the figures are not directly comparable, because of the transition from the older system to the current one.

"Everybody on the wait list is a person; they're not a statistic or a number," Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston said.

Shadow Health Minister Anne Ruston says the government was trying to hide the information. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

The Opposition said the data emerged after the federal government failed to comply with two Senate orders to produce the figures.

"Rather than fixing the system, Labor has put its energy into avoiding scrutiny. And it is older Australians and their families who are paying the price," she said.

"The extent to which the government tried to hide this information from the public is appalling. The prime minister and his ministers clearly just didn't want older Australians and their families to know the truth."

More than 100,000 Australians are stuck in a funding backlog, and many end up in hospital or forced into residential aged care sooner. (ABC News: Jake Grant)

CEO of the Council on the Ageing Australia, Patricia Sparrow, described the figures as "an absolute tragedy", which demonstrated just how badly the system was keeping up with demand.

"This shouldn't be happening … there aren't enough packages in the system [and] we need to make sure people can get the package they need within about 30 days of being assessed," she said.

Ms Sparrow said when people did not get support at home for basic needs like showering or eating they could end up in hospital or be forced to move into residential aged care sooner.

"We need to make sure older people are respected … they don't put their hand up for assistance until they really need it," she said.

A report in May revealed patients were waiting an average of a year for services in aged care. (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

More than 106,000 Australians were on the official waiting list for a Support at Home place as of June 30.

The waitlist, known as the Support At Home priority system, determines how older people are prioritised for funding, and also includes people who are already receiving funding for a lower level of care, and are waiting for a higher level to be allocated.

In August, Four Corners revealed the true number of people waiting for full aged care funding at home was almost 154,000.

Thousands removed from official aged care waitlist A Four Corners investigation can reveal the number of people waiting for full aged care funding at home stands at almost 154,000 — not 100,000 as officially reported.

In May, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese conceded the state of aged care in Australia was "not good enough", after a report revealed patients were waiting an average of a year for services.

The federal government was also accused of burying that report by its political opponents, quietly dropping it during budget-lock up.

Last year, a Senate inquiry into aged care services heard from the families of people who died while waiting for support, including one Hobart man with Parkinson's and cancer who waited over 12 months for a home care package.

His package was approved three days before his death.

Senator David Pocock says the Senate has been pushing the government to improve care for years. ( ABC News: David Sciasci )

Independent Senator David Pocock said the data was "shocking but sadly not surprising".

"The Senate has been pushing the government hard for years to improve the care we're providing to older Australians. Time and again the aged care minister has dismissed and deflected and ultimately failed these older Australians and their families. It is unacceptable," he said.

"I am also dismayed that this data is released quietly and in a way that is hard to find. Even though it tells a grim story, older Australians and their family still deserve transparency from the government on the state of affairs."

Aged care crisis worsens nationwide The number of aged care patients stuck in hospitals has jumped by 35 per cent in less than a year, fuelling fresh demands for the federal government to stem the crisis.

Aged Care Minister Sam Rae said the rate of people who died waiting for Support at Home was "significantly lower than the rate of death for older Australians in the broader population".

"Every single death of someone who is waiting for care is a tragedy. My thoughts and condolences are with every family who has lost a loved one," he said.

Mr Rae said while there was "more work to do" the government had delivered an additional 83,000 home care places in 2025-26, with a further 32,000 rolling out this year.

World.title: High Court's coalmine emissions ruling says 'the quiet part out loud'
World.content:
Resources company MACH Energy probably never expected its High Court appeal over the future of a Hunter Valley coal mine to trigger a legal precedent that has been celebrated by climate activists.

The court's decision has the resources sector nervous, the federal government downplaying the ruling's wider significance, and the opposition apoplectic about its potential to cripple the Australian fossil fuel industry.

The extension of the Mount Pleasant coalmine would add roughly twice Australia's total annual greenhouse gas emissions to the atmosphere. (Supplied: Nearmaps)

Whether the ruling is a narrow interpretation of a planning statute or spells doom for the fossil fuel industry depends on who you talk to.

So, let's step through it all carefully.

What was the case about?

MACH Energy operates the Mount Pleasant open-cut mine near Muswellbrook.

It wants to double the amount of coal it exports from the mine and keep it open until 2048.

NSW's Independent Planning Commission (IPC) approved that expansion in 2022. But the plan came to a dramatic halt when a residents' group convinced the state's Court of Appeal the IPC got it wrong.

The Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (DAMSHEG), led by two retired schoolteachers, said the planning panel failed to properly consider that climate change caused by the exported coal's "downstream" or scope 3 emissions would cause harm to the Hunter.

'Dangerous loophole' in the law In a week of floods and droughts across Australia, the government extended the life of one of the world's largest gas facilities.

What are scope 3 emissions?

Under climate regulations, Scope 1 emissions are those that come from the source, such as methane leaks from a coalmine.

Scope 2 emissions are caused by electricity that has been generated using fossil fuels.

Scope 3 emissions are indirect emissions, and in this case describe the "downstream" or "chain emissions" that occur when a product is sold on and used — in this case, when the exported coal is burned overseas.

Globally, they account for the vast majority of emissions from coalmines and other fossil fuel production.

In July 2025, the NSW Court of Appeal agreed with DAMSHEG's argument, finding that none of the IPC's conditions expressly addressed scope 3 emissions, despite it being a legal requirement to "ensure greenhouse gas emissions are minimised to the greatest extent possible".

The court sent the case to be reviewed again, this time by the Land and Environment Court.

Frustrated with the delays, and in an effort to get some clear guidance on a path forward, the coal company took its case to the High Court, which agreed to review the planning process.

MACH Energy wants to extract more than 440 million tonnes of coal from the site. (Supplied: Climate Media Centre)

University of Melbourne environmental and climate change law expert Jacqueline Peel said it was a "very unusual case" for the High Court to take up, given the case was "largely an issue of statutory interpretation, what the words of the statute meant".

"On one take it's just a narrow decision interpreting a specific provision or provisions of New South Wales planning law," she said.

Jacqueline Peel says it was an unusual case for the court to take up. (Supplied)

What did the High Court find?

In its original approval, the IPC accepted that 860 million tonnes of emissions would be generated overseas from the project, and that this would contribute to climate change.

But the planning panel said that "would be accounted for" by the countries that imported the coal, "through broader national policies and international agreements (such as the Paris Agreement)".

On the hook for fossil fuel exports The International Court of Justice was unequivocal about the consequences for countries that make the climate crisis worse. As one of the world's biggest fossil fuel exporters, it puts Australia on notice.

MACH Energy's appeal to the High Court argued the same: that the Paris Agreement was enough, and that essentially once the coal left Australia, it was not the company's problem.

But the High Court dismissed that argument in a majority 3 to 2 ruling.

The court found NSW law required the IPC to "consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable all greenhouse gas emissions, including Scope 3 emissions".

What does it mean for fossil fuel projects?

Professor Peel said at its most narrow reading, the High Court ruling essentially enforced NSW planning law that already existed.

But she said the potential big change was that the High Court was now "saying the quiet part out loud", which "means taking account or having accountability for those emissions, which is something we really haven't seen in Australia to date".

"If you start requiring mines to actually deal with and be accountable for their scope 3 emissions and have to do something to minimise those, then it makes the coal mine a much different economic prospect than it would be if you can just deal with scope 3 emissions as someone else's problem," she said.

The Australian Conservation Foundation's Adam Bandt said the outcome was something governments and corporations had long been fighting against.

"There came a time when we understood that asbestos was a product that when you used it as intended would cause harm," Mr Bandt said.

"That's now the same with coal and gas. We don't mine and export asbestos anymore."

The Minerals Council's Tanya Constable said she was "very concerned about the decision".

"This will send shudders down everybody's spine," she said.

MACH Energy's Mount Pleasant coal mine can continue operating until the end of 2032. (7.30 Report)

It is the requirement to consider emissions overseas, not just those happening in Australia, that has the industry and conservative politicians so worked up.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said it was "absurd" to ask local planning authorities to consider climate impacts in other countries before approving a mine in New South Wales.

"Under the international rules … emissions are counted where coal is used, not where it is mined," he said.

But those rules appear to be changing.

In July 2025, the International Court of Justice issued an advisory opinion putting accountability for climate-related harm onto coal and other fossil fuel producers at the point of extraction.

The UK Supreme Court also ruled that the future impact of fossil fuel projects must be assessed by planning bodies when deciding whether to approve projects.

High Court Judge Gordon appeared to accept this argument in her own findings from the MACH Energy case.

"The impact of greenhouse gas emissions is the same, regardless of how they are categorised," Judge Gordon found.

The fact that scope 3 emissions were accounted for by other countries through the Paris Agreement did "not address the Commission's obligation … which relates to all greenhouse gas emissions (including Scope 3 emissions), and which requires it to consider imposing conditions to minimise to the greatest extent practicable those emissions".

Advocates for climate action attend the International Court of Justice decision in 2025. (Supplied: Ray Campbell / Pacific Community)

What's next?

Both the NSW and federal governments have downplayed the broader significance of the ruling.

NSW Premier Chris Minns warned climate activists not to "get overexcited" and said the mine's operators were still "looking to continue an application through the IPC" to expand the mine.

Federal Industry Minister Tim Ayres said the High Court decision was "not a big deal" and "confined to the provisions of the NSW Act and the way that the NSW planning authority did their work".

But Professor Peel said that was a "narrow" interpretation of the ruling.

"It's entirely understandable that the minister at the federal level would be trying to say: 'No, this is just a NSW problem,'" she said.

"But I just don't think we've had that argument in the court yet."

She said she expected new litigation to result from the decision.

"Groups will now want to explore what that added set of arguments from the High Court decision might offer in terms of challenging approvals for fossil fuel projects," she said.

World.title: ‘I’ll ring Wayne’: Latrell Mitchell coy on future at South Sydney
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘I’ll ring Wayne’: Latrell Mitchell coy on future at South Sydney Adrian Proszenko Updated October 8, 2026 — 5:49pm ,first published 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Kangaroos centre Latrell Mitchell is relishing the chance to resume his battle with Dane Gagai at international level, but has brushed off questions about his future after South Sydney put contract extension talks on hold. Rabbitohs star Mitchell and Newcastle three-quarter Gagai had a memorable duel during the opening round of the finals. The Knights ultimately prevailed, Gagai declaring afterwards: “I wasn’t going to let him push me around.” Loading The rivalry will continue when Australia host New Zealand in the Rugby League World Cup opener next Thursday, which marks Gagai’s first appearance for the Kiwis after last representing Australia in 2018. After Gagai earned a points victory in the play-off fixture, Mitchell is looking forward to the rematch.



“Let’s go! We love it,” Mitchell said after entering Kangaroos camp at Double Bay on Thursday. “Dane’s a competitor, I’m a competitor, and that’s where we leave it, on the field. I love him, he’s a good man, and you walk off and know you’ve done everything you can to try and win a game. I love Gags. I wish him the best, but yeah, I’m definitely ready.” Latrell Mitchell and Dane Gagai go head-to-head in the finals. NRL Photos Mitchell and Gagai were Rabbitohs teammates for two years, but have for the most part of their careers been rivals at club and state level. “He just never stops talking, never goes away, you know?” Mitchell said. “He gives you shit … and I’m very competitive, so I just can’t let it die really.



“He’s winding back the clock, definitely. He’s shown that, and I think he’s got another two or three [seasons] in him, so let him go.” Mitchell’s future will be one of the big talking points during the off-season. The Blues star is among several centres – along with Herbie Farnworth, Matt Burton, Billy Smith, Jack Wighton, Jack Howarth and Deine Mariner – to hit the open market if they don’t re-sign with their incumbent clubs before November 1. Given he has played just 34 games in three seasons, critics question whether Mitchell remains a million-dollar-a-year player, at a time when the salary cap will soon increase. Mitchell would normally be a signing priority for the Rabbitohs, but they have indicated they will put contract talks on hold, potentially until March. Coach Wayne Bennett, however, is bullish about Mitchell staying. “I think for me, just focusing on camp is most important,” Mitchell said. “I’ve got a different colour on to the Rabbitohs, so for me, it’s all about this camp and focusing on that.” Pressed on his future, Mitchell said, “I’ll ring Wayne”, before ending Thursday’s press conference.



‘I wish I could be half the player Teddy is’: Walsh pays tribute to No.1 rival Tedesco Brisbane superstar Reece Walsh concedes he will struggle to wrestle the Kangaroos No.1 jersey off James Tedesco, saying he would be content to be “half the player” the Roosters captain is. One of the biggest selection calls for Australia coach Kevin Walters is his first-choice fullback. Walsh is the incumbent after being the No.1 on last year’s Ashes tour, while Tedesco made a strong case during a stellar season, which culminated in him winning the Clive Churchill Medal for the best player in Sunday’s grand final win over the Knights. Reece Walsh is back in the green and gold, but he has a lot of work to do to hang onto the No.1 jumper. George Chan “It’s hard to compete with Clive,” Walsh quipped as the Australian squad assembled in Sydney on Thursday.



“I’m obviously grateful to be in camp. I was watching Teddy when I was a kid. To see what he’s done over the last few weeks, it’s going to be hard for myself to push for a position – but I’m confident in my ability. “I can’t wait to be a sponge and learn off him. He’s one of the greats to do it in our game, and I’m lucky enough to be able to rub shoulders as a teammate with him.” Walsh has long admired Tedesco’s ability to perform at the highest level for such a lengthy period. Reece Walsh was the star of the 2025 season, which culminated in him claiming the Kangaroos No.1 jersey. Getty Images “I wish I could be half the player Teddy is, man,” Walsh said.



“Sitting there in school watching him win premierships and all that, it’s pretty amazing for his longevity and how consistent he’s been for so many years. Like I said, it was like last year being on the Ashes tour with Dyl [Dylan Edwards] – to be there and be able to rub shoulders and see the way he prepared. “Now, for myself to be able to see the way Teddy prepares for a game, as a 24-year-old, I’m pretty stoked with that. If there are some small things I can take away and put into my game, if I can be half the player that he’s been, I’ll be happy with that, brother.” Walsh hasn’t played since suffering a high-grade syndesmosis injury in August that required surgery. However, the Maroons ace feels he’s ready to return. Reece Walsh lies injured during the round 24 match against the Warriors with what was feared to be a season-ending injury. Getty Images “At the Broncos, we’ve got such good staff there who manage injuries really well,” he said.



“One of the physios there, Shred, has been thrashing me for the last six weeks. So it’s good to get back into the team environment and be around more players instead of just getting thrashed by myself ... “I’m going to do everything I can to push for this team, whether that’s starting or whether it’s not. I’m just going to try my best.” Related Article NRL 2026 Daniel Tupou retires after Roosters’ grand final win Walsh was the star of the 2025 season, helping steer the Broncos to a drought-breaking premiership. However, he concedes he has not consistently reproduced that form this year. “My form, it’s obviously disappointing after you win a comp and then see yourself back where you are,” he said.



“I feel like I tried hard this year. I feel like I wasn’t happy with where we finished as a team, but there are always lessons in having those years. I feel like those are the ones that drive you to get better, keep learning and want to do better the next year.” Walsh refused to give up on his World Cup dream despite initially suffering what was thought to be a season-ending injury. “I was obviously just taking it week by week and trying to do everything I could to put myself in a position to be fit,” he said. “I’ve done that, so I’m happy to be here. I can’t wait to get to work and prepare us for a good World Cup.”

World.title: Taylor and Abbott say Bondi shooting drove the politics on migration
World.content:
PoliticsFederalImmigration Taylor and Abbott say Bondi shooting drove the politics on migration Paul Sakkal October 8, 2026 — 5:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and ally Tony Abbott have linked the Coalition’s migration clampdown to the Bondi massacre, in the face of continued pressure to explain how the plan stacked up economically. Labor pushed back on deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume’s claim that Labor had brought in “more  executives than carpenters”, citing data showing that four times as many carpenters had arrived in the past four years. Angus Taylor, photographed in Sydney on Thursday. Nadir Tolj-Kinani After former bureaucrat Abul Rizvi cast doubt on Taylor’s 100,000 net migration target, Taylor spent Thursday defending the rigour of the policy and pledging an official set of costings by the next election. A top labour economist told this masthead on Wednesday that cutting the growing number of temporary migrants could help turn around Australia’s productivity malaise by encouraging firms to innovate instead of relying on cheap labour.



On the cultural and political rationale, Abbott echoed One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce in saying the terror attack on December 14 last year lit the fuse for the current debate on migration. Related Article Exclusive

Immigration The cost of cutting foreign workers: Fares spike in Taylor’s migration gamble “Because it was such a dismal milestone in our decline, for millions of Australians the Bondi massacre inspired a determination to retake control of our country,” Abbott said on Thursday. In a veiled critique of One Nation, Abbott argued Taylor had not “just railed against excessive migrant numbers … but provided a considered, costed mechanism to bring numbers down.” The former prime minister used his long-standing line on migrants joining “hotel Australia” rather than “team Australia” in a Substack article. Taylor used the same terms for the first time when announcing the policy two days ago, pointing to Abbott’s influence.



Similar democracies – from Canada to Scandinavia – have faced intense debates on migration and social values, prompting both right and centre-left parties to tighten controls. Related Article University International student cuts risk ‘very significant hole’, universities warn Moderate Liberal MPs speaking anonymously told this masthead they were relieved that Taylor’s office did not pursue a proposal formulated in Sussan Ley’s dying days as opposition leader that would have blocked migration from “terror hotspots”, which could have been characterised by political opponents as a discriminatory, Trump-like Muslim ban. But Taylor acknowledged that cultural as well as numerical considerations drove the policy, which he hopes will stem bleeding to One Nation and head off speculation about his leadership. “It absolutely is both,” Taylor said on Andrew Bolt’s program on News24.



“We’ve seen people come to this country and get visas who should never have come to this country, and should never have been issued visas. One of them was one of the shooters at North Bondi just before Christmas last year.” Related Article Analysis

Immigration A year after Hastie’s warning, Taylor has a solid migration plan. Hanson has the voters Australian-born Naveed Akram and his father, Sajid, a permanent resident who migrated from India in 1998, are accused of carrying out December’s Bondi Beach attack that claimed 15 innocent lives after being radicalised by Islamic State propaganda. The younger Akram survived and is awaiting trial on murder and terrorism charges, while Sajid was shot and killed during the attack. On the week of the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attacks on Israel, Taylor added: “We do not want people coming to our country who do not share our values and Islamist extremists do not share our values.”



The Business Council of Australia and the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry have opposed the Coalition’s plan, arguing it puts up arbitrary targets while exacerbating skills shortages. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announcing Labor’s migration plans last month. Alex Ellinghausen The council, a traditional ally of the pro-business Coalition, called out the “race to the bottom” on migration, but senior Coalition MPs laughed off the complaints, saying business leaders had vacated the debate on migration over the past year just as it had on tax reform brawls, and that they had become addicted to cheap labour. Labor ministers have not launched a full-frontal attack on Taylor’s plan – a sign the government knows it stands to gain little debating a hot-button issue where the populist right is setting the agenda. Instead, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has questioned the Coalition’s maths and said its plan would lead fewer skilled workers to migrate to Australia. Taylor received a series of questions on Thursday about labour shortages in aged care, restaurants and cleaning firms.



“We should not build an economy or businesses on a guest worker foundation; that is not the way to do it,” he said, insisting the party will release costings by the election. “That being said, it is true that there are many students, many students, both international and domestic, by the way, who work in aged care and the healthcare sector, and that’s a good thing.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Subscribers can sign up to our weekly Inside Politics newsletter.

Destination dining doesn’t always involve a plane ride. Sometimes all it takes is a speedy trip on the M80. Xuan Banh Cuon is a restaurant filled with diners hunched over piping hot bowls of noodles from morning to night.

Wiggly rice flour-sheets are the restaurant’s namesake, rolled around pork, prawn and black fungus and improved only by a quick dip in a bowl of funky nuoc cham. Northern-style spring rolls are packed with pork and vegetables, chopped into crunchy inch-long nubbins for snacking ease.

Slurp stans will gravitate towards bun rieu cua cha ca, the shrimp and tomato broth holding vermicelli noodles, pork patties and crab meatballs. Sticky rice stuffed with sweet bean paste might be the best-value side dish on the strip, arriving sky-high and topped with golden-fried shallots all for a cheeky fiver.

World.title: ASX finishes lower as oil jumps again on renewed Iran tensions
World.content:
Updated BusinessMarketsWorld markets ASX finishes lower as oil jumps again on renewed Iran tensions Staff writers Updated October 8, 2026 — 5:37pm ,first published October 8, 2026 — 5:17am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

The Australian sharemarket declined on Thursday, as oil prices jumped on renewed Middle East tensions, stoking concerns about inflation. Miners and banks led the losses. The S&P/ASX 200 finished down 66.8 points, or 0.8 per cent, at 8660.90, with five of its 11 sectors in the red and six in the green. The market decline came after a choppy, directionless session on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.54¢. Global sharemarkets felt pressure as yields climbed in the bond market and oil prices rose again. Bloomberg Oil rose after a report that the White House asked the Pentagon to draw up strike options against Iran that could be executed before the midterm elections, and as a storm shut some US output. Also, Iran-backed Houthis struck two airports in Saudi Arabia, killing three people as the group intensified its attacks on the kingdom, while also fighting Riyadh-backed forces in Yemen. Meanwhile, a tanker was struck by projectiles off the coast of Qatar on Wednesday, according to a report from UK Maritime Trade Operations, a rare attack deep inside the Persian Gulf. It’s the first reported strike on a tanker deep within the gulf in about a month.



Global benchmark Brent rose 2.5 per cent to approach $US103 a barrel in the afternoon. The advance pressured US Treasuries, pushing up the 10-year yield by three basis points to 5.32 per cent, near levels last seen in 2002. Australian 10-year government bonds, however, eased by a basis point to 5.39 per cent. Rising oil prices stoke energy costs for companies, also stoking inflation across the economy, weighing on corporate profits and slowing economic growth. Related Article Updated

AI Firmus float in trouble as investors don’t buy the hype Australia’s mining heavyweights took the brunt in Thursday’s session, leading the market decline. BHP – the biggest stock on the local market – finished down 2 per cent and Rio Tinto shed 2.9 per cent. Lynas Rare Earths slumped 5.3 per cent. Fortescue, the only pure-play iron ore producer, lost 1.4 per cent after saying its iron ore shipments fell 6 per cent in the September quarter to 46.8 million tonnes due to maintenance shutdowns. Inventories rose as it sold less than that – 42.9 million tonnes – amid its protracted negotiations with China’s state buyer. At the same time, net debt ballooned from $US900 million at the end of June to $US2.8 billion as of September 30, after paying out its dividends.



Gold miners also struggled. Northern Star Resources dropped 1.4 per cent, Evolution Mining shed 2.2 per cent and Newmont lost 1 per cent after bullion prices fell to a two-month low as the US dollar strengthened and the heightened Middle East tensions fuelled fears over war-driven inflation; investors weighed prospects for at least one more US rate hike this year. Higher interest rates reduce the investor appeal of gold, which doesn’t earn investors any interest. Bullion steadied in the afternoon, but had dropped as much as 2.3 per cent to below $US4100 an ounce overnight – its lowest intraday price since early August. The banking heavyweights, having been up during morning trade, turned south in the afternoon as oil prices pulled higher. All big four banks closed the session in the red. Commonwealth Bank fell 1.5 per cent, while National Australia Bank, Westpac and ANZ Bank each shed 1.6 per cent. Airline stocks suffered amid concerns over fuel prices, with Qantas Airways both down 1.8 per cent. An 8 per cent slump in Megaport, which sells a software platform that allows big businesses to create and manage network connections, pulled the tech sector down. It was otherwise mixed, with Codan down 1.3 per cent, software makers Xero and WiseTech up 3 per cent and 0.5 per cent and data centre operator NextDC also up 0.5 per cent.



The session’s big loser was construction services company Maas Group, which finished down 22.4 per cent amid concerns over its backing of data centre start-up Firmus’ planned $44 billion sharemarket float. The IPO is on life support after investors baulked at the price, with its bankers scrambling to stop the public offering from being called off. Maas, which owns 3.2 per cent of Firmus and has contracts to help build its facilities, told the ASX it considers that “speculation [about the float] has influenced investor sentiment” towards its shares. Meanwhile, defensive sectors such as utilities did well, with power companies Origin and AGL Energy up 1.7 per cent and 0.7 per cent. Among consumer staples, supermarket chains Woolworths and Coles were up 1.7 per cent and 1.4 per cent, respectively. Related Article Updated

High Court of Australia ‘Pandora’s box’: High Court decision could reopen coal mine approval cases Oil producers jumped thanks to the rise in prices for fuel. Woodside gained 2.6 per cent, Santos rose 1.5 per cent, and refiners Ampol and Viva Energy were up 1 per cent and 1.3 per cent, respectively. Coal mining companies Yancoal (down 0.9 per cent) and Whitehaven (down 0.7 per cent) both fell, after approval for a major Hunter Valley coal mine expansion was declared invalid by the High Court on Wednesday in a landmark decision that will force NSW planning authorities to reckon with emissions from Australian coal burnt overseas.



Legal and industry experts have warned the ruling will ripple across the sector, potentially exposing recent coal mine approvals to judicial review. On Wall Street overnight, the S&P 500 slipped 0.2 per cent, a day after topping its prior all-time high set in August. The Dow Jones dropped 0.7 per cent, while the Nasdaq composite fell 0.2 per cent from its own record. Related Article Opinion

Trade wars Europe raids Trump’s tool box for new ‘trade bazooka’ against China Stephen Bartholomeusz Senior business columnist US stocks felt pressure amid the rising yields swung in the bond market. World.title: ‘I’ll ring Wayne’: Latrell Mitchell coy on future at South Sydney
World.content:
SportNRLNRL 2026 ‘I’ll ring Wayne’: Latrell Mitchell coy on future at South Sydney Adrian Proszenko Updated October 8, 2026 — 5:49pm ,first published 3:30pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Gift icon Gift Gift icon 0 / 3 No gift articles left You've used all of your gift articles. 3 more will become available on the 1st of every month. Close Share A A A

Kangaroos centre Latrell Mitchell is relishing the chance to resume his battle with Dane Gagai at international level, but has brushed off questions about his future after South Sydney put contract extension talks on hold. Rabbitohs star Mitchell and Newcastle three-quarter Gagai had a memorable duel during the opening round of the finals. The Knights ultimately prevailed, Gagai declaring afterwards: “I wasn’t going to let him push me around.” Loading The rivalry will continue when Australia host New Zealand in the Rugby League World Cup opener next Thursday, which marks Gagai’s first appearance for the Kiwis after last representing Australia in 2018. After Gagai earned a points victory in the play-off fixture, Mitchell is looking forward to the rematch.



“Let’s go! We love it,” Mitchell said after entering Kangaroos camp at Double Bay on Thursday. “Dane’s a competitor, I’m a competitor, and that’s where we leave it, on the field. I love him, he’s a good man, and you walk off and know you’ve done everything you can to try and win a game. I love Gags. I wish him the best, but yeah, I’m definitely ready.” Latrell Mitchell and Dane Gagai go head-to-head in the finals. NRL Photos Mitchell and Gagai were Rabbitohs teammates for two years, but have for the most part of their careers been rivals at club and state level. “He just never stops talking, never goes away, you know?” Mitchell said. “He gives you shit … and I’m very competitive, so I just can’t let it die really.



“He’s winding back the clock, definitely. He’s shown that, and I think he’s got another two or three [seasons] in him, so let him go.” Mitchell’s future will be one of the big talking points during the off-season. The Blues star is among several centres – along with Herbie Farnworth, Matt Burton, Billy Smith, Jack Wighton, Jack Howarth and Deine Mariner – to hit the open market if they don’t re-sign with their incumbent clubs before November 1. Given he has played just 34 games in three seasons, critics question whether Mitchell remains a million-dollar-a-year player, at a time when the salary cap will soon increase. Mitchell would normally be a signing priority for the Rabbitohs, but they have indicated they will put contract talks on hold, potentially until March. Coach Wayne Bennett, however, is bullish about Mitchell staying. “I think for me, just focusing on camp is most important,” Mitchell said. “I’ve got a different colour on to the Rabbitohs, so for me, it’s all about this camp and focusing on that.” Pressed on his future, Mitchell said, “I’ll ring Wayne”, before ending Thursday’s press conference.



‘I wish I could be half the player Teddy is’: Walsh pays tribute to No.1 rival Tedesco Brisbane superstar Reece Walsh concedes he will struggle to wrestle the Kangaroos No.1 jersey off James Tedesco, saying he would be content to be “half the player” the Roosters captain is. One of the biggest selection calls for Australia coach Kevin Walters is his first-choice fullback. Walsh is the incumbent after being the No.1 on last year’s Ashes tour, while Tedesco made a strong case during a stellar season, which culminated in him winning the Clive Churchill Medal for the best player in Sunday’s grand final win over the Knights. Reece Walsh is back in the green and gold, but he has a lot of work to do to hang onto the No.1 jumper. George Chan “It’s hard to compete with Clive,” Walsh quipped as the Australian squad assembled in Sydney on Thursday.



“I’m obviously grateful to be in camp. I was watching Teddy when I was a kid. To see what he’s done over the last few weeks, it’s going to be hard for myself to push for a position – but I’m confident in my ability. “I can’t wait to be a sponge and learn off him. He’s one of the greats to do it in our game, and I’m lucky enough to be able to rub shoulders as a teammate with him.” Walsh has long admired Tedesco’s ability to perform at the highest level for such a lengthy period. Reece Walsh was the star of the 2025 season, which culminated in him claiming the Kangaroos No.1 jersey. Getty Images “I wish I could be half the player Teddy is, man,” Walsh said.



“Sitting there in school watching him win premierships and all that, it’s pretty amazing for his longevity and how consistent he’s been for so many years. Like I said, it was like last year being on the Ashes tour with Dyl [Dylan Edwards] – to be there and be able to rub shoulders and see the way he prepared. “Now, for myself to be able to see the way Teddy prepares for a game, as a 24-year-old, I’m pretty stoked with that. If there are some small things I can take away and put into my game, if I can be half the player that he’s been, I’ll be happy with that, brother.” Walsh hasn’t played since suffering a high-grade syndesmosis injury in August that required surgery. However, the Maroons ace feels he’s ready to return. Reece Walsh lies injured during the round 24 match against the Warriors with what was feared to be a season-ending injury. Getty Images “At the Broncos, we’ve got such good staff there who manage injuries really well,” he said.



“One of the physios there, Shred, has been thrashing me for the last six weeks. So it’s good to get back into the team environment and be around more players instead of just getting thrashed by myself ... “I’m going to do everything I can to push for this team, whether that’s starting or whether it’s not. I’m just going to try my best.” Related Article NRL 2026 Daniel Tupou retires after Roosters’ grand final win Walsh was the star of the 2025 season, helping steer the Broncos to a drought-breaking premiership. However, he concedes he has not consistently reproduced that form this year. “My form, it’s obviously disappointing after you win a comp and then see yourself back where you are,” he said.



“I feel like I tried hard this year. I feel like I wasn’t happy with where we finished as a team, but there are always lessons in having those years. I feel like those are the ones that drive you to get better, keep learning and want to do better the next year.” Walsh refused to give up on his World Cup dream despite initially suffering what was thought to be a season-ending injury. “I was obviously just taking it week by week and trying to do everything I could to put myself in a position to be fit,” he said. “I’ve done that, so I’m happy to be here. I can’t wait to get to work and prepare us for a good World Cup.”

World.content:
PoliticsFederalImmigration Taylor and Abbott say Bondi shooting drove the politics on migration Paul Sakkal October 8, 2026 — 5:47pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Opposition Leader Angus Taylor and ally Tony Abbott have linked the Coalition’s migration clampdown to the Bondi massacre, in the face of continued pressure to explain how the plan stacked up economically. Labor pushed back on deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume’s claim that Labor had brought in “more  executives than carpenters”, citing data showing that four times as many carpenters had arrived in the past four years. Angus Taylor, photographed in Sydney on Thursday. Nadir Tolj-Kinani After former bureaucrat Abul Rizvi cast doubt on Taylor’s 100,000 net migration target, Taylor spent Thursday defending the rigour of the policy and pledging an official set of costings by the next election. A top labour economist told this masthead on Wednesday that cutting the growing number of temporary migrants could help turn around Australia’s productivity malaise by encouraging firms to innovate instead of relying on cheap labour.



On the cultural and political rationale, Abbott echoed One Nation’s Barnaby Joyce in saying the terror attack on December 14 last year lit the fuse for the current debate on migration. Related Article Exclusive

Immigration The cost of cutting foreign workers: Fares spike in Taylor’s migration gamble “Because it was such a dismal milestone in our decline, for millions of Australians the Bondi massacre inspired a determination to retake control of our country,” Abbott said on Thursday. In a veiled critique of One Nation, Abbott argued Taylor had not “just railed against excessive migrant numbers … but provided a considered, costed mechanism to bring numbers down.” The former prime minister used his long-standing line on migrants joining “hotel Australia” rather than “team Australia” in a Substack article. Taylor used the same terms for the first time when announcing the policy two days ago, pointing to Abbott’s influence.



Similar democracies – from Canada to Scandinavia – have faced intense debates on migration and social values, prompting both right and centre-left parties to tighten controls. Related Article University International student cuts risk ‘very significant hole’, universities warn Moderate Liberal MPs speaking anonymously told this masthead they were relieved that Taylor’s office did not pursue a proposal formulated in Sussan Ley’s dying days as opposition leader that would have blocked migration from “terror hotspots”, which could have been characterised by political opponents as a discriminatory, Trump-like Muslim ban. But Taylor acknowledged that cultural as well as numerical considerations drove the policy, which he hopes will stem bleeding to One Nation and head off speculation about his leadership. “It absolutely is both,” Taylor said on Andrew Bolt’s program on News24.



“We’ve seen people come to this country and get visas who should never have come to this country, and should never have been issued visas. One of them was one of the shooters at North Bondi just before Christmas last year.” Related Article Analysis

Immigration A year after Hastie’s warning, Taylor has a solid migration plan. Hanson has the voters Australian-born Naveed Akram and his father, Sajid, a permanent resident who migrated from India in 1998, are accused of carrying out December’s Bondi Beach attack that claimed 15 innocent lives after being radicalised by Islamic State propaganda. The younger Akram survived and is awaiting trial on murder and terrorism charges, while Sajid was shot and killed during the attack. On the week of the third anniversary of the October 7 Hamas attacks on Israel, Taylor added: “We do not want people coming to our country who do not share our values and Islamist extremists do not share our values.”



The Business Council of Australia and the Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry have opposed the Coalition’s plan, arguing it puts up arbitrary targets while exacerbating skills shortages. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke announcing Labor’s migration plans last month. Alex Ellinghausen The council, a traditional ally of the pro-business Coalition, called out the “race to the bottom” on migration, but senior Coalition MPs laughed off the complaints, saying business leaders had vacated the debate on migration over the past year just as it had on tax reform brawls, and that they had become addicted to cheap labour. Labor ministers have not launched a full-frontal attack on Taylor’s plan – a sign the government knows it stands to gain little debating a hot-button issue where the populist right is setting the agenda. Instead, Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke has questioned the Coalition’s maths and said its plan would lead fewer skilled workers to migrate to Australia. Taylor received a series of questions on Thursday about labour shortages in aged care, restaurants and cleaning firms.



“We should not build an economy or businesses on a guest worker foundation; that is not the way to do it,” he said, insisting the party will release costings by the election. “That being said, it is true that there are many students, many students, both international and domestic, by the way, who work in aged care and the healthcare sector, and that’s a good thing.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. Destination dining doesn’t always involve a plane ride. Sometimes all it takes is a speedy trip on the M80. Xuan Banh Cuon is a restaurant filled with diners hunched over piping hot bowls of noodles from morning to night.

Wiggly rice flour-sheets are the restaurant’s namesake, rolled around pork, prawn and black fungus and improved only by a quick dip in a bowl of funky nuoc cham. Northern-style spring rolls are packed with pork and vegetables, chopped into crunchy inch-long nubbins for snacking ease.

Slurp stans will gravitate towards bun rieu cua cha ca, the shrimp and tomato broth holding vermicelli noodles, pork patties and crab meatballs. Sticky rice stuffed with sweet bean paste might be the best-value side dish on the strip, arriving sky-high and topped with golden-fried shallots all for a cheeky fiver.

The Australian sharemarket declined on Thursday, as oil prices jumped on renewed Middle East tensions, stoking concerns about inflation. Miners and banks led the losses. The S&P/ASX 200 finished down 66.8 points, or 0.8 per cent, at 8660.90, with five of its 11 sectors in the red and six in the green. The market decline came after a choppy, directionless session on Wednesday. The Australian dollar was trading at US69.54¢. Global sharemarkets felt pressure as yields climbed in the bond market and oil prices rose again. Bloomberg Oil rose after a report that the White House asked the Pentagon to draw up strike options against Iran that could be executed before the midterm elections, and as a storm shut some US output. Also, Iran-backed Houthis struck two airports in Saudi Arabia, killing three people as the group intensified its attacks on the kingdom, while also fighting Riyadh-backed forces in Yemen. Meanwhile, a tanker was struck by projectiles off the coast of Qatar on Wednesday, according to a report from UK Maritime Trade Operations, a rare attack deep inside the Persian Gulf. It’s the first reported strike on a tanker deep within the gulf in about a month.



Global benchmark Brent rose 2.5 per cent to approach $US103 a barrel in the afternoon. The advance pressured US Treasuries, pushing up the 10-year yield by three basis points to 5.32 per cent, near levels last seen in 2002. Australian 10-year government bonds, however, eased by a basis point to 5.39 per cent. Rising oil prices stoke energy costs for companies, also stoking inflation across the economy, weighing on corporate profits and slowing economic growth. Related Article Updated

AI Firmus float in trouble as investors don’t buy the hype Australia’s mining heavyweights took the brunt in Thursday’s session, leading the market decline. BHP – the biggest stock on the local market – finished down 2 per cent and Rio Tinto shed 2.9 per cent. Lynas Rare Earths slumped 5.3 per cent. Fortescue, the only pure-play iron ore producer, lost 1.4 per cent after saying its iron ore shipments fell 6 per cent in the September quarter to 46.8 million tonnes due to maintenance shutdowns. Inventories rose as it sold less than that – 42.9 million tonnes – amid its protracted negotiations with China’s state buyer. At the same time, net debt ballooned from $US900 million at the end of June to $US2.8 billion as of September 30, after paying out its dividends.



Gold miners also struggled. Northern Star Resources dropped 1.4 per cent, Evolution Mining shed 2.2 per cent and Newmont lost 1 per cent after bullion prices fell to a two-month low as the US dollar strengthened and the heightened Middle East tensions fuelled fears over war-driven inflation; investors weighed prospects for at least one more US rate hike this year. Higher interest rates reduce the investor appeal of gold, which doesn’t earn investors any interest. Bullion steadied in the afternoon, but had dropped as much as 2.3 per cent to below $US4100 an ounce overnight – its lowest intraday price since early August. The banking heavyweights, having been up during morning trade, turned south in the afternoon as oil prices pulled higher. All big four banks closed the session in the red. Commonwealth Bank fell 1.5 per cent, while National Australia Bank, Westpac and ANZ Bank each shed 1.6 per cent. Airline stocks suffered amid concerns over fuel prices, with Qantas Airways both down 1.8 per cent. An 8 per cent slump in Megaport, which sells a software platform that allows big businesses to create and manage network connections, pulled the tech sector down. It was otherwise mixed, with Codan down 1.3 per cent, software makers Xero and WiseTech up 3 per cent and 0.5 per cent and data centre operator NextDC also up 0.5 per cent.



The session’s big loser was construction services company Maas Group, which finished down 22.4 per cent amid concerns over its backing of data centre start-up Firmus’ planned $44 billion sharemarket float. The IPO is on life support after investors baulked at the price, with its bankers scrambling to stop the public offering from being called off. Maas, which owns 3.2 per cent of Firmus and has contracts to help build its facilities, told the ASX it considers that “speculation [about the float] has influenced investor sentiment” towards its shares. World.title: NZ First surge extends coalition lead, latest Taxpayers' Union Curia poll shows
World.content:
A new poll shows the coalition has slightly extended its lead over the left bloc thanks to a surge in support for New Zealand First, while both the major parties remain languishing in the twenties.

The Taxpayers' Union Curia poll has National and Labour neck and neck: since its September results, National dropped to 28.5 percent (down 0.5 percentage points), while Labour rose to 28.2 percent (up 2.3).

The Greens dipped slightly to 13.3 percent (down 0.6) while New Zealand First rocketed to 12 percent (up 3.6).

ACT is on 9.2 percent (down 1.3), Opportunity reached 4.8 percent (up 0.3) and Te Pāti Māori has dropped to 1.4 percent (down 0.6).

On these numbers, National, New Zealand First and ACT have a path to power with 65 seats.

However, the left bloc of Labour, the Greens and Te Pāti Māori would have 55 and be unable to form a coalition with Opportunity out of reach of Parliament.

The pollster - which also carries out National's internal party polling - noted due to the margin of error there is a 42 percent chance Opportunity is above the five percent threshold to enter Parliament.
