In the preferred Prime Minister stakes, National's Christopher Luxon is unchanged on 21.2 percent, while Labour's Chris Hipkins has leapt 4.1 points to 21 percent.

New Zealand First's Winston Peters is up 3.2 points to 13.9 percent, ACT's David Seymour is down 1.8 points to 6 percent, and the Greens' Chlöe Swarbrick is down 2.1 points to 4.9 percent.

World.title: Loafers Lodge fire trial: Survivor recounts rescue from burning building
World.content:
A elderly Loafers Lodge resident says he owes his life to firefighters who rescued him.

The claim comes on the fourth day of the manslaughter trial of four people involved in the operation and maintenance of the building.

Five people died, when a deliberately lit fire ripped through the multi-storey accommodation building in 2023.

John Tepania told the Wellington High Court he woke to the smell of smoke and, looking out the window, could see the shadows of a firetruck's ladder in the carpark on the northern side of the building

He said he tried to leave his top-storey room, but was beaten back by the heat and smoke so thick, he could only see about 10cm in front of him.

"I came out and I couldn't, I couldn't." Tepania said. "I tried three times all together.

"I knew where the steps were, but I thought the bottom might be burnt out. I went back to my room."

Tepania said he considered jumping from his fourth-floor window.

"I thought, 'What do I do? I haven't got much choice here', but then, bang, the door flew open and the fireman was standing at the door.

"If they hadn't come in, I would've been history. I would've been cooked.

"I owe my life to those firemen."

Hayden Moncrieff was that fireman.

He had attended two callouts to the lodge before the fire and had worked on the mezzanine floor of the rearward annex of the building.

On Wednesday, the jury heard that, while firefighters received reports of people trapped on "the mezzanine", the plans they had access to were from 2005.

Those plans pre-dated the addition of the forward mezzanine, where the five victims of the fire - Michael Wahrlich, Melvin Parun, Peter O'Sullivan, Kenneth Barnard and Liam Hockings - all lived.

On hearing reports of people trapped on the mezzanine, Moncrieff headed to the rear of the building, where he'd been before.

"I thought this was the mezzanine referred to on the radio as being the one where the people were trapped," he said. "I realised at this stage that there must be another mezzanine."

Moncrieff and another firefighter made their way up an external staircase to the rearward roof level, and helped four trapped residents into the basket of a ladder appliance working from the VTNZ carpark below.

After scanning the roof for others, he headed back down into the building to keep searching for people.

"The smoke was thick and had lowered to approximately chest height," Moncreiff said. "I found an elderly man... sitting in his room by the window, looking out."

He and another firefighter escorted the man - Tepania - from his room, and led him to the third floor, handing him over to another firefighter, who helped him from the building.

When Moncrieff resumed his search, he found conditions had grown even closer to "flashover", where any burnable material in an area spontaneously combusts.

"I could see that the smoke was starting to flicker," he said. "Sparks could be seen in it.

"This showed that the smoke was going to ignite. It would likely have been fatal for us to have been on the fire floor, when the flashover occurred."

Would up-dated floorplans have saved lives?

Assistant Commander Martin Wilby, who took over command of the scene from SSO Clark Townsley, said - on arriving at about 1am - he saw "jets of flames" from the roof of the building.

He surmised they must have come from sky-lights on a level not shown in the plans available to his fire crews.

Wilby told the jury he doubted the availability of accurate plans would have saved the lives of the five residents, who died in the fire.

"Due to the fire dynamics and the intensity of the fire, the data that we had, while it may not have been indicative of the changes in the buildings, I personally believe it would not have made a difference on the night," he said.

Under further examination from counsel for Greg Mein, Christopher Stevenson KC, Wilby conceded that, on his way to the fire, he had stopped to view the building's plans.

Realising they were not up to date, he requested Wellington City Council bring updated plans to the scene. Those plans arrived at about 2 am.

"We've already heard that time is of the essence and that a fire can double in 30 seconds," Stevenson said. "Save time, save lives, yes?

"The reason you stop is that you want more information about this building. Information is power isn't it?

"It's vital that you know the layout of the building."

Stevenson suggested to Wilby that, given the confusion created by calls from residents saying they were on a mezzanine level that did not correlate with the plans the initial response team had, it was reasonable to expect that correct plans would have assisted their response.

"It would've helped, yes," said Wilby.

Water weight threatens to collapse building.

Wilby described the scene as "chaotic", when he arrived shortly after 1am, and said he encouraged staff in the command unit to calm down.

He told the court he formally took over command of the scene from Clark Townsley at 1.09 am, and he quickly counted up the number of hose lines and appliances operational at the scene.

"I estimated the water was being put into the building at a rate of approximately 9000 litres per minute, but the rate of water exiting the building was far lower than that,

"The building contained within it approximately 250,000 litres

He said he was very concerned about the floors "pancaking", where they collapse one after another, due to the weight of water.

Wilby instructed crews to withdraw from the building and would later learn that, at a similar time, crews fighting the blaze on level three were also about to escape, as fire conditions approached unsurvivable levels.

"I knew that this decision may have altered the number of deceased, but I knew I had to do this to protect my staff," he said.

From the outside, he saw sign of extremely high temperatures, as well as the partial collapse of the mezzanine level near the eastern face of the building on Adelaide Road.

"I made the assessment that the collapse would have been insurvivable [sic]," Wilby said.

A short while later, he would meet two of the accused - McAllister and Murphy - and with their advice, a plan was formulated to retrieve a list of the building's occupant's from Murphy's office on the first floor.

On Wednesday, the court was told the court Townsley had also encountered McAllister and had taken keys to the building from him.

Locked rooms slow searches.

Station officer Joshua Leceve was initially tasked with searching for occupants on the third level, where the fire was situated.

His crew took over attacking the fire, as other teams withdrew, due to exhaustion and low oxygen levels.

"All I could see was a long hallway with lots of smoke. There was almost no visibility."

He made a decision not to break down locked doors along the north hall of level three to focus on pushing toward the fire source.

"The situation was deteriorating," Leceve said. "We were making good progress down the hallway on our hands and knees."

At one point, Leceve stood up to get his bearings.

"To my surprise, I felt the ceiling just above my head. When I touched the ceiling I felt heat through my glove and had to pull my hand away."

He told the court this and smoke emanating from the walls around him were clear signs the building was becoming structurally unsafe, and temperatures were nearing flashover.

He told his crew to withdraw and they left the fire floor, leaving their hose in their haste.

After a brief rest and replenishing his air supply, Leceve returned to the second level of the building, using a sledgehammer to smash his way past locked doors, but finding no-one.

Counsel for the prosecution Grant Burston asked Leceve if, had he known master keys to the building had been surrendered to firefighters, he would have used them in his search.

World.title: Southland District Council seeks to revoke resource consent for slink skin factory
World.content:
The Southland District Council is fighting in the Environment Court to strip a slink skin factory of its resource consent, arguing repeated breaches have harmed the environment and neighbouring properties.

Da Cheng "Eddie" Zhi and his Tuturau business, NZAgri Development, have been the subject of court orders and legal action by both local and regional authorities over alleged illegal discharges.

Neighbours have complained about offensive smells and piles of carcasses at the factory.

Zhi, who is representing himself in court, has defended his operation.

Six charges brought by the regional council relate to discharges of blood, leachate and/or contaminants to land where they could enter water, and a seventh alleges failure to comply with abatement notices.

The district council has also laid charges and is seeking to revoke the business' resource consent.

At an Environment Court hearing in Invercargill on Thursday, district council lawyer Laura Bielby said this was a significant step.

"This is one of those rare situations that the provision was intended to capture, where significant non-compliance has been both repeated and ongoing and where over a year of formal enforcement action has failed to achieve compliance," she said.

"For district council the compliance issues at the property kicked off in September of last year when council became aware through complaints that thousands of carcasses were piled up at the property and had not been disposed in accordance with the land use consent."

Nearby resident Alyce Perkins told the court her family had struggled with strong odours from the site.

"Physically you're just smelling that all the time. It makes you gag, it gets in your nose and you feel like you're wearing it," she said.

"It affects the way we live in our home. On when days it's smelly you can't open the windows, you wouldn't hang the washing out."

When cross-examining Perkins, Zhi apologised for her experience but questioned whether she could be certain the smell came from his property.

"There is no mistake where the smell is coming from. It is coming from the thousands of caresses that you have piled up in your yard," Perkins replied.

The Environment Court granted interim enforcement orders on 9 September preventing NZAgri Development from receiving or processing carcasses.

Zhi is separately challenging those orders, arguing his business is being unfairly restricted.

Zhi became emotional in court on Thursday, saying the interim enforcement orders had left his business struggling.

He told the court about workers losing their jobs, unpaid wages and customers who had already paid large sums of money.

"My heart is absolutely shattered. I have had enough. I have really had enough," he said.

World.title: Labour, Greens slam National's promise to drug test unemployed beneficiaries
World.content:
Labour and the Greens have labelled National's promise to drug test unemployed beneficiaries cruel and deplorable, while Winston Peters has warned it borders on fascist.

However, ACT leader David Seymour is on board, saying "people should have to work for their drugs".

National also wants to lower payment rates for people who have received a benefit for more than two years and double the benefit stand down period if they repeatedly leave jobs without good reason.

Social development spokesperson Louise Upston said drug-testing was entirely reasonable, and it was expected of many people to keep or get jobs.

Labour campaign chair Kieran McAnulty told RNZ the idea behind the policy was "frankly rubbish" and "quite offensive" to people who were desperately trying to find a job.

Audio player for " Salvation Army hit back at National's drug testing proposal " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1794026%2Flabour-greens-slam-national-s-promise-to-drug-test-unemployed-beneficiaries

Salvation Army hit back at National's drug testing proposal Checkpoint Download MP3 7m

He said the government's focus should be on creating jobs, not trying to look tough.

"If the National Party want to randomly drug-test beneficiaries, then why don't they randomly drug-test themselves?" he said.

"It's a tried and true Tory approach - kick the beneficiaries and hope that it gives them a bounce in the polls."

McAnulty said his past experience as a Work and Income case manager had taught him that people were not on the Jobseeker by choice.

Labour's campaign chair Kieran McAnulty. RNZ / Samuel Rillstone

"The whole premise behind it is that these people are taking the piss and they're not," he said. "These aren't bludgers."

Earlier this week, Labour confirmed it would not campaign on reversing the new Jobseeker "parental test" - introduced by the coalition - which prevented many 18 and 19-year-olds from getting the benefit.

McAnulty said it did not like the policy, but the party needed to make some trade-offs to ensure its fiscal plan added up.

Greens co-leader Marama Davidson said National's policy was cruel.

"Shame on National," she said.

"[It's] embarrassing, distraction, lazy politics of picking on people who are already struggling. This is just old, lazy, beneficiary , because they do not have the solution to create jobs."

National said 200,000 jobs were on the way, but Greens co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick said they were painting too rosy a picture, citing unemployment at an 11-year high.

"People can't work Luxon's ghost jobs," she said.

Peters warns of attack on freedoms, Seymour wants people to work for their drugs

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters said the policy could be a massive attack on people's freedoms.

"How quickly can that go straight from there to fascist behaviour? You've got to be very concerned about those sorts of suggestions."

New Zealand First leader Winston Peters. RNZ / Baz Macdonald

National leader Christopher Luxon said he was open to MPs being drug-tested and Peters said he would agree to that.

ACT leader David Seymour supported National's drug-testing plan, but said its proposal to lower the rate of payment for those who had been on the benefit for two of the previous three years was a "cop-out".

Seymour said, if people believed being on benefit required them to be ready for work, rather than a lifestyle of being dependent, then they must be able to pass a drug test.

"I look at guys that get up and go to work at five in the morning, go to a depot, get in a ute, and get driven out into the forest, work like hell in a dangerous environment," he said. "Why should those people have to pass a drug test so they can keep getting paid, when the alternative is to get stoned, stay in bed, and actually get the money from people who do have to go and work?

"That's not right, people should have to work for their drugs."

On National's plan to lower the benefit rate for longer-term jobseekers, Seymour said he preferred ACT's plan to put beneficiaries on electronic income management.

"I'd much rather say we'll give you the same amount on a plastic card that works at Pak'nSave, that will make sure your rent and power are paid," he said. "Then people say 'what about freedom?'

"No problem, get a job"

'Really, really cruel'

Auckland Action Against Poverty volunteer advocate Pip Colgan told RNZ Checkpoint the policy's authors had no idea what it was like to be on a benefit.

"It made me feel sick actually," she said. "It just feels really, really cruel.

"People are trying to get jobs, there are none. There are some, but I know endless people who have tried and tried and tried to get a job, and haven't been able to.

"You have to remember this government has caused tens of thousands of jobs to fold, particularly in the public service sector and other sectors as well.

Audio player for " Beneficiaries will face random drug tests, have some payments cut if National re-elected " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/politics_election-2026/1794026%2Flabour-greens-slam-national-s-promise-to-drug-test-unemployed-beneficiaries

Beneficiaries will face random drug tests, have some payments cut if National re-elected Checkpoint Download MP3 6m

"In most walks of life, you'll find people take drugs and I'm not sure why you would just pick on people on Jobseeker to test people. People offering jobs will drug-test people where it is needed, but it feels like they're just sniping vulnerable people again."

Colgan insisted people with drug issues needed help, not sanctions.

"Word on the ground is why would you even apply for Jobseekers, when you're only going to be turned down. It's very hard to get on a Jobseeker benefit, even if you're entitled to it.

"If you've been trying to get a job, how can [reducing benefits] be an incentive? All it will do is make it harder.

"Being on a benefit now really doesn't make ends meet. The moment something goes wrong, you're having to ask for an advance and get into debt, so if you haven't been able to get a job, receiving less money just creates more stress, more worries, more domestic violence, more illness, more truancy, more of all those negative things.

"Beneficiaries need to be treated with absolute dignity and given enough to live on, and supported in a much more comprehensive way than they are currently."

The Salvation Army also opposed the proposals and was alarmed that sanctions against beneficiaries would just exacerbate child poverty in New Zealand.

"The Salvation Army also opposed the 2012 Social Security Amendment Bill, which was a similar bill with related sanctions," Emma Hunter told Checkpoint.

"The consequences are that it could increase material hardship and, as we know, there are currently 169,000 children in child poverty. Children don't get to choose parental circumstances and the impacts of material hardship could be lifelong.

"A policy recommending benefit sanctions is inconsistent with a harm-reduction approach.

"If people are experiencing problematic substance abuse, we want to see access to treatment and the right support, and the right support for whanau.

"There's no evidence to suggest that drug-taking is related to unemployment."

Hunter cited a 2018 report, commissioned by Ministry of Social Development and written by the Welfare Expert Advisory Group, which found "very limited evidence about whether welfare benefit drug-testing and sanctions achieved their intended outcome".

World.title: Man took his own life after paying money to ‘sextortion’ blackmail involving AI-generated woman
World.content:
This article deals with the subject of suicide and may be distressing for some people.

A man fooled by a "sextortion" scam sent images to an AI-generated woman online, which criminals used to blackmail him.

The distressed man sent the blackmailers money and took his own life later that day.

The 41-year-old's suicide has prompted a coroner to issue a warning and advice about what to do if caught in such a scam.

The man died in 2024, within hours of making contact with someone online who identified themselves as "Donna Chase".

He exchanged messages and images of a sexual nature with "Donna", and she immediately began blackmailing him.

Police do not believe Donna Chase existed, but that she was an AI-generated persona used to trick the man into sharing sexually explicit images.

They told Coroner Janet Anderson they believed the bank account the man paid money into was associated with an organised criminal network based overseas.

"I have no doubt that the actions of 'Donna' were the primary relevant factor in [his] death," Coroner Anderson said.

"She deliberately solicited images of a sexual nature ... and then used these to blackmail him. This is a practice known as 'sextortion'."

The man died "within hours" of his first communication with Donna, the coroner said.

In a published summary, Coroner Anderson said the man was under stress when he died.

A relative had died, he was struggling with a relationship break-up, was on medical leave from work and had financial issues.

The man had told a relative he was finding it hard to get out of bed.

However, he had no significant history of mental health problems and no record of self-harm.

He had been due to return to work on the day he died.

That morning he sent "farewell messages" to his family, who went to check on him and found him dead.

Donna Chase

The man used Signal, a secure messaging account, to communicate with "Donna Chase".

After the images were sent, "Donna" immediately threatened to send them to the man's contacts and demanded money, via bank account transfer and codes for pre-paid Steam gift cards.

The summary said the man handed money over, but did not specify how much.

The exchanges with Donna, which included voice calls, ended with a final message from the man at 10.09am on the day he died.

The coroner said it was reasonable to conclude the man was in a highly emotional and vulnerable state when he ended his life.

"His actions would have been impulsive and taken in direct response to the difficult and stressful situation he found himself in."

Man's suicide a second 'sextortion' case

The man's suicide was the second involving a sextortion attempt before the Coroners Court this year.

A teen who had dreams of becoming a policeman took his own life just hours after he was sexually extorted online in 2023.

The 18-year-old met a person on Facebook who called herself Laura Wilson, who wanted to exchange intimate images.

He had no way of knowing he was talking to a scammer in West Africa who then threatened to share the teen's videos with all his contacts if he didn't pay $5000.

The online safety organisation Netsafe advised Coroner Anderson that sextortion is a serious global issue and the scammers are highly organised professional criminals who can be based anywhere.

She said the Auckland man's tragic death showed "the harm inflicted by those who engage in sextortion activities goes beyond extreme emotional distress and financial loss".

"In this case, it led to the senseless loss of a father, partner and friend."

Police advice for people caught in a sextortion scam is to pay nothing, to shut down all social media and contact Netsafe for further advice.

Netsafe has also published a step-by-step guide on how to deal with sextortion on its website.

Netsafe's advice for people subject to sextortion

Don't give in to demands

The most important thing is not to give in to the blackmailer's demands or share more pictures or videos. If you do, they are more likely to continue asking for more money or content. If you have already given them money - do not give them more. Even if you have given money, the remaining steps can still help.

Get evidence

If possible, take screenshots of the threats, but don't take pictures of the private images or videos. Note down the blackmailer's account name and where this is happening online.

Let others know

It might be helpful to write a message for your friends and family, letting them know that someone is trying to scam you (you don't have to go into detail about what has happened) and ask them not to accept message requests from unknown accounts online.

Report to the platform

Report to the social media platform (e.g. Instagram, Snapchat, PornHub) where the scammer contacted you. Give them all the information you can. If your content is shared we also recommend you report to that platform.

Cut off contact

Stop talking to the blackmailer and block them on all platforms.

The scammer will focus on the people they believe will most likely pay them or send more content. The scammer will 'drop' others very quickly who block the scammer and refuse to contact them, so it is very important that all contact from them is blocked immediately.

Secure social media accounts

Ensure all your social media accounts are as private as possible or deactivate them temporarily.

Keep an eye out

Ask someone you trust to help by keeping an eye on social media activity for you. This can help keep you informed and give you a break from social media if you need it.

Get the content hashed for removal

If you are under 18, and if you have copies of the private images or videos the blackmailer is threatening you with, you can use a free tool called Take It Down.

Take It Down creates a special code or digital fingerprint from the pictures or videos, and it shares that code with online platforms that may help to find and remove them from being shared online. The tool can also be used for synthetic images (deep fakes), which deals with it in the same way as genuine content.

If you are 18 or older you can use StopNCII.

StopNCII will generate a digital fingerprint, called a hash, of the images/videos on your device. STOPNCII shares the hash with Industry Partners so they can try to help detect and remove the images/videos from being shared online. StopNCII.org also accepts synthetic images (deep fakes) and deals with them in the same way as genuine content.

You can report to the police

You can make a report to police by calling 105. If you are at immediate risk please call police on 111.

Where to get help:

If it is an emergency and you feel like you or someone else is at risk, call 111.

* This story originally appeared in the New Zealand Herald.

World.title: Are you feeling wealthier?
World.content:
Audio player for " Can my landlord put a political billboard on my home? " removed for printing Visit page to play audio: https://www.rnz.co.nz/news/eyJhbGciOiJIUzI1NiJ9._Q.VKhexyL5oal5uCV3AUQmI1EOdryHi3hh73RdibV20lY/personal-finance/1794216%2Fare-you-feeling-wealthier

Can my landlord put a political billboard on my home? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 9m

Are you feeling wealthier?

Stats NZ has released updated national accounts data that shows household wealth slipped in the June quarter, although we are still better off than a year ago.

In the three months to June, household net wealth dropped by 0.3 percent, or $8.4 billion to $2.593 trillion but was still 1.9 percent higher than a year earlier.

Stats NZ said New Zealand has about two million households, which would mean wealth of about $1.3 million per household, but that hides very significant variations.

The fall in the most recent quarter was driven by a drop in housing and land values, which were down $16.6 billion or 1.4 percent. They were also 0.9 percent lower than a year earlier.

Westpac senior economist Satish Ranchhod said housing assets had recorded no growth since late 2023.

Financial wealth increased 0.6 percent to $1.39 trillion, 4.6 percent higher than June 2025.

Superannuation fund assets rose strongly over the quarter. Disposable incomes rose 5.2 percent over a year, led by income from self-employed businesses, up 12 percent.

Ranchhod said that would include stronger earnings from the agricultural sector, which has been boosted by strong commodity prices.

The amount that households were spending on interest was up in the June quarter, which Ranchhod said was the first increase in two years.

"Over the past few years, many borrowers saw their debt servicing costs fall as they rolled off earlier high mortgage rates and on to lower ones. That helped to support household spending.

"However, the easing in average borrowing cost has now ended. Recent months have seen mortgage rates pushing higher as the RBNZ has begun to hike the Official Cash Rate, with further hikes expected over the coming year.

"Looking ahead, we don't expect a significant increase in average household borrowing costs. However, we won't see the same support for spending that we did over the past few years."

Financial liabilities were up 4.9 percent compared to 2025.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said both the drop in house values and the wider increase in the cost of living, particularly in essentials, would be making people feel worse off.

"For those who bought during the last decade, it's been a ****show on house prices. But those who bought before are still ahead. But it's not rising. That means we aren't moving as much, aren't renovating ... that shows up in house sales, furniture, hardware."

He said how the impact was felt would vary across different parts of the economy.

Infometrics chief forecaster Gareth Kiernan said house price falls were probably not a significant drag on many households anymore, except those who bought at the peak of the market.

"It's probably more in terms of the cost of living, essentials going up in price overlaid with fuel prices being at levels we haven't seen before."

Incomes and employment were growing, he said, and GDP was increasing more than it had in recent years.

"Things are heading in the right direction but not enough to feel like we've really crawled out of the hole we've found ourselves in."

Otago University economist Murat Ungor said changes in wealth would affect spending but the effect was small.

"A study from 2018 on NZ finds that the estimated elasticity of consumption spending to housing wealth is about 0.22 percent. In dollar terms, the average marginal propensity to consume out of a one-dollar increase in housing wealth is around 2.2 cents. Income and the prices people pay every week matter more.

"It does depend on who we are talking about. For older homeowners with little or no mortgage, a fall in house values is largely a paper change. For people who bought recently with a high loan relative to the value of the house, or who need to refinance soon, falling values are more worrying, because their equity cushion is thinner.

"For renters and would-be first-home buyers, lower prices may be welcome news. Aggregate figures hide these differences.

"I would say the sense of being worse off is driven more by what is happening to prices and incomes than by house values."

World.title: Serial rapist, convicted murderer Malcolm Rewa appeals for earlier release
World.content:
One of the country's worst serial rapists is appealing to remain eligible for release next year.

In April, Malcolm Rewa was sentenced at the Auckland High Court to 10 years in prison, after pleading guilty to raping a 16-year-old in Onehunga in June 1988.

He was already serving a preventive detention sentence, with a minimum non-parole period of 22 years, after being convicted of sexual attacks on 25 women.

Rewa, now 73, was also serving a life sentence for murdering Susan Burdett in 1992.

His sentence for the Burdett murder meant he was eligible for release in 2027, but this year's sentencing extended that eligibility out to 2029.

In the Auckland Court of Appeal on Thursday, Rewa appealed the April sentence, asking to keep a parole eligibility date of next year.

Lawyer David Allan said Rewa's sentence did not need an extension, given he was already serving an indefinite sentence of preventive detention.

Allan said the court should consider the totality of the case.

"To extend the parole period out any further than the current eligibility date of 6 February 2027 is manifestly excessive and a disproportionate punishment," he said.

Rewa was already subject to an indeterminate sentence for the same series of offending and becoming eligible for parole did not necessarily mean he would be released on 6 February next year, Allan said.

The most recent sentence came after the now-adult survivor of the rape - who did not know who her attacker was at the time - asked police to run her medical swabs against its DNA database, revealing a match with Rewa.

Allan said it wasn't clear why the 1988 rape had not been merged with Rewa's other rape cases, as was done in 1996.

Crown lawyer Zannah Johnston said the court should look at the 1988 case separately, rather than grouping it with the rest of Rewa's crimes.

"It doesn't follow that a court sentencing in 2026 must only sentence that which would have been imposed back in the 90s or 80s, if this had come up earlier," she said.

"This offending has come to light later and does warrant separate recognition."

The panel of Justice David Johnstone, Justice Grant Powell and Justice Paul Radich reserved their decision.

Another man, Teina Pora, was wrongfully convicted of Susan Burdett's rape and murder in 1994.

He was found guilty again at a retrial in 2000, but eventually had his convictions quashed by the Privy Council in 2014.

World.title: Whangārei rough sleepers braced for eviction as deadline arrives
World.content:
Controversial plans to evict rough sleepers from a disused sports ground in Whangārei have put on hold, mayor Ken Couper says.

The district council had ordered the 10 people staying in tents, makeshift shelters and a bus at the Old Boys' Rugby Club to leave by the end of today.

However, after visiting the site this afternoon, Couper said any further action had been paused.

That was to give people living there more time to work with social agencies on accommodation and support options.

Couper said the council would also continue to address its safety concerns at the site.

At its peak earlier this year, about 50 people - including teenage children - were living at the hilltop sportsground.

Couper said today's meeting with the residents was "very productive".

"All parties need to be congratulated for a constructive approach to the problem," he said.

"The next step will be, I will go back to the council, we will talk to the agencies involved and council staff. We do have to look after public safety but clearly there are people up there who require help from society, and we have to make sure they can get it."

Some of the rough sleepers told RNZ they had nowhere else to go.

Elliot Jackson said he had been homeless since his house burnt down two years ago.

He had spent much of that time couchsurfing at friends' homes, but for the past five months, he had lived in a tent on the hill at the Old Boys' sportsground.

He was "most definitely" worried about the eviction notice.

"I talked to the council women who came up here," Jackson said. "They said it was alright for us to stay, they had no problem with it and now it seems like they do have a problem.

"If this somehow changes things and it gets one person in a house, then it's worth doing, because living in a tent, you can't move. It's confining, it's cold and damp, and there's no locks on it.

More than 50 people turned out at the Old Boys' Rugby Club to support rough sleepers facing eviction. Supplied

"In this day and age, you definitely need locks."

Jackson said he was not eligible for emergency housing, because he still owned the land where his house used to stand.

The 59-year-old said it was hard to find a job and start saving money to rebuild.

"The thing is, at my age, no-one really wants to hire you and you don't earn enough on the benefit to rent a house yourself, so I'm in a no-win situation."

Jackson, who had injured his back getting in and out of the tent, said the nearest tap was in a park on the other side of Port Road, at the bottom of a steep hill.

The nearest toilet was about half a kilometre away by the Hātea River.

Jason Poutai, who lived in a tent at the sports ground until he got a flat in a new Kāinga Ora complex in June, said it would have been distressing to get the eviction notice.

"That'd be heart-breaking to be honest, because, well, you've got these move-on laws coming in as well. Where are they supposed to go?"

Poutai was pleased the Old Boys' residents would now get a reprieve, at least until the council decided its next steps.

He was also campaigning for a night shelter, which he said was badly needed in the city.

Poutai said homelessness in Whangārei was mostly out of sight and far bigger than the 10 people in tents at the Old Boys' sports ground.

The last official survey, in December 2025, found 237 people in Whangārei were without nay kind of shelter, and a further 1900 were couchsurfing or living in condemned buildings.

Earlier today, around 7am, about 50 people gathered at the hilltop site in a peaceful show of support for the rough sleepers.

Northland-based Green MP Hūhana Lyndon, who also visited the sportsground, urged the council to put the eviction notice on hold.

She said agencies were working hard to find homes for the remaining residents, but many had complex needs and it would take time.

"These are people, these are whānau, they need love and care and respect," Lyndon said. "We need to put dignity at the forefront in the way we handle those most vulnerable in these times of need and we know Whangārei's better than this."

World.title: Dropped Aussie opener out of Sheffield Shield match with concussion
World.content:
Jake Weatherald's wretched run has continued, with the discarded Test opener forced out of the start of the domestic cricket season with concussion.

Weatherald was subbed out of South Australia's opening game against Victoria at Junction Oval on Thursday, before the start of day two.

He crashed into the picket fence while chasing the ball on Wednesday during Victoria's first innings.

Weatherald then faced only faced six balls at the end of day one before Victorian debutant Harry Hoekstra had him caught behind for a duck.

It is understood Weatherald had delayed symptoms, prompting the decision on Thursday morning to take him out of the game.

Matthew Gilkes took Weatherald's place in the SA line-up.

Weatherald was dropped from the Test team in August after their shock first-Test loss to Bangladesh in Darwin.

Hoekstra also top-scored with 45 at number nine as Victoria rallied to reach 244 in their first innings.

South Australia resumed at 1-4 and were 5-185 approaching tea.

Opener Henry Hunt made 71 before David Moody bowled him in a crucial breakthrough for the fourth wicket.

Jake Lehmann was 52 not out and Hoekstra had continued his fine debut with three wickets.

AAP

World.title: 'Live on forever': Brock inspires Bathurst 20 years on
World.content:
Just as he does every year, Craig Lowndes is drawing on memories of Australian motorsport legend Peter Brock to fuel yet another attempt at the Bathurst 1000.

It is just that this year's Great Race feels a bit more special, with Australian motorsport marking 20 years since the nine-time Mount Panorama conqueror's tragic death.

A long-time protege of Brock, seven-time Bathurst 1000 winner Lowndes will line up for his 33rd bid at claiming the holy grail of Australian motorsport.

Bathurst 1000: How to watch, race start time and weather forecast Here is what you need to know about this weekend's Bathurst 1000, including when the race begins and how you can follow the action.

The 52-year-old will share the number 15 Team 18 wildcard with Super2 racer Bayley Hall after Triple Eight Racing Engineering ditched Chevrolet for Ford last year.

Lowndes has paired with rookies since former Triple Eight teammate Jamie Whincup's retirement in 2021, a move that helps the three-time Supercars champion pass on Brock's legacy.

"I'm somewhat gone full circle," Lowndes said today.

"Bayley, we did a track walk the other day, and I literally recalled everything that Peter taught me; from Turn 1, from Hell Corner, all the way around to Murray's Corner.

"For me, I'm hopefully passing on that legacy in some way … it is a milestone year. There's no doubt about that."

Peter Brock, pictured in 2004, won the Bathurst 1000 a record nine times. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

Ask Lowndes what he remembers of Brock's counsel, and he will condense his knowledge of the track's 23 corners into a minute: advice like doing all your braking over Skyline or looking for the kink on the inside of the Elbow for your turn-in point.

"Peter was more than just a teammate," Lowndes said.

"His legacy will live on forever. He was bigger than the sport in some regards.

"He was just very much a person that could capture people's attention, hold their attention, but also inspire them for greatness.

"Those are the parts that I miss 20 years on."

Just weeks after Brock died in 2006, Lowndes roared to an emotional Bathurst 1000 win with an up-and-coming Jamie Whincup to pay tribute to his great mate.

Just weeks after Peter Brock's death, Craig Lowndes (left) and Jamie Whincup won the Bathurst 1000 in 2006. (Getty Images: LAT Images/Mark Horsburgh)

"History shows that the gap at the end of the day was 0.5, and that was Brock's number for a long time," Lowndes said.

Whincup added: "The minute's silence, I'll never forget that."

"You generally got someone on the hill yell out or whatnot, but that day, even the birds stopped chirping.

"It was my first (Bathurst) win for the team and a memory that I'll take to the grave."

Seven-time champion Whincup won't be on the grid for the first time since his 2002 debut, making way for Nick Percat to link up with title contender Broc Feeney, and allowing him to focus on his duties as Triple Eight team principal.

Feeney and Percat will be smarting after a horror outing at last month's The Bend 500, finishing 24th out of 26 cars at the Bathurst 1000 curtain-raiser.

The Triple Eight star has never won the 1,000km epic and is second in the standings behind last year's race winner and Grove Racing star Matt Payne.

World.title: NZ Rugby goes to court over PNG 'Chiefs' name
World.content:
Rugby union officials have launched New Zealand High Court proceedings to prevent the National Rugby League's (NRL) new Papua New Guinea-based franchise from using the "Chiefs" name in New Zealand.

New Zealand Rugby (NZR) said the move was an effort to protect the brand of the Waikato-based Chiefs, who have played in the Super Rugby competition across Australasia since rugby union turned professional in 1996.

The NRL, which is Australia-based but has one team in the New Zealand city of Auckland, announced the expansion of the league to Papua New Guinea in 2024.

The island nation's Prime Minister James Marape unveiled the name "Chiefs" the following year.

James Marape (front, second from right) announced the PNG Chiefs' name in October 2025. (Supplied: NRL)

NZR said attempts to engage the Australian Rugby League Commission (ARLC) over the issue had been unsuccessful and it was seeking an interim and final injunction against the use of the name before the Papua New Guinea team was officially launched later this month.

"For 30 years the Chiefs and their players have built an incredibly strong identity that is widely recognised and loved by fans," NZR chief executive Steve Lancaster said in a statement today.

"We have raised our concerns with the ARLC directly and consistently over the last year in attempting to find a resolution. We now have a responsibility to protect the Chiefs brand."

Action branded 'hypocritical'

ARLC executive chairman Peter V'landys said the complaint was hypocritical given the New South Wales rugby league team had used the "Blues" brand for more than half a century before the Auckland Blues Super Rugby franchise was launched 30 years ago.

"We will defend this vigorously," he said.

"The hypocrisy is mind-blowing, considering the Auckland Blues in 1996 used the NSW Blues name without any consultation or approval.

"Rugby union is obviously feeling threatened by rugby league in New Zealand, with sell-outs at most rugby league games."

Rugby league split from rugby union in the late 19th century in a dispute about amateurism.

PNG Chiefs face 'danger of brand confusion' over team name Australia's intellectual property agency tells PNG's rugby league franchise that its chosen name, the Chiefs, risks being confused with the name of a Super Rugby club.

While union is the more popular game globally, league rules the roost on Australia's eastern seaboard and has been making great strides in New Zealand.

Papua New Guinea is the only country in the world where rugby league is the most popular sport.

The new team has already signed a slew of top NRL players ahead of its first season in 2028, and will be backed by hundreds of millions of dollars in funding from the Australian government, which is looking to shore up its influence in the Pacific Islands.

"We want to be absolutely clear, this is not about rugby league's growth in the Pacific," Mr Lancaster said.

"We welcome the development of the Pacific region through sport and the passion that the people of Papua New Guinea have for both rugby and rugby league."

The ABC has contacted PNG Chiefs CEO Lorna McPherson, IP Australia and Mr Lancaster for comment.

Reuters/ABC

World.title: Amateur players' chance to win $1m against pros returns to Australian Open
World.content:
The Australian Open's 1 Point Slam will again have some star power in January with Carlos Alcaraz, Coco Gauff, Naomi Osaka and Jannik Sinner among the players set to compete against pros and amateur qualifiers for a $1 million prize.

At the Australian Open launch today, organisers said qualifying events for the 1 Point Slam are underway at clubs across the country, and a further two days of qualifying will be held during opening week ahead of the first grand slam tournament of the year from January 17 to 31.

The 1 Point Slam final will see the pros competing against amateurs and wild cards for the prize at Rod Laver Arena on January 13.

Jordan Smith, a little-known local amateur player, beat Sinner and went on to make himself a millionaire after winning the 1 Point Slam last January.

Smith won on the third stroke of the final when Joanna Garland, the women's number 117 from Taiwan, sent a two-handed backhand wide.

Jordan Smith cashes in Jordan Smith comes from a tennis-mad family in Sydney and is now a millionaire thanks to a couple of days' work at the Australian Open.

All the matches lasted just one single point in a knockout bracket that included men and women, professionals and amateurs, plus celebrities such as Taiwanese pop star Jay Chou, who was knocked out without hitting a ball after an ace from Petar Jovic.

"At the heart of the creation of the 1 Point Slam is our desire to even more deeply connect the Australian Open to every tennis community in the country," Andrew Abdo, Tennis Australia's new chief executive, said.

More than 1.3 million fans attended the 2026 Australian Open, and organisers are planning to increase viewing capacity, seating and offer more shade across the Melbourne Park precinct next year.

AP

World.title: Wallabies resist urge to shift Suaalii from wing for Bledisloe Cup Test
World.content:
The Wallabies have kept Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii on the wing for Saturday night's Bledisloe Cup Test at Auckland's Eden Park, with Isaac Henry named in the centres.

Henry has been included at outside centre to partner Len Ikitau in the Wallabies' midfield against the All Blacks.

Ikitau, who has recovered from an ankle injury, moves from outside to inside centre in the wake of Hunter Paisami's suspension.

Wallabies upset Boks in Perth The Wallabies manage to overcome four late yellow cards to defeat world champions South Africa 42-38 in a pulsating Test in Perth.

Wallabies coach Les Kiss resisted the temptation to shift Suaalii from the wing back to the centres.

He has shown faith in 27-year-old Henry, who he coached at the Queensland Reds.

Kiss also handed Henry his Test debut two months ago, against Japan in Osaka.

Henry, who will be playing his fifth Test, is the only change to the Wallabies' starting XV following their stunning 42-38 win over world champions South Africa in Perth late last month.

The Wallabies made four changes on the reserves bench, opting for a 5-3 (forwards-back split).

Hooker Josh Nasser, prop Massimo De Lutiis, back-rower Nick Champion de Crespigny and fly half Declan Meredith earned call-ups.

De Lutiis and Champion de Crespigny are the respective replacements for Taniela Tupou and Tom Hooper, who have returned to their European clubs.

Isaac Henry will wear the number 13 jersey against the All Blacks. (Getty Images: Paul Miller)

"Keeping consistency in the starting side gives us a solid foundation, while adding some freshness on the bench will provide energy late in the game," Kiss said in a statement.

The Wallabies have enjoyed a six-match unbeaten streak after beginning the Test season with defeats to Ireland and France in the Nations Championship.

Since Kiss took over from Joe Schmidt as coach, the Wallabies have recorded four wins and a draw.

But the All Blacks pose an almighty challenge, especially at Eden Park.

The Wallabies have lost 24 consecutive Tests against the All Blacks at the venue, with their most recent victory coming in 1986.

They did, however, beat Wales at Eden Park in the third-place play-off at the 2011 Rugby World Cup.

"There aren't many tougher challenges than playing New Zealand at Eden Park, but it's one we're excited by and know that we will need to be at our best in all aspects of our game," Kiss said.

Damian McKenzie will start at fly half for the All Blacks. (Getty Images: Fiona Goodall)

Meanwhile, injury has forced the All Blacks to name Damian McKenzie at fly half as they look to maintain their stranglehold on the Bledisloe Cup.

McKenzie will start at 10 after Ruben Love (ankle) and Richie Mo'unga (calf) were ruled out.

Beauden Barrett will play fullback, with McKenzie having held down the role for all four Tests in the All Blacks' recent 3-1 series loss to the Springboks.

All three Barrett brothers will start against the Wallabies, with ex-captain Scott named at lock and Jordie slotting in the backline at inside centre.

The All Blacks have held the Bledisloe Cup since 2003.

Wallabies squad (1-15): Angus Bell, Brandon Paenga-Amosa, Allan Alaalatoa, Jeremy Williams, Lukhan Salakaia-Loto, Rob Valetini, Fraser McReight, Harry Wilson (C), Ryan Lonergan, Ben Donaldson, Joseph-Aukuso Suaalii, Len Ikitau, Isaac Henry, Max Jorgensen, Tom Wright

Replacements: Josh Nasser, Aidan Ross, Massimo De Lutiis, Lachlan Shaw, Nick Champion de Crespigny, Tate McDermott, Declan Meredith, Harry Potter

All Blacks squad (1-15): Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor (C), Fletcher Newell, Scott Barrett, Josh Lord, Tupou Vaa'i, Peter Lakai, Wallace Sititi, Cam Roigard, Damian McKenzie, Leroy Carter, Jordie Barrett, Quinn Tupaea, Will Jordan, Beauden Barrett

Replacements: Asafo Aumua, George Bower, Pasilio Tosi, Shannon Frizell, Anton Segner. Kyle Preston, Rieko Ioane, Josh Moorby

World.title: Roosters lose fifth NRL premiership player as Leniu joins Eels
World.content:
Spencer Leniu has signed a four-year deal with Parramatta just days after winning his fourth NRL premiership with the Sydney Roosters.

Leniu finished his three-year stint at the Tricolours on a high after a stellar performance in the 19-18 win over Newcastle to secure the 2026 trophy.

The NSW Origin representative added the Roosters' premiership ring to the three he won with Penrith between 2021 and 2023.

Leniu was granted a release from the final year of his Roosters contract, which will give the club some salary cap reprieve.

Whyte primed to be even better following GF win Naufahu Whyte wouldn't have looked out of place should he have won the Clive Churchill Medal after the Roosters' grand final victory, and the Tricolours prop is adamant we have yet to see his best.

The hard-hitting forward's Eels contract is reportedly worth more than the $850,000 a year he was making with Easts, where he spent much of his time coming off the bench.

He is expected to play a more active role in blue and gold, leading the line for the Eels' forward pack.

The move will see the former Panther reunite with good friend Jarome Luai, but first the pair will both suit up for Toa Samoa at the Rugby League World Cup.

Earlier, the Roosters announced that the 26-year-old had been granted an immediate release from the final year of his contract, allowing him to join Parramatta.

From the premiership line-up, Angus Crichton and Mark Nawaqanitawase are rugby-bound, Daly Cherry-Evans is joining Hull FC, while Daniel Tupou has retired this week after his 307-game career.

Connor Watson, who missed the title decider due to concussion, has signed for a season with St George Illawarra Dragons.

With his exit announced at the Roosters' awards night on Wednesday, Leniu said he would leave the club on a high.

"I'm proud to have worn the Roosters jersey, and I'll always have a lot of love and respect for the club, the boys and everyone who has supported me during my time here," Leniu said.

"Winning a premiership with this group and sharing that with the boys, our families and everyone at the club is something I'll carry with me for the rest of my life."

AAP

World.title: Sally 'couldn't run to the mailbox'. Now she tackles ultramarathons
World.content:
Sally Beggs has been running for 10 hours.

Traversing tough terrain since 6am, it's now late afternoon, and the downhill course allows her to pick up speed.

"This race owes no-one anything," she tells herself.

"No dilly dallying; I'm not allowed to stop for photos. Stop for nothing. Just keep going as fast as you can."

Beggs is competing in the Grampians Peaks Trail 50-kilometre ultramarathon, and is on her way to cross the finish line in a personal best time of 10 hours and 24 minutes.

Sally Beggs says running has helped her make changes to her lifestyle. (ABC: Tony Hill)

Chasing a runner's high wasn't how Beggs imagined life would look in her 50s, but she, like more and more Australians, has made heading off the beaten track for hours on end her sport of choice.

Beggs says when her interest in running began, she "couldn't even run to the mailbox".

"My sister phoned me up and said, 'Sal, come and run a half marathon'. I actually had a cigarette in one hand and a drink in the other," she tells ABC iview's Back Roads.

Unfit and overwhelmed by small decisions, Beggs took to running laps of the paddocks on her family's wool farm in regional Victoria to help escape the "craziness of the world".

Now, she runs 50 kilometres on race day.

The GPT 100 is the main event and is 100 miles or about 160 kilometres long. (ABC iview: Back Roads)

An ultramarathon, or ultra, is any running race longer than a regular marathon's 42.2 kilometres. Trail runs use forest and hiking tracks rather than the road.

Ultra events and trail running are seeing more sell-out events, larger participant numbers and greater diversity in entrants, according to president of the Australian Ultra and Trail Running Association (AUTRA) John Claridge.

"While the sport has traditionally attracted runners in their 30s and 40s, we're seeing increasing numbers of younger adults looking for experiences beyond road running, alongside older runners who value the variety of terrain and the social nature of trail events," he says.

Loading...

There are events of varying lengths, from short introductory runs to the longest ultras, which exceed 300 kilometres and take days to complete.

Claridge says this means there's something for all runners.

"We're seeing increasing participation across different ages, abilities and backgrounds, which is helping to build a stronger and more inclusive community," he says.

Unlike many sports, trail and ultra running is said to be as much about the journey as the result.

"Every course is different, with changing terrain, weather and conditions, so success is often defined by completing a personal challenge rather than simply achieving a placing," Claridge says.

A sense of adventure

The Grampians Peaks Trail 100 Miler is right on Beggs's doorstep.

Grampians Peaks Trail 100 miler is not the faint-hearted. (ABC iview: Back Roads)

It's one of more than 100 organised ultra-marathon events held across the country annually and is recognised as one of 10 World Trail Major events, alongside races in Canada, the USA, Japan, Spain and South Africa.

Hosting races of varying distances, the event traverses Gariwerd/Grampians National Park from Mt Zero to Dunkeld, over tough terrain and often through tumultuous weather.

The main event, the 100 miler, features 7,700 metres of elevation and is completed over four days.

The 50-kilometre event is Beggs's race of choice, and it's the beauty of the outdoors that keeps her coming back for more.

Ultramarathons offer races across all kinds of terrain. (ABC New England: Matt Bedford)

"I just love being in nature. I love all the surprises that you get. You never know what you're going to see," she says.

Claridge says this strong connection with Australia's landscape draws people in.

"People are increasingly looking for experiences that combine physical activity with time outdoors and a sense of adventure," he says.

It's a sense of adventure that John Claridge says is increasing the sport's popularity. (Supplied: GPT 100)

Camaraderie alongside competition

Halls Gap police officer Greg Kew and his wife Nicole are self-proclaimed running addicts.

They serve as each other's support crew and travel the world to participate in ultra marathons.

"People go out for cake and coffee on a date. We go running," Greg Kew says.

In the 2025 Grampians Peaks Trail 100 miler, they ran for almost 44 hours through wild weather and bitter cold.

Greg and Nicole Kew met through the running community.

But on the trails, Greg Kew says people look out for each other and are mindful of the landscape.

The couple are active members of the ultra and trail-running community and volunteer at local events.

Claridge says members like the Kews help foster the sport's strong camaraderie between competitors.

"While people challenge themselves individually, the culture of the sport is notably supportive, and that sense of belonging is something many participants talk about," he says.

Women are finding new ways to move and connect outdoors A growing number of women say they want community, physical activity and time outdoors — just without the gasps for air that come with trying to chat mid-run.

Not to mention the health benefits of being active. For Beggs, this has helped her kick old habits.

"I've quit smoking. I used to drink a lot, and now I don't," she says.

"I feel like I'm setting a better example to my boys, and I just find that it just brings me such enormous pleasure. It's a way that I recharge."

Stream Back Roads free on ABC iview or watch Thursdays at 8pm on ABC TV.

World.title: Adelaide 36ers coach claims he was 'targeted' by refs in United loss
World.content:
Adelaide 36ers coach Trevor Gleeson says he was "targeted" by NBL referees in his side's 96-91 Ignite Cup loss to Melbourne United on Wednesday night.

Gleeson was left flabbergasted after being whistled for a technical foul by referee James Griguol during the second quarter of the 36ers' third straight defeat.

Griguol made the call from the opposite corner of the court at the Adelaide Entertainment Centre.

"I was talking to one referee [Andrew Goodman], because Whitey [36ers guard Isaac White] got a backhand right in the face," Gleeson said.

"The other referee on the other side of the floor gives me a technical foul, when I'm having a conversation with [Goodman].

"I think I was targeted for that today."

Gleeson was also frustrated by an incident in the third quarter.

With 7:17 left in the term, Gleeson requested to challenge an offensive foul against centre Nick Rakocevic, who scored while colliding with Melbourne's Fabijan Krslovic.

After a lengthy delay, Gleeson was told the decision would stand and the replay centre would not entertain his challenge.

"They already reviewed it [Rakocevic's foul] and you can't challenge a review," Gleeson said.

"No-one told me.

"I'll talk to [NBL head of referees] Scott Butler and say, 'Why?', and send him [video] clips again."

A 23-16 disparity in free-throw attempts, favouring Melbourne, also earned Gleeson's ire.

That was on the back of a similar 23-14 differential in foul shots favouring the New Zealand Breakers in the 36ers' blowout 88-72 home loss on Sunday.

"It's frustrating when the opposition team comes here and they shoot more free throws than us both times," Gleeson said.

"The guys deserve more than that.

"Coming back [to the NBL] after five years, I would have thought the referees would really go in front.

"I've got a good relationship with Scott [Butler], but it just seems that when the bright lights come on, something else happens."

The 36ers' loss leaves the club second last on the NBL ladder.

AAP

Tech.title: BMW’s iX4 SUV is a 428-mile defensive weapon against China’s EV takeover
Tech.content:
is transportation editor with 10+ years of experience who covers EVs, public transportation, and aviation. His work has appeared in The New York Daily News and City & State.

While much of the automotive world sits dumbfounded as China gobbles up all its customers, BMW continues to roll out extremely well-crafted, technologically advanced electric vehicles that impress in both drive quality and price. The latest is the BMW iX4, a coupe-shaped SUV that puts a sportier spin on the automaker’s iX3.

The iX4 is the third vehicle to be released on BMW’s next-generation Neue Klasse platform, following the iX3 and i3 models. The iX4 50 xDrive will come first in March 2027, followed by an even more high-performance M60 xDrive version later in the year. The automaker is positioning this new lineup as its bulwark against the flood of Chinese imports that is currently decimating other European brands. But while the iX4 can certainly compete on range and tech, it’s unclear whether BMW can rival China in terms of sheer affordability.

In that respect, the BMW iX4 50 xDrive starts at $66,200 (excluding fees for destination and handling). And it bears all the hallmarks of BMW’s other Neue Klasse models, such as the “Gen6” high-voltage battery with 112.2kWh of usable energy, an 800-volt architecture for lightning-quick charging top-ups, and up to 428 miles of range based on EPA estimates.

That’s more range than the Tesla Model Y, the best-selling electric vehicle in the world. BMW has been blowing away expectations on range to such a degree that even the experts at InsideEVs are left wondering whether it’s overkill. After all, Tesla and others have done plenty well with EVs in the mid-300s, while Lucid continues to struggle despite exceeding 500 miles in range.

The BMW iX4 50 xDrive (left) and M60 xDrive (right).

But BMW wants to go the distance, believing that range and efficiency are two of its biggest selling points. The third would be performance, and thanks to a dual-motor setup in both the 50 xDrive and M60 xDrive, the iX4 is sure to delivery plenty of giddy up. The 50 xDrive’s motors put out 463 horsepower and 475lb-ft of torque, for a 0–60mph acceleration of 4.7 seconds. Meanwhile, the M60 xDrive’s motors produce 603hp and 645lb-ft of torque, for a 0–60 time a whole second less than the 50 xDrive.

Like other Neue Klasse vehicles, the electrically excited synchronous motor (EESM) in the rear axle serves as the primary drive axle, using electricity instead of permanent magnets to power both its stator outer frame and interior spinning rotor. An inverter acts as the brain of the system, converting direct current from the battery into alternating current for the motor, regulating the electromagnets, and monitoring performance to keep the motor running as efficiently as possible. BMW says this combination helps slash drive-system energy losses by 40 percent and weight by 10 percent.

Previous Next







1 / 5

The Gen6 batteries are built with cylindrical lithium-ion cells measuring 46mm in diameter and 95mm in height that provide a 20 percent increase in energy density compared to the prismatic cells used in BMW’s Gen5 batteries. BMW has eliminated the traditional modules in favor of a “pack-to-open-body” construction where the battery housing serves as the vehicle’s underbody, lowering weight and increasing torsional rigidity.

Like Hyundai and Kia, BMW is building its Neue Klasse EVs to take fast charging to the next level. With its 800V architecture, the iX4 can accept up to 400kWs of DC fast charging, replenishing up to 184 miles of range in 10 minutes, and 10–80 percent charge in just 21 minutes. With a NACS charging port, the iX4 will be compatible with over 80,000 Tesla Supercharger connectors around the world.

Previous Next









1 / 6

The Panoramic iDrive infotainment system is BMW’s redesigned digital dashboard that replaces traditional gauge clusters with a heads-up-style projection along the full width of the lower windshield. The 17.9-inch central touchscreen presents as a free-cut display where you can drag and drop up to six widgets like media, weather, or navigation from the screen directly onto the windshield display.

And like the i3 and iX3, the iX4 can do all sorts of extra stuff, including bidirectional charging with vehicle-to-load and vehicle-to-home capabilities, an intelligent charging flap that opens when a driver approaches a known charging point, and Plug & Charge for automatic charging at 10 different charging providers.

Previous Next









1 / 6

If you look at the whole package, there’s a lot to like. Sure, the Model Y beats the iX4 in a few categories, most importantly price. It’s a bit quicker off the line, and of course, the Model Y comes with the option for Full Self-Driving (Supervised). BMW has something it calls “Symbiotic Drive,” which it describes as a Level 2 system designed for “fluid, intuitive interaction.” In other words, drivers can adjust the steering or even brake without canceling the automated functions. The iX4 also allows for hands-free driving on the highway — but no point-to-point assisted driving. Not until 2027 at the earliest.

Where BMW still bests Tesla is variety. You can get the iX4 50 xDrive, or if you want something sportier, try the M60 xDrive. If you’re rather have a sedan, there’s the i3. Or if you want something a bit more affordable, there’s the iX3. And don’t forget the flagship 7 series. Yep, those are getting Neue Klasse makeovers as well.

Tesla has the Model 3 and Model Y — and that’s about it. (Yes, there’s the Cybertruck, but clearly most people aren’t interested in that. And there’s the Cybercab, but it won’t be on sale anytime soon.) BMW knows its customers want options. And it’s doing it’s best to deliver.

Tech.title: Teenage Engineering’s CEO says it’ll stop making synths
Tech.content:
Kouthoofd tells me that, as part of a reorganization last fall, he announced to his team he is planning to stop making synthesizers altogether. The OP-1 is no exception. Launched in 2011, it put Teenage Engineering on the map and has been central to its success ever since.

“Everyone was like, ‘What are you talking about?’ But I’ve come to the conclusion that, for us, the products aren’t the business,” Kouthoofd says. “We can be so much more than that.”

Tech.title: Android’s physical navigation buttons are back on Googlebooks, but not the way you think
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

A common misconception I’ve seen with Googlebooks is that the Quick Insert and Google logo keys are new. They’re not, as they first debuted a couple of years ago on some Chromebooks. But there is something new for Googlebooks that’s ripped straight from Android phones circa 2014.

On every Googlebook keyboard, the F1, F2, and F3 keys are the old triangle, circle, and square navigation icons that first debuted on Android 5.0 Lollipop. These were the back, home, and app switcher buttons long before everything went to gesture-based navigation, and they’re still built into phones on Android 17 as an alternative. On Googlebook OS, these keys do what you expect: the left-pointing triangle goes back, the circle goes “home” by minimizing all open apps, and the square tiles your open apps like Mission Control on macOS / Task View on Windows.

If I stare at these keys long enough, I can pretend I’m holding my old Nexus 6. Photo: Antonio G. Di Benedetto / The Verge

It’s useful to have these buttons, and to have them matched across all Googlebooks. The back button seems sometimes necessary when using Android apps that aren’t really optimized for a desktop interface or mouse controls. I just wish a second press of the home button brought all your apps back to where they were, but that’s another feature called desktop peeking that uses a different keyboard shortcut.

If you’re an Android nerd of yore, it’s kind of fun to see these buttons live on. But they’re also a reminder that you sometimes need a fallback when Android gets all Android on you.

Tech.title: We found some great October Prime Day deals under $50
Tech.content: Getting in on the Prime Day action doesn’t have to result in an empty wallet. Just as we found a couple handfuls of goodies that are under $25, there are plenty of deals during Amazon’s October sale that are $50 or less, many of which offer a lot of practical value. Everything from chargers to coffee makers are discounted until 3 AM ET on October 8th, 2026, so you only have a few hours to take advantage of some of these deals.

Tech.title: Roku’s OLED TVs are up to $400 off during Prime Day, starting at $700
Tech.content:
is an editor covering deals and gaming hardware. He joined in 2018, and after a two-year stint at Polygon, he rejoined The Verge in May 2025.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Just over a week ago, we covered a deal at Amazon that knocked around 30 percent off Roku’s new (and first-ever) OLED TVs. The deal expired, but has returned for the final day of October Prime Day.

The 55-inch Pro Series OLED is $699.99 at Amazon, which is 30 percent off its list price. The 65-inch model is $799.99, which is $400 off its list price, also at Amazon. Both models support a native 120Hz refresh rate, which is great for gaming, plus four HDMI 2.1 ports for 4K gaming at its full refresh rate, and support for Dolby Vision and HDR10 Plus. You’ll also get a backlit Roku remote control.

There have been a few TV deals during Prime Day, though these are the lowest prices on OLEDs by a wide margin. We haven’t tested this model, but it’s an affordable way to get unbeatable contrast for your next movie or game night.

Tech.title: ChatGPT’s ‘Intelligent UI’ update fills its responses with pictures, charts, and buttons
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

OpenAI is launching a new Intelligent UI feature in ChatGPT that allows the chatbot to answer your questions with interactive visuals. The update, which is rolling out to all users alongside GPT-6, gives ChatGPT the ability to combine a text response with diagrams, charts, forms, tappable buttons, and more.

In a blog post explaining the change, OpenAI says it trained GPT-6 when to generate interactive visuals over text, as well as how to format them in its response. An example shared by OpenAI shows how ChatGPT might show a diagram of a seven-speed bicycle if you ask about its design, complete with interactive buttons that highlight different parts.

ChatGPT generates a diagram showing the design of a seven-speed bicycle. Image: OpenAI

Another shows how ChatGPT can teach you to play Mahjong by generating visuals of each tile and placing them into categories that you can scroll through. You can also ask ChatGPT to generate tools for different tasks, such as a retirement savings calculator, retro game, or bill splitter. It will then generate the tool in-line with its response.

OpenAI announced its first GPT-6 models last month, but now it’s bringing the Sol and Luna versions to ChatGPT. In addition to enabling Intelligent UI, OpenAI says its GPT-6 allows ChatGPT to perform better web searches and provide quicker, partial answers to users while it gathers information. The company notes that GPT-6 “showed stronger resistance to attempts to bypass its safety training” as well.

GPT-6 with Intelligent UI is rolling out globally to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users starting today, but will expand to Go and free tiers on Thursday. While higher-tier subscribers will gain access to the mid-range GPT-6 Sol model, Go and free users will get to use the more efficient GPT-6 Luna.

Tech.title: The first Nvidia RTX Spark laptops cost up to $7,000
Tech.content:
is a reviewer covering laptops and the occasional gadget. He spent over 15 years in the photography industry before joining The Verge as a deals writer in 2021.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

The first array of laptops powered by Nvidia’s new RTX Spark chip are designed to compete with high-end MacBook Pros — and they’ve got some high-end prices to match.

The flagship Surface Laptop Ultra and RTX Spark laptops from Dell, Lenovo, MSI, HP, and Asus start as low as $2,599 for configurations with an 18-core CPU, 24GB of unified memory, and 512GB of storage. That’s close in price to a similarly specced 14-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Pro chip, though Apple includes 1TB of storage. But the prices for both RTX Spark and Apple laptops of course go much, much higher.

Of the pricing we’ve seen so far, a kitted-out Asus ProArt P16 RTX Spark laptop with a 20-core chip, 128GB of unified memory, and 2TB of storage costs up to $6,999.99. We don’t yet know the full breadth of configuration options for Microsoft’s Surface Laptop Ultra, as the preorder page only has an email sign-up box to get updates, but a 48GB model on Best Buy costs $3,999.99.

Asus’ ProArt P14 and P16 range in price from $2,599.99 to $6,999.99. Image: Asus

Wildly expensive laptops aren’t really anything new: you can configure a 16-inch MacBook Pro with M5 Max chip to nearly $10,000 if you max out all options. But the first volley of RTX Spark options are obviously aimed at the high-end side of creators and local AI users. And RAMageddon certainly isn’t helping make this any easier on peoples’ wallets.

Will they be worth it? We’ll find out soon. The Surface Laptop Ultra and other RTX Spark laptops are launching this month — as early as October 16th.

Tech.title: It appears .agent and .agi are about to be the hot new domains
Tech.content:
For the first time in years, the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers — better known as ICANN — is accepting applications for new top-level domains. These are the suffixes at the end of all URLs, and you may know them as things like .com, .org, and .pizza.

ICANN just announced the 1,615 applications that have been submitted so far, from 481 different applicants. The trend will not surprise you: AI is everywhere. Ten different companies, including both Meta and OpenAI, applied for the .agent domain. Seven, including OpenAI, applied for .agi. Six, including OpenAI, applied for .asi, clearly attempting to get in on President Trump’s demand to switch from “artificial intelligence” to “super intelligence.” Four companies applied for .intelligence, and Meta is one of two interested in the preposterously long .superintelligence. (OpenAI applied for a total of 15 TLDs; Meta wants a whopping 21.)

There are, broadly, two types of domains in these applications. One is more generic, the kind of thing lots of people or companies might use. There are hundreds of those in this current batch, from .geek to .haha to .anime to .jackpot. There’s also my personal favorite new one, .itiswhatitis.

The other is purely branded, giving a company its own TLD to use for its own purposes. There are 345 brand applications in this batch, including everything from .applebees and .bankofamerica to .zillow and .zoom. Meta applied for .facebook, .instagram, .messenger, .meta, .frommeta, and .threads, which it could use for many purposes; Bluesky applied for .bsky with the apparent intention of weaving the domain into its usernames; OpenAI applied for .chatgpt, .codex, .openai, .gpt, and others; Anthropic wants .anthropic and .claude. These strings could ultimately make for memorable product pages, social media usernames, and much more besides.

It has mostly been a tough road for these alternate TLDs over the last few years. Some, like .ai or .app, have become somewhat popular thanks to various tech trends, but most people just never got used to the idea of typing .restaurant or .babysitting, and .com and a few others have actually become more important than ever. It’s interesting to see so many brands go for their own domain, which only Google and a few others have accomplished before.

This is but one step in the process of creating a new top-level domain, and nothing will be made official before sometime next year. But it appears that even as the world becomes more filled with and mediated by AI, great domain names continue to matter. Even the AI companies think so.

Tech.title: India rejects Elon Musk’s claim of discrimination over Starlink launch
Tech.content:
India has rejected Elon Musk’s claim that Starlink, SpaceX’s satellite internet service, is being unfairly blocked from launching in the country. The pushback comes as SpaceX struggles to turn years of regulatory work and partnerships with India’s biggest telecom operators into a commercial launch in one of the world’s largest internet markets.

On Wednesday, Musk accused unnamed “oligarchs” of blocking Starlink’s launch in India to maintain what he called their “monopolistic chokehold” on the country, without identifying them or providing evidence for his claim. He called the alleged blocking a “crime against the people of India” and argued that Starlink could bring affordable, high-speed internet to people who lack internet access.

Hours later, India’s Ministry of Communications pushed back, saying its regulatory framework for satellite communications is “fair and non-discriminatory.” The ministry said in a statement that Starlink and two other licensed satellite operators are all at “broadly the same regulatory stage.” It added that all three companies are undergoing security assessments that must be completed before they can seek spectrum, the radio frequencies that satellites use to send signal.

Starlink has spent over five years trying to enter India, a market with more than a billion internet subscribers. But it has yet to begin commercial services despite securing key regulatory approvals and partnering with telecom giants Reliance Jio and Bharti Airtel last year. SpaceX has also set up a local team as it prepares for a launch, appointing former Payoneer executive Prabhakar Jayakumar to lead its India operations in December.

Musk’s comments came hours after Lauren Dreyer, Starlink’s vice president of business operations, appeared at a telecom industry conference, India Mobile Congress, in New Delhi and reiterated the company’s commitment to the market. “We stand ready to serve India,” Dreyer said, adding that Starlink wants to help realize Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s goal of achieving universal connectivity across the country.
